310:
## 12. Jhānavibhaṅga
## 1. Suttantabhājanīyaṃ
## Mātikāvaṇṇanā
Now, in this Jhānavibhaṅga which follows the Maggavibhaṅga, in this Mātikā (Matrix) placed first for the entire Suttantabhājanīya method, the word "Idha" (In this Dispensation) illustrates the Dispensation (Sāsana) as the support for a person who has fulfilled the preliminary duties and produces all types of jhāna. It also serves to exclude other dispensations from being such a support. For it was said by the Blessed One: "Only here, monks, is there a recluse... other doctrines are empty of recluses [who know the Four Noble Truths]" (A. Ni. 4.241).

"Bhikkhū" (Monk) illustrates the person who produces those jhānas. "Pātimokkhasamvarasamvuto" (Restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha) illustrates the monk's established state in the restraint of the Pātimokkha. "Viharati" (Dwells) illustrates the monk's possession of postures suitable for that restraint. "Ācāragocarasampanno" (Possessed of proper conduct and resort) illustrates the qualities that are helpful for the Pātimokkha restraint mentioned below and for the application to jhāna mentioned above. "Aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī" (Seeing danger in the slightest faults) illustrates the monk's nature of not falling away from the Pātimokkha restraint. "Samādāya" (Having undertaken) illustrates the monk's taking up of the training rules without exception. "Sikkhati" (Trains) illustrates the monk's state of being endowed with training. "Sikkhāpadesu" (In the training rules) illustrates the things that the monk must train in.

"Indriyesu" (In the senses) illustrates the basis for being one with guarded doors; it is also said to illustrate the place to be guarded. "Guttadvāro" (Guarded in the doors) illustrates the monk's state of having well-arranged protection over the six doors. "Bhojane mattaññū" (Moderate in eating) illustrates the monk's virtues such as contentment. "Pubbarattāpararattaṃ jāgariyānuyogamanuyutto" (Devoted to wakefulness in the first and last watches of the night) illustrates the monk's state of being an exertive cause. "Sātaccaṃ nepakkaṃ" (Perseverance and prudence) illustrates the monk's state of acting with perseverance through effort grasped by wisdom. "Bodhipakkhikānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhāvanānuyogamanuyutto" (Devoted to the development of the factors of enlightenment) illustrates the monk's practice as belonging to the part of the path that pierces through defilements.

"So abhikkante ... tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī hoti" (He acts with clear comprehension in going forward ... in silence) illustrates the monk's state of being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension in all activities. "So vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ bhajati" (He resorts to a secluded lodging) illustrates the monk's acquisition of a suitable lodging. "Araññaṃ ... paṭisallānasāruppaṃ" (Forest ... suitable for seclusion) illustrates the types of lodgings, their faultlessness, and their benefits.
311:
"So araññagato vā" (Whether he has gone to the forest) illustrates the monk's state of being endowed with the aforementioned types of lodgings. "Nisīdati" (Sits) illustrates the monk's posture suitable for meditative application (kammaṭṭhāna). "Parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā" (Setting up mindfulness in front) illustrates the monk's beginning of meditative effort. "So abhijjhaṃ loke pahāya" (Having abandoned covetousness for the world) etc., illustrates the monk's abandoning of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) through meditative application. For one who has thus abandoned the hindrances, the words "Vivicceva kāmehi" (Quite secluded from sensual pleasures) etc., illustrate the sequential arising of the jhānas.

Alternatively, "Idha bhikkhū" means the monk who produces jhāna in this Dispensation. Since a monk who produces jhāna must purify the four types of virtue, the words "Pātimokkhasamvarasamvuto" point to the purification of his Pātimokkha restraint virtue. The words "Ācāragocarasampanno" etc., point to the purification of livelihood (ājīvapārisuddhisīla). The words "Samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu" point to the undertaking of those two virtues without remainder. "Indriyesu guttadvāro" points to the virtue of sense restraint (indriyasamvarasīla). "Bhojane mattaññū" points to the virtue regarding the use of requisites (paccayasannissitasīla). "Pubbarattāpararattaṃ" etc., point to the qualities helpful for jhāna development for a monk established in virtue. "So abhikkante" etc., point to the application of mindfulness and clear comprehension to prevent the decline of those qualities and the loss of the meditation subject. "So vivittaṃ" etc., point to the acquisition of a lodging suitable for development. "So araññagato vā" etc., point to the posture suitable for jhāna and the start of jhāna development for a monk who has reached that lodging. "So abhijjhaṃ" etc., point to the abandoning of states adverse to jhāna by starting jhāna development. "So ime pañca nīvaraṇe pahāya" etc., point to the sequence of the arising of all jhānas for a monk who has thus abandoned the states adverse to jhāna.

## Mātikāvaṇṇanā.
## Niddesavaṇṇanā
Now, to explain the established matrix (Mātikā) in order, the text begins with "Idha imissā diṭṭhiyā" (Here, in this view) etc. Therein, by the ten terms beginning with "imissā diṭṭhiyā", the Dispensation of the All-Knowing Buddha, known as the Three Trainings (sikkhā), is spoken of. That Dispensation is called "Diṭṭhi" (View) because it was seen by the Blessed Buddha himself. It is called "Khanti" (Patience/Acceptance) due to the power of being pleased with it, "Ruci" (Preference) due to the power of liking it, "Ādāya" (Adoption) due to the power of taking it up, and "Dhamma" (Doctrine) because it has a true and unerring nature.
312:
It is called Vinaya because it is to be trained in; Dhamma-vinaya because of both meanings; Pāvacana because it is the excellent word; Brahmacariya because it is the noble practice; and Satthusāsana because it provides the Teacher's instruction. Therefore, in the phrases beginning with 'this view' (imissā diṭṭhiyā), it means: in this dispensation seen by the Buddha, in this dispensation liked by the Buddha, in this dispensation desired by the Buddha, in this dispensation taken up by the Buddha, in this Dhamma which is the nature of the Buddha, and in this Vinaya which is the instruction of the Buddha.

'Gotamī, whatever qualities you may know: "These qualities lead to passion, not to dispassion; to being fettered, not to being unfettered; to accumulating, not to shedding; to clinging, not to relinquishing; to muchness of wishing, not to fewness of wishing; to discontent, not to contentment; to socializing, not to seclusion; to laziness, not to arousal of energy; to being difficult to support, not to being easy to support"—you may definitely hold, Gotamī: "This is not the Dhamma, this is not the Vinaya, this is not the Teacher's instruction." Gotamī, whatever qualities you may know: "These qualities lead to dispassion, not to passion... to being easy to support, not to being difficult to support"—you may definitely hold, Gotamī: "This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher's instruction."' (Thus He taught).

When it is said thus, the meaning should be understood as: in this Buddha-Dhamma-Vinaya, in this Buddha-Pāvacana, in this Buddha-Brahmacariya, in this Buddha-Satthusāsana.

Furthermore, it is called diṭṭhi (view) because the entire dispensation, known as the three trainings, is seen by the Blessed One, because it is the cause of right view, and because it is preceded by right view. It is called khanti (patience/acceptance) by way of the Blessed One's acceptance, ruci (preference) by way of His liking, and ādāya (taking up) by way of His grasping. It is called Dhamma because it upholds the practitioner so that they do not fall into the lower realms. That very Dhamma is called Vinaya because it removes the side of unwholesome defilements. It is called Dhamma-vinaya because it is both Dhamma and Vinaya. Alternatively, it is called Dhamma-vinaya because it is the removal of unwholesome states by means of wholesome states. For that very reason, the Blessed One taught: 'Gotamī, whatever qualities you may know: "These qualities lead to dispassion, not to passion... this is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher's instruction."''
313:
It is called 'Dhamma-vinaya' because it is disciplining through the Dhamma, or disciplining by means of the Dhamma and not by means of sticks and so forth. This has also been said:

'Some tame with sticks, with hooks, and with whips; but the elephant was tamed by the Great Sage without stick or weapon.'

Likewise:
'What envy can there be for those who are led by the Dhamma, for those who understand?'

Alternatively, it is 'Dhamma-vinaya' because it is discipline for the sake of the faultless Dhamma (anavajjadhamma). Indeed, this dispensation is for the sake of the faultless Dhamma, not for the sake of material gains of life. Therefore, the Blessed One taught in detail: 'Monks, this holy life is not lived for the sake of deceiving or surprising people.' The Elder Puṇṇa also said: 'Friend, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging.'

Alternatively, it is called 'Vinaya' because it leads (nayati) to the distinguished [Nibbāna]. It is 'Dhamma-vinaya' because it leads by way of the Dhamma. Indeed, this dispensation leads to the distinguished Nibbāna away from the phenomena of saṃsāra or from phenomena such as sorrow. Alternatively, it is 'Dhamma-vinaya' because it is the discipline of the Dhamma, not of the sectarians; for the Blessed One is the embodiment of Dhamma (dhammabhūta), and this is His discipline. Or, because only the Dhammas are to be fully known, thoroughly understood, abandoned, developed, and realized, this is the discipline regarding the Dhammas, not regarding beings or souls; thus it is 'Dhamma-vinaya'.

It is called 'Pāvacana' because it is the principal speech compared to the speech of others, due to its being with meaning and phrasing, etc. That very 'Pāvacana' is also called 'Pāvacana'. It is 'Brahmacariya' because it is the distinguished practice among all practices. It is 'Satthusāsana' because it is the instruction of the Blessed One, who is the Teacher of devas and humans. Or, it is 'Satthusāsana' because the instruction itself is the Teacher. For it was said, 'That Dhamma and Vinaya shall be your Teacher after my passing,' thus the Dhamma-Vinaya itself is called the Teacher; in this way, the meaning of these words should be understood.

However, since a monk who produces all types of jhānas is seen only in this dispensation and not elsewhere, it should be understood that the restriction 'this' and 'in this' is made in various places. This is the explanation of the matrix term 'idha' (here).

In the explanation of the term 'bhikkhu' (monk), 'samaññāya' means by way of designation or common usage. For some are known as 'monks' merely by designation. Therefore, when counting monks for invitations and so forth, even novices are included and people say, 'a hundred monks, a thousand monks.' 'Paṭiññāya' means by way of one's own claim [to be a monk].
314:
A monk capable of producing all types of jhāna is found only in this Dispensation, not in any other. Therefore, in various Pali passages, the determination is made by specifying 'in this Dispensation' (idha). This is the meaning of the introductory term 'idha'.

In the explanation of the term 'bhikkhu', 'by designation' (samaññāya) means he is called a bhikkhu by way of name, designation, and appellation. Some are known as 'monks' by their own claim (paṭiññā). When such a person is asked, "Who is there, friend?", and he replies, "I am a monk, friend," etc., he is to be understood as a monk by claim. This claim is a righteous claim when spoken by the Elder Ānanda. However, at night, even those of immoral conduct, while traveling on the road, when asked "Who is there?", make an unrighteous and false claim, saying, "We are monks."

He is a 'bhikkhu' because he begs (bhikkhati); begging means receiving alms. Whoever begs for alms-food, or seeks it out, whether he receives that alms-food or not, is called a 'bhikkhu' because he begs. The word 'bhikkhaka' is an expansion of the term by its syllables; the meaning is 'bhikkhu' because of the nature of begging.

He is one who has 'entered upon the practice of alms-gathering' (bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhuupagato) because he has undertaken the practice of alms-gathering as accepted and practiced by the Buddha and others. Whoever renounces a mass of wealth, whether small or large, goes forth from the home life into homelessness, abandons livelihoods such as farming or cattle-herding, and enters upon the practice of alms-gathering simply by accepting the outward marks of a monk, is called a 'bhikkhu'. Or, because his life is dependent on others, even if he eats a meal brought by a carrying-pole into the midst of the monastery, he is still called a 'bhikkhu' as one who has entered upon the practice of alms-gathering. Or, because he has developed enthusiasm for the monkhood depending on a morsel of alms-food, he is called a 'bhikkhu' as one who has entered upon the practice of alms-gathering.

He is a 'wearer of broken cloth' (bhinnapaṭadhara) because he wears cloth that is broken (ruined) in terms of value, texture, and color. Herein, the ruin of value is to be understood by cutting with a small knife. Even a cloth worth a thousand pieces of money, when cut into pieces with a knife, has its value ruined and is not worth even half its former price. The ruin of texture is to be understood by sewing with thread. Even a cloth of soft texture, when sewn with threads, has its texture ruined and becomes coarse to the touch. The ruin of color is to be understood by the stains of the needle and so forth. Even a very pure cloth, from the time it is worked with a needle, has its color ruined by the stains of the needle, hand-sweat, grime, and so forth, and finally by the process of dyeing; it loses its original color. Thus, because he wears cloth ruined in these three ways, he is a 'bhikkhu' as a 'wearer of broken cloth'. Or, simply by wearing the saffron-colored robes which are distinct from the clothes of laypeople, he is a 'bhikkhu' as a 'wearer of broken cloth'.

He is a 'bhikkhu' because he destroys (bhindati) evil, unwholesome states. He is a 'bhikkhu' because he destroys five defilements with the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga). He is a 'bhikkhu' because he destroys four defilements with the path of once-returning (sakadāgāmimagga), four with the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga), and eight defilements with the path of arahantship (arahattamagga). With this much sequence of words, the four persons established in the Path are shown. By the word 'because of being broken' (bhinnattā), the four persons established in the Fruit are shown. A monk who is a stream-enterer stands having destroyed five defilements with the path of stream-entry. Thus, the four monks established in the Fruit are called 'bhikkhu' because they have destroyed evil, unwholesome states. In the Pali phrase 'by the abandoning of defilements by limit' (odhiso kileṣānaṃ pahānā), 'limit' (odhi) is a boundary, and there are two kinds: the limit of the Path and the limit of defilements. A monk who is a stream-enterer is called a 'bhikkhu' because he abandons defilements according to their limit by the limit of the Path.
315:
With this sequence of words, the four individuals established in the Path (maggaṭṭha) have been shown. However, by the word 'bhinnattā', the four individuals established in the Fruit (phalaṭṭha) are shown. For the Sotāpanna monk stands having destroyed five defilements (kilesa) by the Path of Stream-entry. The Sakadāgāmī monk stands having destroyed four defilements by the Path of Once-returning; the Anāgāmī monk stands having destroyed four defilements by the Path of Non-returning; and the Arahant stands having destroyed eight defilements by the Path of Arahatship. Thus, this fourfold individual established in the Fruit is called a 'bhikkhu' because of having destroyed (bhinnattā) evil unwholesome states.

In the phrase 'odhisova kilesānaṃ pahānā' (abandoning defilements with a limit), there are two kinds of limits (odhi): the limit of the path (maggodhi) and the limit of defilements (kilesodhi). 'Odhi' means a limit or a boundary. Between these two limits, the Sotāpanna monk is called a 'bhikkhu' because of abandoning defilements with a limit according to the limit of the path. For him, defilements are abandoned by only one limit among the four paths, not by the entire set of four paths. The same method applies to the Sakadāgāmī and Anāgāmī. The Sotāpanna monk is also called a 'bhikkhu' because of abandoning defilements with a limit according to the limit of defilements. For him, among the defilements to be abandoned, they are abandoned only by way of a limit, not entirely and completely. The Arahant, however, is called a 'bhikkhu' because of abandoning defilements without a limit (anodhisova). For that Arahant, defilements are abandoned without a limit by the four paths, not by the limit of a single path. And among the defilements to be abandoned, they are abandoned without a limit. Not even a single limit of defilement remains. Thus, that Arahant is called a 'bhikkhu' because of abandoning defilements without a limit in both ways—by the limit of the path and the limit of defilements.

'Sekha' (Trainee) refers to the seven noble individuals (ariya) together with the noble worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana). They are called 'sekha' because they are still training in the three trainings (sikkhā). Among them, any trainee individual should be understood as a 'bhikkhu'. One is called 'asekha' (Non-trainee) because one no longer trains (having completed the training). Because he has transcended the states of a trainee and stands in the highest fruit, and because there is nothing further to be trained in beyond that fruit, the one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) is called 'asekha'. The remaining worldling monk (puthujjana-bhikkhu) should be understood as 'nevasekkhanāsekha' (neither trainee nor non-trainee) because he is neither currently training in the three trainings nor stands having completed the training.

One is called 'agga-bhikkhu' (foremost monk) because of standing having reached this excellence: the excellence of virtue, the excellence of concentration, the excellence of wisdom, and the excellence of liberation (the fruit of Arahatship). 'Bhadra' means one who is not evil. Individuals starting from the noble worldling up to the Arahant are reckoned as 'bhadra-bhikkhu' because they are endowed with auspicious virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. 'Maṇḍa-bhikkhu' means a pure monk; the meaning is one who is especially pure and undisturbed, like the cream of clarified butter (sappimaṇḍa). 'Sāra' (essential) should be understood as 'sāra-bhikkhu' because of being endowed with the essence of virtue and so on, just as a cloth endowed with blue color is called a blue cloth. Alternatively, only the one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) should be understood as 'sāra' because of the absence of the pithless nature of defilements.
316:
Among the contexts showing the meaning of the word 'bhikkhu', the seven trainees (sekha) are spoken of in these three instances: the instance 'He is a bhikkhu because he destroys evil unwholesome states', the instance 'He is a bhikkhu because of abandoning defilements with a limit', and the instance 'A trainee bhikkhu'.

Only the one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) is spoken of in these five instances: 'He is a bhikkhu because of having destroyed evil unwholesome states', 'He is a bhikkhu because of abandoning defilements without a limit', 'An asekha bhikkhu', 'A foremost bhikkhu', and 'An essential bhikkhu'. In the instance 'Neither a trainee nor a non-trainee', only the worldling (puthujjana) is spoken of. In the remaining instances, all these—the noble worldling monk, the seven trainees, and the one whose taints are exhausted—are spoken of.

Having thus shown the 'bhikkhu' by way of common designation (samaññā) and so on, he now said 'by a harmonious Saṅgha' (samaggena saṅghena) etc., to show him by way of higher ordination (upasampadā). In that passage, 'by a harmonious Saṅgha' means by a Saṅgha that has reached a state of harmony in a single legal act, because the five monks—which is the minimum requirement—who are eligible to perform the act have arrived, because the consent (chanda) of those entitled to give consent has been brought, and because there is no protest from those present.

'By a motion as the fourth' (ñatticatutthena) means by an act to be performed with one motion (ñatti) and three proclamations (anussāvanā). 'By an act' (kammena) means by a legal act of the Vinaya that is in accordance with the Dhamma. 'By an unshakeable act' (akuppena) means by an act that has reached a state of being irreproachable and not to be protested because it is endowed with the perfections (sampatti) of the object (vatthu), the motion, the proclamation, the boundary (sīmā), and the assembly (parisā). 'By a fitting act' (ṭhānārahena) means by an act that is suitable to the cause and suitable to the Teacher's Dispensation.

'Upasampanna' means one who has attained or reached the higher state. Indeed, the state of a bhikkhu is a higher state. And because he has attained that state through the aforementioned legal act, he is called 'upasampanna'. By this term 'upasampanna', among the eight kinds of higher ordination mentioned—namely, Ehibhikkhu-upasampadā, Saraṇagamana-upasampadā, Ovādapaṭiggahaṇa-upasampadā, Pañhabyākaraṇa-upasampadā, Garudhamma-upasampadā, Dūtena-upasampadā, Aṭṭhavācikā-upasampadā, and Ñatticatutthakamma-upasampadā—only these three are permanent: Ñatticatutthakamma-upasampadā, Dūtena-upasampadā, and Aṭṭhavācikā-upasampadā. The others existed only while the Buddha was alive. Among those kinds of higher ordination, in this context, only this Ñatticatutthakamma-upasampadā is intended.

## In the Exposition on the Restraint of the Pātimokkha

'Pātimokkha' refers to the virtue of the training rules (sikkhāpada-sīla). For if a monk guards (pāti) it, it releases (mokkheti) him from sufferings such as those of the states of deprivation; therefore, it is called 'Pātimokkha'. Phrases such as 'Virtue is the foundation' (sīlaṃ patiṭṭhāti) are synonyms (vevacana) for that very Pātimokkha. Among them, the word 'sīla' (virtue) indeed arises together with the conclusion of the formal act (kammavācā).
317:
This is a synonym for the Pātimokkha that has reached completion. Even so, in terms of its ultimate reality, this virtue (sīla) should be understood as the states such as volition (cetanā) of one who abstains from killing living beings (pāṇātipāta) and so forth, or of one who fulfills the duties and practices. For it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "What is virtue? Volition is virtue, mental factor is virtue, restraint (saṃvara) is virtue, non-transgression (avītikkama) is virtue."

Among those, 'volition as virtue' refers to the volition of one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth, or of one who fulfills the duties and practices. 'Mental factor as virtue' refers to the abstinence (virati) of one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth. Alternatively, 'volition as virtue' refers to the seven volitions of the courses of action (kammapatha cetanā) of one who abandons misconduct such as killing living beings. 'Mental factor as virtue' refers to the states of non-covetousness (anabhijjhā), non-ill will (abyāpāda), and right view (sammādiṭṭhi) as taught in the Mahāvagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya in the manner beginning with: "Having abandoned covetousness, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness."

In the phrase "restraint is virtue," it should be understood that there are five kinds of restraint: restraint by the Pātimokkha, restraint by mindfulness (sati), restraint by knowledge (ñāṇa), restraint by patience (khanti), and restraint by energy (vīriya). The distinctions between these types of restraint are explained in the Visuddhimagga. "Non-transgression is virtue" refers to the non-transgression by body and speech of one who has undertaken the precepts.

Here, it should be understood that restraint-virtue and non-transgression-virtue are virtue in the literal sense (nippariyāya), while volition-virtue and mental-factor-virtue are virtue in the figurative sense (pariyāya).

Because a monk is established in the Dispensation (Sāsana) by means of the Pātimokkha-restraint-virtue, it is called 'foundation' (patiṭṭhā). Or, a monk stands upon this virtue, or wholesome states are established upon this virtue; thus it is called 'foundation'. This meaning should be understood through the following verses and suttas:

"When a wise man, established in virtue,
Develops concentration and wisdom,
Then as a monk, ardent and sagacious,
He succeeds in disentangling this tangle."

And: "Great King, virtue is the foundation for all wholesome states." And: "Great King, for one established in virtue, all wholesome states do not decline."

That same virtue is called 'beginning' (ādi) in the sense of being the first to arise. This is also stated as: "Therefore, Uttiya, you should first purify the very beginning of wholesome states. And what is the beginning of wholesome states? It is virtue that is well-purified and view (diṭṭhi) that is straight."
318:
For example, just as a city builder (or an expert in city planning) who wishes to build a city first clears the site for the city, and after clearing it, divides it into sections such as main roads, crossroads, and junctions before building the city; in the same way, a practitioner (yogāvacara) first purifies virtue at the very beginning. Only after purifying virtue does he subsequently realize tranquillity (samatha), insight (vipassanā), the path (magga), fruition (phala), and Nibbāna.

Alternatively, just as a washerman first washes a cloth with three kinds of alkaline ashes (from wood, straw, and cow dung), and only when the cloth is clean does he apply the desired dye; or just as a skilled painter who wishes to paint a figure first prepares the wall (parikamma) and subsequently paints the figure; in the same way, a practitioner first purifies virtue and subsequently realizes states such as tranquillity and insight. Therefore, virtue is called the 'beginning' (ādi).

That virtue is called 'conduct' (caraṇa) because it is like feet. Caraṇa means feet. Just as a man whose feet are severed cannot make the effort to go to another direction, while it is possible only for one with sound feet; in the same way, if a person's virtue is broken, flawed, or incomplete, the movement of knowledge for going to Nibbāna cannot be accomplished. But if his virtue is unbroken, flawless, and complete, the movement of knowledge for going to Nibbāna can be accomplished. Therefore, virtue is called 'conduct' (caraṇa).

That virtue is called 'restraint' (saṃyama) in the sense of refraining, and 'restraint' (saṃvara) in the sense of guarding. By both terms, virtue-restraint (sīla-saṃyama) and virtue-restraint (sīla-saṃvara) are taught. The meaning here is: it is called 'saṃyama' because it refrains from the agitation of transgression, or it restrains the person, not allowing him to be agitated by way of transgression. It is called 'saṃvara' because it guards or closes the door of entry for transgression.

'Mokkha' means the foremost or that which is like a mouth (entrance). Just as the four kinds of nutriment for beings enter through the mouth and pervade the limbs and parts of the body, so too the wholesome states of the four planes of the yogi enter through the mouth of virtue and bring about the accomplishment of the goal. Therefore, it is called 'mokkha'. It is called 'pāmokkha' because it is good in the beginning; it means the precursor, the most excellent, the chief. It should be understood as the pre-eminent (pāmokkha) state—the precursor, the most excellent, the chief—for the attainment of wholesome states.

'Non-transgression by body' refers to the three kinds of good bodily conduct. 'By speech' refers to the four kinds of good verbal conduct. 'By body and speech' refers to both. By this, it shows the inclusion of virtue with livelihood as the eighth (ājīvaṭṭhamaka sīla). 'Restrained' (saṃvuta) means having the sense faculties closed or guarded.
319:
It means one whose faculties are closed (pihitindriya). Just as a house with closed doors is called a 'closed house' (saṃvutageha or pihitageha), similarly, here, one whose faculties are restrained is called 'restrained' (saṃvuta). 'By the restraint of the Pātimokkha' (pātimokkhasaṃvarena) means being endowed with both the Pātimokkha and other forms of restraint, or being endowed with the restraint known as the Pātimokkha. The meaning of terms such as 'endowed with' (upeto) is exactly as previously stated (in the Satippaṭṭhāna Vibhaṅga).

By the seven terms beginning with 'iriyati' (moves/behaves), the monk's dwelling in postures while established in the virtue of the restraint of the Pātimokkha is described.

In the explanation of conduct and resort (ācāra-gocara-niddesa), the Blessed One, wishing to teach the conduct of a recluse (samaṇācara) and the resort of a recluse (samaṇagocara), extracted the phrase from 'endowed with conduct and resort' (ācāragocarasampanno), saying, "There is good conduct (ācāra) and there is bad conduct (anācāra)." Just as a man skilled in paths, when explaining a route, first points out the dangerous wrong path to be avoided, saying, 'Leave the left, take the right,' and then points out the safe, straight path to be taken; similarly, the King of Dhamma, who is like a man skilled in paths, wishing to teach good conduct (ācāra) after first pointing out the bad conduct (anācāra) that should be abandoned and is loathed by the Buddhas, said, "Therein, what is bad conduct?" and so on. While a path shown by a human might or might not be correct, the path shown by the Tathāgata is unerring, like the thunderbolt (vajira) hurled by Indra; it leads directly to the city of Nibbāna. Therefore, He said: "Tissa, 'a man skilled in paths' is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One."

Alternatively, just as for a man who has bathed his head and washed away sweat and dirt, the adornment with garlands and perfumes is more complete, so too for a yogi who has abandoned evil states, the association with good states is truly complete. Therefore, wishing to teach good conduct (ācāra) after first pointing out the bad conduct (anācāra) that should be abandoned like sweat and dirt, He said, "Therein, what is bad conduct?" and so on. Among those bad conducts, bodily transgression (kāyika-vītikkama) refers to the three types of bodily misconduct; verbal transgression (vācasika-vītikkama) refers to the four types of verbal misconduct. Transgression by both body and speech refers to both. Thus, He showed the transgression of the virtue with livelihood as the eighth (ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla).

Since bad conduct is practiced not only through body and speech but also through the mind, to show bad conduct practiced through the mind, He said, "All lack of virtue (dussīlya) is called bad conduct."
320:
Wishing to explain in detail some of those improper conducts, He said, "Here, someone [gives] by way of giving bamboo (veḷudānena)," and so on. In that context, 'veḷudānena' means making a living by giving bamboo for the sake of requisites. It is not proper to give bamboo grown in the monastery or brought from the forest and preserved, to supporters with the thought, "If I give this, they will offer me requisites such as alms-food." For a monk who makes a living by giving bamboo in this way lives by improper search and blameworthy wrong livelihood (micchā-ājīva). Such a monk incurs blame in this very life and fills the states of deprivation (apāya) in the next life. A monk who gives even his own personal bamboo for the sake of currying favor with families (kula-saṅgaha) commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for corrupting families (kula-dūsaka). If he gives another's bamboo with a mind to steal, the offense must be decided according to the value of the bamboo. The same rule applies to communal (saṅghika) bamboo. If he gives that communal bamboo as if he were the owner, he commits a grave offense (thullaccaya) for disposing of heavy property (garubhaṇḍa).

What kind of bamboo is heavy property, and what kind is not? Bamboo that grows naturally is heavy property only in the area designated by the Saṅgha; outside that area, it is not. In a place where it is planted, all of it is heavy property. If the bamboo is the size of an oil-tube (tela-nāḷi), it is heavy property; if smaller, it is not. If a monk needs bamboo for an oil-tube or a walking stick, he must take it by performing compensation (phātikamma). In performing phātikamma, it is proper to exchange it for an item of equal or greater value; exchanging it for an item of lesser value is not proper. Regarding manual labor (hatthakamma), merely fetching water or clearing grass is not enough; it is only proper if one performs some permanent service. Therefore, it is proper to take it after dredging silt from a pond, laying steps, or leveling uneven ground, etc. Bamboo taken without phātikamma should be used only while staying in that monastery; when leaving for another place, it must be left as communal property. If taken inadvertently, it must be sent back from wherever one remembers. If there is danger on the way, it should be deposited at the monastery one has reached.

People come to the monastery and ask for bamboo. The monks, saying "It is communal property," do not dare to give it. If people ask repeatedly or threaten, they should be told, "Take it by performing a penalty task (daṇḍakamma)"; this is not considered 'giving bamboo'. If they offer knives, axes, etc., or food as a penalty, it is not proper to accept them. However, in the Vinaya Commentary, it is said: "If people whose houses have burned down take it, they should not be prevented."
321:
If pests (or small parasitic plants) that destroy bamboo appear in a bamboo grove belonging to the Saṅgha, and the bamboo will be ruined if those destructive elements are not removed, what should be done? People should be informed during the alms round. If they do not wish to clear them, one should say, 'You will receive an equal share.' If they still do not wish to do so after being told this, one should say, 'You will receive two shares.' If they still do not wish to do so even after this, one should say, 'There is no benefit if the grove is ruined; when you are free, perform this task and take the bamboo.' This is not considered 'giving away' bamboo. The same principle applies to bamboo groves caught in a fire or bamboo swept away by water. The same rule applies to trees. However, a tree the size of a stylus handle is considered 'heavy goods' (garubhaṇḍa). It is permissible to have Saṅghika trees cut down to build a Saṅghika dwelling (āvāsa) even without informing the Saṅgha. However, to prevent criticism, it should be built only after informing them.

Is it permissible to build a private dwelling (puggalika āvāsa)? It is not permissible. However, based on the importance of manual labor (hatthakamma), one may obtain the space for a single couch in one building as private property; if three buildings are constructed, one building may be obtained. If the timber materials are private property but the land belongs to the Saṅgha, one receives an equal share in one building; if two buildings are constructed, one building is obtained. If a Saṅghika tree obstructs a Saṅghika dwelling, is it permissible to remove it without informing the Saṅgha? It is permissible. However, to prevent criticism, it should be removed only after informing them. If the Saṅgha receives great gains depending on that tree, it should not be removed. If a private tree obstructs a Saṅghika dwelling, the owner of the tree should be informed. If they do not wish to remove it, it should be cut and removed. If the owner demands, 'Give me my tree,' the tree should be appraised and its value paid. The same principle applies if a Saṅghika tree obstructs a private dwelling, or if a private tree obstructs a private dwelling. The same rule applies to creepers (valli). However, in a place where creepers are sold and are rare, they are considered heavy goods. Such a creeper is heavy goods from the length of half an arm upwards; a piece of creeper smaller than that is not heavy goods.

Regarding the giving of leaves and so forth, everything starting with 'by giving leaves' (pattadānena) based on the four requisites should be understood in the same manner as described under 'giving bamboo' (veḷudāna). Regarding the status of heavy goods in this matter of giving leaves, this is the decision: In a place where leaves are sold and perfumers and others buy them for purposes such as wrapping perfumes, only in such a place where they are rare are they considered heavy goods. This is the decision regarding Pauk leaves, palm leaves used for ear ornaments, and so forth.
322:
Palm leaves should also be discussed in this same context (of giving leaves). In a naturally grown palm grove, only the palm leaves in the area designated by the Saṅgha are heavy goods; those beyond that are not. In the case of planted palm trees, all palm leaves are heavy goods. The minimum size for such a leaf is a blank palm leaf (not yet written upon) of at least eight finger-breadths. Grass should also be included and discussed here. In places where there is no grass, they also roof with Muñja grass, straw, coconut leaves, and so forth. Therefore, those (Muñja grass, etc.) are also included under the term 'grass'. Thus, among Muñja grass, straw, and so forth, even a handful of grass, or among coconut leaves and so forth, even a single leaf, is heavy goods if it is given to the Saṅgha, or grown there, or grown in a Saṅgha-owned meadow outside the monastery and is guarded and protected. If there is a surplus of such grass and leaves after the work for the Saṅgha and the Cetiya is completed, it is permissible to give them for private use. The same principle applies to the bamboo mentioned above.

Regarding the giving of flowers: Flowers in a designated area are heavy goods only if it is specified, 'Use the flowers from these many trees for gruel, food, and robes; use the flowers from these many trees for the repair of dwellings.' On the other bank, novices pick flowers and make a heap; a monk who is a flower-distributor (pupphabhājaka) endowed with the five qualities counts the community of monks and makes portions. He is allowed to give them to the assembled group without informing the Saṅgha. If he is not an appointed distributor, he must give them only after informing the Saṅgha. To whom is a monk allowed to give flowers, and to whom is he not? He is allowed to give them to his parents, whether by carrying them to their house or by calling them from the house, saying, 'Perform an offering to the Triple Gem'; he is not allowed to give them for the purpose of wearing. For other relatives, he should not carry them to their house to give, but may give them after calling them and saying, 'Perform an offering.' For other people who have arrived at the place of offering, he should give them without expecting anything in return; such giving is not considered (prohibited) 'giving of flowers'.

Many flowers bloom in the monastery. A monk wandering for alms, upon seeing people, should say, 'Many flowers are blooming in the monastery; perform an offering.' There is no fault in the mere words. However, he should not say it with the thought, 'People will bring snacks and food.' If he says it with such a thought, he must not consume the snacks and food (they bring). If people, of their own accord, ask, 'Are there flowers in the monastery?' and say, 'We will come to the monastery on such-and-such a day; do not let the novices pick the flowers,' the monk might forget to tell the novices. The novices then pick the flowers and set them aside. If the people approach the monk and say, 'Venerable Sir, we told you on such-and-such a day not to let the novices pick the flowers, why did you not forbid them?' (the monk should say), 'I forgot; they have only just been picked and the offering has not yet been made; take them.'
323: We said: 'Do not allow the novices to pick flowers.' If [people] ask, 'Why did you not forbid them?' one should say, 'My mindfulness was lapsed; they were merely picking the flowers, the offering had not yet been made.' One should not say, 'Take them and offer them.' If one says so, the material gifts [given by them] should not be consumed. Another monk tells the novices, 'The villagers of such-and-such a village said, "Do not pick the flowers."' People also bring material gifts, give them as an offering, and say, 'Our people are not many; please order the novices to pick flowers with us.' One should say: 'Lay followers, the novices have received their alms-food; those who do not go for alms-round will know for themselves.' Having obtained this method, there is no fault in having novices pick flowers by treating them like sons or brothers; this is not considered 'giving flowers' [as a gift of communal property]. In the case of giving fruits, fruits, like flowers, are designated as garubhaṇḍa (heavy property). When there are many fruits, large and small, in the monastery, sick people come and ask for them. Monks, considering them as saṅghika (communal property), do not dare to give them. The people, becoming dissatisfied, revile and threaten [the monks]. In such a case, what should be done? An agreement should be made by demarcating fruits or trees: 'Those who take this many fruits from such-and-such trees, or those who take fruits from this many trees, should not be forbidden.' However, if thieves or rulers take them by force, they should not be forbidden; for if they become angry, they might destroy the entire monastery. But the disadvantage [of using communal property] should be explained. In the case of giving bath powder, pounded bath powders are not garubhaṇḍa. Only the unpounded tree bark is garubhaṇḍa. As for the powder, it is allowable for a non-sick monk if it is the bark residue left from boiling dye. For a sick monk, any kind of powder is allowable. Fine clay should also be included and discussed here. Fine clay is garubhaṇḍa only in places where it is difficult to find. Even then, it is garubhaṇḍa only if it is at least the size of a ball of molasses weighing thirty pala; if it is less than that, it is not garubhaṇḍa. In the case of giving tooth-sticks, only the uncut tooth-stick is garubhaṇḍa. Those novices whose turn it is to fetch tooth-sticks from the Saṅgha are not allowed to give them separately to their own teachers or preceptors (upajjhāya). However, those who have taken their turn after the Saṅgha has specified, 'This many tooth-sticks must be brought,' are allowed to give the surplus tooth-sticks to their teachers and preceptors. A monk [taking] many tooth-sticks from the tooth-stick shed...
324: Many tooth-sticks should not be taken; only one should be taken daily. Even a monk living separately and alone should count the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and take only as many tooth-sticks as fall to his share before leaving. If visiting monks arrive in the meantime, or if he departs for another region, he should take the [surplus] tooth-sticks and place them back in the same spot from which they were taken. In the terms beginning with 'cāṭukamyatā', 'cāṭukamyatā' refers to speech spoken in praise because of a desire to be liked, placing oneself in a low position like a servant and even correcting the mistakes in another's speech to make it right. 'Muggasūpyatā' is a name for livelihood by means of speech that mixes truth and falsehood, similar to bean soup. Just as when bean soup is cooked, most beans are done while a few remain uncooked, similarly, in a person who makes a living by mixing truth and falsehood, there is much falsehood and only a little truth. Or, just as there is no meal that bean soup cannot enter, similarly, there is no speech that a person of truthful-falsehood livelihood cannot enter; it stands like a crossroads where currents from all directions meet. Therefore, that person's lying is called 'muggasūpyatā'. 'Pāribhaṭayatā' is the state of being a nursemaid. The work of a nursemaid is pāribhaṭaya, and its state is pāribhaṭayatā. It is a name for making children play and smile by means of decorating them and so forth. 'Jaṅghapesanika' refers to the carrying of messages and replies for various laypeople from one village to another, or from one region to another. This work of a messenger is allowable if one carries a message for one's parents or for those who look after one's parents. It is also allowable to carry messages for the Pagoda, for the Saṅgha, or for the carpenters who are doing work for oneself. If people say, 'We will give a gift, we will perform a puja; please inform the Bhikkhu Saṅgha,' or if they give alms-food, medicine, or robes saying, 'Give this to such-and-such an Elder,' or if they entrust flowers, scents, perfumes, etc., or banners and flags, etc., saying, 'Perform a puja at the monastery,' it is allowable to carry all of these; it is not considered 'jaṅghapesanika'. For a monk who goes carrying the messages of others [not mentioned above], there is an offense (dukkata) at every footstep. 'Aññataraññatarena' means by any one of these wrong livelihoods such as giving bamboo, etc., or by any of the livelihoods such as medical practice, acting as a storekeeper, bartering alms-food, or improperly managing Saṅgha property or Pagoda property. 'Buddha-paṭikuṭṭhena' means that which is censured and forbidden by the Buddhas. All this [improper conduct] is called 'anācāra'. The explanation of 'ācāra' (proper conduct) should be understood by the method of the opposite of what has been said about 'anācāra'.
325:
In the Explanation of Resort (Gocaraniddesa), the reason for first teaching improper resort (agocara) should be understood in the same manner as previously stated in the Explanation of Conduct (Ācāraniddesa). In this context, gocara (resort) refers to a place suitable for approaching for the sake of requisites such as alms-food, while agocara (improper resort) refers to an unsuitable place. 

'Vesiyāgocara' means one whose resort is a courtesan; it implies a place approached through friendship and intimacy. In this term, vesiyā (courtesans) refers to women who live by their beauty and are easily accessible for misconduct through some material gain. One who approaches them out of affection or friendship is said to have a courtesan as a resort. Therefore, it is not proper to approach them in such a manner. Why? Because of the failure of protection. For a monk who approaches in this way, the ascetic dharma (samaṇadhamma) that has been long protected and guarded perishes in just a few days; even if it does not perish, he incurs blame. However, a monk who approaches for the sake of an offering should do so by establishing mindfulness. 

Vidhavā refers to widows or women separated from their husbands. Thullakumāriyo refers to elderly unmarried maidens. Paṇḍaka refers to eunuchs who are full of talk related to worldly pleasures, whose defilements are thick, and whose fever of defilements is not calmed. The danger in approaching all these should be understood in the same way as stated for the courtesan resort. The same method applies to bhikkhunīs. Furthermore, monks are those with abundant holy life (brahmacariya), and so are bhikkhunīs. Through mutual association, they can destroy the well-guarded ascetic dharma in just a few days. However, it is proper to go to visit a sick bhikkhunī. It is also proper for a monk to go for the purpose of making an offering after obtaining flowers, or for the purpose of giving an exhortation (ovāda).

Pānāgāra refers to a tavern or liquor shop. Such a place is not secluded from drunkards who cause obstacles to the holy life. It is not proper to approach such a tavern as a drinking companion with those drunkards, as it causes obstacles to the holy life. In the passages such as 'He lives in association with kings,' 'kings' refers to those who rule the country, whether consecrated or unconsecrated. Rājamahāmattā refers to high ministers endowed with great authority similar to that of kings. Titthiyā refers to external wanderers with wrong views. Titthiyasāvakā refers to those who give requisites to heretics out of devotion. It means being in association with these kings and others.

Ananulomika-saṃsagga (inappropriate association) refers to association that is unsuitable and contrary to the three trainings (sikkhā). Through such association, one encounters obstacles to the holy life, transgression of training rules, and the decline of the practice of effacement (sallekha). How? By sharing sorrow, sharing joy, and sharing happiness and suffering with kings and royal ministers.
326:
When duties and affairs arise for kings or royal ministers, one personally exerts effort for them; or having the same desires, preferences, and conduct as heretics and their disciples, or having affection, great esteem, and intimacy that brings about the state of having the same desires, preferences, and conduct. Among these associations, associating with kings and royal ministers creates obstacles to the holy life. Associating with the remaining heretics and their disciples leads to adopting their views. However, it is proper for one who is capable of breaking their views and making them adopt one's own view to approach them.

Now, to show improper resort by another method, the Buddha began the discourse with 'Whatever families...' (yāni vā pana tāni kulāni). In that context, assaddhāni (faithless) refers to families devoid of faith in the Three Jewels, such as the Buddha. They do not believe that 'The Buddha is omniscient, the Dhamma is leading out of suffering, and the Saṅgha is practicing well.' Appasannāni (unbelieving) means they are unable to make their minds clear and untroubled. Akkosakapari-bhāsakāni refers to families that are both abusive and threatening. They abuse with the ten grounds of abuse, saying: 'You are a thief, you are a fool, you are an idiot, you are a camel, you are an ox, you are a donkey, you are one headed for a state of deprivation, you are one headed for hell, you are an animal, there is no good destination for you, only a bad destination is to be expected.' They threaten by showing danger, saying: 'Let it be, now we will beat you, bind you, or kill you.'

Anatthakāmā means they do not desire benefit but desire only harm. Ahitakāmā means they desire only what is not beneficial and do not desire what is beneficial. Aphāsukakāmā means they do not desire comfort but desire only discomfort. Ayogakkhemakāmā means they do not desire Nibbāna, which is secure and fearless from the four yokes, but desire only the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa-dukkha) which is accompanied by danger. In the term 'of monks' (bhikkhūnaṃ), novices (sāmaṇeras) are also included. In the term 'of nuns' (bhikkhunīnaṃ), probationary nuns (sikkhamānās) and novice nuns (sāmaṇerīs) are also included. Indeed, for all four assemblies who have gone forth or taken refuge dedicated to the Blessed One, those families desire only harm. 

Tathārūpāni kulāni refers to families of such nature, such as royal families. Sevati means living in dependence. Bhajati means approaching. Payirupāsati means approaching again and again. This is called improper resort (agocara), which should be understood as three types: the courtesan-resort etc. for a monk who has such a resort; the king-association etc. for a monk associated with kings; and the faithless-family-resort etc. for a monk who frequents faithless families.

The state of being an improper resort for that monk should be understood by the following reason. First, the courtesan etc. should be understood as an improper resort because they are a basis for the five cords of sensual pleasure. As it is said: 'Monks, what is the improper resort, the wrong range for a monk? It is the five...'
327:
"Sensual pleasures" (Saṃ. Ni. 5.372) refers to persons such as kings who are an unsuitable resort (agocara) because they are not a support for the practice of meditative absorption (jhāna), because they can cause the thunderbolt of gain and honor to fall, and because they are a cause for the ruin of right view. Likewise, families lacking faith are an unsuitable resort because they bring about the decline of faith and cause mental distress. In the explanation of resort (gocara), terms such as "resort of prostitutes" (vesiyāgocara) should be understood as the opposite of the aforementioned unsuitable resorts.

Regarding the terms beginning with "opānabhūtāni": "opānabhūtāni" refers to houses that are like wells or ponds. Like a lotus pond dug at a four-way crossroads, they are houses like that of the high official Citta, which are capable of being comfortably entered by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. It is said that in that official's house, a sun-dial pillar (kālatthambho) was indeed erected. For the monks who arrived at the door of the house, there was no such thing as a lack of requisites. Even for medicinal requisites alone, sixty kahāpaṇas were spent daily. "Kāsāvapajjotāni" refers to houses like that of the merchant Bhūtapāla, which are filled with a single mass of light from the radiance of the saffron-dyed robes worn by the bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs. "Isivātapativātāni" refers to houses that are blown upon by the wind from the robes of the sages (isī)—namely the bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs—who enter and leave the house, and by the wind from their bodies generated by movements such as bending and stretching, or houses where the stains of evil have been blown away.

In the explanation of "seeing danger in the slightest faults": "anumattāni" means the size of an atom. "Vajjā" means faults. "Yāni tāni vajjāni" means those things called faults because they are blameworthy. "Appamattakāni" means those of small measure. "Oramattakāni" means those of a measure even lower than small. "Lahusāni" means light. "Lahusammattāni" means those considered as light faults. "Saṃyamakaraṇīyāni" means those to be remedied through restraint. "Saṃvarakaraṇīyāni" means those to be remedied through restraint (indriya-saṃvara). "Cittuppādakaraṇīyāni" means those to be remedied by a mere thought. "Manasikārapaṭibaddhāni" means those to be remedied by mere mental reflection.

What are those faults? First, the Elder Suma, who resided at Divāvihāra, said: "These are faults that do not amount to a formal offense (āpatti) but are mere arisings of thought, which are purified by the mere mental reflection, 'I will not do such a thing again.' This is called 'declaration by resolution' (adhiṭṭhānāvikamma)." However, his pupil, the Elder Tipitaka Cūḷanāga, said: "This is only an analysis of the Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla. Therefore, the faults here should be understood as the dukkaṭa and dubbhāsita offenses, which are the lightest of all offenses. This is called 'declaration for rehabilitation' (vuṭṭhānāvikamma)."
328:
"Iti imesu" means in these faults of such a nature. "Vajjadassāvī" means having the habit of seeing a fault as a fault or as a defect. "Bhayadassāvī" means having the habit of seeing them as danger because they are the cause of the four types of fear. "Ādīnavadassāvī" means having the habit of seeing them as disadvantages in various ways: because they bring blame in this life, because they result in suffering in the future, because they create obstacles to higher virtues, and because they generate remorse.

"Nissaraṇadassāvī" means having the habit of seeing the escape that exists from those faults. What is the escape here? In the view of the teacher, the Elder Mahāsuma, it is said: "When an offense has not yet been reached, making the fault clear through mental resolution is the escape." In the view of the pupil, the Elder Tipitaka Cūḷanāga, it is said: "When an offense has been reached, making the fault clear through the confession of the offense for rehabilitation is the escape."

In those two traditions, such a bhikkhu is said to see faults of the size of an atom as faults and as danger. To illustrate such a bhikkhu, this method of measurement is stated: Paramāṇu, Aṇu, Tajjarī, Rathareṇu, Likkhā, Ūkā, Dhanyamāsa, Aṅgula (finger-breadth), Vidatthi (span), Ratana (cubit), Yaṭṭhi (rod), Usabha, Gāvuta, and Yojana. Among these, the "Paramāṇu" belongs to the realm of space and does not come into the range of the physical eye; it can only be seen by the divine eye. An "Aṇu" is the mote seen circling in the form of tiny balls in the sunlight entering through holes in walls or keyholes. A "Tajjarī" is the dust that breaks off and rises on both sides of cattle paths, footpaths, or chariot paths. A "Rathareṇu" is the dust that clings to those same places. Likkhā and the others are well known.

Among these measurements, 36 paramāṇus equal the size of 1 aṇu. 36 aṇus equal the size of 1 tajjarī. 36 tajjarīs equal 1 rathareṇu. 36 rathareṇus equal 1 likkhā. 7 likkhās equal 1 ūkā (louse). 7 ūkās equal 1 dhanyamāsa (grain of paddy). The measure of 7 dhanyamāsas is 1 aṅgula (finger-breadth). By that finger-breadth, 12 aṅgulas make 1 vidatthi (span). 2 spans make 1 ratana (cubit). 7 cubits make 1 yaṭṭhi (rod). By that rod, 20 yaṭṭhis make 1 usabha. 80 usabhas make 1 gāvuta. 4 gāvutas make 1 yojana. By that yojana, Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, is 168,000 yojanas in height. A bhikkhu who is able to see a fault the size of an atom as being equal to Mount Sineru, which is 168,000 yojanas high—this bhikkhu...
329:
Regarding 'seeing danger in the slightest faults': This means that a monk is able to perceive a fault that is as small as an atom—one that does not reach the level of an offense but is merely a mental occurrence—as being like Mount Sineru, which is 168,000 yojanas high. Such a monk is known as one who sees danger in the slightest faults, both as a fault and as a danger. Furthermore, a monk who is able to perceive an offense that is the lightest of all offenses, such as a dukkaṭa or a dubbhāsita, as being like the first pārājika offense, is also known as one who sees danger in the slightest faults, both as a fault and as a danger.

In the definition of the phrase 'takes up and trains in the training rules' (samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu): 'Bhikkhu-sikkhā' refers to the training to be practiced by monks. Whether that training is shared with bhikkhunīs or not, it is called bhikkhu-sikkhā. 'Bhikkhunī-sikkhā' refers to the training to be practiced by bhikkhunīs. Whether that training is shared with bhikkhus or not, it is also called bhikkhunī-sikkhā. The training of sāmaṇeras, sikkhamānās, and sāmaṇerīs is also included within these trainings of bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs. 'Upāsaka-sikkhā' refers to the training to be practiced by male lay followers. It is established by way of the five precepts and the ten precepts. 'Upāsikā-sikkhā' refers to the training to be practiced by female lay followers. It is also established by way of the five precepts and the ten precepts. Among these, the training of bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs lasts until the path of Arahantship (arahattamagga). The training of upāsakas and upāsikās lasts until the path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga). Among these trainings, this monk trains only in the training rules that he himself should practice. The remaining trainings are mentioned for the purpose of showing the meaning of the training rules by extracting the relevant meanings.

'Thus in these trainings' means in trainings of such a nature. 'Entirely in every way' means all training by taking up all training. 'In every manner, all' means all training through every manner of training to be practiced. 'Without remainder, completely' means 'without remainder' because nothing is left out; it means 'completely' because even a training rule broken through forgetfulness is restored to its original state. 'Takes up and practices' means having taken up and accepted, he practices. Therefore, it is said: 'Because he takes up and practices, fulfilling all these training rules in every manner to be practiced, it is said "he takes up and trains in the training rules".'

517-8. In the definition of the two terms 'guarded in the sense doors' (indriyesu guttadvāro) and 'moderate in eating' (bhojane mattaññū), the purpose of teaching the unwholesome side (kaṇhapakkha) first should be understood in the same way as stated in the definition of conduct (ācāra-niddesa). In that definition, whatever should be said regarding 'What is unguardedness in the sense doors?' and so on, has already been stated in the explanation of the Nikkhepa-kaṇḍa.

In the definition of devotion to wakefulness (jāgariyānuyoga-niddesa), in the phrase 'the former part and the latter part of the night' (pubbarattāpararattaṃ), the first half of the night is called pubbaratta. By this term pubbaratta, the first watch (paṭhama-yāma) and the afternoon period (pacchābhatta) are taken. ...
330:
... is taken. By the word 'apararatta', which is the latter part of the night, the last watch (pacchima-yāma) and the time before the meal (purebhatta) are taken. The middle watch (majjhima-yāma) is not taken because it is the opportunity for the monk to dispel the fatigue of sleepiness. 'Devotion to wakefulness' (jāgariyānuyoga) means the repeated effort of being awake without sleeping. 'Is devoted' (anuyutto hoti) means being endowed with the repetition and development known as that effort. In this definition, by the words 'here, a monk during the day' (idha bhikkhu divasaṃ), all three parts of the day—morning, noon, and evening—are taken.

'By walking and sitting' (caṅkamena nisajjāya) means living throughout the whole day using only these two postures of walking and sitting, and purifying or liberating the mind from the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) or all unwholesome states that obstruct the mind. Although the posture of standing (ṭhāna) is not mentioned here, it should be understood as being included by relying on walking and sitting. 'During the first watch' (paṭhamayāmaṃ) means during the entire first watch. 'During the middle watch' (majjhimayāmaṃ) means the middle watch, which is the sixth part when the day and night are divided into six parts.

Regarding 'the lion's sleep' (sīha-seyyā), there are four types of sleep: the sensualist's sleep (kāmabhogī-seyyā), the hungry ghost's sleep (peta-seyyā), the lion's sleep (sīha-seyyā), and the Tathāgata's sleep (tathāgata-seyyā). Among these, 'Monks, generally those who enjoy sensual pleasures sleep on their left side' is the sensualist's sleep. Among them, there is generally no one who sleeps on the right side. 'Monks, generally hungry ghosts sleep on their backs' is the hungry ghost's sleep. Because they have little flesh and blood and are entangled in a skeleton, they cannot sleep on one side and only sleep on their backs. 'Monks, the lion, the king of beasts, lies down on his right side ... and is glad and joyful' (A. Ni. 4.246)—this sleep is the lion's sleep. The majestic lion king, possessing great power, places his two front paws in one place and his two hind paws in another, tucks his tail between his thighs, notes the position where the front paws, hind paws, and tail are placed, and then sleeps with his head resting on top of the two front paws. Even after sleeping all day, when he wakes up, he does so without being startled. He lifts his head and observes the position of his front paws and so on. If any part has moved even slightly from its original position, he becomes displeased, thinking, 'This is not suitable for your birth and your bravery,' and he sleeps right there again, not going out for food. If it remains unmoved, he becomes glad and joyful, thinking, 'This is suitable for your birth and your bravery,' and having risen, he stretches himself with the movement of a lion.
331:
(The lion) shakes off the burden of its mane, roars the lion's roar three times, and then departs for its hunting ground. The dwelling in the fourth jhāna, however, is called the Tathāgata-seyya (the Buddha's posture). Among those four types, the Sīha-seyya (lion's posture) is intended here. This Sīha-seyya is called the noble posture because it is a posture of great power.

"Foot by foot" means placing the left foot upon the right foot. "Overlapping" means placing it slightly beyond. This is because if the ankles or the knees strike against each other, pain constantly arises, the mind does not become one-pointed, and the sleep is uncomfortable. However, if placed overlapping so they do not strike, pain does not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, and the sleep is comfortable. Therefore, it is said, "placing foot by foot overlappingly." "Mindful and clearly comprehending" means being endowed with mindfulness and the wisdom of clear comprehension. By this, the mindfulness and clear comprehension that delimits sleep is spoken of. "Reflecting on the perception of rising" means placing in the mind the perception of rising that delimits the time of rising, such as "I shall rise at such and such a time." One who lies down having done this is one who makes an effort to rise exactly at the delimited time.

520-521. "Sātacca and Nepakka": Sātacca refers to energy (vīriya) because it should be constantly maintained, and Nepakka refers to wisdom (paññā) because it has reached maturity. Only one endowed with these dwells constantly devoted to the practice of wakefulness (jāgariyānuyoga). Here, energy is spoken of as a mixture of mundane and supramundane; wisdom also follows the nature of energy. If energy is mundane, wisdom is mundane; if energy is supramundane, wisdom is supramundane.

"Of the Bodhipakkhiya-dhammas" means of the dhammas that exist on the side of the path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) which realizes the Four Noble Truths. By this much, taking all thirty-seven Bodhipakkhiya-dhammas as a group, and wishing to show only the Bojjhaṅgas (factors of enlightenment) which are capable of occurring together on a single object even in mundane meditation, he said "seven factors of enlightenment," etc. It should be understood that those Bojjhaṅgas are spoken of as a mixture of mundane and supramundane. The remaining meanings are clear according to the method already mentioned below.

In the description beginning with "Abhikkante," in the phrase "Abhikkante paṭikkante," first, going forward is called "abhikkanta." Turning back or retreating is called "paṭikkanta." Both of these in the four...
332:
...postures are obtained. In walking, first, conveying the body forward is called 'abhikkama' (going forward); turning back is called 'paṭikkama' (going backward). Even while standing, leaning the body forward while standing is called 'abhikkama'; leaning backward is called 'paṭikkama'. Even in sitting, moving toward the front of one's seat while sitting is called 'abhikkama'; moving back toward the rear is called 'paṭikkama'. In lying down, the method is the same.

'Sampajānākārī hoti' means one who habitually performs all actions with clear comprehension (sampajañña), or one who habitually practices clear comprehension itself. That monk indeed practices clear comprehension in matters such as going forward; he is never devoid of clear comprehension. Since that clear comprehension is always associated with mindfulness, in its description it is said, "Mindful and clearly comprehending, he goes forward; mindful and clearly comprehending, he goes backward."

This monk, whether going forward or backward, is not unmindful or without clear comprehension. Being endowed with mindfulness and clearly comprehending with wisdom, he both goes forward and goes backward. In all matters such as going forward, he applies the fourfold clear comprehension. There are four types of clear comprehension: Sātthaka-sampajañña, Sappāya-sampajañña, Gocara-sampajañña, and Asammoha-sampajañña. Among those four, when the thought of going forward arises, instead of going according to the mind's whim, one delimits whether it is beneficial or not, thinking, "Is there benefit for me in going here, or not?" Taking what is beneficial is 'Sātthaka-sampajañña'. In that benefit, progress in accordance with the Dhamma through seeing a shrine (cetiya), seeing a Bodhi tree, seeing the Sangha, seeing elder monks, or seeing a foul object (asubha), etc., is called 'benefit'. For, having seen a shrine or a Bodhi tree and having produced joy (pīti) with the Buddha as the object, or having seen the Sangha and having produced joy with the Sangha as the object, one who contemplates that very joy in terms of rise and fall (khayavaya) reaches Arahantship. Having seen elder monks and established oneself in their advice, or having seen a foul object and produced the first jhāna therein, and then contemplating that very jhāna in terms of rise and fall, one reaches Arahantship. Therefore, seeing these things is beneficial. Some teachers, however, say, "Obtaining the four requisites is also a benefit, because one practices to support the holy life (brahmacariya) by depending on those requisites."

In that going, delimiting what is suitable and unsuitable and taking what is suitable is 'Sappāya-sampajañña'. For example: seeing a shrine is indeed beneficial. However, if there is a great festival at the shrine and within ten or twelve yojanas there is a crowd...
333:
...they gather. Women and men, decorated according to their wealth, move about like painted figures. At that time, greed arises in that monk for a pleasant object, hatred for an unpleasant object, and delusion for lack of reflection. Or there may be an offense through physical contact with a woman, or danger to life and the holy life (brahmacariya). Such a place is called unsuitable (asappāya). If the aforementioned dangers are absent, it is called a suitable (sappāya) place. The same principle applies to visiting the Bodhi tree. Visiting the Saṅgha is also beneficial. However, if there is a gathering of people and danger as described above when people build a large pavilion in the village and listen to the Dhamma all night, then that place is unsuitable. It is suitable only if there is no danger. The same principle applies to visiting senior elders who are surrounded by a large following.

Viewing a corpse (asubha) is also beneficial. To clarify this point, there is this story: It is said that a young monk took a novice (sāmaṇera) and went to the forest for tooth-sticks. The novice stepped off the path and, walking ahead, saw a corpse and attained the first jhāna. Using that very jhāna as a basis, he contemplated formations (saṅkhāra), realized the three lower fruits (phala), and stood there maintaining his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) for the sake of the higher path. The young monk, not seeing the novice, called out, "Novice!" The novice thought, "Since the day I was ordained, I have never spoken even two words of idle chatter with a monk; I will attain the higher distinction on another day," and replied, "What is it, Bhante?" When told, "Come here," he came at that single word and said, "Bhante, please go along this path and stand for a moment at the place where I stood, facing the east, and look." The young monk did so and attained the same distinction that the novice had reached. Thus, a single corpse became beneficial for two people. However, for a man, the corpse of a woman is unsuitable, and for a woman, the corpse of a man is unsuitable. Only the same sex (sabhāga) is suitable. Such discernment of suitability is called 'clear comprehension of suitability' (sappāya-sampajañña).

For a monk who has thus discerned what is beneficial and suitable, taking up his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) known as the 'resort' (gocara) according to his preference among the thirty-eight meditation subjects, and going on the alms round without letting go of that meditation subject, is called 'clear comprehension of the resort' (gocara-sampajañña). To clarify this gocara-sampajañña, this fourfold grouping should be understood:

In this Dispensation, a certain monk carries (the meditation subject) and does not bring it back. A certain monk does not carry it but brings it back. A certain monk neither carries it nor brings it back. A certain monk both carries it...
334:
...and brings it back. Among those (four types), a certain monk purifies his mind from the hindering (nīvaraṇa) states by walking and sitting during the day. Likewise, in the first watch of the night, and having slept in the middle watch, he spends the last watch also in sitting and walking. Early in the morning, he performs the duties of the Cetiya courtyard and the Bodhi tree courtyard, pours water at the Bodhi tree, sets out drinking water and water for use, and practices by undertaking all the Khandhaka duties, such as the duties toward teachers and preceptors (upajjhāya). Having performed his bodily ablutions and entered the refectory, he sits cross-legged two or three times to allow the body to warm up, applies himself to his meditation subject, and then rises at the time for alms round. Taking his bowl and robes with the meditation subject foremost, he leaves the monastery and goes to the Cetiya courtyard while still reflecting on the meditation subject.

If his meditation subject is the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati), he enters the Cetiya courtyard without letting go of that meditation subject. If it is another meditation subject, he stands at the foot of the stairs and leaves it there like a bundle held in the hand, takes up the joy (pīti) that has the Buddha as its object, and ascends the Cetiya courtyard. If it is a large Cetiya, he should circumambulate it three times and pay homage at the four sides. If it is a small Cetiya, he should likewise circumambulate it and pay homage at eight places. Having worshipped the Cetiya, when he reaches the Bodhi tree courtyard, he should worship the Bodhi tree, showing respect as if he were in the presence of the Blessed Buddha.

Having thus worshipped the Cetiya and the Bodhi tree, he goes to the place where he left his meditation subject. As if picking up a stored bundle with his hand, he takes back the meditation subject he had set down. Then, near the village, with the meditation subject still foremost, he puts on his robes and enters the village for alms. Then, when people see him, they come out to meet him, saying, 'Our noble lord has arrived,' take his bowl, and have him sit in the rest house or a house. They offer him gruel and, until the meal is finished, wash his feet, anoint them with oil, and sit before him, either asking questions or wishing to hear the Dhamma. Even if they do not ask, the teachers of the Commentaries say, 'A Dhamma talk should indeed be given for the sake of favoring the people.' Indeed, there is no Dhamma talk that is devoid of the meditation subject. Therefore, having partaken of the food with the meditation subject foremost and given the blessing (anumodanā), he leaves the village followed by the people who are seeing him off, and having sent them back, he continues on his way.

Then, the novices and young monks who had left earlier and finished their meal duties outside the village, seeing him, come out to meet him and take his bowl and robes. It is said that ancient monks did not perform duties by looking at faces, thinking, 'This is our preceptor, this is our teacher'; they performed duties simply according to the order of arrival. Those young monks ask him, 'Bhante, these...'
335:
"How are these people related to you? Are they relatives from your mother's side or your father's side?" they asked. When asked in return, "What did you see that makes you ask this?" they replied, "Their love and reverence for you are very great." "Friends, these people do for us what even parents find difficult to do. Our alms-bowls and robes belong to them; because of their influence, even when there is danger, we do not know danger, and when there is hunger, we do not know hunger. We have no such benefactors as these," he said, praising their virtues as he went. This monk is said to be one who "carries but does not carry back."

For a monk who performs the aforementioned duties early on, the fire element born of kamma (kammaja-tejo-dhātu) blazes up. It leaves the non-clung-to (external food) and takes the clung-to (internal body); sweat pours from his body, and the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) cannot enter the path. That monk, taking his bowl and robes early, quickly pays homage to the shrine and enters the village for congee at the very time the cattle go out. Having received the congee, he goes to the assembly hall and drinks it. Then, by merely swallowing two or three times, the fire element born of kamma leaves the clung-to and takes the non-clung-to. As if bathed with a hundred jars of water, he attains the cooling of the fire element's heat. Keeping the meditation subject at the forefront, he partakes of the congee, washes his bowl and mouth, and during the interval before the main meal, he reflects on the meditation subject. He wanders for alms in the remaining places, partakes of the meal while keeping the meditation subject at the forefront, and from then on, he returns while holding onto the meditation subject that arises continuously. This monk is said to be one who "does not carry but carries back." Such monks, having drunk congee and undertaken insight meditation (vipassanā), and attained Arahantship in the Buddha's Dispensation, are beyond counting. In the island of Sīhaḷa, there is no seat in the assembly halls of various villages where a monk has not attained Arahantship after drinking congee.

One who dwells negligently, has laid down the burden, has broken all duties, and dwells with a mind bound by the five mental spikes and the five fetters, without even the perception that "there is such a thing as a meditation subject," enters the village for alms, wanders and eats while associating with laypeople in an unsuitable manner, and comes out empty-handed—this monk is said to be one who "neither carries nor carries back."

As for the one who is said to "carry and carry back," he should be understood by way of the duty of going and coming back (gatapaccāgatika-vatta). Indeed, sons of good family who desire their own welfare in the Dispensation...
336:
...having gone forth, while living together for ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or even a hundred years, they dwell having made a pact: "Friends, you did not go forth because of debt, nor because of fear, nor because of a difficult livelihood; rather, you went forth in this Dispensation desiring to be liberated from suffering. Therefore, suppress the defilements (kilesa) that arise while walking, even while walking. Suppress the defilements that arise while standing, sitting, or lying down, even while standing, sitting, or lying down." 

Having made such a pact, when they go for alms, they mark stones at distances of half an usabha, one usabha, half a gāvuta, or one gāvuta, and they go while reflecting only on the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). If defilement arises in any monk while walking, he suppresses it right there. If he is unable to do so, he stands still. Then the monk coming behind him also stands still.
