That monk admonishes himself, "This monk knows the thought that has arisen in you; this is not suitable for you," and by developing insight meditation (vipassanā), he enters the stage of the Noble Ones (ariyabhūmi). If he is unable to do so, he sits down. Then the monk coming behind him also sits down; the method is the same. Even if he is unable to enter the stage of the Noble Ones, he goes on while reflecting on the meditation subject, having pushed aside that defilement. He does not lift a foot with a mind devoid of the meditation subject; if he does lift it, he turns back and returns to the previous spot, like the Elder Mahāphussadeva who dwelt in Ālindaka.

That Elder, it is said, lived for nineteen years fulfilling the duty of going and coming back (gatapaccāgatika-vatta). People, while plowing, sowing, and threshing in the fields along the way, seeing the Elder going in that manner, would say, "This Elder is turning back again and again; is he perhaps confused about the way, or has he forgotten something?" The Elder, without paying attention to those words, practiced the recluse's duties (samaṇadhamma) with a mind associated only with the meditation subject, and within twenty years, he attained Arahantship. On the day he attained Arahantship, a deity residing at the end of his walking path stood lighting a lamp with her fingers. The four Great Kings, Sakka the king of devas, and Sahampati Brahma also came to attend to him. Seeing that radiance, the Elder Vanavāsī Mahātissa asked him the next day, "During the night, there was a radiance in your presence. What was that radiance?" The Elder, wishing to deflect the question, said, "Radiance can be the light of a lamp, or the light of a gem," and so on. Then, being repeatedly entreated, "Venerable sir, please do not hide it," he acknowledged it by saying "Yes" and told him.
337:
It is also like the Elder Mahānāga, a resident of Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa. That Elder, while fulfilling the duty of going and returning (gatapaccāgatavatta), thought, "First, I will honor the Great Exertion (mahāpadhāna) of the Blessed One." He undertook the practice of only standing and walking for seven years. Thereafter, he fulfilled the duty of going and returning for sixteen years and attained Arahatship. That Elder would lift his foot only with a mind associated with the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna); if he lifted his foot with a mind dissociated from the meditation subject, he would turn back. Upon reaching the village boundary, he would stand at a place where one might wonder, "Is it a cow? Is it a renunciant?" and then put on his robe. He would wash his bowl with water from a flask and keep a mouthful of water. Why? With the intention: "May there be no distraction from my meditation subject even by the mere words 'May you live long' to the people who come to offer alms or to pay homage to me." If he was asked about the date, the number of monks, or a question, he would swallow the water and answer. If there was no one asking about the date and so on, he would spit out the water at the village gate upon leaving and depart.

It is also like the fifty monks who entered the Rains Retreat at Kalambatittha Monastery. It is said that on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, they made a pact: "We will not speak to one another until we have attained Arahatship." When entering the village for alms, they would enter with a mouthful of water. If asked about the date and so on, they acted in the manner already described. The people in that village, seeing the place where the water was spat out, knew: "Today one has come; today two have come." They also thought: "Is it that these monks do not speak only with us, or do they not speak with each other either? If they do not speak with each other, they must surely be in a quarrel. Come, let us go and make them apologize to one another." All of them went to the monastery, but among the fifty monks, they did not see even two monks in the same place. Then, a wise man among them said: "Friends, a place where quarreling people live cannot be like this. The courtyard of the shrine and the courtyard of the Bodhi tree are well-swept; the brooms are well-stored; the drinking water and washing water are well-provided." They turned back from there. Those monks attained Arahatship within the three months of the Rains and performed the Pavāraṇā of purity (visuddhipavāraṇā) on the day of the Great Pavāraṇā.

Thus, like the Elder Mahānāga, a resident of Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa, and like the monks who entered the Rains Retreat at Kalambatittha Monastery, lifting the foot only with a mind associated with the meditation subject...
338:
Going near the village, having rinsed the mouth with water, and having carefully observed the streets, one should enter a street where there are no drunkards, scoundrels, or such quarrelsome people, nor fierce elephants, horses, and so on. When wandering for alms there, one should not go with speed like one in a great hurry, for there is no such ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) as "alms-gathering with speed." One should go steadily, like a water-cart that has reached an uneven piece of ground. When entering houses in order, one should wait for a suitable time to know whether the person wishes to give or not. After receiving alms, one should sit in a comfortable and suitable place, whether inside the village, outside the village, or in the monastery. While reflecting on the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and establishing the perception of the repulsiveness of food, one should consume the food endowed with eight factors, reflecting on it with the similes of greasing an axle, anointing a wound, or eating the flesh of one's own son. In consuming it, it should not be for fun, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification... but only for living comfortably. After eating, having performed the duties with water and having rested for a moment to relieve the fatigue of the meal, one should reflect only on the meditation subject in the period after the meal, in the first watch, and in the last watch, just as before the meal. This practice is called "carrying out and carrying back."

A person who fulfills this duty of going and returning (gatapaccāgatavatta), known as carrying out and carrying back, if endowed with the sufficing conditions (upanissaya), can attain Arahatship even in the first stage of life. If not in the first stage, then in the middle stage; if not in the middle stage, then in the last stage; if not in the last stage, then at the time of death; if not at the time of death, then upon becoming a deity (devaputta); if not upon becoming a deity, then being born when no Buddhas have arisen, he realizes Private Enlightenment (paccekabodhi). If he does not realize Private Enlightenment, then upon meeting with Buddhas, he becomes one of quick intuition like the Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya, or one of great wisdom like the Elder Sāriputta, or one of great psychic power like the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, or a bearer of ascetic practices like the Elder Mahākassapa, or one with the divine eye like the Elder Anuruddha, or a bearer of the Vinaya like the Elder Upāli, or a Dhamma-preacher like the Elder Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, or a forest-dweller like the Elder Revata, or one of great learning like the Elder Ānanda, or one who is desirous of training like the Elder Rāhula, the son of the Buddha. Thus, for one who performs "carrying out and carrying back" in this group of four, his clear comprehension of the resort (gocarasampajañña) is said to have reached its pinnacle.
339:
Non-delusion in moving forward and so forth is called clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña). This clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood as follows: In this Dispensation, when a monk is moving forward or moving backward, he does not become deluded like the foolish worldlings who, in moving forward and so forth, are deluded thinking, 'The self moves, the movement is produced by the self,' or 'I move, the movement is produced by me.' Instead, when the thought 'I will move forward' arises, the mind-produced air element (vāyodhātu), together with that mind, arises, producing bodily intimation (viññatti). Thus, by the power of the mental activity and the diffusion of the air element, this skeleton, which is conventionally called 'the body,' moves forward.

When moving forward in such a manner, in the lifting of each foot, the two elements of earth (pathavī) and water (āpo) are weak and sluggish, while the other two elements (fire and air) are strong and powerful. The same applies to the swinging forward and the carrying across. In the letting down of the foot, the two elements of fire (tejo) and air (vāyo) are weak and sluggish, while the other two elements (earth and water) are strong and powerful. The same applies to the placing down and the pressing against the ground.

In that process, the physical and mental phenomena that arise during the lifting of the foot do not reach the swinging forward. The phenomena that arise during the swinging forward do not reach the carrying across. The phenomena that arise during the carrying across do not reach the letting down. The phenomena that arise during the letting down do not reach the placing down. The phenomena that arise during the placing down do not reach the pressing against the ground. In each and every place, they break up joint by joint, segment by segment, and part by part, crackling like sesame seeds thrown into a hot pan. In that breaking up, who is the individual that moves forward? Or whose movement forward is it? In the ultimate sense, it is only the going of elements, the standing of elements, the sitting of elements, and the lying down of elements. In each of those parts, together with the material phenomena—

One mind arises,
Another mind ceases;
It proceeds in an uninterrupted connection
Like a river current.

Thus, non-delusion in moving forward and so forth is called clear comprehension of non-delusion.

## The explanation of the phrase 'he is one who acts with clear comprehension in moving forward and moving backward' is finished.

In the phrase 'in looking ahead and looking aside' (ālokite vilokite), looking ahead (ālokita) means looking straight forward. Looking aside (vilokita) means looking in various directions. There are also other types such as looking down (olokita), looking up (ullokita), and looking behind (apalokita).
340:
These are the names [of the types of looking]. They are not included here. However, these two are included as they are appropriate. Or, by this method, all of them are indeed included.

Among them (looking ahead and looking aside), when the thought 'I will look' arises, the consideration of whether it is beneficial or not before looking according to the mind's desire is called 'clear comprehension of purpose' (sātthaka-sampajañña). This clear comprehension of purpose should be understood by taking the Venerable Nanda as a witness. For this was said by the Blessed One:

'Monks, if Nanda has to look towards the eastern direction, he looks towards the eastern direction only after having fully attended to it with his mind, thinking: "While I am looking towards the eastern direction in this way, covetousness, dejection, and evil unwholesome states will not follow and flow into me." In this way, he is one who has clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajāna). Monks, if Nanda has to look towards the western direction, the northern direction, the southern direction, upwards, downwards, or towards the intermediate directions... [Venerable Nanda] is one who acts with clear comprehension.' Thus it was taught (in the Aṅguttara Nikāya).

Furthermore, in this context as well, the purposefulness (sātthakatā) and suitability (sappāyatā) should be understood in the same way as mentioned before, such as in the case of seeing a shrine (cetiya).

Not abandoning the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is called 'clear comprehension of the domain' (gocara-sampajañña). Therefore, those who meditate on the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana) should look ahead and look aside by the power of their own meditation subject. Those who meditate on kasinas and so forth should do so by making the meditation subject the primary focus.

In the ultimate sense, there is no 'self' (attā) inside who is the looker or the one who looks around. When the thought 'I will look' arises, the mind-produced air element (vāyodhātu), together with that mind, arises, producing intimation (viññatti). Thus, by the power of the mental activity and the diffusion of the air element, the lower eyelid sinks down and the upper eyelid rises up. There is no one who is opening them with a machine. Thereafter, eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa), performing the function of seeing, arises. Knowing in this way is called 'clear comprehension of non-delusion' (asammoha-sampajañña) in this context.
341:
Furthermore, in this context, clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) should be understood by way of original full understanding (mūlapariññā), the state of being a guest (āgantukatā), and the state of being temporary (tāvakālikabhāva).

To explain first by way of original full understanding: there are the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), adverting (āvajjana), seeing (dassana), receiving (sampaṭicchana), investigating (santīraṇa), determining (votthabbana), and the seventh, impulsion (javana). Among these, the bhavaṅga occurs performing the function of a factor of the rebirth-process (upapattibhava). Turning that bhavaṅga aside, the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu) occurs performing the function of adverting. With its cessation, the eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) occurs performing the function of seeing. With its cessation, the resultant mind-element (vipāka-manodhātu) occurs performing the function of receiving. With its cessation, the resultant mind-door-consciousness-element (vipāka-manoviññāṇadhātu) occurs performing the function of investigating. With its cessation, the functional mind-door-consciousness-element (kiriya-manoviññāṇadhātu) occurs performing the function of determining. With its cessation, the impulsion (javana) impels seven times.

Among those impulsions, even in the first impulsion, there is no looking forward or looking aside by way of lust, hatred, or delusion, thinking, "This is a woman, this is a man." This is the same for the second... up to the seventh impulsion. However, just like soldiers on a battlefield, it is only when those mental states have broken up and fallen in succession that looking forward or looking aside occurs by way of lust and so on, thinking, "This is a woman, this is a man." Thus, in this context, clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood "by way of original full understanding."

When a visible form comes into range at the eye-door, after the vibration of the bhavaṅga, adverting and so on arise and cease by way of performing their respective functions, and finally, impulsion arises. That impulsion is like a guest man in the eye-door, which is like the house of the previously arisen adverting and so on. Just as it is not proper for a guest man, who has entered another's house to ask for something, to give orders while the house-owners themselves remain silent, so too, it is improper for (impulsion) to have lust, hatred, or delusion in the eye-door—the house of adverting and so on—while adverting and so on themselves are without lust, hatred, or delusion. Thus, clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood "by way of the state of being a guest."

Those consciousnesses that arise in the eye-door ending with determining, break up right there along with their associated states; they do not see one another. Therefore, they are brief and temporary. In that (temporariness), for example, in a house where all the people have died, it is not proper for the one remaining person, who is himself subject to death at that very moment, to delight in dancing and singing. Similarly, in a single door, along with the associated states...
342:
...when adverting and so on have died right there, it is not proper for the impulsion consciousness, which is also subject to death at that very moment, to have delight (abhirati) by way of lust, hatred, or delusion. Thus, clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood "by way of the state of being temporary."

Furthermore, this clear comprehension of non-delusion should also be understood by way of reflecting on the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), and conditions (paccaya). In this reflection, the eye and visible forms are the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha); seeing is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha); the feeling associated with that consciousness is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha); perception is the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha); and contact and so on are the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). Thus, in the combination of these five aggregates, looking forward and looking aside are manifested. Therein, who is the single one that looks forward? Who is the one that looks aside?

Likewise, the eye is the eye-base (cakkhāyatana), the visible form is the form-base (rūpāyatana), seeing is the mind-base (manāyatana), and the states such as feeling associated with that consciousness are the mental-object-base (dhammāyatana). Thus, in the combination of these four bases, looking forward and looking aside are manifested. Therein, who is the single one that looks forward? Who is the one that looks aside?

Likewise, the eye is the eye-element (cakkhudhātu), the visible form is the form-element (rūpadhātu), seeing is the eye-consciousness-element (cakkhuviññāṇadhātu), and the states such as feeling associated with that consciousness are the mental-object-element (dhammadhātu). Thus, in the combination of these four elements, looking forward and looking aside are manifested. Therein, who is the single one that looks forward? Who is the one that looks aside?

Likewise, the eye is the support condition (nissaya-paccaya), the visible form is the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), adverting is the proximity, contiguity, decisive support, absence, and disappearance conditions (anantara, samanantara, upanissaya, natthi, vigata-paccaya), light is the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya), and feeling and so on are the conascence and other conditions (sahajātādi-paccaya). Thus, in the combination of these conditions, looking forward and looking aside are manifested. Therein, who is the single one that looks forward? Who is the one that looks aside? Thus, in this context, clear comprehension of non-delusion should also be understood by way of reflecting on the aggregates, bases, elements, and conditions.

"In bending and stretching" (samiñjite pasārite) refers to the bending and stretching of the joints. In that bending and stretching, not doing so merely according to the whim of the mind, but rather discerning the presence or absence of purpose in the cause of bending and stretching the hands and feet, and choosing that which has purpose, is called "clear comprehension of purpose" (sātthaka-sampajañña). For one who remains with hands and feet bent or stretched for too long, painful feelings arise at every moment, the mind does not attain one-pointedness, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) falls away, and one does not achieve distinction. But for one who bends at the proper time and stretches at the proper time, those painful feelings do not arise, the mind is one-pointed, the meditation subject reaches growth, and one can achieve distinction. Thus, "discerning the presence or absence of purpose" should be understood.
343:
Even when there is a purpose, distinguishing between what is suitable and unsuitable and choosing the suitable is called 'clear comprehension of suitability' (sappāya-sampajañña). In this regard, the method is as follows: It is said that on the terrace of the Mahācetiya, young monks were reciting their studies. Behind them, young nuns were listening to the Dhamma. Among them, one young monk, while stretching out his hand, came into bodily contact with a young nun and, for that very reason, returned to the lay life. Another monk, while stretching out his foot, stretched it into a fire. His foot was burned down to the bone. Another monk stretched his foot into an anthill; he was bitten by a viper. Another monk stretched his foot against the post of a robe-hut; he was bitten by a green pit viper. Therefore, one should not stretch [one's limbs] in such unsuitable places but only in suitable ones. This is 'clear comprehension of suitability' in this context.

Furthermore, 'clear comprehension of the resort' (gocara-sampajañña) should be illustrated by the story of the Great Elder: It is said that a Great Elder, while sitting in his daytime quarters and conversing with his disciples, suddenly bent his hand, then returned it to its original position and bent it again slowly. His disciples asked, 'Venerable sir, why did you suddenly bend your hand, then return it to its original position and bend it again slowly?' He replied, 'Friends, since I began to apply my mind to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), I have never bent my hand while letting go of the meditation subject. But just now, while conversing with you, I bent it while letting go of the meditation subject. Therefore, I returned it to its original position and bent it again.' The disciples said, 'Excellent, venerable sir! A monk should indeed be like this.' Thus, in this context, not abandoning the meditation subject is to be understood as 'clear comprehension of the resort' (gocara-sampajañña).

To understand thus: 'In the internal sense, there is no such thing as a "self" (atta) that bends or stretches. Rather, through the diffusion of the air element (vāyodhātu) produced by the aforementioned mental activity, bending and stretching occur, just like the movement of the hands and feet of a wooden puppet pulled by strings'—this is to be understood as 'clear comprehension of non-delusion' (asammoha-sampajañña).

In the phrase 'in wearing the outer robe, bowl, and robes' (saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe), 'wearing' (dhāraṇam) refers to the use of the outer robe and robes by way of dressing and covering, and the bowl by way of receiving alms-food and so on. Therein, regarding the wearing of the outer robe and robes, for one who dresses and covers himself and wanders for alms, the 'purpose' (attho) is the benefit as stated by the Blessed One in such ways as 'for the sake of receiving alms, for warding off cold,' and so on. Through the power of that purpose, 'clear comprehension of purpose' (sātthaka-sampajañña) is to be understood.
344:
For one who is of a hot nature or who is weak, a fine, soft robe is suitable; for one who is sensitive to cold, a thick double-layered robe is suitable. The opposite is unsuitable. For anyone, a worn-out robe is unsuitable, because it causes an impediment (palibodha) to him through the need for patching and so on. Similarly, robes made of silk, fine cloth, and the like, which are desirable to thieves, are unsuitable. Such a robe can be a danger to the clothing and even to the life of one living alone in the forest. In the ultimate sense, however, whatever robe is obtained through wrong livelihood (micchā-ājīva) such as hinting (nimittakamma) and the like, or a robe by the use of which unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, that is unsuitable. The opposite is suitable. By knowing what is suitable in this way, 'clear comprehension of suitability' (sappāya-sampajañña) is to be understood here, and by not abandoning the meditation subject, 'clear comprehension of the resort' (gocara-sampajañña) is to be understood.

Internally, there is no person called 'self' (atta) who puts on the robe. Rather, the putting on of the robe occurs only through the diffusion and movement of the air element (vāyodhātu) produced by the aforementioned mind. In that process, the robe is insentient (acetana), and the body is also insentient (acetana). The robe does not know, 'I am being worn by the body,' nor does the body know, 'I am being covered by the robe.' Only elements are covering a collection of elements, just as a puppet made of rags is covered with cloth. Therefore, one should not be joyful (somanassa) upon receiving a good robe, nor should one be displeased (domanassa) upon receiving a poor one. For at the Nāgavammika shrine, trees, and so on, some people perform acts of veneration with flowers, scents, incense, and cloth, while others show disrespect by striking them with excrement, urine, mud, sticks, or weapons. Because of such actions, the Nāgavammika tree and others do not feel joy or displeasure. In the same way, one should not feel joy upon receiving a good robe, nor displeasure upon receiving a poor one. Through such reflective contemplation, 'clear comprehension of non-delusion' (asammoha-sampajañña) is to be understood here.

In carrying the bowl as well, one should not take the bowl thoughtlessly, but with the purpose of the benefit to be obtained by taking the bowl, thinking, 'By taking this and wandering for alms, I shall receive alms-food.' Thus, 'clear comprehension of purpose' (sātthaka-sampajañña) is to be understood. For one with a thin and weak body, a heavy bowl is unsuitable. For anyone, a bowl that has been reinforced with four or five knots/repairs and is difficult to clean is unsuitable. A bowl that is not well-washed is not proper; cleaning it becomes an impediment (palibodha) for that monk. A bowl as bright as a gem is also unsuitable, as it is desirable [to others], just as mentioned regarding the robe. A bowl obtained through hinting (nimittakamma) and the like, or one by the use of which unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, is absolutely unsuitable. The opposite is suitable. By knowing what is suitable in this way, 'clear comprehension of suitability' (sappāya-sampajañña) is to be understood here, and by not abandoning the meditation subject, 'clear comprehension of the resort' (gocara-sampajañña) is to be understood.
345:
Internally, there is no such person called a 'self' (atta) who holds the bowl. The act of holding the bowl occurs only through the diffusion and movement of the air element (vāyodhātu) produced by the mind as previously described. In that holding, the bowl is insentient, and the hands are also insentient. The bowl does not know, 'I am being held by the hands.' The hands also do not know, 'The bowl is being held by us.' Only the elements hold the collection of elements, just as a red-hot iron plate is held with tongs. Through the reflection that occurs in this way, 'clear comprehension of non-delusion' (asammoha-sampajañña) should be understood here.

Alternatively, just as compassionate people, seeing a helpless sick person in an almshouse—whose hands and feet are severed, with pus, blood, and maggots oozing from the wounds, and surrounded by bluebottles—offer them rags for binding the wounds and medicines in bowl-fragments and the like. Among those, some receive soft rags while others receive coarse ones. Some receive well-formed medicine containers while others receive poorly-formed ones. Those sick people are neither pleased nor displeased by those things. For their purpose is served merely by the rags for covering the wounds and by the bowl-fragments for holding the medicine. In the same way, a monk should regard the robe like a wound-bandage, the bowl like a medicine container, and the almsfood received in the bowl like the medicine in the container. Such a monk should be known as one who acts with supreme clear comprehension (sampajānākārī) through the clear comprehension of non-delusion in wearing the double-robe, bowl, and robes.

Among the terms beginning with 'asita': 'asita' refers to the eating of almsfood and the like. 'Pīta' refers to the drinking of gruel and the like. 'Khāyita' refers to the chewing of hard food and the like. 'Sāyita' refers to the tasting of honey, molasses, and the like. In that eating and drinking, the eightfold benefit described by the method 'not for play,' etc., is called 'purpose' (attha). Through that benefit, 'clear comprehension of purpose' (sātthaka-sampajañña) should be understood.

Among coarse, fine, bitter, and sweet foods, whatever food causes discomfort to someone is 'unsuitable' for them. Whatever is obtained through signs and hints (nimittakamma), etc., and whatever food, when eaten, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline, that is absolutely 'unsuitable.' The opposite is 'suitable.' Through knowing what is suitable, 'clear comprehension of suitability' (sappāya-sampajañña) should be understood here, and through not abandoning the meditation subject, 'clear comprehension of the resort' (gocara-sampajañña) should be understood.

Internally, there is no such person called a 'self' (atta) who eats. The act of receiving the bowl occurs only through the diffusion and movement of the air element produced by the mind as previously described. The lowering of the hand into the bowl occurs only through the diffusion and movement of the air element produced by the mind. The making of a morsel, the lifting of a morsel...
346:
...and the opening of the mouth occur. No one opens the jaw with a key or a machine. The placing of the morsel in the mouth, the upper teeth performing the function of a pestle, the lower teeth performing the function of a mortar, and the tongue performing the function of a hand occur only through the diffusion and movement of the air element produced by the mind. Thus, in that mouth, thin saliva from the tip of the tongue and thick saliva from the root of the tongue smear the morsel. That morsel, turned over by the tongue-hand in the lower-teeth-mortar, moistened by the saliva-water, and crushed by the upper-teeth-pestle—there is no one who pushes it inside with a ladle or a spoon; it enters only by the air element. As it enters again and again, there is no one who prepares a straw mat to support it; it stays only by the power of the air element. As it stays again and again, there is no one who makes a hearth, lights a fire, and cooks it; it is cooked only by the fire element (tejodhātu). As it is cooked again and again, there is no one who extracts it outside with a stick or a staff; only the air element extracts it. Thus, the air element carries, moves from place to place, supports, turns over, crushes, dries, and extracts (the morsel). The earth element (pathavīdhātu) also supports, turns over, crushes, dries, and extracts. The water element (āpodhātu) provides cohesion and maintains the state of moisture. The fire element repeatedly cooks the morsel that has entered inside. The space element (ākāsadhātu) serves as the path. The consciousness element (viññāṇadhātu) knows by following the right effort in various places. Through the power of reflection that occurs in this way, 'clear comprehension of non-delusion' (asammoha-sampajañña) should be understood in this (eating).

Furthermore, 'clear comprehension of non-delusion' should also be understood here through the reflection on the repulsive nature in ten ways: by way of going, seeking, consuming, the receptacle, the store, the undigested, the digested, the fruit, the discharge, and the smearing. The detailed explanation of this should be taken from the 'Description of the Perception of Repulsiveness in Food' in the Visuddhimagga.

## In the act of defecating and urinating (Uccārapassāvakamme)
This refers to the performing of defecation and urination. In that (act), for one who does not defecate or urinate when the time for discharge has arrived, sweat is released from the whole body, the eyes roll, the mind is not concentrated, and other diseases arise. But for one who performs the discharge, all those dangers do not occur; this is the meaning here. Through the power of that (benefit), 'clear comprehension of purpose' (sātthaka-sampajañña) should be understood.

For one who defecates or urinates in an unsuitable place, an offense (āpatti) occurs, ill-repute increases, and there may be danger to life. For one who does so in a suitable place, all...
347:
The non-occurrence [at an unsuitable time] is here 'clear comprehension of suitability' (sappāya-sampajañña). Through the power of that clear comprehension of suitability, and through the power of not abandoning the meditation subject, 'clear comprehension of the domain' (gocara-sampajañña) should be understood.

Within the body, there is no such thing as a 'self' (attā) that performs the act of voiding excrement and urine. The act of voiding excrement and urine occurs only through the diffusion of the wind element (vāyodhātu) produced by mental activity. For example, just as when a ripe boil bursts, pus and blood come out without intention, and just as water comes out of an overfilled water pot without intention, so too, the excrement and urine accumulated in the receptacle for digested food (pakkāsaya) and the bladder (muttavatthi), being pressed by the force of the wind, come out even without intention. These excrement and urine that come out in this way belong neither to that monk himself nor to others; they are merely the outflow of the body's impurities. To give another example: just as for someone pouring out old water from an old water pot, that water belongs neither to himself nor to others, but is merely the act of cleaning; so it is here. Through the power of the reflection that occurs in this way, 'clear comprehension of non-delusion' (asammoha-sampajañña) should be understood.

In the phrase gatādīsu (in going, etc.), gate means in going; ṭhite means in standing; nisinne means in sitting; sutte means in sleeping. In these instances of going, etc., the state of acting with clear comprehension (sampajāna-kārī) should be understood in the same manner as previously described for 'advancing' (abhikkanta), etc.

There is also another method here: one monk, while going, goes thinking of something else and reflecting on something else. Another monk, however, goes without abandoning his meditation subject. Similarly, one monk, while standing, sitting, or sleeping, sleeps thinking of something else and reflecting on something else. Another monk, however, sleeps without abandoning his meditation subject.

Since it is not yet clear with this much, they illustrated it by means of the walking meditation (caṅkama). A monk who has descended to the walking path and stands at the end of the path, comprehends thus: 'The mental and physical phenomena (rūpārūpa-dhamma) that arose at the eastern end of the path have ceased right here without reaching the western end; those that arose at the western end have ceased right here without reaching the eastern end; those that arose in the middle of the path have ceased right here without reaching either end; the mental and physical phenomena that arose during the act of walking have ceased right here without reaching the state of standing; those that arose in standing have ceased right here without reaching sitting; and those that arose in sitting have ceased right here without reaching sleeping.' While repeatedly comprehending in this way, he enters the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). When waking up, he wakes up only after taking up his meditation subject. This monk is called one who acts with clear comprehension (sampajāna-kārī) in going, etc.
348:
In sleeping, the meditation subject becomes unmanifest by the aforementioned method. One should not let the meditation subject become unmanifest. Therefore, as long as he is able to maintain comprehension, a monk, after walking, standing, and sitting, when lying down, comprehends thus: 'The body is insentient (acetana); the bed is insentient. The body does not know: "I am lying on the bed." The bed also does not know: "The body is lying on me." The insentient body is lying on the insentient bed.' Comprehending thus repeatedly, he lets the mind enter the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). When waking up, he wakes up only after taking up his meditation subject. This monk is called one who acts with clear comprehension (sampajāna-kārī) in sleeping. 

In waking (jāgarite): 'When there is the non-occurrence of the continuous functional process (kiriya-maya-pavatta) that produces bodily and vocal actions, it is not called waking; when that functional process is in use, it is called waking.' A monk who comprehends thus is one who acts with clear comprehension in waking. Furthermore, a monk who divides the night and day into six parts and remains vigilant for five parts to prevent unwholesome states from arising is also called one who acts with clear comprehension in waking. 

In speaking (bhāsite): 'When there is the non-occurrence of the sound-base (saddāyatana) which is derived matter (upādā-rūpa), it is not called speaking; when that sound-base occurs, it is called speaking.' A monk who comprehends thus is one who acts with clear comprehension in speaking. Also, a monk who teaches the Dhamma with the fruit of Arahantship as the goal, or a monk who, having abandoned the thirty-two kinds of animal talk (tiracchāna-kathā), speaks words based on the ten subjects of discourse (kathāvatthu), is one who acts with clear comprehension in speaking. 

In keeping silence (tuṇhībhāve): 'When there is the occurrence of the sound-base which is derived matter, it is not called silence; when there is its non-occurrence, it is called silence.' A monk who comprehends thus is one who acts with clear comprehension in silence. Also, a monk who sits having taken up a meditation subject from among the thirty-eight objects according to his mental preference, or a monk who enters the second absorption (dutiya-jhāna), is indeed called one who acts with clear comprehension in silence. 

And here, the single posture of 'going' appears in two places. Below, in the passage 'in advancing and retreating' (abhikkante paṭikkante), it is spoken of in terms of traveling a long distance by a monk going to and returning from the village for alms. In the passage 'in going, standing, sitting' (gate ṭhite nisinne), it should be understood as being spoken of in terms of the posture of taking small steps within the monastery. In that Pali text, all the phrases such as 'What is mindfulness?' (katamā sati) have an obvious meaning.
349:
What is shown by this word starting with 'He [resorts to] a secluded [lodging]'? It shows the suitable lodging (senāsana), which is the path of exertion and the place for practicing meditation, similar to an archery practice range for this monk.

Indeed, for a monk who possesses such qualities within himself (such as the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint), living in the forest is appropriate. However, for one who does not possess these qualities, living in the forest is inappropriate. The forest-dwelling of such a monk (lacking virtue) is like the forest-dwelling of black monkeys, other wild beasts, leopards, deer, and so on. Why? Because he enters [the forest] while remaining in evil desires. For such a monk, there is no benefit to be gained from forest-dwelling. He only destroys the reputation of forest-dwelling and of those who are good forest-dwellers. He also causes lack of faith in the Dispensation (Sāsana).

Only for a monk who possesses such qualities within himself is that forest-dwelling appropriate. That monk, relying on forest-dwelling, can develop insight (vipassanā), attain the fruit of Arahatship, and realize Parinibbāna. He beautifies the entire practice of forest-dwelling. He washes the heads (exalts the status) of forest-dwelling monks. He also spreads the entire Dispensation. Therefore, the Teacher, wishing to show the training ground, the path of exertion, and the suitable lodging for such a monk, said: 'He resorts to a secluded lodging,' and so forth.

In that passage, 'secluded' (vivittaṃ) means a lodging that is empty, free from human voices, and free from the noise of towns and villages. To show this very meaning, the words 'it is not crowded with people' and so forth were said. In that context, 'not crowded' (anākiṇṇam) means unmixed and not cramped.

Regarding the meaning of 'unmixed' (asaṅkiṇṇam): if a lodging is surrounded by mountains, thickets, or rivers within a distance of one gāvuta or half a yojana, such that no one can approach it at an improper time, this is called 'not crowded' even if it is nearby. If it is located half a yojana or one yojana away, it is called 'not crowded' simply because of its distance.

It is called 'lodging' (senāsana) because one sleeps (seti) and sits (āsati) there. To show the different types of lodging, the words 'bed, chair' and so forth were said. In that context, 'bed' (mañca) refers to four types of beds: masāraka (a bed with legs slotted into the frame), bundikābaddha (a bed with legs tied or bolted), kuḷīrapādaka (a bed with curved legs like crab legs), and āhaccapādaka (a bed with legs removable/plugged in). The chair (pīṭha) is likewise of four types.

'Bolster' (bhisi) refers to five types of bolsters: wool-stuffed, cloth-stuffed, bark-stuffed, grass-stuffed, and leaf-stuffed. A pillow for the head is called bimbohana. That pillow should be one span and four finger-breadths in width, and its length should be equal to the width of the bed.

'Dwelling' (vihāra) is a lodging made with a surrounding walkway and designated places for night and day use only within. 'Half-roofed house' (aḍḍhayoga) is a house with a roof curved like a garuda's wing. 'Mansion' (pāsāda) is a long building constructed with two peaks. 'Tower' (aṭṭo) is a special type of residence with thick walls made of bricks, having four or five stories, for the purpose of warding off enemy kings and others. 'Pavilion' (māḷo) is a circular hall similar to a dining hall. However, in the Vinaya Commentary...
350:
...it is said that a square mansion with a single peak is a māḷo. 'Shelter' (leṇa) is a lodging made by excavating a mountain or by raising a wall in a place under a cliff that is not habitable. 'Cave' (guhā) refers to an earth-cleft or a cave in a mountain or an excavated earth-cave where a lamp is needed day and night. 'Foot of a tree' (rukkhamūla) refers to the area under a tree, whether enclosed or not. 'Bamboo thicket' (veḷugumba) is a cluster of bamboo. Or, 'wherever monks resort' (yattha vā pana bhikkhū paṭikkamanti) means that, excluding these beds and so forth, any place where monks assemble and which is suitable for their assembly is all called 'lodging' (senāsana).

'Resorts to' (bhajati) means approaches. 'Fully resorts to' (sambhajati) means approaches well without boredom due to delight in that lodging. 'Uses' (sevati) means uses by way of dwelling. 'Closely uses' (nisevati) means uses by relying on it well without boredom. 'Thoroughly uses' (saṃsevati) means uses properly while fulfilling the duties of the lodging.

Now, to show the different types of what was called 'secluded,' the passage beginning with 'forest, foot of a tree' was started. In that passage, 'forest' (arañña) is first defined according to the Vinaya method: 'Excluding the village and its precincts, all the rest is called forest.' According to the Suttanta method, referring to a forest-dwelling monk: 'A lodging is called a forest-dwelling if it is at least five hundred bow-lengths away.' Both the Vinaya and Suttanta methods are called figurative teaching (pariyāya-desanā). Since the Abhidhamma is non-figurative teaching (nippariyāya-desanā), to show the forest by the Abhidhamma method, it is said: 'Going out beyond the village gate-post (indakhīla).' This means going out beyond the village gate-post [constitutes the forest].

Because the foot of a tree (rukkhamūla) and other lodgings are naturally easy to understand, it is said: 'The foot of a tree is just the foot of a tree,' and so forth. Furthermore, among these, 'foot of a tree' refers to any secluded foot of a tree with cool shade. 'Mountain' (pabbata) refers to a rocky mountain. For, in such a mountain, for a monk who has performed his water duties in the rock-pools and sits in the cool shade of a tree, while the various directions appear clearly and he is fanned by the cool breeze, his mind becomes one-pointed. 'Glen' (kandara) is so called because 'ka' means water, and it refers to a mountain region cleft or broken by that water. They also call it a mountain slope (nitumba) or a river glen (nadīkuñja). In such a place, there are white sands like silver plates. Above, the forest thicket is like a jeweled canopy. Waters as clear as a block of gems flow there. Having descended into such a glen, having drunk the water and cooled the body, and having piled up the sand, [he spreads] his rag-robe...
351:
Descending into a valley with white sands like silver plates, where trees overhead form a canopy like a ruby ceiling, and waters as clear as rubies flow, a monk drinks the water, cools his body, spreads his rag-robe on a heap of sand, and sits down to practice the Dhamma of a recluse; the mind of such a monk attains one-pointedness. Giriguhā refers to the space between two mountains, or a large cave-like opening within a single mountain. The characteristics of a cemetery (susāna) have already been described in the Visuddhimagga.

Vanapattha refers to a place beyond the vicinity of a village, where people do not frequent or travel, and where there is no plowing or sowing. For this reason, in the definition (niddesa) of the word vanapattha, it is stated: "Vanapattha is a name for remote lodgings," and so on. Alternatively, since only this vanapattha is explained in detail among terms like rukkhamūla (root of a tree), it should be understood that the definition is given at the very end of all terms, rather than following the order of the table of contents (mātikā). Abbhokāsa refers to the open air, without cover or shelter. When one wishes to stay in the open air, one makes a small hut out of robes and resides there. Palālapuñja refers to a heap of straw. Recluses pull out straw from the middle of a large straw heap to create a space like a mountain cleft or a cave. Alternatively, they place straw on top of bushes and sit underneath to practice the Dhamma of a recluse. Both of these methods are intended by the term palālapuñja.

In the definition of vanapattha, "salomahaṃsānaṃ" refers to lodgings that are so frightening that they cause one's hair to stand on end upon entering. "Pariyantānaṃ" refers to lodgings situated at the outskirts because of their remoteness. "Na manussūpacārānaṃ" refers to forest lodgings situated beyond the areas frequented by people for activities such as plowing and sowing. "Durabhisambhavānaṃ" refers to lodgings where it is difficult for monks who have not yet attained the taste of seclusion (viveka) to reside by overcoming fear.

In the definition of appasadda etc., "appasaddaṃ" means being free from the noise of talking. "Appanigghosaṃ" means being free from the noise of towns and villages. Since both are identical in the sense of being noiseless, it is stated in the definition: "That which is appasadda is the same as that which is appanigghosa." "Vijanavātaṃ" means being free from the scent (or air) of people passing by. There is also a variant reading "vijanavādaṃ," which means being free from the sound of people talking within the lodging. Since a lodging that is appanigghosa is also free from the movement and talk of people, it is stated in the definition: "That which is appanigghosa is the same as that which is vijanavāta." "Manussarāhasseyyakaṃ" refers to a place suitable for the private actions of humans. Since such a lodging is free from the movement of people, it is stated: "That which is vijanavāta is the same as that which is manussarāhasseyyaka." "Paṭisallānasāruppaṃ" means being suitable for seclusion. Since such a lodging is always suitable for human privacy, it is stated: "That which is manussarāhasseyyaka is the same as that which is paṭisallānasāruppa."

In the definitions beginning with araññagata, the terms "arañña" (forest) and "rukkhamūla" (root of a tree) have already been explained. All remaining lodgings such as pabbata (mountain) and kandara (glen) are included under the term "suññāgāra" (empty dwelling). "Pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā" means sitting with the legs folded in a circle. "Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya" means keeping the upper body erect. For a monk who sits by aligning the eighteen vertebrae end to end, his skin, flesh, and sinews...
352:
That lodging is always suitable for the manner of a place of human privacy. Therefore, in the definition of that term, it is said: "That which is suitable for human privacy is the same as that which is suitable for seclusion (paṭisallānasāruppa)."

In the definition of terms beginning with araññagata, the forest (arañña) has already been explained. Likewise, the root of a tree (rukkhamūla) has also been explained. All other remaining lodgings (senāsana), however, are included under the term "empty dwelling" (suññāgāra).

"Having folded his legs crosswise" (pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā) means sitting by locking the thighs in a circle. "Having set his body erect" (ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya) means keeping the upper body straight and aligning the eighteen vertebrae (backbone) end to end. For one who sits in this manner, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not sag. Consequently, the pains that would arise moment by moment due to the sagging of the skin, flesh, and sinews do not occur. When those pains do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) does not fall away, and it reaches growth and increase.

This statement, "The body is straight, steady, and well-placed," is also said with this same meaning in mind.

"Having established mindfulness in front" (parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā) means setting mindfulness toward the meditation object, or keeping it near the mouth. Therefore, it is said: "This mindfulness is well-established at the tip of the nose or at the sign of the mouth (mukhanimitta)." Here, "the sign of the mouth" should be understood as the center of the upper lip, where the air from the nose strikes. Alternatively, the prefix "pari" has the sense of grasping (pariggaha), "mukha" has the sense of leading out (niyyāna), and "sati" has the sense of establishing (upaṭṭhāna). Therefore, the meaning should also be understood here according to the method mentioned in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. The summary of that method in the Paṭisambhidāmagga is: "Having made mindfulness that has a grasped leading out."

The definition of covetousness (abhijjhā) is quite clear in meaning. However, here is a brief explanation: In the phrase "having abandoned covetousness in the world," the "world" (loka) refers to the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha) because of their nature of breaking up and disintegrating. Therefore, the meaning here is: having abandoned greed (rāga) and suppressed sensual desire (kāmacchanda) regarding the five aggregates of clinging.

"With covetousness gone" (vigatābhijjhēna) means having covetousness gone because it has been abandoned through suppression; it does not mean that it is naturally absent like in eye-consciousness.
353:
“He purifies the mind from covetousness” (abhijjhāya cittaṃ parisodheti) means cleansing the mind thoroughly of covetousness. The meaning is that he acts in such a way that he releases that covetousness, and having released it, does not take it up again. In the descriptive terms (niddesa), however, it should be understood as: he cleanses it while practicing (āsevanto), he cleanses it especially while developing (bhāvento), and he cleanses it thoroughly while frequently repeating (bahulīkaronto). The same method applies to terms like “he liberates” (moceti) and so on.

542-543. The meaning of the terms beginning with “having abandoned the taint of ill-will” (byāpādadadosaṃ pahāya) should also be understood in this same way. Because of this anger, the mind abandons its natural state, like rotten barley-gruel and such; because it thus abandons its natural state, it is called ill-will (byāpāda). It perishes by itself through reaching a state of transformation, or it causes others to perish or destroys them; because it is such, it is called malice (padosa). Both of these are synonyms for anger (kodha). Therefore, it was said: “Whatever is ill-will, that is malice; whatever is malice, that is ill-will.” Since this anger is pointed out by way of including all beings and formations, it was not said “one who has compassion for the welfare of all living beings,” but only “one with a mind free from ill-will” (abyāpannacitto).

Sloth (thina) is the sickness of the mind, and torpor (middha) is the sickness of the mental factors. The combination of sloth and torpor is called thinamiddha. “They are calmed” (santā honti) means that both these states are calmed through cessation. With reference to these two states, a distinction in grammatical number (vacanabheda) is made here.

“Percipient of light” (ālokasaññī) means being endowed with a pure perception, free from hindrances, capable of recognizing the light seen either by night or by day.

“Mindful and clearly comprehending” (sato sampajāno) means being endowed with both mindfulness and wisdom. Both of these are mentioned because they are helpful to the perception of light.

In the descriptive terms for the absence of sloth and torpor and for the perception of light, terms such as “relinquished” (cattattā) and so on are merely mutual synonyms. Among those terms, “relinquished” (cattattā) is due to the cause of having been given up. In the remaining terms, the method is the same. This term “relinquished” (cattattā) is spoken by way of abandoning its own nature. This term “vomited” (vantattā) is spoken by way of showing the state of not taking it up again. This term “freed” (muttattā) is spoken by way of liberation from the mental continuum. This term “abandoned” (pahīnattā) is spoken by way of the non-existence of even the freed sloth and torpor in any place. This term “renounced” (paṭinissaṭṭhattā) is spoken by way of showing the giving up of sloth and torpor that was previously grasped. Or, because of being liberated from re-grasping by the power of meditation...
354:
...it means the state of being released after overcoming. “Because of being abandoned and renounced” (pahīnapaṭinissaṭṭhattā) means that the abandonment occurs by way of suppression (vikkhambhana), and it is renounced so that it does not arise again in the mental continuum. “It becomes luminous” (ālokā honti) means it becomes radiant. It is “open” (vivaṭā) in the sense of being unobstructed. It is “thoroughly pure” (parisuddhā) in the sense of being without defilements. It is “bright” (pariyodātā) in the sense of being brilliant.

In this term “restlessness and remorse” (uddhaccakukkucca), the state of agitation is restlessness (uddhacca). The transgression regarding an object due to indecision is remorse (kukkucca). Here too, in the phrase “they are calmed” (santā honti), the distinction in grammatical number should be understood according to the previous method.

“One who has crossed over doubt” (tiṇṇavicikiccho) is one who stands having crossed over and transcended doubt. In its description, “crossed” (tiṇṇo) is spoken by way of showing the state of not being submerged in doubt. “Ascended” (uttiṇṇo) is spoken by way of showing the transcendence of it. “Completely crossed” (nittiṇṇo) is spoken by way of showing the state of having crossed over the danger by overcoming it through the power of meditation. “Gone to the further shore” (pāraṅgato) means having gone to the further shore of doubt, which is the state of being without doubt. “Reached the further shore” (pāramanuppatto) means having reached that same further shore through the practice of meditation. Thus, it shows the fruitfulness of his practice.

“Free from ‘how-so’” (akathṃkathī) means one who is devoid of the questioning that occurs as “How is this? How is that?”. “In wholesome states” (kusalesu dhammesu) means in blameless states. “Does not hesitate” (na kaṅkhati) means he does not give rise to the doubt, “Are these indeed wholesome?”. “Does not doubt” (na vicikicchati) means he does not find it difficult or exhausting to determine those states according to their nature. “Becomes free from ‘how-so’” (akathṃkathī hoti) means he is devoid of the questioning, “How indeed are these wholesome?”. “Nikkathaṃkathī” and “vigatakathaṃkatho” are synonyms for that same “akathṃkathī”. As for the word-meaning, one who has emerged from questioning is “nikkathaṃkatha”. One whose questioning has gone away is “vigatakathaṃkatha”.

“Defilements” (upakkilese) means those things that are defilements. For they approach the mind and defile it; therefore, they are called defilements (upakkilesā).

“Weakening wisdom” (paññāya dubbalīkaraṇe) means that when these hindrances arise, they do not allow unarisen mundane and supramundane wisdom to arise; and even if they have arisen, they cut off and cause the eight attainments or the five direct knowledges to fall away. Therefore, they are called “those that weaken wisdom.” The statement “and unarisen wisdom does not arise” is also said with this meaning in mind.
355:
The statement "arisen wisdom ceases" is also spoken with reference to the sense of making this wisdom weak. All the remaining meanings in this description are clear, as they have already been explained in various places below.

In the descriptions beginning with "secluded from sensual pleasures," whatever should be said has already been stated below in the Cittuppāda-kaṇḍa, in the description of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), and in various places within this Vibhaṅga itself. Specifically, in the descriptions of the second, third, and fourth jhanas, they are not described as they were below—where it was said, "there is a three-factored jhana, there is a two-factored jhana"—but rather, because of the statement "internal composure" (ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ) and so on, those factors are taken together with composure (sampasāda) and others by way of figurative description (pariyāya). Thus, each jhana is described in detail in such a way as: "jhana means composure, joy, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind." This is the distinction here.

In the description of the phrase "which the Noble Ones declare," although all the words such as "declare" (ācikkhanti) and "teach" (desenti) are synonyms of one another, they still have specific nuances: they "declare" (ācikkhanti) by way of the brief instruction (uddesa) such as "one who dwells in equanimity, mindful, and happy"; they "teach" (desenti) by way of the detailed exposition (niddesa); they "describe" (paññāpenti) by way of the supplementary exposition (paṭiniddesa); they "establish" (paṭṭhapenti) by setting down the meaning in various ways; they "reveal" (vivaranti) by showing the reason for each meaning; they "analyze" (vibhajanti) by showing the classification of syllables and words; they "make clear" (uttāniṃ karonti) by bringing out the hidden and profound nature to establish knowledge in the listeners; and they "manifest" (pakāsenti) by dispelling the darkness of ignorance in the listeners through all these modes. This is how the meaning should be understood.

In the description of "transcending" (samatikkama) as well, the meaning should be understood as follows: "passing" (atikkamanto) because of emerging from those respective states in those respective jhanas; "transcending" (vītikkamanto) especially for the attainment of higher stages; and "well-transcended" (samatikkamanto) by way of non-decline from that higher stage.

## Commentary on the Suttanta Analysis

## 2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma Analysis

In the Abhidhamma Analysis, the text is laid down exactly according to the method that appeared below in the Cittuppāda-kaṇḍa. Therefore, in that Abhidhamma Analysis, the meaning of all the jhanas described by way of wholesome (kusala), resultant (vipāka), and functional (kiriya) should be understood according to the method already stated in that Cittuppāda-kaṇḍa. All the various methods, such as the Pure Ninefold (suddhikana-vaka) and so on, are also exactly the same as the method stated in that Cittuppāda-kaṇḍa.
356:
In that Abhidhamma Analysis, the meaning of the jhanas should be understood exactly as stated in that method. All the various classifications, such as the Pure Ninefold (suddhikana-vaka) and so on, are also exactly the same as what was stated there.

## Commentary on the Abhidhamma Analysis

## 3. Commentary on the Questioning Section

In the Questioning Section (Pañhāpucchaka), the wholesome nature and so on of the jhanas should be understood according to the sequence of the Pali text. Furthermore, in the triads of objects (ārammaṇa-ttika), it should be understood that the three lower jhanas cannot be described as having limited objects (parittārammaṇa) and so on, because they have the sign (nimitta) of the kasina as their object. Among these, the supramundane (lokuttara) jhanas, whether at the time of the Path or the Fruit, have the immeasurable (appamāṇa) as their object.

In the passage "the fourth jhana may have a limited object," there are thirteen types of wholesome fourth jhanas. They are: the fourth jhana as a basis for all powers (sabbatthapādaka-catuttha), the fourth jhana of supernormal powers (iddhividha-catuttha), the fourth jhana of the divine ear (dibbasota-ñāṇa-catuttha), the fourth jhana of knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa-catuttha), the fourth jhana of knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa-catuttha), the fourth jhana of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa-catuttha), the fourth jhana of knowledge of passing away and rebirth according to kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa-catuttha), the fourth jhana of knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa-catuttha), the four fourth jhanas such as the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana), and the supramundane fourth jhana.

Among those thirteen fourth jhanas, the fourth jhana as a basis for all powers has an object that cannot be described as limited and so on.

The fourth jhana of supernormal powers has a limited object at the time of performing a miracle with an invisible body by directing the body according to the mind. It has an exalted object (mahaggatārammaṇa) for one who goes to the Brahma world after performing a miracle with a visible body by directing the mind according to the body, because the object is the mind of attainment (samāpatti-citta).

The fourth jhana of the divine ear has a limited object because its object is sound.

The fourth jhana of knowledge of others' minds has a limited object at the time of knowing a mind of the sensual sphere (kāmāvacara). It has an exalted object at the time of knowing a mind of the fine-material or immaterial sphere. It has an immeasurable object at the time of knowing a supramundane mind.

A worldling (puthujjana) who has attained the knowledge of others' minds knows only the minds of worldlings, not those of the Noble Ones (ariya). A Stream-enterer (sotāpanna) knows the minds of Stream-enterers and worldlings. A Once-returner (sakadāgါmī) knows the minds of Once-returners and the two below (worldlings and Stream-enterers). A Non-returner (anāgāmī) knows the minds of Non-returners and the three below. An Arahant (khīṇāsava) knows the minds of all.
357:
The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa) has a limited object (parittārammaṇa) when recollecting the aggregates of the sensual sphere (kāmāvacara). It has an exalted object (mahaggatārammaṇa) when recollecting the aggregates of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara). It has an immeasurable object (appamāṇārammaṇa) when recollecting: 'In the past, the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants developed the path and realized the fruit.' It has an object that is not to be designated (navattabba) when recollecting names and clans.

The fourth jhāna of the divine eye knowledge (dibbacakkhuñāṇa) has a limited object because its object is visible form.

The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of passing away and rebirth according to kamma (yathākammūpagañāṇa) has a limited object when recollecting kamma of the sensual sphere. It has an exalted object when recollecting kamma of the fine-material and immaterial spheres.

The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa) has a limited object when knowing the arising in the sensual element in the future. It has an exalted object when knowing the arising in the fine-material and immaterial existences. It has an immeasurable object when knowing: 'In the future, the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants will develop the path and realize the fruit.' It has an object that is not to be designated when recollecting names and clans, such as: 'In the future, there will be a king named Saṅkha.'

The fourth jhānas of the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana) and the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) have objects that are not to be designated. The fourth jhānas of the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) have exalted objects.

The supramundane (lokuttara) fourth jhāna has an immeasurable object.

This same arrangement of objects applies to those twelve functional (kiriya) jhānas as well. Regarding the statement 'The three jhānas do not have the path as object,' it means that either the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa) or the knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariyañāṇa), etc., can take the path as an object. Since the three lower jhānas do not occur in that way (taking the path as an object), they do not have the path as an object. However, they may be 'having the path as root' (maggahetuka) by the power of the conascent root. When developing the path by making energy (vīriya) or investigation (vīmaṃsā) predominant, they have the path as predominant (maggādhipati). At the time when desire (chanda) and consciousness (citta) are predominant, and at the time of the fruit, they are not to be designated (as having the path as object or predominant).

In this term 'fourth jhāna,' among the thirteen wholesome (kusala) fourth jhānas, the fourth jhānas of the 'basis for all' (sabbatthapādaka), supernormal powers (iddhividha), divine ear (dibbasota), divine eye (dibbacakkhu), and knowledge of rebirth according to kamma (yathākammūpagañāṇa), as well as the four immaterial fourth jhānas, are not to be designated as 'having the path as object' and so forth. However, the fourth jhānas of the knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariyañāṇa), knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa), and knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa) do have the path as an object. They are not to be designated as 'having the path as root' or 'having the path as predominant.' The supramundane fourth jhāna does not have the path as an object; at the time of the path consciousness...
358:
...however, by the power of the conascent root, it is 'having the path as root' (maggahetuka). Due to the development of the path led by energy (vīriya) or investigation (vīmaṃsā), it is 'having the path as predominant' (maggādhipati). In the development of the path led by desire (chanda) or consciousness (citta), and at the time of the fruit, it is not to be so designated. This same method applies to the twelve functional jhānas.

The statement that the three jhānas are not to be designated (as having a past object, etc.) should be understood as such because they do not occur by taking even a single state among the past and so forth as an object.

Regarding the 'fourth jhāna,' among the thirteen wholesome fourth jhānas, the fourth jhāna which is the basis for all supernormal knowledges (sabbatthapādaka) has only an object that is not to be designated. The fourth jhāna of supernormal powers (iddhividha) is 'having a past object' (atītārammaṇa) when, in connection with the body, one inclines the mind and takes the attainment-consciousness as an object. It is 'having a future object' (anāgatārammaṇa) when making a resolution: 'In the future, may these flowers not wither, may these lamps not go out, may a mass of fire arise, may a mountain arise.' It is 'having a present object' (paccuppannārammaṇa) when, in connection with the mind, one inclines the body and takes the body as an object. The fourth jhāna of the divine ear knowledge (dibbasotañāṇa) is 'having a present object' because its object is sound. The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariyañāṇa) is 'having a past object' when knowing a mind that arose and ceased within the past seven days. It is 'having a future object' when knowing a mind that will arise within the future seven days. As stated in the Sutta: 'The mental formations of this venerable one are thus established; immediately after this mind, he will think such and such a thought.' Even if he points out many, it happens exactly so and not otherwise—thus the occurrence of the knowledge of penetration of minds is explained. When it occurs taking the present as an object by way of 'duration-present' (addhānapaccuppanna) or 'continuity-present' (santatipaccuppanna), it is 'having a present object.' The detailed explanation here should be understood according to the method already stated in the commentary on the Aṭṭhakathā-kaṇḍa below.

The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa) is 'having a past object' when recollecting past aggregates. It has an object that is not to be designated when recollecting names and clans. The fourth jhāna of the divine eye knowledge (dibbacakkhuñāṇa) is 'having a present object' because its object is visible form. The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of rebirth according to kamma (yathākammūpagañāṇa) is 'having a past object' because it takes only past kamma as its object. The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa) is 'having a future object' when recollecting future aggregates. It has an object that is not to be designated when recollecting names and clans. The fourth jhānas of the base of infinite space and the base of nothingness have only objects that are not to be designated. The fourth jhānas of the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are only 'having a past object.' The supramundane fourth jhāna has only an object that is not to be designated. This same method applies to the twelve functional fourth jhānas.
359:
The three jhānas have external objects (bahiddhārammaṇa); this means they are called bahiddhārammaṇa because they occur by taking as an object a kasiṇa sign that is external to one's own continuity (attasantāna).

Here also, among the thirteen types of fourth jhāna that are wholesome (kusala), the fourth jhāna which is the basis for all direct knowledges (sabbattha-pādaka-catuttha) is exclusively bahiddhārammaṇa.

The fourth jhāna of the supernormal powers (iddhividha) is internal-object (ajjhattārammaṇa) when it occurs by taking one's own body or mind as an object, such as when directing the mind towards the body or directing the body towards the mind. When it occurs in such ways as "showing an elephant externally," it is bahiddhārammaṇa.

The fourth jhāna of the divine ear knowledge (dibbasota-ñāṇa) is ajjhattārammaṇa when taking sounds within one's own belly as an object. When taking the sounds of others as an object, it is bahiddhārammaṇa. By way of both, it is internal-external-object (ajjhatta-bahiddhārammaṇa).

The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa) is exclusively bahiddhārammaṇa.

The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa) is ajjhattārammaṇa when recollecting one's own past aggregates (khandhas). When recollecting the aggregates, names, and clans of others, it is bahiddhārammaṇa.

The fourth jhāna of the divine eye knowledge (dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa) is ajjhattārammaṇa when taking one's own visible form as an object. When taking the visible form of others as an object, it is bahiddhārammaṇa. By way of both, it is ajjhatta-bahiddhārammaṇa.

The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of passing away and rebirth according to kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa) is ajjhattārammaṇa when knowing one's own kamma. When knowing the kamma of others, it is bahiddhārammaṇa. By way of both, it is ajjhatta-bahiddhārammaṇa.

The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) is ajjhattārammaṇa when knowing one's own future rebirth. When recollecting the aggregates, names, and clans of others, it is bahiddhārammaṇa. By way of both, it is ajjhatta-bahiddhārammaṇa.

The fourth jhāna of the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana) is bahiddhārammaṇa. The fourth jhāna of the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) has an object that cannot be described (navattabbārammaṇa). The fourth jhānas of the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) are ajjhattārammaṇa.

The supramundane (lokuttara) fourth jhāna is exclusively bahiddhārammaṇa. This same method applies to the twelve jhānas that are functional (kiriya).
360:
In this Jhānavibhaṅga, however, the Fully Enlightened One taught only the jhānas that are mixed mundane and supramundane in the Suttantabhājanīya (Sutta classification); and similarly in the Abhidhammabhājanīya (Abhidhamma classification) and the Pañhāpucchaka (Questionnaire). Indeed, these three methods have a single definition because they are mixed with the states of the three planes (tebhūmaka). Thus, this Jhānavibhaṅga has been shown by analyzing it through the extraction of the three modes.

## The Explanation of the Jhānavibhaṅga
## in the Vibhaṅga Commentary named Sammohavinodanī is finished.
361:
## 13. Appamaññāvibhaṅga
## 1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

Now, in this Appamaññāvibhaṅga which follows that [Jhānavibhaṅga], the word 'four' is a numerical limit. They are called 'appamaññā' (illimitables) because they are limitless in terms of pervasion. For these [states] either pervade limitless beings by way of the object, or they pervade even a single being by way of pervasion without remainder; thus they are called 'appamaññā' by way of the limitlessness of pervasion.

'A bhikkhu in this Dispensation' refers to a bhikkhu in this Sāsana. 'With [a mind] accompanied by loving-kindness' means endowed with mettā. 'With a mind' means with consciousness. 'One direction' is said by way of pervading beings included in one direction, starting with the being first grasped. 'Having pervaded' means having touched, having made it an object. 'Dwells' means he maintains the dwelling in the postures (iriyāpathavihāra) based on the divine abodes (brahmavihāra). 'Likewise the second' means just as he dwells having pervaded any one direction among the east and so on, likewise he dwells pervading the second, third, and fourth directions immediately following that.

'Thus upwards' means the upward direction is intended by that same method. 'Downwards, across' means the same applies to the downward direction and the intermediate (across) directions. Here, 'downwards' means below, and 'across' means the intermediate directions. In this way, in all directions, he sends the mind accompanied by loving-kindness forward and back, like a horse in a racecourse. By this much, the pervasion of mettā by way of limitation (odhiso) is shown by grasping each direction individually.

However, the passage beginning with 'sabbadhī' (everywhere) is stated to show pervasion without limitation (anodhiso). Therein, 'sabbadhī' means in all places. 'Sabbattatāya' (to all as to oneself) means without making the distinction 'this is another being' among all beings classified as low, medium, high, friend, enemy, neutral, etc., but by way of equality with oneself. Or, 'sabbattatāya' means with the entire state of mind, not allowing even a little to be distracted externally. 'Sabbāvantaṃ' means containing all beings, or joined with all beings. 'Lokaṃ' means the world of beings (sattaloka).

Because of showing the synonyms beginning with 'vipulena' (abundant), the phrase 'accompanied by loving-kindness' is stated again here. Or, because the word 'likewise' (tathā) or 'thus' (iti) is not mentioned here as it was in the limited pervasion, the phrase 'with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness' is stated again. Or, it is stated by way of conclusion. In the word 'vipulena', abundance should be understood by way of pervasion. By way of the plane, that mind is sublime (mahaggata). By way of proficiency, it is limitless. By way of the object of beings, it is also limitless. It is called 'without enmity' (avera) because of the abandonment of the opposing enemy, ill-will (byāpāda). It is called 'without suffering' (abyāpajja/anīgha) because of the abandonment of mental pain (domanassa). This is the meaning of the matrix (mātikā) of mettā and so on, placed first in the Suttantabhājanīya.

643. Now there is the Padabhājanīya (Word-by-word Analysis) taught by the method beginning with 'How does he dwell?'. In that Padabhājanīya, this mettā meditation is suitable for one of hateful temperament. Therefore, to show first the person who is the basis of that mettā, in whom this mettā reaches attainment (appanā), the words beginning with 'Just as [one might see] a single person' are stated.

In that passage, the phrase 'seyyathāpi nāma' is a particle in the sense of a simile. The meaning is: just as one develops mettā upon seeing a single person. 'Piyaṃ' means dear; 'manāpaṃ' means one who increases the mind's joy. [One feels mettā] towards that dear and beloved person either because of having lived together in the past or because of being benefited in the present life...
362:
Being without limit, and also being without limit by way of the object of beings, is called 'immeasurable' (appamāṇa). Being 'free from enmity' (avera) is due to the abandoning of ill-will (byāpāda), which is its opposite. Being 'free from affliction' (abyāpajjha) is due to the abandoning of mental distress (domanassa); it means being without mental suffering. This is the meaning of the matrix (mātikā) established by the method beginning with 'with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness.'

Now, in the word-by-word commentary (padabhājanīya) taught by the method beginning with 'And how, monks, [does one dwell] with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness?', since this meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is suitable for one of a hateful temperament, in order to first show the person who is the object of loving-kindness—the kind of person in whom this loving-kindness reaches absorption (appanā)—it is said: 'just as [one might see] a single person,' and so on. Therein, 'seyyathāpi nāma' is a particle in the sense of a simile, meaning 'just as [one might see] a single person [and develop loving-kindness].' 'Piya' means a beloved person. 'Manāpa' means one who causes the heart to increase (pleasing). In that regard, one is called 'dear' (piya) either because of having lived together in the past or because of performing a present benefit. One is called 'pleasing' (manāpa) because of being endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla).

Alternatively, the state of being dear (piyatā) should be known through giving (dāna) and impartiality (samānattatā); the state of being pleasing (manāpatā) through kindly speech (piyavacana) and useful conduct (atthacariyā). Here, because of the state of being dear, there is the abandoning of ill-will; because of that abandoning, loving-kindness pervades happily.
