Because of the state of being pleasing, indifference does not remain, and shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa) appear. Thus, loving-kindness protected by shame and fear of wrongdoing does not decline. Therefore, using that person as a simile, it is said: 'dear and pleasing.' 'Mettāyeyya' means one should pervade with loving-kindness; it means one should perform or practice loving-kindness towards that person. 'Just so, all beings' means that just as one would practice loving-kindness towards a dear person, so too, with loving-kindness that has reached absorption and attained mastery (vasībhāva) in that person, one gradually pervades all beings, including those who are neutral and those who are enemies. The terms 'metti, mettāyanā,' etc., have the meanings already stated.

The word 'vidiisaṃ vā' (or an intermediate direction) is stated to clarify the meaning of the word 'tiriyaṃ vā' (or across).

'Pharitvā' (having pervaded) means having touched by way of making [it] an object. 'Adhimuñcitvā' (having resolved) means having released with an exceeding state; it means having released in such a way that what is released is well-released, well-extended, and well-expanded.

In the description of 'sabbadhi' (everywhere) and so on, since all these three words are all-inclusive, in order to show their meaning together, it is said 'sabbena sabbaṃ' (entirely in every way), and so on. Its meaning has already been stated below.
363:
In the description of 'vipula' (expansive) and so on, because the mind accompanied by loving-kindness is expansive by way of pervading infinite beings after reaching absorption, it is certainly 'sublime' (mahaggata) by way of its plane. That which is sublime is 'immeasurable' (appamāṇa) by way of its object, which is the immeasurable concept of beings. That which is immeasurable is 'free from enmity' (avera) by way of the destruction of opposing enemies. That which is free from enmity is 'free from affliction' (abyāpajjha) because of having ill-will (domanassa) removed. Therefore, it is said: 'that which is expansive is sublime,' and so on. Here, 'avero abyāpajjo' is stated with a change of gender. Otherwise, it should be connected with the word 'mana' (mind): 'that immeasurable mind is a mind free from enmity; that mind free from enmity is a mind free from affliction.' Furthermore, here it should be understood that the preceding word is the meaning of the succeeding word, or the succeeding word is the meaning of the preceding word.

'Just as [one might see] a single person who is miserable and ill-fated' is also stated to show the person who is the object of compassion (karuṇā). For towards such a person, strong compassion arises. Therein, 'duggata' (miserable) means one who has reached a state of being endowed with suffering. 'Durupeata' (ill-fated) means one who is endowed with bodily misconduct and so on. Alternatively, a person who stands in a state of darkness (tamabhāva) by way of destination, family, wealth, etc., is called 'miserable' (duggata); a person who stands in a state of being bound for darkness because of being endowed with bodily misconduct and so on is called 'ill-fated' (durupeata). Thus should the meaning be understood.

'Just as [one might see] a single person who is dear and pleasing' is also stated to show the person who is the object of appreciative joy (muditā). Therein, a person who stands in a state of light (jotibhāva) by way of destination, family, wealth, etc., should be known as 'dear' (piya); a person who stands in a state of being bound for light because of being endowed with bodily conduct and so on should be known as 'pleasing' (manāpa).

'A person who is neither pleasing nor unpleasing' is also stated to show the person who is the object of equanimity (upekkhā). Therein, one should be known as 'not pleasing' (neva manāpa) because of not yet having reached the state of a friend, and 'not unpleasing' (na amanāpa) because of not yet having reached the state of an enemy. All other things that should be said here have already been stated in the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness (Cittuppādakaṇḍa) below. The method of developing these meditation subjects has also been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

## The Explanation of the Suttanta Analysis.
364:
## 2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma Exposition

The Abhidhamma exposition has been analyzed by way of wholesome (kusala), resultant (vipāka), and functional (kiriya) states, exactly according to the method of analysis in the Section on the Arising of Consciousness (Cittuppādakaṇḍa) explained below. The meaning of this Abhidhamma exposition should also be understood exactly as stated in that Section on the Arising of Consciousness.

## 3. Commentary on the Questioning Section

In the Questioning section (Pañhāpucchaka), the nature of loving-kindness (mettā) and so forth as wholesome and so on should be understood according to the sequence of the Pali text. However, regarding the Triads of Objects (ārammaṇattika), all the illimitables (appamaññā) have objects that are not to be called [limited, etc.] (i.e., the concept of beings) in the three triads. In the Triad of Internal Objects, they have external objects. In this Analysis of the Illimitables (Appamaññāvibhaṅga), the Sammasambuddha has taught only the mundane (lokiya) illimitables in the Suttanta exposition, the Abhidhamma exposition, and the Questioning section. This is because these three methods, being mundane, have the same scope. Thus, this Analysis of the Illimitables is also shown analyzed by extracting the three rounds (teparivaṭṭa).

## From the Sammohavinodanī, the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga,
## the Commentary on the Analysis of the Illimitables is finished.
365:
## 14. Analysis of the Training Rules (Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga)
## 1. Commentary on the Abhidhamma Exposition

Now, following the Analysis of the Illimitables, in the Analysis of the Training Rules, there is a numerical limit of five. "Sikkhāpadāni" means factors of training (sikkhitabbapadāni), which are groups of things to be trained in. Furthermore, all the wholesome states mentioned above are called "sikkhā" because they should be trained in. Among the five factors of virtue (sīla), any one factor is called "pada" (footing) in the sense of being the basis for those wholesome trainings; because they are the footing for the trainings, they are called "sikkhāpada" (training rules). "Pāṇātipātā" means causing a being to fall quickly, killing, or slaying. "Veramaṇī" means abstinence (virati). "Adinnādānā" means taking what is not given, the carrying away of what is possessed by another. "Kāmesu" means in the objects of sense-desire (vatthukāma). "Micchācārā" means low conduct by the power of defiled lust (kilesakāma). "Musāvādā" means from speaking what is not true. In the phrase "surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā," "surā" refers to five kinds of liquor: liquor made from flour, liquor made from cakes, liquor made from rice, liquor with yeast added, and liquor mixed with ingredients. "Meraya" refers to five kinds of fermented draughts (āsava): draughts made from flowers, draughts made from fruits, draughts made from sugar, draughts made from honey, and draughts mixed with ingredients. Both of these are called "majja" (intoxicant) because of their intoxicating nature. The volition (cetanā) with which one drinks that intoxicant is called "pamādaṭṭhāna" (the occasion for negligence) because it is the cause of negligence; therefore, it is called "surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā." This is the meaning of the summary (mātikā) laid down in this Analysis of the Training Rules.

In the Exposition of Terms (Padabhājanīya), the entire passage beginning with "yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ" follows the method already stated below (in the Cittuppādakaṇḍa) and its meaning is quite clear. Since abstinence (virati) alone is not the only training rule, but volition (cetanā) is also a training rule, the second method is shown to demonstrate that training rule of volition. And since not only these two states are training rules, but the more than fifty states associated with volition are also training rules as they are groups of things to be trained in, the third method is also shown.

Therein, training rules are of two kinds: the figurative training rule (pariyāyasikkhāpada) and the non-figurative training rule (nippariyāyasikkhāpada). Among those two, abstinence is the non-figurative training rule. For it appears in the Pali as "abstinence from taking life," not volition. And one who abstains does so from this or that [act of] taking life only through that abstinence, not through volition. Nevertheless, [the Buddha] showed it by adducing volition. Likewise, he showed the remaining states associated with volition. For at the time of transgression, the volition of enmity is called "immorality" (dussīlya). Therefore, that volition is also spoken of by way of "good conduct" (susīlya) at the time of abstinence. States such as contact (phassa) are included because they are associated with that abstinence and volition.
366:
Now, for the purpose of sharpening knowledge regarding these training rules, the determination of these [actions] such as killing living beings should be understood by way of nature (dhamma), category (koṭṭhāsa), object (ārammaṇa), feeling (vedanā), root (mūla), action (kamma), blameworthiness (sāvajja), and effort (payoga).

Among those [nature, etc.], 'by way of nature (dhamma)' means that these five, such as killing living beings, are only the dhamma of volition (cetanā). 'By way of category (koṭṭhāsa)' means that all five are indeed courses of action (kammapatha).

'By way of object (ārammaṇa)' means that killing living beings has the life faculty as its object. Taking what is not given has either a being or formations (saṅkhāra) as its object. Sexual misconduct has a woman or a man as its object. False speech has either a being or formations as its object. Drinking intoxicants has formations as its object.

'By way of feeling (vedanā)' means that killing living beings has painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā). Taking what is not given has all three feelings. Indeed, for one who takes what is not given while being joyful and delighted, there is pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā); at a time of fear, there is painful feeling; for one who takes with a neutral (upekkhā) mind, there is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Sexual misconduct has either pleasant feeling or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. False speech, like taking what is not given, has all three feelings. Drinking intoxicants has pleasant or neutral (upekkhā) feeling.

'By way of root (mūla)' means that killing living beings has the roots of hatred and delusion (dosa-moha). Taking what is not given sometimes has the roots of greed and delusion (lobha-moha), and sometimes the roots of hatred and delusion. Sexual misconduct has the roots of greed and delusion. False speech sometimes has the roots of greed and delusion, and sometimes the roots of hatred and delusion. Drinking intoxicants has the roots of greed and delusion.

'By way of action (kamma)' means that among these [actions] such as killing living beings, false speech is verbal action (vacīkamma). The rest are bodily action (kāyakamma) only.

'By way of blameworthiness (sāvajja)' means that killing living beings is sometimes of little blame and sometimes of great blame. Likewise for taking what is not given, etc. The distinction between little and great blame has already been shown below [in the Dvārakathā].

This is another method: the killing of a bug, an ant, a termite, or a moth is of little blame; the killing of a creature larger than those is of greater blame. Even that [killing of a larger creature] is of little blame [compared to others]; the killing of a female bird larger than that is of greater blame. Greater than that is the killing of a monitor lizard, then a rabbit, then a deer, then a gayal, then a horse, then an elephant. Greater than killing an elephant is the killing of an immoral human. Greater than that is the killing of a human with naturally virtuous (gorūpasīlaka) conduct [who is as free from evil as cattle], then one who has gone for refuge, then one who possesses the five precepts, then a novice (sāmaṇera), then a worldling monk, then an Arahant—it is of extremely great blame.

Taking what is not given is of little blame in taking the property of an immoral person. Greater than that is taking the property of one with naturally virtuous conduct. From there, through those who have gone for refuge, those with the five precepts, and so on, taking the property of an Arahant is of extremely great blame, even more than taking from a non-returner (anāgāmi).

Sexual misconduct is of little blame in transgressing with an immoral woman. Greater than that is transgressing with a woman of naturally virtuous conduct. From there, through women who have gone for refuge, and so on, transgressing with a bhikkhunī who is not an Arahant is certainly of extremely great blame.
367:
Greater than killing a worldling monk is killing a stream-enterer (sotāpanna), then a once-returner (sakadāgāmi), then a non-returner (anāgāmi), then an Arahant—it is of extremely great blame.

Taking what is not given from an immoral person is of little blame; greater than that is taking from a person of naturally good (gorūpasīlaka) virtue. Greater than that is taking from one who has gone for refuge, then one with the five precepts, then a novice, then a worldling monk, then a stream-enterer, then a once-returner, then a non-returner. Greater than that, taking from an Arahant is of extremely great blame.

Sexual misconduct with an immoral woman is of little blame; greater than that is misconduct with a woman of naturally good virtue. Greater than that is misconduct with a woman who has gone for refuge, one with the five precepts, a female novice, a worldling bhikkhunī, a stream-enterer, a once-returner, then a non-returner bhikkhunī. But misconduct with a bhikkhunī who is not an Arahant is certainly of extremely great blame.

False speech for the sake of a mere kākaṇika (a small coin) is of little blame. Greater than that is false speech for the sake of an aḍḍhamāsaka, a māsaka, five māsakas, an aḍḍhakahāpaṇa, a kahāpaṇa, and then for priceless goods. But for one who causes a schism in the Sangha by speaking falsely, it is certainly of extremely great blame.

Drinking intoxicants to the extent of a pasata (a small measure) is of little blame. Drinking to the extent of an añjali (a handful) is of great blame. But for one who drinks so much that it causes the body to sway and tremble, and commits the act of destroying a village or a market town, it is certainly of extremely great blame.

In truth, regarding killing living beings, killing an Arahant is of great blame. Regarding taking what is not given, taking the property of an Arahant; regarding sexual misconduct, violating a bhikkhunī who is not an Arahant; regarding false speech, causing a schism in the Sangha through lying; regarding drinking intoxicants, drinking so much that the body sways and destroying a village or market town—these are of great blame. However, among all these, causing a schism in the Sangha through false speech is the greatest blame. That schism of the Sangha is a great evil capable of causing one to be cooked in hell for an entire aeon (kappa).
368:
Regarding the term ‘payoga’ (effort), killing (pāṇātipāta) is both personal (sāhatthika) and commanded (āṇattika). Stealing (adinnādāna) is the same. Sexual misconduct (kāmesumicchācāra), lying (musāvāda), and taking intoxicants (surāpāna) are only personal (sāhatthika). In this way, having understood the decision regarding unwholesome acts such as killing by way of dhamma etc. in this Vibhaṅga of Training Rules, one should also understand the decision regarding the training rules such as ‘abstaining from killing’ (pāṇātipātā veramaṇီ) by way of dhamma, category (koṭṭhāsa), object (ārammaṇa), feeling (vedanā), root (mūla), action (kamma), breach (khaṇḍa), undertaking (samādāna), and effort (payoga).

Among those, ‘dhamma’ refers to the five volitional states (cetanā-dhamma) in sequence by way of conventional virtue (pariyāya-sīla). ‘Koṭṭhāsa’ means all five training rules are indeed courses of action (kammapatha).

‘Ārammaṇa’ means the training rule of abstaining from killing takes the life faculty of another as its object and abstains from one's own volition of enmity. The same method applies to the other training rules. Indeed, all these abstinences (virati) take the object that should not be transgressed (such as life, etc.) as their object and abstain through volitions of enmity.

‘Vedanā’ means all training rules are associated with either pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) or neutral feeling (upekkhā-vedanā).

‘Mūla’ means for one who abstains with a mind associated with wisdom, the roots are non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa), and non-delusion (amoha); for one who abstains with a mind dissociated from wisdom, the roots are non-greed and non-hatred.

‘Kamma’ means among these training rules, only abstinence from lying is verbal action (vacī-kamma); the remaining abstinences are bodily action (kāya-kamma).

‘Khaṇḍa’ means for laypeople, whichever training rule they transgress, only that transgressed training rule is breached and destroyed; the remaining ones are not destroyed. Why? Because laypeople do not have permanent virtue (nibadda-sīla); they protect whichever training rule they are able to protect. For novices (sāmaṇera), however, if they transgress one training rule, all training rules are destroyed. Not only these five, but the remaining virtues such as abstaining from eating at the wrong time (vikālabhojana) are also destroyed. The transgression of those novices has the disciplinary penance (daṇḍakamma) as its basis. After deciding ‘I will not do such a thing again’ and undergoing the penance, the virtue becomes complete.

‘Samādāna’ means for one who undertakes by oneself saying ‘I undertake the five precepts,’ or for one who undertakes them individually, they are well-undertaken. For one who sits in the presence of another and says ‘I undertake the five precepts,’ or for one who undertakes them individually, they are also indeed undertaken.

By way of ‘payoga’, all training rules should be understood as having personal effort (sāhatthika-payoga).

Now, since these five training rules have been mentioned as a group of trainings, in order to show those trainings, this section on training (sikkhāvāra) is begun with ‘Which states are trainings?’ (katame dhammā sikkhā). In that section on training, all wholesome states belonging to the four planes...
370:
## 15. Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga
## 1. Suttantabhājanīya
## 1. Saṅgahavāravaṇṇanā

Now, in the Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga, which immediately follows the Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga, the word "catasso" (four) is a delimitation of number. "Paṭisambhidā" means distinctions (or discriminations). However, since it is stated later that "knowledge in the meaning is attha-paṭisambhidā," and so forth, it should be understood that these are not distinctions of anything else, but distinctions of knowledge alone. Thus, by the phrase "catasso paṭisambhidā," the meaning of four distinctions of knowledge is encompassed.

Attha-paṭisambhidā is the discrimination in the meaning (attha). It means the knowledge that has reached the state of distinction regarding the meaning, being capable of performing the noting, manifesting, and determining of the distinctions of meaning. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Knowledge that has reached the state of distinction regarding the cause (dhamma), being capable of performing the noting, manifesting, and determining of the distinctions of cause, is called dhamma-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge that has reached the state of distinction regarding the expression (nirutti) directed towards the meaning, being capable of performing the noting, manifesting, and determining of the distinctions of the uttered sounds, is called nirutti-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge that has reached the state of distinction regarding the perspicuity (paṭibhāna), being capable of performing the noting, manifesting, and determining of the distinctions of the knowledge that has appeared before one, is called paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā.

Now, wishing to show the discriminations by classifying them according to the established summary (mātikā), the Teacher said: "Knowledge in the meaning is attha-paṭisambhidā," and so forth. Therein, "meaning" (attha), in brief, is the result of a cause. That result is called "attha" because it is to be known, reached, or attained by means of a cause. In terms of distinctions, however, these five things should be understood as "attha": whatever is produced by conditions, Nibbāna, the meaning of what is spoken, the resultant (vipāka), and the functional (kiriya). The knowledge that has reached the state of distinction regarding that meaning in one who is reviewing that meaning is attha-paṭisambhidā.

"Dhamma," in brief, is the cause. It is called "dhamma" because it arranges, produces, and brings about various results. In terms of distinctions, however, these five things should be understood as "dhamma": any cause that produces a result, the Noble Path, the spoken word, the wholesome (kusala), and the unwholesome (akusala). The knowledge that has reached the state of distinction regarding that dhamma in one who is reviewing that dhamma is dhamma-paṭisambhidā.

Therein, "knowledge in the expression of the dhamma" (dhamma-niruttābhilāpe ñāṇaṃ) refers to the knowledge in the utterance of the natural expression (sabhāvanirutti) that exists in both that meaning and that cause. In uttering that natural expression, [taking] that sound of natural expression...
371:
...making it an object and reviewing it, the knowledge that has reached the state of distinction regarding that utterance of natural expression is called nirutti-paṭisambhidā. Thus, this nirutti-paṭisambhidā is said to have sound as its object (saddārammaṇa), not concepts (paññatti) as its object. Why? Because upon hearing a sound, they know: "This sound is a natural expression; this sound is not a natural expression." Indeed, when the word "Phasso" is uttered, one who has attained the discriminations knows: "This sound is a natural expression." But when "Phassā" or "Phassaṃ" is uttered, they know: "This sound is not a natural expression." The same method applies to "Vedanā" and so forth.

Does that person know other sounds such as nouns (nāma), verbs (ākhyāta), prefixes (upasagga), and particles (byañjana) other than the Magadhan expression? It is said that to the extent they hear a sound and know "This is natural expression, this is not," to that same extent they will also know those sounds uttered in other languages. However, rejecting this by saying that such knowledge is not the function of the Paṭisambhidā, this story is told:

It is said that Elder Tissadatta, while at the Great Bodhi Tree, took a golden slip and made an invitation, saying: "In which of the eighteen languages shall I preach?" That invitation was made by the Elder based on his own learned mastery (uggaha), not by standing in the power of Paṭisambhidā. For he, being of great wisdom, had learned those various languages by having others teach them to him; therefore, he made such an invitation based on his learned mastery.

Regarding the statement that beings learn languages, this is said: Parents, in the child's infancy, lay the child on a bed or a stool and perform various tasks while speaking various words. The children note those various languages of the parents, thinking: "This person said this for this reason; this person said this for that reason." As time goes by, they come to know the entire language. If the mother is a Damili woman and the father is an Andhaka man, the child born to them will speak the Damila language if they hear the mother's speech first; if they hear the father's speech first, they will speak the Andhaka language. However, if they hear the speech of neither parent, they will speak the Magadhan language (Māgadhabhāsā).

Even one born in a great forest where there is no village and no one else to speak to, when they naturally produce speech on their own, they will speak only the Magadhan language. In hell, in the animal realm, in the realm of hungry ghosts, in the human world, and in the deva world—in all these places, the Magadhan language is predominant. The other eighteen languages, such as Oṭṭa, Kirāta, Andhaka, Yonaka, and Damila, are subject to change. Only this Magadhan language, which is called the correct and unchanging usage of the Ariyas, is...
372:
(The eighteen languages) change. Only this Magadhi language, known as the language of truth, the language of Brahmās, and the language of the Noble Ones, does not change. Even the Blessed One, when placing the Buddha's words—the Tipiṭaka—into the textual tradition, did so only in the Magadhi language. Why? Because only when placed in Magadhi is it easy to convey the meaning. Indeed, for those who have attained the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), the Buddha's words placed in the textual tradition of Magadhi are such that the meaning appears through hundreds and thousands of methods as soon as they strike the ear; the only delay is the time it takes to reach the ear. However, teachings placed in other languages must be learned with difficulty, striking the vocal organs repeatedly. Even after much learning, a worldling (puthujjana) never attains the analytical insights. Yet, there is no Noble Disciple (ariya-sāvaka) who has not attained the analytical insights.

'Knowledge within knowledges' refers to the analytical insight of ready wit (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā), which is the distinctive knowledge that arises in one who contemplates knowledge by taking all knowledges (of meaning, law, and language) as objects. These four analytical insights should be understood as reaching distinction in two stages and becoming clear through five causes. What are the two stages? They are the stage of the trainee (sekha-bhūmi) and the stage of the adept (asekha-bhūmi). Among these, the analytical insights of the eighty great elders, such as the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the Venerable Mahākassapa, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita, reached distinction in the stage of the adept. The analytical insights of the Venerable Ānanda, Citta the householder, Dhammika the lay follower, Upāli the householder, Khujjuttarā the laywoman, and others, reached distinction in the stage of the trainee. Thus, they reach distinction in these two stages.

Through which five causes do the analytical insights become clear? They are through attainment (adhigama), learning (pariyatti), hearing (savana), inquiry (paripucchā), and former practice (pubbayoga). Among these, 'attainment' refers to the fruit of Arhatship (arahattaphala). The analytical insights of one who has reached that fruit of Arhatship become clear. 'Learning' refers to the Buddha's words. The analytical insights of one who learns those Buddha's words become clear. 'Hearing' refers to listening to the Dhamma. The analytical insights of one who listens to the Dhamma respectfully become clear. 'Inquiry' refers to the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā). The analytical insights of one who explains and teaches the meaning of the Pali texts they have learned become clear. 'Former practice' refers to having systematically practiced meditation in previous lives through the method of 'carrying and bringing back' (haraṇa-paccāharaṇa). The analytical insights of one who has practiced in the past become clear. Among these causes, the analytical insights of Tissa Thera, the son of the householder Punabbasu, became clear due to his attainment of the fruit of Arhatship. That elder, after learning the Buddha's words in the island of Tambapaṇṇi, went to the other shore and learned the Buddha's words in the presence of the Venerable Yonaka Dhammarakkhita...
373:
Among those five causes, the analytical insights of Tissa Thera, the son of the householder Punabbasu, became clear due to his attainment of the fruit of Arhatship. It is said that this Tissa Thera, after learning the Buddha's words in the island of Tambapaṇṇi, went to the other shore and learned the Buddha's words in the presence of the Venerable Yonaka Dhammarakkhita. While returning, at the port where he was to board a boat, a doubt arose regarding a single word. He turned back and traveled a distance of a hundred leagues (yojana) to return to his teacher. On the way, he answered a question for a householder, who, out of devotion, offered him a woolen blanket worth a hundred thousand. Tissa Thera took that blanket and offered it to his teacher. The teacher elder cut it with a small adze and made a border (paribhaṇḍa) for his sitting place. For what purpose did he do this? It was to favor the community of monks who would come later. The thought occurred to that elder: 'Reflecting on the path we have taken, fellow practitioners in the future will consider that they ought to fulfill the practice (paṭipatti).' Tissa Thera, having cleared his doubt in the presence of his teacher, disembarked at the port of Jambukola. At the time of sweeping the courtyard of the shrine, he arrived at Vālikā Monastery and swept it. Seeing the place he had swept, people realized, 'This is the place swept by a monk free from passion (vītarāga),' and they asked him questions to test him. Because the elder had attained the analytical insights, he answered all the questions asked.

Through learning (pariyatti), the analytical insights of Tissadatta Thera and Nāgasena Thera became clear. Through respectful hearing of the Dhamma, the analytical insights of Sudhamma Sāmaṇera became clear. That Sudhamma Sāmaṇera was the nephew of Dhammadinna Thera of Talangara; he attained Arhatship while his hair was being shaved. While sitting and listening at the place where his uncle elder was making Dhamma decisions, he became proficient in the three Pitakas. However, in explaining the meaning of the learned Pali, only the analytical insights of Tissadatta Thera were clear. As for those who have been practitioners (yogāvacara) in previous lives, who fulfilled the 'going and returning' duty (gatapaccāgata-vatta) and practiced meditation up to the stage of conformity (anuloma), and thus arrived at clear analytical insights, they are infinitely numerous.

Among these causes, these three—learning, hearing, and inquiry—are the powerful causes for reaching distinction (in knowledge). Former practice is a powerful condition for the attainment of the fruit of Arhatship. As to whether (former practice) is a powerful cause for distinction in knowledge: it is, but not always so. Whether learning, hearing, and inquiry existed in previous lives or not, there is no such thing as analytical insight without the contemplation of formations (saṅkhāra-sammasana) through former practice, both in the past and in the present. These two—former practice and attainment—together support the analytical insights and make them clear and bright.

## Description of the Summary Section (Saṅgahavāra-vaṇṇanā).
374:
## 2. Commentary on the Section on Truths, etc.
Now, in order to analyze the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) by way of showing the distinctions of the five meanings (attha) and five phenomena (dhamma) included in the Summary Section (Saṅgahavāra), the Section on Classifications (Pabhedavāra) has been undertaken once more starting with the method "Four...". That Section on Classifications is fivefold: the Section on Truths (Saccavāra), the Section on Causes (Hetuvāra), the Section on Phenomena (Dhammavāra), the Section on the Mode of Conditions (Paccayākāravāra), and the Section on the Scriptures (Pariyattivāra).

Among these five, the **Section on Truths** is spoken to show the state of being a result (attha) of the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca), which is produced by causes, and of Nibbāna, which is to be attained through causes; and to show the state of being a cause (dhamma) of the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca), which produces the result, and of the Noble Path (ariya-magga), which leads to Nibbāna.

The **Section on Causes** is spoken to show the state of being a cause (dhamma) of any cause that produces a result, and the state of being a result (attha) of the result of a cause. In this Section on Causes, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā) is pointed out first, in reverse of the regular order of cause and result.

The **Section on Phenomena** is spoken to show the state of being a result (attha) of those result-phenomena that have arisen from various causes, such as material and immaterial distinctions, and to show the state of being a cause (dhamma) of those various material and immaterial causes.

The **Section on the Mode of Conditions** is spoken to show the state of being a result (attha) of result-phenomena such as aging and death (jarā-maraṇa), and to show the state of being a cause (dhamma) of causal phenomena such as birth (jāti), which are said to be the origin of aging and death, etc.

After that, the **Section on the Scriptures** is spoken to show the state of being a cause (dhamma) of the various spoken words known as the scriptures (pariyatti), and to show the state of being a result (attha) of the meaning of what is spoken, which is to be attained through the cause known as the spoken word.

In that Section on the Scriptures, because the meaning of the spoken word is known only after knowing the spoken word itself, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā) is pointed out first, in reverse of the order of the spoken word and its meaning. For the purpose of showing the distinctions of the scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-dhamma), the Section on the Detailed Exposition (Paṭiniddesavāra) is spoken, preceded by the question: "Among those analytical knowledges, what is the analytical knowledge of phenomena?" In that Section on the Detailed Exposition, the Canon (tanti) is taken without remainder by way of the nine factors such as Suttanta, etc. Even in this context, "This is the meaning of this spoken word," the Canon is taken without remainder in connection with the speaker.

## Commentary on the Suttanta Classification

## 2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma Classification
In that Suttanta Classification method, the three analytical knowledges are purely mundane (lokiya). The analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā) is a mixture of mundane and supramundane (lokuttara). Indeed, that analytical knowledge of meaning, by way of the path-knowledge and fruition-knowledge which have Nibbāna as their object...
375:
...is also supramundane. In the Abhidhamma Classification (Abhidhamma-bhājanīya), it is analyzed by way of four sections: wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), resultant (vipāka), and functional (kiriya). In those sections, however many wholesome consciousnesses were analyzed previously in the Section on the Arising of Consciousness (Cittuppāda-kaṇḍa), it should be understood that by way of all those wholesome consciousnesses, four analytical knowledges are analyzed in each individual exposition of consciousness. The same method applies to unwholesome consciousnesses. In the sections on resultants and functionals, because resultants and functionals are included as results (attha), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā) is excluded, and only three analytical knowledges are analyzed in each individual resultant consciousness and functional consciousness. The Pali text, however, shows only a mere indication and is abbreviated. That abbreviated Pali text should be understood exactly according to the detailed method that appeared previously.

But why is it that, just as in the wholesome and unwholesome sections it is said, "The knowledge of the resultant of those (wholesome and unwholesome states) is the analytical knowledge of meaning," here (in the resultant and functional sections) it is not said, "The knowledge of those phenomena of which these are the resultants is the analytical knowledge of phenomena"? It is because it has already been stated previously. If that is so, since it was stated previously that "The knowledge of the resultant of those is the analytical knowledge of meaning," should this analytical knowledge of meaning also not be stated here (in the resultant and functional sections)? It is not that it should not be stated; (it should indeed be stated). Why? Because it has not yet been stated previously by way of the arising of resultant consciousness and functional consciousness. And in the functional section, the statement "of those phenomena of which these are the functionals" is itself inappropriate. Therefore, in these two sections, only three analytical knowledges each are analyzed.

In those (two sections), there is a designation of those phenomena by whatever vocal expression is uttered; thus, by the method starting with "by whatever expression (nirutti) there is contact," a designation occurs for those phenomena as "this is contact, this is feeling." In that context, "knowledge in the expression of the phenomena-language" (dhamma-niruttābhilāpe ñāṇaṃ) means the knowledge in the utterance of that language of phenomena (dhamma-nirutti), which is a nature-designation (sabhāva-paññatti) occurring in those results (attha) and causes (dhamma). Here too, only the knowledge that arises by taking the uttered sound as an object is spoken of. "By which knowledge" means by which analytical knowledge of perspicacity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa). "Knows those knowledges" means it knows the other three analytical knowledges.

Now, just as that knowledge knows those knowledges, in order to show its occurrence in them, it is said: "These knowledges illuminate this meaning." In that context, "illuminators of this meaning" (idamatthajotakāni) means they are the illuminators or clarifiers of this meaning; the meaning is that they illuminate, clarify, and delimit this particular meaning. Thus, the knowledge in the three knowledges that occurs in this manner is called the analytical knowledge of perspicacity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā).
376: Among these four analytical knowledges, this analytical knowledge of perspicacity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā) knows the function of the other analytical knowledges, saying, 'This is the function of this analytical knowledge, that is the function of that analytical knowledge,' yet it cannot perform those functions itself. It is like a learned Dhamma-preacher who cannot perform the function of a less learned Dhamma-preacher. It is said that there were two monks: one was very learned (bahussuta) and the other was less learned (appassuta). They both learned a single method of Dhamma-preaching together. Among them, the less learned monk was endowed with a beautiful voice, while the other had a poor voice. The less learned monk, wherever he went, would preach the Dhamma, moving the entire assembly with the excellence of his voice. Those listening to the Dhamma, with joyful and satisfied minds, would say, 'Judging by the way he preaches the Dhamma, he must be a bearer of the Tipitaka (tipiṭakadhara).' The learned monk, however, said, 'When you listen to the Dhamma, you will know whether this person is a bearer of the Tipitaka or not.' Although the learned monk said this, he did not have the ability to preach the Dhamma in a way that could move the entire assembly like the less learned monk. Just like that example, it should be understood that the analytical knowledge of perspicacity knows the functions of the other analytical knowledges, just as the learned monk knows the function of the less learned monk, but it cannot perform those functions itself. The remaining words are clear in meaning. Having thus classified the analytical knowledges by way of the arising of wholesome consciousness and so on, he now said, 'Again, the four analytical knowledges,' and so forth, to show the field that is the place of their arising. Therein, the statement that 'three analytical knowledges occur in the four types of consciousness associated with knowledge in the sense-sphere wholesome' is said by way of trainees (sekha). For those trainees, when reflecting on the cause (dhamma), the analytical knowledge of principles (dhammapaṭisambhidā) arises in the four wholesome consciousnesses associated with knowledge, taking as object the fivefold Dhamma mentioned below. Similarly, when reflecting on language (nirutti), the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā) arises taking sound as the object. When reflecting on knowledge (ñāṇa), the analytical knowledge of perspicacity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā) arises taking as object the knowledge that pertains to all aspects of meaning, cause, and language. The statement that 'they occur in the four functional consciousnesses' is said by way of adepts (asekha). For those adepts, when reflecting on the Dhamma, the analytical knowledge of principles arises in the four functional consciousnesses associated with knowledge, taking as object the fivefold Dhamma mentioned below. Similarly, when reflecting on language, the analytical knowledge of language arises taking sound as the object. When reflecting on knowledge, the analytical knowledge of perspicacity arises taking as object the knowledge that pertains to all aspects. The statement that 'the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) also arises in these consciousnesses' is said by way of both trainees and adepts. To explain this: for trainees, when reflecting on the result (attha), taking as object the various meanings mentioned below, in the four wholesome consciousnesses associated with knowledge...
377:
This atthapaṭisambhidā (analytical knowledge of meaning) also arises in the path-consciousness and fruition-consciousness at the time of the path and fruition. However, at the time of reviewing the benefit of an asekha (one beyond training), it arises in the four functional consciousnesses associated with knowledge, taking as object the meaning which has five aspects (such as being produced by conditions) as mentioned below. At the time of fruition, it arises in the highest fruit of asceticism (sāmaññaphala), which is the fruition of arahantship. Thus, these analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), when they arise in the continuities of sekhas (trainees) and asekhas, arise in these planes (bhūmi); this method is shown for the purpose of demonstrating the planes of occurrence.

## Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya.

## 3. Commentary on the Pañhāpucchaka.

In the Pañhāpucchaka, the state of the four analytical knowledges as wholesome and so forth should be understood according to the sequence of the Pali text. Regarding the triads of objects (ārammaṇa-ttika), niruttipaṭisambhidā (analytical knowledge of language) has a limited object (parittārammaṇa) because it takes only sound as its object. Atthapaṭisambhidā has a limited object in the continuity of one who reviews the effect produced by causes, known as sense-sphere resultant and functional [consciousness]. It has a sublime object (mahaggatārammaṇa) in the continuity of one who reviews the effects of the fine-material and immaterial spheres of the aforementioned types. It has an immeasurable object (appamāṇārammaṇa) in the continuity of one who reviews the effect of supramundane resultant and the ultimate reality, Nibbāna.

Dhammapaṭisambhidā (analytical knowledge of origin) has a limited object in the continuity of one who reviews wholesome states, unwholesome states, and causal states of the sense sphere. It has a sublime object in the continuity of one who reviews wholesome states and causal states of the fine-material and immaterial spheres. It has an immeasurable object in the continuity of one who reviews supramundane wholesome states and causal states.

Paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā (analytical knowledge of perspicuity) has a limited object in the continuity of one who reviews sense-sphere wholesome, resultant, and functional knowledges. It has a sublime object in the continuity of one who reviews fine-material and immaterial wholesome, resultant, and functional knowledges, as well as in the continuity of one who knows the objects of those knowledges. It has an immeasurable object in the continuity of one who reviews supramundane wholesome and resultant knowledges.

Atthapaṭisambhidā may be "having the path as cause" (maggathetuka) by way of conascent cause. It may be "having the path as predominant" (maggādhipati) at the time of developing the path with energy as the predominant factor. However, when desire (chanda) or consciousness (citta) is the predominant factor, it should not be called "having the path as cause" or "having the path as predominant." Likewise, it should not be so called at the time of fruition. Dhammapaṭisambhidā has the path as object (maggārammaṇa) at the time of reviewing the path. In the continuity of one who reviews the path by giving it importance, it has the path as predominant by way of object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati). Paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā has the path as object at the time of reviewing the path-knowledge. In the continuity of one who reviews the path by giving it importance, it has the path as predominant. At the time of reviewing the remaining knowledges...
378:
They have objects that cannot be said to be (past, future, or present). The Analytical Insight into Language (Nirutti-paṭisambhidā) is called 'having a present object' (paccuppannārammaṇā) because it takes only present sound as its object.

The Analytical Insight into Meaning (Attha-paṭisambhidā) has a past object in the mental continuum of one who reflects on the meaning of past results (vipāka), functional states (kiriya), and effects produced by causes (paccayasamuppanna). It has a future object in the continuum of one who reflects on the future. It has a present object in the continuum of one who reflects on the present. It has an object that cannot be said to be (past, future, or present) in the continuum of one who reflects on the supramundane ultimate reality (Nibbāna). The Analytical Insight into Origin (Dhamma-paṭisambhidā) has a past object in the continuum of one who reflects on past wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), and causal states (paccaya-dhamma). It has a future object in the continuum of one who reflects on the future. It has a present object in the continuum of one who reflects on the present. The Analytical Insight into Perspicacity (Paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā) has a past object in the continuum of one who reflects on past wholesome knowledge, resultant knowledge, and functional knowledge. It has a future object in the continuum of one who reflects on the future. It has a present object in the continuum of one who reflects on the present.

Nirutti-paṭisambhidā has an external object (bahiddhārammaṇā) because its object is sound. Among the remaining three, Attha-paṭisambhidā has an internal object (ajjhattārammaṇā) when reflecting on the meaning of results, functional states, and effects produced by causes within one's own continuum. It has an external object when reflecting on the external (the continuum of others). It has an internal-external object when reflecting on both one's own and others' continua. However, when reflecting on the ultimate reality (Nibbāna), it has only an external object. Dhamma-paṭisambhidā has an internal object at the time of reflecting on wholesome, unwholesome, and causal states within one's own continuum. It has an external object at the time of reflecting on wholesome, unwholesome, and causal states occurring externally. It has an internal-external object at the time of reflecting on wholesome, unwholesome, and causal states occurring both within oneself and externally. Paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā has an internal object at the time of reflecting on wholesome, resultant, and functional knowledge within one's own continuum. It is said that it has an internal-external object at the time of reflecting on wholesome, resultant, and functional knowledge occurring both within oneself and externally (and similarly for the external).

In this [Pañhāpucchaka] method also, the three analytical insights are mundane only; the Analytical Insight into Meaning is both mundane and supramundane. In this Analysis of the Analytical Insights (Paṭisambhidā-vibhaṅga), the Blessed One has taught the three methods with uniform divisions because they are a mixture of the mundane and supramundane. In those three methods also, it is taught that these three analytical insights are mundane, while the Analytical Insight into Meaning is both mundane and supramundane. Thus, this Analysis of the Analytical Insights has also been shown by classifying it according to the three cycles (teparivaṭṭa).

## The Explanation of the Analysis of the Analytical Insights
## in the Vibhaṅga Commentary named Sammohavinodanī is finished.
379:
## 16. Analysis of Knowledge (Ñāṇa-vibhaṅga)

## 1. Commentary on the Matrix of the Singles, etc.

Now, in the Analysis of Knowledge which immediately follows that Analysis of the Analytical Insights, the Exposition (Niddesa) is made according to the sequence of the matrix terms laid down, starting with the method "Basis of knowledge in a single way" (ekavidhena ñāṇavatthu), first establishing the matrix with ten sections ending with the tenfold way.

Among those matrix terms, "ekavidhena" means in one way or as one portion. In the term "ñāṇavatthu", it is called "basis of knowledge" because it is both knowledge and the basis for various kinds of attainments (sampatti). It is also called "basis of knowledge" in the sense of being the location or occasion for knowledge. In this context, however, "basis of knowledge" should be understood only in the former sense. Therefore, at the end of the singlefold section, it is stated: "Wisdom that clarifies the reality of things is thus the basis of knowledge in a single way."

"Five consciousnesses" (pañca viññāṇā) refers to the five such as eye-consciousness. The terms starting with "not a root" (na hetu) should be understood in the same manner as stated below in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Commentary. Briefly, what should be said here will be made clear in the Section of the Exposition (Niddesa-vāra). Just as in these terms of the Matrix of the Singles, what should be said in the terms of the Matrix of the Dyads, etc., will also be made clear in that same Exposition Section. However, in this Section of the Summary (Uddesa-vāra), the extent of the layout of the matrix should be understood as follows:

Among these matrices, first, the Matrix of the Singles (Ekaka-mātikā) is laid down with seventy-eight terms in two brief divisions: by way of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī matrix with terms such as "Not a root, rootless" (na hetu ahetukā), and by way of other texts outside the matrix with terms such as "Impermanent, overcome by decay" (aniccā jarābhibhūtā).

The Matrix of the Dyads (Duka-mātikā) is laid down with thirty-five dyads suitable for the dyad form.

The Matrix of the Triads (Tika-mātikā) is laid down with eighty-eight triads as follows: by way of the four external triads (bāhira-tika) such as "Wisdom consisting in reflection" (cintāmayā paññā); by way of the fourteen matrix triads stated by way of unspecified wisdom such as "Wisdom that is a result" (vipākā paññā); in the triad of initial application (vitakka-tika), thirteen triads stated by way of wisdom specified by the first term, seven by the second term, and twelve by the third term; and in the triad of rapture (pīti-tika), thirteen triads stated by way of wisdom specified by the first term, similarly thirteen by the second term, and twelve by way of wisdom specified by the third term.
380:
The Blessed One set forth the Matrix of Fours (Catukka-mātikā) by way of twenty-one fours, such as "knowledge of ownership of kamma" (kammassakatā-ñāṇa); the Matrix of Fives (Pañcaka-mātikā) by way of two fives; the Matrix of Sixes (Chakka-mātikā) by way of one six; the Matrix of Sevens (Sattaka-mātikā) by way of eleven sevens briefly taught as "seventy-seven bases of knowledge" (sattasattati ñāṇavatthūni); the Matrix of Eights (Aṭṭhaka-mātikā) by way of one eight; and the Matrix of Nines (Navaka-mātikā) by way of one nine.

## 10. Commentary on the Matrix of Tens (Dasaka-mātikā).

The Matrix of Tens is set forth by way of a single ten, beginning with "Ten are the Tathāgata's powers of a Tathāgata." In that Pali text, "ten" (dasa) is a numerical delimitation. "Of the Tathāgata" (tathāgatassa) means of the one who has come (āgata) just as the previous sages such as Vipassī came, and who has gone (gata) just as they have gone. "The Tathāgata's powers" (tathāgata-balāni) are powers belonging only to the Tathāgata, not shared with others. Alternatively, it means powers that have come (āgata) in the same way as the powers of previous Buddhas came through the fulfillment of the accumulation of merit.

Among those powers, the Tathāgata's power is twofold: physical power (kāya-bala) and the power of knowledge (ñāṇa-bala). Among these, physical power should be understood according to the lineage of elephants. Thus, the ancient teachers said:

Kāḷāvaka, Gaṅgeyya, Paṇḍara, Tamba, Piṅgala,
Gandha, Maṅgala, Hema, Uposatha, and Chaddanta are the ten.

These are the ten lineages of elephants. Among these elephant lineages, "Kāḷāvaka" refers to the ordinary lineage of elephants. The physical strength of 10 men is equal to the strength of 1 Kāḷāvaka elephant. The strength of 10 Kāḷāvaka elephants is equal to the strength of 1 Gaṅgeyya elephant. The strength of 10 Gaṅgeyya elephants is equal to the strength of 1 Paṇḍara elephant. The strength of 10 Paṇḍara elephants is equal to the strength of 1 Tamba elephant. The strength of 10 Tamba elephants is equal to the strength of 1 Piṅgala elephant. The strength of 10 Piṅgala elephants is equal to the strength of 1 Gandha elephant. The strength of 10 Gandha elephants is equal to the strength of 1 Maṅgala elephant. The strength of 10 Maṅgala elephants is equal to the strength of 1 Hemavata elephant. The strength of 10 Hemavata elephants is equal to the strength of 1 Uposatha elephant. The strength of 10 Uposatha elephants is equal to the strength of 1 Chaddanta elephant. The strength of 10 Chaddanta elephants is equal to the strength of the Tathāgata. This very power is also called the power known as Nārāyaṇa. This power...
381: In terms of the count of ordinary elephants, it is the strength of a thousand crores of elephants; in terms of the count of men, it is the strength of ten thousand crores of men. This is first of all the physical power (kāya-bala) of the Tathāgata. Knowledge power (ñāṇa-bala), however, refers to the Ten Powers of Knowledge (dasabala-ñāṇa) directly mentioned here in the text of the Ñāṇavibhaṅga; the Ten Powers of Knowledge mentioned in the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, the four kinds of intrepidity (vesārajja-ñāṇa), the knowledge of being unshakable in the eight assemblies, the knowledge that distinguishes the four modes of birth (yoni), the knowledge that distinguishes the five destinations (gati), the seventy-three kinds of knowledge mentioned in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the seventy-seven kinds of knowledge, and so on, including many other thousands of knowledges—this is called knowledge power. Here too, only knowledge power is intended. Indeed, knowledge is called 'power' (bala) because of its aspect of being unshakable by opposing states and because of its aspect of providing support. 'Endowed with which powers' means the Tathāgata who is possessed of, well-endowed with, those ten powers of knowledge. 'The supreme station' (āsabha-ṭṭhāna) means the noble station, the highest station (Omniscience). Or 'āsabha' refers to the previous Buddhas; thus it means their station. Furthermore, a bull that is the leader of a hundred cows is called 'usabha'. A bull that is the leader of a thousand cows is called 'vasabha'. Or, the leader of a hundred cow-pens is an 'usabha', and the leader of a thousand cow-pens is a 'vasabha'. A bull that is noble among all cattle, capable of enduring all dangers, pure white, pleasing to behold, capable of bearing great burdens, and unshakable even by the sound of a hundred thunderclaps is called 'nisabha'. In this context, that 'nisabha' is intended by the term 'usabha'. This is indeed a synonymous term for it. Because it belongs to the 'usabha' bull, it is called 'āsabha'. 'Station' (ṭṭhāna) refers to standing unshakably by pressing the earth with four feet. This Omniscience is called 'āsabha' because it is like the 'āsabha' (the stance of the bull). Just as the bull known as 'nisabha', being endowed with the strength of a bull, stands in an unshakable position by pressing the earth with four feet, so too the Tathāgata, being endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, stands in an unshakable position in the world including the devas, unable to be moved by any adversary or enemy, by pressing the earth of the eight assemblies with the four feet of intrepidity (vesārajja-ñāṇa). Standing thus, he claims that supreme station (the Omniscience which is the domain of previous Buddhas), attains it, does not reject it, and takes it upon himself. Therefore, it is said, 'He claims the supreme station.' 'In the assemblies' means in the eight assemblies. 'Roars the lion's roar' means he utters a noble roar, a fearless roar, or he utters a roar similar to that of the king of lions. This meaning should be understood through the Sīhanāda Sutta. Or, just as a lion is called 'sīha' because of its endurance (sahana) and its ability to strike down (hanana), so too the Tathāgata, regarding the worldly conditions...
382:
He is called a lion (sīha) because of his endurance and because he destroys the doctrines of others. The sound of such a lion is called a lion's roar (sīhanāda). In this context, just as a lion, endowed with leonine strength, is confident in all places and roars his lion's roar without trepidation, so too the Buddha-lion, endowed with the powers of a Tathāgata (tathāgata-bala), is confident in the eight assemblies and, without trepidation, roars the lion's roar endowed with the elegance of various teachings in such ways as 'Such is form,' and so on. Therefore, it is said, 'He roars the lion's roar in the assemblies.'

In the phrase 'He sets in motion the Brahma-wheel (brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti),' 'Brahma' means excellent, noble, and especially pure. The word 'wheel' (cakka) is seen in the following senses:
In prosperity, in marks, in a chariot part,
In postures, in giving, in a gem, in the Dhamma,
In the torture-wheel, and so on;
Here, it is intended as the Dhamma-wheel, and that should be understood in two ways.

In such passages as 'Monks, these four wheels, possessed of which, devas and humans...' (A. Ni. 4.31), this word 'cakka' is seen in the sense of prosperity (sampatti). In the phrase 'On the soles of his feet, wheel-marks (cakka) appeared' (Dī. Ni. 2.35), it is in the sense of marks (lakkhaṇa). In 'The wheel (cakka) follows the hoof of the ox that draws the load' (Dha. Pa. 1), it is in the sense of a chariot part. In 'Four wheels (four postures), nine doors' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.29), it is in the sense of postures (iriyāpatha). In 'Give and enjoy, do not be negligent; set the wheel (cakka) of giving in motion for all living beings' (Jā. 1.7.149), it is in the sense of giving (dāna). In 'The divine gem-wheel (cakkaratana) appeared,' it is in the sense of a gem-wheel. In 'The wheel (cakka) set in motion by me' (Su. Ni. 562), it is in the sense of the Dhamma-wheel. In 'The wheel (torture-wheel) spins on the head of the man overcome by evil desire' (Jā. 1.1.104, 1.5.103), it is in the sense of a torture-wheel (uracakka). In 'Even with a wheel (cakka) with a razor-edge,' it is in the sense of a weapon-wheel. In 'The lightning-circle,' it is in the sense of a lightning-circle (asani-maṇḍala). Here, however, it is intended as the Dhamma-wheel.

That Dhamma-wheel is of two kinds: the knowledge of penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa). Among them, the knowledge produced by wisdom that brings about one's own noble fruition is called paṭivedha-ñāṇa. The knowledge produced by compassion that brings about the noble fruition of disciples is called desanā-ñāṇa. Among these, the knowledge of penetration is of two types: arising and arisen. Indeed, from the Great Renunciation until the Path of Arahatship...
383:
...it is 'arising'; at the moment of fruition, it is called 'arisen' (uppanna). Or, from the Tusita heaven until the Path of Arahatship at the seat of the Great Enlightenment, it is 'arising'; at the moment of fruition, it is called 'arisen'. Or, from the time of receiving the prophecy from the Buddha Dīpaṅkara until the Path of Arahatship, it is 'arising'; at the moment of fruition, it is called 'arisen'. The knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa) is also of two kinds: proceeding (pavattatā) and proceeded (pavatta). Indeed, until the Stream-entry Path of Aññā Koṇḍañña, it is 'proceeding'; at the moment of fruition, it is called 'proceeded'. Among these, the knowledge of penetration is supramundane (lokuttara), and the knowledge of teaching is mundane (lokiya). Both of these are the Buddha's own (orasa) knowledge, not shared with others.

Now, to show in detail those ten powers endowed with which the Tathāgata claims his noble station, which were initially stated as 'The ten powers of the Tathāgata are ten,' [the text asks] 'What are the ten?' Here, it says, 'The Tathāgata understands the cause as cause,' and so on. There, 'the cause as cause' (ṭhānañca ṭhānato) means the cause as the state of being a cause. A cause is called 'ṭhāna' because the effect stands (tiṭṭhati) there, and because it arises and proceeds depending on that. The Blessed One, knowing 'Whatever states are the root (hetu) and condition (paccaya) for the arising of certain states, that is the cause (ṭhāna),' and 'Whatever states are not the root and not the condition for the arising of certain states, that is the non-cause (aṭṭhāna),' understands the cause as cause and the non-cause as non-cause as they really are. 'Yampī' means 'by which knowledge.' 'Idampi tathāgatassa' means 'this knowledge of cause and non-cause is also a power of the Tathāgata (tathāgata-bala).' The application of terms in all instances should be understood in this way.

'Of the undertakings of kamma' (kamma-samādānānaṃ) means of the wholesome and unwholesome kammas performed after undertaking them. Or, kamma itself is called 'kamma-samādāna.' 'By way of condition and cause' (ṭhānaso hetuso) means by way of condition (paccaya) and root-cause (hetu). There, destination (gati), physical excellence (upadhi), time (kāla), and effort (payoga) are the 'ṭhāna' (condition) for the result (vipāka), and kamma is the 'hetu' (root-cause).

'Leading everywhere' (sabbattha-gāminiṃ) means leading to all destinations (gati) and leading to the non-destination (Nibbāna). 'The way' (paṭipadaṃ) means the path (magga). 'Understands as it really is' means that even when many people kill a single living being, he understands the nature of the practices known as wholesome and unwholesome intentions without error, in this way: 'The intention of this person will lead to hell; the intention of this person will lead to the animal realm,' even regarding a single object.
384:
‘Anekadhātu’ means having many elements, such as the eye element and so on, or elements such as the sense-sphere element and so on. ‘Nānādhātu’ means having various kinds of elements due to the different characteristics of those very elements. ‘Loka’ means the world of aggregates (khandha), the world of bases (āyatana), and the world of elements (dhātu). ‘He knows as it really is’ means He penetrates and knows the nature of those various elements correctly and without distortion.

‘Nānādhimuttikata’ means the state of having various dispositions (adhimutti/ajjhāsaya), such as low dispositions and so on.

‘Parasattānaṃ’ means of the noble or primary beings. ‘Parapuggalānaṃ’ means of the inferior beings other than those noble ones. Or, these two terms have the same meaning, but are taught in two ways according to the needs of those to be disciplined (veneyya). ‘Indriyaparopariyatta’ means the superiority (increase) and inferiority (decrease) of the faculties (indriya) such as faith (saddhā) and so on.

‘Jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpatti’ refers to [the diversity of] the four jhānas starting with the first jhāna; the eight liberations (vimokkha) starting with “one possessing form sees forms”; the three kinds of concentration (samādhi) such as that with initial and sustained thought; and the nine successive attainments (anupubbasamāpatti) starting with the first jhāna attainment. ‘Saṃkilesa’ means states belonging to decline. ‘Vodāna’ means states belonging to distinction. ‘Vuṭṭhāna’ means the cause by which they emerge from jhāna and so on; it refers to that cause of emergence.

‘Pubbenivāsānussati’ means the recollection of aggregates lived in the past.

‘Cutūpapāta’ means passing away and rebirth.

‘Destruction of taints’ means Nibbāna, which is the destruction and cessation of taints (āsava) such as the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava).

‘These [powers]’ means He concludes that these [powers of knowledge such as right and wrong] are the very same “Ten Tathāgata Powers” mentioned below. Having thus understood the explanation of the terms in this table (mātikā) in sequence, now: first, the Tathāgata, through the knowledge of right and wrong (ṭhānāṭhānañāṇa), sees the absence of the obstacle of defilements (kilesāvaraṇa), which is the basis (ṭhāna) and non-basis (aṭhāna) for the attainment or non-attainment of the destruction of taints in beings to be disciplined. This is through seeing the basis of mundane right view and seeing the absence of the basis of fixed wrong view. Then, He sees the absence of the obstacle of resultants (vipākāvaraṇa) in those beings through the knowledge of kamma-result (kammavipākañāṇa), by seeing triple-rooted rebirth (tihetukapaṭisandhi). Through the knowledge of the way leading everywhere (sabbatthagāminīpaṭipadāñāṇa), He sees the absence of the obstacle of kamma (kammāvaraṇa), by seeing the absence of weightier kamma (ānantariyakamma). Thus, for those without obstacles, He sees the specific character (caritavisesa) through the knowledge of many and diverse elements (anekadhātunānādhātuñāṇa) in order to teach the appropriate Dhamma. This is by seeing the diversity of elements. Then
385:
He sees the firm disposition (adhimutti) through the knowledge of their diverse dispositions (nānādhimuttikatañāṇa). This is for the purpose of teaching Dhamma by the power of disposition, without even considering current effort (payoga). Then, to teach Dhamma to those whose dispositions are thus seen, according to their capacity and strength, He sees the sharpness or dullness of the faculties such as faith through the knowledge of faculties (indriyaparopariyattañāṇa). If these persons whose faculties are thus distinguished are far away, He approaches them quickly through specific psychic powers because of His mastery in jhāna and so on, using the knowledge that understands jhāna and so on.

Having approached, He sees their past habits through the knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa), and their specific present state of mind through the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyayañāṇa) obtained by the power of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu). Then, through the power of the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa), being free from delusion regarding the path leading to the destruction of taints, He teaches Dhamma for the sake of the destruction of taints. Therefore, it should be understood that these ten powers are taught in this sequence. This is the explanation of the meaning of the table (mātikā).

## (1.) Explanation of the Description of the Single (Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā)

Now, in the section of the description (niddesavāra) begun according to the table laid down, with the method “The fivefold consciousness are not roots,” etc., “na hetum eva” is the description showing the rejection of roots along with delimitation. In that term “na hetum eva,” all the decisions that should be stated by way of the four kinds of roots—root-root (hetu-hetu), causal-root (paccaya-hetu), supreme-root (uttama-hetu), and common-root (sādhāraṇa-hetu)—have already been stated in the explanation of the terms “All form is not a root,” etc., in the Section on Form (Rūpakaṇḍa).

In the terms “ahetukam eva,” etc., it should be understood that the letter ‘m’ is included by the power of euphonic junction (sandhi); it means “ahetukā eva” (only without associated roots). In the remaining terms, this same method applies. Furthermore, among the groups of Dhamma such as “Root dhammas, Not-root dhammas,” the fivefold consciousness are neither root dhammas nor dhammas with roots (sahetuka). But definitely, they are “only not roots” and “only without roots”—in this way, the meaning should be understood in all terms in this section of the description.

The term “abyākatam eva” is taught by way of resultant indeterminate (vipākābyākata). The term “sārammaṇam eva” is taught by way of an object that is leaned upon (olubbhārammaṇa). For objects are of two kinds: causal object (paccayārammaṇa) and leaned-upon object (olubbhārammaṇa). In this context, the leaned-upon object is primary, but the causal object is also certainly obtained.

The term “acetasikam eva” is taught with reference only to the mind (citta) among the three non-mental factors: mind, matter, and Nibbāna. “No apariyāpannam eva” means they are only “included” (pariyāpanna) because of being included in destinations (gati), included in death (cuti), and included in the existence of the round of rebirth (saṃsāravaṭṭa); they are not “unincluded” (apariyāpanna). Because they do not lead out from the world, from the round...
386:
These states are called aniyyānikā because they do not lead out from the round of rebirths. The phrase 'cognizable only by mind-consciousness' (manoviññāṇaviññeyyam eva) means that in the section on matter (rūpakaṇḍa), since eye-consciousness and the others occur by taking present visible objects and so forth as their objects, mind-consciousness—which has past objects and so forth as its domain—is also treated as falling within the stream of the fivefold consciousness, and it is said: 'It is cognizable by the six appropriate consciousnesses' (Dhs 584). However, although the fivefold consciousnesses are present, they are not the objects of eye-consciousness and the others; they are objects only for mind-consciousness. Therefore, it is said: 'Cognizable only by mind-consciousness.' They are 'impermanent' (anicca) in the sense of non-existence after having come to be. They are 'overcome by decay' (jarābhibhūta) because they are overwhelmed by aging.

762. The phrase 'having an arisen base and an arisen object' (uppannavatthukā uppannārammaṇā) is a term that excludes the future. Indeed, these states do not arise in relation to future bases or objects.

The phrase 'having a pre-arisen base and a pre-arisen object' (purejātavatthukā purejātārammaṇā) is a term that excludes simultaneous arising. Indeed, they do not arise depending on a base or an object that arises simultaneously; rather, they themselves arise later, occurring in relation to bases and objects that have arisen previously.

'Having an internal base' (ajjhattikavatthukā) is stated by way of the internal-internal. Indeed, these states arise depending on the five sensitive matters (pasāda-rūpa) within the internal continuity as their base. 'Having external objects' (bāhirārammaṇā) means they have objects such as external visible forms and so forth. In this regard, the fourfold combination should be understood: the fivefold consciousnesses, because they have sensitive matter as their base, are internal states and have internal bases; mind-consciousness, when it arises depending on the heart-matter (hadaya-rūpa), is an internal state and has an external base; the three mental aggregates associated with the fivefold consciousness are external states and have internal bases; the three mental aggregates associated with mind-consciousness, when they arise depending on the heart-matter, are external states and have external bases.

'Having an undestroyed base' (asambhinnavatthukā) means having a base that has not yet ceased. Indeed, they do not arise depending on a past base that has ceased. The same method applies to 'having an undestroyed object' (asambhinnārammaṇā).

In the Pali passages such as 'The base of eye-consciousness is one thing, and the object is another,' the base of eye-consciousness is distinct, and its object is distinct. The base and object of ear-consciousness and the others are also distinct. Eye-consciousness cannot arise by taking any of the sensitive matters such as ear-sensitivity as its base, or any of the objects such as sound as its object, even if one were to travel from one aeon to another; it arises only by taking eye-sensitivity as its base and visible form as its object. Thus, the base, the door, and the object of that eye-consciousness are fixed; it does not shift to another base, door, or object. It arises having a fixed base, a fixed door, and a fixed object. The same method applies to ear-consciousness and the others.

763. In this passage beginning with 'Not of each other's...' the meaning is: the eye-sensitivity of one is not for that ear-sensitivity, and the ear-sensitivity is...
387:
Eye-consciousness arises having a fixed base, a fixed door, and a fixed object. The same method applies to ear-consciousness and the others.

'They do not experience each other's range and domain'—in this phrase, it means that one does not experience the range and domain of the other, such as the eye for the ear, or the ear for the eye. If one were to collect various visible forms such as blue and bring them near the ear-faculty and say, 'Come, distinguish and clarify this object—what is its name?', the eye-consciousness, though it has no mouth, would by its own nature say: 'You blind fool! Even if you run about for a hundred or a thousand years, where else besides me will you find the consciousness that can know this visible form? Bring it here; bring it to the eye-sensitivity. I shall know this object, whether it be blue or yellow. This is not the domain of another; it is my domain alone.' The same method applies to the remaining consciousnesses. In this way, these consciousnesses are said not to experience each other's range and domain.

'To one who attends' means to one who attends solely by way of adverting (āvajjana).

'To one who attends' means to one who attends solely by way of adverting. Indeed, these consciousnesses arise only at the time when there is adverting and attention.

'Not interspersed' (na abbokiṇṇā) means they do not arise continuously without being interspersed by other consciousnesses. By this, their immediate succession (anantarata) is denied.

'Not before, not after'—by this, the simultaneous arising of all consciousnesses is denied. 'Not immediately contiguous to each other'—by this, immediate contiguity (samanantarata) is denied.

The four names beginning with āvaṭṭanā are all names for adverting (āvajjana) itself. That adverting is called āvaṭṭanā because it turns the life-continuum (bhavaṅga); it is called ābhoga because it bends that same life-continuum; it is called samannāhāra because it brings together visible forms and so forth; and it is called manasikāra because it attends to those same visible forms. Thus, in this context, the possibility of the fivefold consciousnesses standing in the place of adverting and performing functions such as adverting is briefly denied.

'Does not specifically cognize any state' means it does not specifically cognize even a single state, whether wholesome or unwholesome, as stated in 'Mind is the forerunner of all states' (manopubbaṅgamā dhammā).
388:
"Aññatra abhinipātamattā" means excluding the mere impact of visible objects and so forth upon the fivefold consciousness. The intended meaning is this: even a very wise man, excluding the mere impact of visible objects and so forth that have come into range, cannot distinguish even a single wholesome or unwholesome state by means of the fivefold consciousness. Among these five types of consciousness, eye-consciousness is merely the act of seeing. Ear-consciousness and the others are merely the acts of hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching. There is no such thing as distinguishing wholesome and other states by these five types of consciousness, which are free from anything beyond the mere extent of seeing and so forth.

"Manodhātuyāpi" means that one cannot distinguish by the receiving mind-element either. Here, the syllable "pi" has the sense of conjunction. Therefore, the meaning should be understood thus: one cannot distinguish any wholesome or unwholesome state by the mind-element, nor by the mind-consciousness elements that arise after it, nor by any of the five-door consciousnesses.

The same method applies to the passages beginning with "Na kañci iriyāpathaṃ kappeti" (He does not arrange any posture). Indeed, by means of the five-door consciousnesses, one cannot perform any posture such as walking; one cannot initiate bodily action or verbal action; one cannot undertake wholesome or unwholesome states; one cannot enter into mundane or supramundane concentration; one cannot emerge from mundane or supramundane concentration; one cannot pass away from a life-existence, nor be reborn in another existence. All these functions, from the distinguishing of wholesome and unwholesome states to passing away, occur only through the mind-door consciousness, not through the five-door consciousness. Therefore, in the performance of all these functions, the five-door cognitive process-consciousnesses together with impulsion (javana) are excluded. Just as these functions do not exist for those five-door cognitive process-consciousnesses, so too functions such as entering into the path of certainty (niyāma) do not exist. Indeed, through five-door impulsion, one does not enter the wrong path of certainty (micchatta-niyāma) nor the right path of certainty (sammatta-niyāma). That impulsion does not occur by taking a name or lineage as its object, nor does it take a concept (paññatti) such as a kasina as its object. It does not proceed by way of insight (vipassanā) taking characteristics as its object, nor by way of powerful insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā). It does not occur by taking fine-material or immaterial states as its object, nor does it take Nirvana as its object. Along with that five-door impulsion, the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidāñāṇa) do not arise, nor do the direct knowledges (abhiññā), the knowledge of a disciple's perfection, the knowledge of a Silent Buddha, or the knowledge of omniscience. All such distinctions are found only in mind-door impulsion.

By the passage "Na supati na paṭibujjhati na supinaṃ passati" (He does not sleep, does not wake, does not see a dream), it is meant that by any five-door consciousness, one does not fall into sleep, does not sleep, does not wake, and does not see any dream. In these three instances, the cognitive process-consciousness together with impulsion is excluded.
