Indeed, when a large wick is lit and a lamp is brought near the eyes of a sleeping person, first, the adverting (āvajjana) at the eye-door does not turn the life-continuum (bhavaṅga); only the adverting at the mind-door turns the life-continuum.
389:
Then, after the impulsion (javana) has run, it descends into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). On the second occasion, the adverting at the eye-door turns the life-continuum. After that, the cognitive process-consciousnesses ending with impulsion, such as eye-consciousness, occur. Immediately after those cognitive process-consciousnesses, the life-continuum occurs. On the third occasion, when the life-continuum has been turned by the mind-door adverting, the mind-door impulsion runs. Knowing with that consciousness, one understands, "What kind of light is this in this place?"

Similarly, when musical instruments are played near the ears of a sleeping person, or when flowers with a fragrant or foul smell are brought near the nose, or when ghee or molasses is placed in the mouth, or when a blow is given with the hand on the back—first, the advertings such as the ear-door adverting do not turn the life-continuum; only the mind-door adverting turns the life-continuum. Then, after the impulsion has run, it descends into the life-continuum. On the second occasion, the advertings such as the ear-door adverting turn the life-continuum. After that, the cognitive process-consciousnesses ending with impulsion, such as ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness, occur. Immediately after those cognitive process-consciousnesses, the life-continuum occurs. On the third occasion, when the life-continuum has been turned by the mind-door adverting, the mind-door impulsion runs. Knowing with that consciousness, one becomes one who says, "What kind of sound is this in this place? It is the sound of a conch, it is the sound of a drum," or "What kind of smell is this in this place? It is the smell of a root, it is the smell of heartwood," or "What kind of taste is this placed in my mouth? It is the taste of ghee, it is the taste of molasses," or "Who struck me on the back? The blow to me was very hard." In this way, one wakes up only by mind-door impulsion, not by five-door impulsion. One sees a dream also only by that mind-door impulsion, not by five-door impulsion.

Furthermore, a person seeing a dream sees it due to four causes: due to the disturbance of elements (dhātukkhobha), due to previous experience (anubhūtapubba), due to the influence of deities (devatopasaṃhāra), or due to prophetic signs (pubbanimitta). Among these four, a person whose elements are disturbed by conjunction with causes that disturb the bile and so forth sees a dream "due to the disturbance of elements." When seeing, he sees various kinds of dreams—as if falling from a mountain, as if going through the sky, or as if being chased by wild beasts, elephants, thieves, and so forth. One who sees "due to previous experience" sees an object previously experienced in the past. To one who sees "due to the influence of deities," the deities, because they desire his welfare or ill-fare, bring various objects for his benefit or harm. He sees those objects through the power of those deities. One who sees "due to prophetic signs" sees a dream that is a prophetic sign of benefit or harm that is about to arise by the power of merit or demerit. It is like the dream of the Bodhisatta's mother, which was the sign of obtaining a son.
390:
Just as the Bodhisatta saw the five great dreams, and King Kosala saw the sixteen dreams (these were seen due to prophetic signs). Among those four types of dreams, the dream seen due to the disturbance of the [bodily] elements (dhātukkhobha) and the dream seen due to previous experience (anubhūtapubba) are not true. The dream seen due to the influence of deities (devatopasaṃhāra) may be true or may be false. This is because angry deities, wishing to destroy someone by a certain means, may show a dream that is reversed. Regarding such reversed displays, there is this story: In the Naga Mahāvihāra of the Rohana region, a Great Elder had a Mesua ferrea (Nāga) tree cut down without informing the Saṅgha of monks. The deity residing in that tree was angry with the Great Elder and, after first enticing him (with a true dream), later informed him in a dream: "Seven days from today, the King who is your supporter will die." The Great Elder took that word and told the King's harem, and the women of the harem all wailed loudly at once. When the King asked, "What is that sound?", they reported, "The Great Elder said this." The King had the days counted, and when the seventh day had passed, he became angry and had the Great Elder's hands and feet cut off.

However, the dream seen due to prophetic signs (pubbanimitta) is absolutely and certainly true. Various types of dreams can also occur through the mixture of these four root causes. Only trainees (sekkha) and worldlings (puthujjana) see these four types of dreams because they have not yet abandoned the distortions (vipallāsa). Arahants (asekkha) do not see dreams because they have abandoned the distortions.

Does the person who sees a dream see it while asleep, or while awake, or in a state that is neither asleep nor awake? In this problem, if one sees it while asleep, it would contradict the Abhidhamma. This is because one sleeps with the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta). That bhavaṅga-citta does not have objects such as visual signs, nor is it associated with greed and so on. Yet, for one who sees a dream, such [active] thoughts do arise. If one sees it while awake, it would contradict the Vinaya. This is because whatever an awake person sees, they see with fully functional consciousness (sabbavohārika-citta). If a transgression is committed with such consciousness, there is no such thing as not being an offense (anāpatti). However, if a person seeing a dream commits a transgression, it is certainly not an offense. If one sees it while neither asleep nor awake, one would not be able to see what is called a dream. If this were the case, would it not lead to the non-existence of dreams? No (dreams do exist).
391:
Dreams are not non-existent. Why? Because one who is overcome by monkey-sleep sees dreams. For it has been said: "O Great King, one who is overcome by monkey-sleep sees dreams" (Milindapañhā). 'Kapimiddhapareto' means one who is possessed of monkey-sleep. Just as the sleep of a monkey is quickly changing, so too is this sleep, which is quickly changing because it is repeatedly interspersed with wholesome and other types of consciousness; one who is possessed of that sleep, in the occurrence of which there is repeated emerging from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), sees dreams. Therefore, this dream may be wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), or indeterminate (abyākata). Therein, for one who performs acts such as worshipping a pagoda, listening to the Dhamma, or preaching the Dhamma in a dream, it is wholesome. For one who performs acts such as killing living beings (pāṇātipāta) and so on, it is unwholesome. At the moments of adverting (āvajjana) and registration (tadārammaṇa), which are free from those two extremes, it should be understood as indeterminate. Even at the time of saying within the dream, "It is as if I saw, it is as if I heard," it is only indeterminate.

Do wholesome and unwholesome deeds performed in a dream have results (vipāka) or no results? They have results. However, because they are weak, they are unable to pull in a rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) result. They have results that are to be experienced during the course of existence (pavatti) when rebirth-linking has been given by another karma.

Thus, wisdom that clarifies the object as it really is (yāthāvaka-vatthu-vibhāvanā paññā) means: the non-causal nature of the five [sensory] consciousnesses is the true nature (yāthāvaṭṭha). Because it clarifies that true object, it is called 'yāthāvaka-vatthu-vibhāvanā'. Likewise, the rootless nature (ahetukaṭṭha) of the five consciousnesses, the nature of being oppressed by decay (jarā), and the nature of not seeing dreams are the true natures. Because it clarifies that true object, it is called 'yāthāvaka-vatthu-vibhāvanā'. Thus, that wisdom which was set forth in the matrix (mātikā) below as "yāthāvaka-vatthu-vibhāvanā paññā" should be understood as such. Only by the power of that wisdom is there the basis of knowledge in this singlefold way. Thus, it is the counting of knowledge by individual groups or the defining of knowledge by a single mode.

## Explanation of the Singlefold Description
## (2.) Explanation of the Twofold Description
In showing the twofold basis of knowledge, "catūsu bhūmīsu kusale" refers to the wholesome wisdom of trainees and worldlings occurring in the four planes. Among the five mentioned in the Vibhaṅga of the Paṭisambhidāmagga...
392:
Among the results, it is called 'Atthajāpikā' because it produces, generates, and causes the occurrence of the result known as fruition (vipāka) pertaining to its respective plane. For an Arahant who is producing supernormal knowledge (abhiññā) or an attainment (samāpatti), the sense-sphere functional wisdom (kāmāvacara-kiriya-paññā) occurring at the time of preliminary work (parikamma) for both abhiññā and samāpatti is also called Atthajāpikā. This is because that sense-sphere functional wisdom produces, generates, and causes the occurrence of the result known as functional consciousness (kiriya) consisting of various abhiññā and samāpatti; thus it is called 'Atthajāpikā-paññā'. This, however, is another method from the Commentaries not directly found in the Pāli: even a preceding sense-sphere functional consciousness is a condition for a succeeding sense-sphere functional consciousness by way of proximity (anantara), etc.; that preceding functional consciousness is also called Atthajāpikā-paññā because it produces that functional result. The same method applies to the fine-material and immaterial spheres.

In the exposition of the second term, among the four planes, wisdom in resultants (vipāka) is called 'Jāpitatthā' because it stands having produced the result of sense-sphere vipāka by way of conascence (sahajāta) and other conditions. The same method applies to the resultant wisdom of the fine-material sphere and so on. Alternatively, all such wisdom is called Jāpitatthā because it is produced, generated, and caused to occur by its own respective causes, and is itself a result (attha). The same method applies to the aforementioned functional wisdom in the abhiññā and samāpatti that have arisen for an Arahant. This is also another method from the Commentaries not directly found in the Pāli: sense-sphere functional wisdom is called Jāpitatthā because it stands having produced the result known as sense-sphere functional consciousness by way of conascence and so on. The same method applies to the functional wisdom of the fine-material and immaterial spheres. Alternatively, all such wisdom is called Jāpitatthā because it is produced, generated, and caused to occur by its own respective causes, and is itself a result. All other remaining meanings in this exposition of the Dyad are clear, as they follow the method already stated in the Atthasālinī (Dhammasaṅgaṇī Commentary).

## Explanation of the Exposition of the Dyad (Dukaniddesavaṇṇanā)

## (3.) Explanation of the Exposition of the Triad (Tikaniddesavaṇṇanā)

In the exposition of the three-fold grounds of knowledge (ñāṇavatthu), in the term 'yoga-vihitesu', 'yoga' refers to wisdom (paññā). The meaning is 'prepared by wisdom' or 'matured by wisdom'. In the term 'kammāyatanesu', the work itself is the base of work (kammāyatana). Alternatively, it is called kammāyatana because the work is the base or cause for livelihood and so on.
393:
It is called 'kammāyatana' because it is the base or cause for livelihood and so on. The same method applies to the bases of crafts (sippāyatana). That work (kamma) is of two kinds: low and high. Among them, low work includes carpentry, the work of flower-scavengers, and so on. High work includes agriculture, trade, cattle-breeding, and so on. Craft (sippa) is also of two kinds: low and high. Among them, low craft includes the craft of basket-makers, weavers, potters, leather-workers, barbers, and so on. High craft includes finger-calculation (muddā), arithmetic (gaṇanā), writing (lekha), and so on. The branch of knowledge (vijjāṭṭhāna) is indeed the knowledge of mantras and spells. In that regard, only righteous knowledge is taken. Medical sciences such as snake-charming, chanting/blowing, ophthalmology (sālākiya), and surgery (sallakattiya), although included in the bases of crafts because of the statement "Teacher, I wish to learn this craft" (Mahāvagga), are not taken here.

In this context, a certain wise person, for the sake of the comfortable living of people and by his own innate nature (dhamma-tā), invents houses, palaces, vehicles, boats, and so on. Indeed, he, thinking "These people suffer without a place to live," and being established in doing good, invents houses of various shapes such as rectangular ones. To protect against cold and heat, he builds palaces with one or two stories and so on. Thinking "Traveling is painful without a vehicle," he invents litters, carts, carriages, and so on to dispel the fatigue of the legs. Thinking "Without a boat, there is no travel on oceans and the like," he invents various kinds of boats. He does not see all these being done by others, nor does he learn them from others, nor does he hear from those who speak of them; rather, he does them by his own innate nature and thought. For when something is done by a wise person through his own nature, it is just like that which is done by those who have learned it from others. This is the method regarding low work (hīna-kamma).

Regarding high work (ukkaṭṭha-kamma) also, a certain wise person, thinking "Without agriculture, the life of people cannot proceed," invents agricultural implements such as yokes and plows for the comfortable living of people. Likewise, he invents various kinds of trade and cattle-breeding. He does not see all these being done by others... (as before) ... it is just like that which is done by others. This is the method regarding high work.

Regarding the two kinds of bases of crafts (sippāyatana) also, a certain wise person, for the sake of the comfortable living of people, invents low crafts such as basket-making, and high crafts such as finger-calculation known as 'muddā', arithmetic known as 'gaṇanā', and writing (lekha) of various brief and detailed forms. He does not see all these being done by others... (as before) ... it is just like that which is done by others. This is the method regarding the bases of crafts.
394: A certain wise person, for the purpose of treating people oppressed by dangers such as non-humans, snakes, and scorpions, brings forth righteous arts such as the Naga-subduing mantras. This wise person has never seen others performing these arts, has not learned them after they were performed, and has not heard them being spoken; rather, he performs them by contemplating through his own natural wisdom. This is because the art performed by a wise person through his own nature is identical to the art performed by those who learn it from others. Kammassakata-ñāṇa is the knowledge that knows: "This kamma is the property of beings; this kamma is not one's own." Vipassanā-ñāṇa is called Saccānulomika-ñāṇa (knowledge in conformity with the truths) because it conforms to the Four Truths. Now, to show the manner of its occurrence, it is said: "Form is impermanent," and so on. Here, although only the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa) is directly shown, it should be understood that the characteristics of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa) and non-self (anatta-lakkhaṇa) are also included by way of meaning. For whatever is impermanent is suffering; whatever is suffering is non-self. All the words such as anulomika-khanti (conformable patience), which have the nature described above, are merely synonyms for wisdom (paññā). That wisdom is called anulomikā because it sees conformably without opposing the five causes such as kammāyatana mentioned below. Likewise, it is called anulomikā because it conforms to the practice for the welfare of beings, conforms to the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca), and conforms to the ultimate truth, Nibbāna. It is called khanti because it can endure (is able to know) all these causes; it is called diṭṭhi because it sees; it is called ruci because it finds pleasure; it is called mudi because it rejoices; it is called pekkhā because it observes. All those phenomena such as kammāyatana can withstand the absolute scrutiny of that wisdom. In particular, it is called dhammanijjhānakkhanti because the phenomena known as the five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā) can withstand absolute scrutiny when repeatedly contemplated by way of impermanence, suffering, and non-self. The wisdom obtained by contemplating on one's own without hearing the words of guidance from another is called cintāmaya-paññā (wisdom based on reflection). This cintāmaya-paññā does not arise in just any ordinary person, but only in very distinguished Great Beings (Mahāsatta). Among those Great Beings, saccānulomika-ñāṇa arises only in the two types of Bodhisattas (the Buddha-to-be and the Paccekabuddha-to-be). It should be understood that the remaining types of wisdom, such as kammāyatana, arise in all great wise persons who have fulfilled the perfections (pāramī).
395: In the phrase "obtained by hearing from others," all wisdom obtained by seeing the fields of activity (kammāyatana) etc. being performed or already performed by others, or by hearing the words of someone speaking, or by learning in the presence of a teacher, should be understood as "wisdom obtained only by hearing from others" (sutamaya-paññā). "Of one who has attained" refers to one who is endowed with an attainment (samāpatti); the wisdom occurring within the attainment is called "wisdom based on mental development" (bhāvanāmaya-paññā). "Based on giving" means because of the volition of giving (dāna-cetanā). "Of one who reaches giving" means the wisdom that arises in the continuum of a person who reaches the volition of giving. Thus, wisdom associated with the volition of giving is called "wisdom based on giving" (dānamaya-paññā). That wisdom arises in three ways: as the preliminary volition (pubba-cetanā) of one who thinks "I will give," as the volition at the moment of giving (muñca-cetanā), and as the subsequent volition (apara-cetanā) of one who reflects after having given. In the phrase "based on virtue, because of reaching virtue," here too, wisdom associated with the volition of virtue is intended as "wisdom based on virtue" (sīlamaya-paññā). This wisdom also arises in three ways: as the preliminary volition of one who thinks "I will fulfill virtue," as the volition while fulfilling it, and as the subsequent volition of one who reflects after having fulfilled it. Bhāvanāmaya-paññā has already been mentioned above. In the sections on higher virtue (adhisīla) etc., virtue and higher virtue, mind and higher mind, wisdom and higher wisdom should each be understood in two ways. Therein, according to the manner included in this text: "Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, that element remains, the stability of phenomena, the fixed course of phenomena," the five precepts and the ten precepts are called "virtue" (sīla). That virtue exists whether a Buddha arises or not. When a Buddha has not arisen, who prescribes them? Hermits (tāpasa), wanderers (paribbājaka), Omniscient Bodhisattas, and Wheel-turning monarchs prescribe them. When a Fully Enlightened Buddha has arisen, the Saṅgha of monks, the Saṅgha of nuns, laymen (upāsaka), and laywomen (upāsikā) prescribe them. However, Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla (virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha) is superior to all other virtues and arises only when a Tathāgata has arisen, not when one has not arisen. Only Omniscient Buddhas prescribe it. For prescribing that "due to this cause, due to this transgression, there is such a training rule" is not the domain of others; it is the domain of Buddhas alone, the power (knowledge) of the Buddhas. Thus, because Pātimokkha-saṃvara is higher virtue (adhisīla), it is said: "Of one who restrains with the Pātimokkha restraint," and so on, to show the wisdom in that higher virtue.
396:
In the Pali text mentioned above, the eight attainments (samāpatti) which are the basis for the round of rebirth are called 'citta' (mind). This 'citta' exists whether a Tathāgata has appeared or not. Who brings it about when a Buddha has not appeared? Ascetics (tāpasa), wanderers (paribbājaka), Omniscient Bodhisattas, and Cakkavatti kings bring it about. When the Blessed One has appeared, those such as monks who desire the distinguished Dhamma can also bring it about. However, the eight attainments which are the basis for insight (vipassanā) are superior to all [other] minds; they arise only when a Tathāgata has appeared, not when he has not appeared. Only the Omniscient Buddhas make these known. Thus, since the eight attainments are 'adhicitta' (higher mind), in order to show the wisdom (paññā) occurring in the higher mind, it was said: "For one who enters the fine-material sphere and immaterial sphere attainments," and so on.

In the Pali text mentioned above, the knowledge of the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā-ñāṇa) is called 'paññā' (wisdom). This wisdom exists whether a Tathāgata has appeared or not. When a Buddha has not appeared, it arises by way of the offerings of King Velāma, King Vessantara, and others. When a Buddha has appeared, there is no limit to the number of those who perform great acts of giving (mahādāna) with that knowledge. However, the wisdom of the Path and Fruit (magga-phala paññā) is superior to all [other] wisdom; it occurs extensively only when a Tathāgata has appeared, not when he has not appeared. Thus, since the wisdom of the Path and Fruit is 'adhipaññā' (higher wisdom), in order to show the superior wisdom, it was said: "In the four Paths," and so on.

In this matter, a question may arise: Among these six categories—virtue (sīla) and higher virtue (adhisīla), mind (citta) and higher mind (adhicitta), wisdom (paññā) and higher wisdom (adhipaññā)—in which category is insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) included? Insight-wisdom is included in the category of higher wisdom. Therefore, just as a parasol or a banner of a smaller size is used as a reference to call a larger parasol 'aticchatta' (superior parasol) and a larger banner 'atidhaja' (superior banner), even so, the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla) is called 'adhisīla' in reference to the five precepts and ten precepts. The eight attainments which are the basis for insight are called 'adhicitta' in reference to the eight attainments which are the basis for the round of rebirth. It should be understood that insight-wisdom, Path-wisdom, and Fruit-wisdom are called 'adhipaññā' in reference to the knowledge of the ownership of kamma.

In the explanations (niddesa) such as 'skill in progress' (āya-kosalla), 'āya' means increase; that increase is of two kinds: the decrease of the disadvantageous and the arising of the advantageous. 'Apāya' means non-increase (decline); that decline is also of two kinds: the decrease of the advantageous and the arising of the disadvantageous. Therefore, in order to show that 'āya' and 'apāya', it was said: "For one who attends to these dhammas," and so on. "This is said" means the wisdom concerning the non-arising and abandoning of unwholesome dhammas, and the arising and persistence of wholesome dhammas—this is "this āya-kosalla". This...
397:
...is called 'skill in progress' (āya-kosalla). The wisdom concerning the non-arising and ceasing of wholesome dhammas, and the arising and persistence of unwholesome dhammas—this is the meaning of 'skill in decline' (apāya-kosalla).

Granted that skill in progress is wisdom, how does skill in decline come to be called wisdom? Indeed, only a wise person understands: "Because I attend [to things] in this way, unarisen wholesome dhammas do not arise, and arisen wholesome dhammas cease. Unarisen unwholesome dhammas arise, and arisen unwholesome dhammas increase." Having known this, he does not allow unarisen unwholesome dhammas to arise and abandons those that have arisen. He causes unarisen wholesome dhammas to arise and brings arisen wholesome dhammas to the fulfillment of development (bhāvanā). Thus, it should be understood that skill in decline is also indeed wisdom.

In that regard, all knowledge of the cause that arises at that moment to remedy an urgent matter or a danger that has arisen is to be understood as 'skill in means' (upāya-kosalla). The meaning of the remaining words is clear in all places.

## Commentary on the Triplets (Tika-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)
## (4.) Commentary on the Quadruplets (Catukka-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

In the explanation of the four types of knowledge-objects (ñāṇavatthu-niddesa), among the words beginning with "atthi dinnaṃ" (there is [result of] giving), the meaning should be understood by the method: "there is a fruit due to the cause of giving." "This knowledge of the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā-ñāṇa) is said" means the wisdom that knows: "This kamma is my own, this kamma is not my own"—this is the meaning. In that regard, these dhammas—the three types of bodily misconduct, the four types of verbal misconduct, and the three types of mental misconduct—are not called 'one's own kamma'. Only the ten types of good conduct occurring in the three doors are called 'one's own kamma'. Whether it be one's own kamma or another's, all unwholesome [kamma] is not 'one's own kamma'. Why? Because it destroys welfare and produces harm. Whether it be one's own or another's, all wholesome [kamma] is indeed called 'one's own kamma'. Why? Because it destroys harm and produces welfare.

There is no limit to the number of virtuous people who, established in this knowledge of the ownership of kamma which is capable of knowing thus, have performed many acts of giving, fulfilled virtue, undertaken the Uposatha, and having experienced happiness after happiness and prosperity after prosperity, reached Nibbāna. For example, a wealthy man loads five hundred carts with ghee, honey, molasses, and so on, as well as salt, sesame, rice, and so on. While traveling on a difficult road, if any necessary task arises, because he has brought all the provisions, he does not worry or tremble, but with ease...
398:
Just as one can safely reach a place free from danger, so too, those who, established in this knowledge of the ownership of kamma (kammasakata-ñāṇa), give many gifts... and reach Nibbāna are so numerous they cannot be counted. "Excluding the knowledge in conformity with the truths" (saccānulomika-ñāṇa) means that, setting aside insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) which is so named because it conforms to the Truth of the Path and the Ultimate Truth (Nibbāna), all other remaining mundane wholesome wisdom is simply knowledge of the ownership of kamma.

In the phrase "the knowledge of one possessed of the path is knowledge regarding suffering," the single path knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) is included in four places (such as knowledge regarding suffering, etc.) by virtue of the simultaneous penetration of the four truths.

In the phrase "knowledge of the Dhamma" (dhamme ñāṇa), let path wisdom be called knowledge of the Dhamma because of the simultaneous penetration of the four truths; but how is fruition wisdom (phala-prajñā) called knowledge of the Dhamma? It should be said that it is because of its relation to the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). Both types of wisdom (path and fruition) should be understood as knowledge of the Dhamma because they occur through their own function and object regarding the Noble Truths, which are realized personally without depending on others. In the phrase "that person through this Dhamma," path knowledge is called "Dhamma" because the Noble Truths are its range (gocara), using the term for the range; or, using the instrumental case in the sense of the accusative, it means "by one who has known these four truths," referring to the path knowledge that stands having known the four truths. "By seeing" (diṭṭhena) means by the path knowledge that stands having seen the four truths. "By reaching" (pattena) means by the path knowledge that has reached the four truths. "By knowing" (viditena) means the four truths have been made clear and known by the path knowledge, and thus those truths are called "known"; it refers to the path knowledge that possesses such known truths. "By plunging into" (pariyogāḷhena) means by the path knowledge that stands having plunged into the four truths. "He leads the way" (nayaṃ neti) means he carries or sends the method into the past and the future. This, however, is not the function of path knowledge, but the function of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). Nevertheless, the Teacher described path knowledge as being like that which leads the way in the past and future. Why? Because reviewing knowledge has path knowledge as its root. Indeed, reviewing occurs for one who has developed the path. Therefore, the Teacher made path knowledge itself appear as if it leads the way. Alternatively, the meaning should be understood thus: whatever path knowledge with the four truths as its range has been attained by this person, through that path knowledge as the cause, he leads the method known as reviewing knowledge into the past and future.

Now, to show the manner in which he leads the way with that knowledge, the Teacher said: "Whoever in the past..." and so on. In that passage, "they fully understood" (abbhanyaṃsu) means they knew and penetrated. "This very [suffering]" (imaññeva) means that the suffering they fully understood in the past and the suffering they will fully understand in the future is not literally this present suffering, but it is spoken of as "this very one" in the sense of similarity. For in the past, excluding craving...
399:
In the past, excluding craving, they penetrated the aggregates of the three planes as the Truth of Suffering; they penetrated craving alone as the Truth of Origin, Nibbāna alone as the Truth of Cessation, and the Noble Path alone as the Truth of the Path. In the future, they will penetrate them in this very same way, and in the present, they penetrate them in this very same way. Thus, "this very [suffering]" is said in the sense of similarity. This knowledge (which follows the sequence) is called inferential knowledge (anvaye ñāṇa); it is also called following knowledge (anugamana-ñāṇa), leading knowledge (nayana-ñāṇa), and causal knowledge (kāraṇa-ñāṇa).

"Knowledge of [others'] minds" (pariye ñāṇa) is the knowledge that defines the mind (cittapariccheda-ñāṇa). "Of other beings" (parasaṭṭānaṃ) means excluding oneself, the minds of remaining beings. The subsequent term "of other persons" (parapuggalānaṃ) is a synonym for the former. "He knows the mind with his own mind" means that with his own mind, he distinguishes and knows the minds of others in various ways, such as being with lust, etc. What should be said regarding the phrases "a mind with lust," etc., has already been stated in the Satipaṭṭhāna Vibhaṅga. However, there is this distinction: here, in the phrases "unsurpassed mind" or "liberated mind," supramundane minds are also included. For even the supramundane mind of others (not yet reached by oneself) can indeed be the object of the knowledge of others' minds for one who has not yet reached that insight.

"Remaining wisdom" means that, excluding the three kinds of wisdom such as knowledge of the Dhamma, etc. (Dhamma, Inferential, and Others' minds), all other wisdom is called conventional knowledge (sammuti-ñāṇa) because it is recognized as knowledge. The etymological meaning here is: knowledge regarding conventions is conventional knowledge.

Wisdom in sense-sphere wholesome states (kāmāvacara-kusala) definitely accumulates death and rebirth in the round of existence; therefore, it is said to be "for accumulation (ācaya), not for reduction (apacaya)." Supramundane path wisdom, however, definitely reduces death and rebirth; therefore, it is said to be "for reduction, not for accumulation." Wisdom of the fine-material and immaterial spheres accumulates death and rebirth, yet it also reduces defilements and states rooted in defilements through the power of suppression (vikkhambhana); therefore, it is said to be "for both accumulation and reduction." The remaining wisdom (resultant and functional) neither accumulates nor reduces death and rebirth; therefore, it is said to be "neither for accumulation nor for reduction."

"Does not penetrate the higher knowledges" is said with reference to the wisdom associated with the first jhāna. For that wisdom, being attainable through seclusion from sensual pleasures, leads to revulsion (nibbidā) toward defilements. Through that, the person becomes dispassionate toward sensual pleasures; however, because of not having reached the state of being a basis for higher knowledges, he neither penetrates the five higher knowledges nor, because of having a sign as an object (nimittārammaṇa), does he penetrate the truths. Thus, this wisdom is for revulsion, not for penetration. "That very person" refers to one who stands having attained the first jhāna. "Being dispassionate toward sensual pleasures" means being dispassionate by way of those sensual pleasures that have been suppressed. The higher knowledges...
400:
“He penetrates” means he penetrates the five superknowledges (abhiññā). This is said with reference to the wisdom associated with the fourth jhāna. Indeed, fourth-jhāna wisdom can certainly penetrate the five superknowledges, both as the basis for superknowledge and by attaining the state of superknowledge itself. Therefore, that fourth-jhāna wisdom leads to penetration. Since one has already become weary of defilements even through first-jhāna wisdom, [fourth-jhāna wisdom] is not for the sake of revulsion (nibbidā).

As for the wisdom of the second and third jhānas, to which category do they belong? By the power of joy (somanassa), they belong to the first jhāna; by the power of being without initial application (avitakka), they belong to the fourth jhāna. Thus, this wisdom should be understood as depending on either the first or the fourth jhāna. “For the sake of revulsion and for the sake of penetration” means path-wisdom (magga-paññā) is for revulsion because it is weary of the entire round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), and for penetration because it penetrates the sixth superknowledge.

In the words “one who attains the first jhāna,” etc., a person attains the first jhāna which is not well-mastered (appaguṇa). When that person emerges from that jhāna, perceptions and mental applications (saññā-manasikāra) accompanied by sense-desire (kāma) occur by way of the object; they strike, they urge [towards sense-desire]. Due to those perceptions and mental applications that rush into sense-desire, that first-jhāna wisdom declines, it deteriorates. Therefore, it is called ‘hāna-bhāginī’ (partaking of decline). ‘Tadanudhammatā’ means having a nature consistent with that [first jhāna]. The phrase “mindfulness remains” (sati santiṭṭhati) is said with reference to wrong mindfulness (micchā-sati), not right mindfulness (sammā-sati). For to one who sees the first jhāna as peaceful and sublime, consistent with its nature, and enjoys it, delights in it, attachment (nikanti) arises. For that person, by the power of that attachment, that first-jhāna wisdom neither declines nor increases, but remains in the category of stability. Therefore, it is called ‘ṭhiti-bhāginī-paññā’ (wisdom partaking of stability).

‘Avitakka-sahagatā’ (accompanied by the absence of initial application) means perceptions and mental applications accompanied by the second jhāna, which is without initial application, occur by way of the object for one who adverts to it as peaceful and sublime. ‘Samudācaranti’ (they occur) means they strike and urge the person who has emerged from the well-mastered first jhāna for the sake of attaining the second jhāna. For that person, due to the power of those perceptions and mental applications that rush into the higher second jhāna, that first-jhāna wisdom is called ‘visesa-bhāginī’ (partaking of distinction) because it is the basis for the arising of the distinguished second jhāna. ‘Nibbidā-sahagatā’ (accompanied by revulsion) means perceptions and mental applications accompanied by insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) called revulsion occur for the person who has emerged from that same first jhāna. Indeed, insight-knowledge becomes weary of and dissatisfied with the various jhāna factors as they occur; therefore, it is called ‘nibbidā’ (revulsion). ‘Samudācaranti’ means they strike and urge for the sake of realizing Nibbāna. ‘Virāgūpasañhitā’ means perceptions and mental applications connected with Nibbāna, which is called dispassion (virāga). It is called ‘virāgūpasañhitā’ because it occurs with the thought, “By this path, one can realize Nibbāna, which is dispassion, through insight-knowledge.” The perceptions and mental applications associated with that insight-knowledge are also called ‘virāgūpasañhitā’. For that person, by the power of those perceptions and mental applications, that first-jhāna wisdom...
401:
...is called ‘nibbedha-bhāginī’ (partaking of penetration) because it is the proximate cause for the penetration of the Noble Path. Thus, in these four instances, only first-jhāna wisdom is discussed. The meaning should be understood in the same way for second-jhāna wisdom and so on.

For one who produces supramundane concentration (lokuttara-samādhi), in the preliminary stage at the time of its arrival, it is called “producing concentration with difficulty and hardship” (kicchena kasirena samādhiṃ uppādentassa) because one arrives having suppressed the defilements while being exhausted by painful effort (saṅkhāra) and exertion (payoga). After suppressing the defilements and dwelling for a long time in the cultivation of insight, one penetrates and attains that state called supramundane concentration slowly and with direct knowledge; thus it is called “slowly knowing with direct knowledge” (dandhaṃ abhijānantassa). This wisdom that arises in this way is called “painful practice and slow direct knowledge” (dukkha-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā) by way of its arrival, even though it arises in a single mind-moment at the time of the path, because the practice of suppressing defilements is painful and the wisdom of insight-cultivation is slow. The meaning in the three subsequent phrases should also be understood in this same way.

One who does not obtain concentration as desired is called “one who does not obtain concentration at will” (samādhissa na nikāmalābhī). This means one who attains a jhāna that is not well-mastered, such that the concentration does not serve as a condition for ascending to higher attainments. “Pervading a small object” (ārammaṇaṃ thokaṃ pharantassa) means performing the preliminary work on a small object, about the size of a tray or a water cup, and reaching absorption (appanā) right there, pervading only that small, unenlarged object. The same method applies to the remaining phrases. For, as the opposite of one who does not obtain it at will, one who attains a well-mastered jhāna is here called “one who obtains it at will” (nikāmalābhī). And as the opposite of an unenlarged object, an enlarged object is called “extensive” (vipula). The rest is just the same.

“This knowledge is also of aging and death” (jarāmaraṇepetaṃ ñāṇaṃ) is said by way of the single penetration of the four truths, taking only Nibbāna as the object. But “starting with aging and death” (jarāmaraṇaṃ ārabbha), etc., are said by way of defining the truths individually in the preliminary stage before the path, when occurring with reference to each single basis. In all places, the remaining meaning is clear.

## Explanation of the Description of the Fours (Catukka-niddesa-vaṇṇanā).
402:
## (5.) Commentary on the Exposition of the Fivefold

In the exposition of the five kinds of objects of knowledge, among the suffusion with rapture and so forth, the wisdom occurring in the two jhānas (the first and second jhānas) because of suffusing with rapture is called 'suffusion with rapture' (pītipharaṇatā). The wisdom occurring in the three jhānas (the lower three jhānas) because of suffusing with bliss is called 'suffusion with bliss' (sukhapharaṇatā). The knowledge of discerning others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) because of suffusing the minds of others is called 'suffusion with mind' (cetopharaṇatā). The divine-eye wisdom (dibbacakkhupaññā) because of suffusing with light is called 'suffusion with light' (ālokapharaṇatā). Reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa) is called the 'sign of reviewing' (paccavekkhaṇānimitta). For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "Wisdom in the two jhānas is suffusion with rapture," and so forth.

Among those types of wisdom, suffusion with rapture and suffusion with bliss are like the two feet; suffusion with mind and suffusion with light are like the two hands; the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññāpādakajjhāna), is like the middle of the body; and the sign of reviewing is like the head. Thus, the Blessed One demonstrated the five-factored right concentration (sammāsamādhi) by comparing it to a man endowed with major and minor limbs. By the words, "This is the five-factored right concentration," He taught the concentration of the basic jhāna (pādakajjhānasamādhi), which is endowed with five factors similar to hands, feet, and the head.

In the passages beginning with, "This concentration is both happy in the present," the concentration of the fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphalasamādhi) is intended. That concentration is 'happy in the present' because it is blissful at the moment of its attainment. It has a 'happy result in the future' because each preceding concentration is a condition for the subsequent bliss of concentration. The peaceful and subtle fruition-consciousness produces a sublime and sweet-natured form (rūpa). For one who has emerged from the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), body-consciousness accompanied by bliss arises, dependent on the tangible object (phoṭṭhabba) consisting of a pleasant touch that pervades the entire body. In this way also, it has a happy result in the future.

It is called 'noble' (ariya) because it is remote from defilements. It is 'non-carnal' (nirāmisa) because of the absence of the baits of sensuality, the baits of the round, and the baits of the world. It is 'cultivated by great men' (akāpurisasevita) because it is cultivated by Great Beings such as the Buddhas. It is 'peaceful' (santa) because of the peacefulness of the jhāna factors, the peacefulness of the object, and the stilling of the fever of all defilements. It is 'sublime' (paṇīta) in the sense of being unsurpassable. It is 'attained through tranquility' (paṭippassaddhiladdha) because it is obtained through the stilling of defilements, or because it has the state of the stilling of defilements. These two terms, 'paṭippassaddhi' and 'paṭippassaddha', are the same in meaning. Alternatively, it is 'attained through tranquility' because it is obtained by an Arahant whose defilements are stilled.

It is 'attained through unification' (ekodibhāvādhigata) because it is obtained by the higher concentration that increases noble concentration, or because it has reached that very unification. It is 'not reached by suppression and prevention' (na sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagata) because it is not a state obtained by suppressing opposing states and preventing defilements with a consciousness accompanied by effort and application, like mundane concentration which is not fully mastered. A person entering that concentration from that...
403:
...or emerging from it, enters only mindfully and emerges only mindfully because of having reached an abundance of mindfulness. Or, he enters mindfully and emerges mindfully by the power of a predetermined time. Therefore, in this concentration, for one who reviews thus: "This concentration is both happy in the present and has a happy result in the future," the knowledge that arises within himself, not depending on others, is one factor. This is the method for the remaining factors as well. Thus, because of these five kinds of reviewing knowledge, this concentration is called the 'fivefold-knowledge right concentration'.

## Commentary on the Exposition of the Fivefold.

## (6.) Commentary on the Exposition of the Sixfold

In the exposition of the six kinds of objects of knowledge, 'knowledge of the modes of supernormal power' (iddhividhañāṇa) is the knowledge regarding various powers occurring in the manner beginning with: "Being one, he becomes many." By this, only the absorption wisdom (appanāpaññā) of a single mind-moment is spoken of, which is without initial and sustained thought, accompanied by equanimity, belongs to the fine-material sphere, and accomplishes the state of becoming many and so forth.

'Knowledge of the purification of the ear-element' (sotadhātuvisuddhiñāṇa) is the knowledge of the divine ear-element which has as its object the various sounds, distant and near. By this also, only the absorption wisdom of a single mind-moment is spoken of, which is without initial and sustained thought, accompanied by equanimity, belongs to the fine-material sphere, and has as its object sounds that transcend the range of the natural ear-consciousness.

'Knowledge of others' minds' (paracitte ñāṇa) is the knowledge in discerning the minds of other beings. By this also, only the absorption wisdom of a single mind-moment of the aforementioned kind is spoken of, which has as its object the minds of others accompanied by lust and so forth.

'Knowledge of the recollection of past lives' (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa) is the knowledge associated with the recollection of past lives. By this also, only the absorption wisdom of a single mind-moment of the aforementioned kind is spoken of, which is associated with the mindfulness that recollects the aggregates previously lived in.

'Knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings' (sattānaṃ cutūpapāte ñāṇa) is the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. By this also, only the absorption wisdom of a single mind-moment of the aforementioned kind is spoken of, which has as its object the element of appearance (vaṇṇadhātu) of beings who are about to pass away or have just been reborn.

'Knowledge of the destruction of the taints' (āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇa) is the knowledge that knows by discerning the Four Noble Truths. This knowledge of the destruction of taints is exclusively supramundane (lokuttara). The remaining types of knowledge are mundane (lokiya).

## Commentary on the Exposition of the Sixfold.
404:
## (7.) Commentary on the Exposition of the Sevens and so forth

In the Exposition of the Seven Bases of Knowledge (Ñāṇavatthuniddesa), by way of the method "with birth as condition, aging and death" and so on, through the occurrence (pavatti) and cessation (nivatti) in the round of rebirths, the Buddha taught reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa) for each of the eleven factors of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) according to the three periods of time. Then, with the words "Whatever is his knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa)," that same knowledge was taught in brief by way of the nature of destruction and so forth.

Therein, the two knowledges: "with birth as condition, aging and death" and "when there is no birth, there is no aging and death," are taught by way of the present time. In the past time and in the future time, there are likewise two knowledges for the past and two for the future, making six. These six, together with the knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma, make seven. Therein, "knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma" means knowledge of the mode of conditions (paccayākārañāṇa). Because the mode of conditions (Dependent Origination) is the cause for the occurrence and stability of phenomena (dhamma), it is called "stability of the Dhamma" (dhammaṭṭhiti); knowledge regarding that is "knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma." This is indeed the name for those six kinds of knowledge. Thus, by making these seven for each factor, there are seventy-seven (77) knowledges for the eleven factors.

Therein, "khayadhamma" means having the nature of destruction; "vayadhamma" means having the nature of decay; "virāgadhamma" means having the nature of fading away; "nirodhadhamma" means having the nature of cessation. What is taught by this Pali? It teaches the contemplation of a preceding insight by a subsequent insight. By teaching thus, insight and insight into insight (vipassanā-paṭivipassanā) are taught seven times.

Indeed, having seen all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) as impermanent, suffering, and non-self with the first insight knowledge, it is proper to see that knowledge with the second knowledge, the second with the third, the third with the fourth, the fourth with the fifth, the fifth with the sixth, and the sixth with the seventh. Thus, the seven insights and insights into insight are taught.

## Commentary on the Exposition of the Sevens.

In the Exposition of the Eight Bases of Knowledge, "wisdom in the path of stream-entry" (sotāpattimagge paññā) means wisdom existing in the path of stream-entry. By this Pali, only the wisdom associated with the path is taught. The same method applies to the remaining terms.

## Commentary on the Exposition of the Eights.

In the Exposition of the Nine Bases of Knowledge, "in the attainments of successive abidings" (anupubbavihārasamāpattīsu) means wisdom occurring in the attainments known as successive abidings. They should be understood as "successive abidings" (anupubbavihāra) in the sense that they should be dwelt in according to their order or sequence, and as "attainments" (samāpatti) in the sense that they should be attained. Therein, the eight wisdoms, such as wisdom in the attainment of the first jhāna, are associated wisdoms.
405: The ninth, the wisdom of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇapaññā), should also be known. That wisdom arises in one who reviews the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) as peaceful and sublime. Therefore, the Buddha said: "The knowledge of reviewing of one who has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling." ## Commentary on the Explanation of the Nines. ## (10.) Commentary on the Explanation of the Tens ## Explanation of the First Power In the explanation of the ten bases of knowledge, the word "impossible" (aṭṭhānaṃ) is the rejection of a cause. "No possibility" (anavakāso) is the rejection of a supporting condition. By both words, only the cause is rejected. For a cause is called the "place" (ṭhāna) and "opportunity" (avakāsa) of its own fruit because the fruit's existence depends on it. "Which" (yaṃ) means "by which cause." "One possessed of right view" (diṭṭhisampanno) refers to a noble disciple, a stream-enterer, possessed of the path-view. It is impossible for that noble disciple to regard any single formation (saṅkhāra) among the conditioned formations in the four planes as "permanent." "This is not possible" (netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati) means this cause does not exist, it cannot be found by knowledge. "That a worldling" (yaṃ puthujjano) means "by which cause a worldling (might regard)." "This is possible" (ṭhānametaṃ vijjati) means this cause exists. Indeed, a worldling, through the view of eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi), might regard any formation among the formations in the three planes as "permanent." However, a formation in the fourth plane (supramundane) is of intense power, and just as a red-hot iron ball that has been heated all day does not become a resting place for flies, it does not become an object for wrong view or other unwholesome states. In this way, the meaning should be understood in the passages such as "regarding any formation as pleasant," etc. "Might regard as pleasant" (sukhato upagaccheyya) is said with reference to the clinging to pleasure by the power of the self-view (attadiṭṭhi), such as "after death, the self is exclusively happy and free from disease." However, with a mind dissociated from wrong view, a noble disciple, when oppressed by the heat of defilements, might resort to (experience) some formation as pleasant in order to calm that heat, just as a brahmin desiring cleanliness might run into a cesspool when terrified by a rutting elephant. In the doctrine of self (attavāda), in order to include concepts such as kasiṇa, etc., the word "any state" (kañci dhammaṃ) is used instead of "formation" (saṅkhāra). Here too, the distinction should be understood by way of the four planes for the noble disciple and by way of the three planes for the worldling. Or, in all sections, the distinction by way of the three planes for the noble disciple is also appropriate. For whatever state the worldling regards (as permanent, etc.), the noble disciple dispels the clinging to that very state. Whatever state the worldling regards as permanent, pleasant, or self, the noble disciple, regarding it as impermanent (suffering, non-self), dispels the clinging.
406: An ordinary person (puthujjana) grasps (at things as permanent, pleasant, and self); from that grasping, the noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) unties the bond. Indeed, whatever an ordinary person grasps as permanent, pleasant, and self, the noble disciple, grasping it as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, unties the bond of attachment. In the words beginning with 'mother' (mātaraṃ), only the biological mother is called 'mother'. By 'arahant' (arahaṃ), only an Arahant who is a human being (khīṇāsava) is intended. Would a noble disciple deprive another being of the life faculty (jīvitindriya), other than their mother? This too is impossible. Even if a noble disciple who has reached another life and does not know their status as a noble disciple were told by someone, 'Deprive this insect of the life faculty and take the sovereignty of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) over the entire universe,' they would not deprive it of the life faculty. Or if they were told, 'If you do not kill this person, we will cut off your head,' they would rather have their own head cut off than kill that person. This is stated to show the grave fault of being an ordinary person and to demonstrate the power of a noble disciple. The intention here is this: the state of an ordinary person is blameworthy, for an ordinary person can even commit heinous crimes (ānantariya kamma) such as matricide. A noble disciple possesses great power; they do not commit these deeds. 'With a corrupt mind' (paduṭṭhena cittena) means a mind associated with hatred and the intent to kill. 'Causing blood to flow' (lohitam uppādeyya) means causing even as much blood as a small fly might drink to flow from the body of a living Buddha. 'Splitting the Sangha' (saṅghaṃ bhindeyya) means dividing the Sangha of the same communion (saṃvāsa) residing within the same boundary (sīmā) through five means. It is said: 'Upāli, the Sangha is split by five means: by a formal act (kamma), by the recitation (uddesa), by speaking (vohara), by proclamation (anussāvana), and by taking voting slips (salākaggāha).' Among those five, 'by a formal act' (kammema) means by any of the four types of formal acts such as an act of proposal (apalokana). 'By the recitation' (uddesena) means by any of the five recitations of the Pātimokkha. 'By speaking' (vohara) means explaining and pointing out the eighteen grounds for schism, such as 'what is not Dhamma is Dhamma,' based on various occurrences. 'By proclamation' (anussāvana) means making it known by whispering in the ear in this manner: 'Do you not know that I am one who went forth from a high-born family and am very learned? It is not proper for you even to think that someone like me would grasp what is not Dhamma or not Vinaya as the Teacher's instruction. Is Avīci hell as cool as a forest of blue lotuses (nīluppalavana) to me? Do I not fear the lower realms?' and so on.
407: ...by proclamation. 'By taking voting slips' (salākaggāha) means, after proclaiming in this way and supporting their minds to make them firm and unwavering, saying 'Take this voting slip.' Among these five, only the formal act (kamma) or the recitation (uddesa) is the decisive factor. Speaking, proclamation, and taking voting slips are merely the preliminary parts (of the act of splitting the Sangha). In truth, although a monk who speaks by pointing out the eighteen grounds makes a proclamation to generate preference for that view and has voting slips taken, the Sangha is not yet split. However, when four or more monks, having taken voting slips in this manner, perform a separate formal act or recitation, then the Sangha is said to be split. Thus, it is impossible for a person endowed with right view (a noble disciple) to split the Sangha. By this much, the five heinous crimes (ānantariya kamma) which an ordinary person commits but a noble disciple does not, such as matricide, have been shown. To clarify these heinous crimes: The decision should be understood by way of action (kamma), door (dvāra), duration of stay in hell (kappaṭṭhitiya), and likewise by the sharing of results (pākasādhāraṇa), etc. In that verse, first, the decision by way of 'action' (kamma) will be stated: In the matter of heinous crimes, for one who is a human being to deprive of life a mother or father who is also a human being, even if they have changed their gender (parivattaliṅga), that action is a heinous crime (ānantariya). Even if one fills the entire universe with golden stupas the size of the Great Stupa (Mahācetiya) with the intention of blocking the result of that heinous crime, or gives a great offering (mahādāna) to the Sangha of monks sitting and filling the entire universe, or walks behind the Blessed Buddha without letting go of the corner of his robe (saṅghāṭikaṇṇa), upon the breakup of the body (after death), they will surely be reborn in hell. However, if one who is a human being kills a mother or father who is an animal, or if one who is an animal kills a parent who is a human being, or if an animal kills an animal parent, that action does not constitute a heinous crime. Nevertheless, that action is very heavy and stands as if it were a heinous crime. This problem (decision) is taught in terms of human beings. Here, the tetrad of the sheep (eḷaka), the tetrad of the battle (saṅgāma), and the tetrad of the thief (cora) should be discussed. Indeed, even if one intends to kill a sheep, if they kill their human mother or father who is in the place of the sheep, they incur a heinous crime. However, if they kill a sheep with the intention of killing a sheep or with the intention of killing a parent, they do not incur a heinous crime. If they kill their parents with the intention of killing their parents, they certainly incur it. This is the method.
408:
In the other two tetrads (battlefield and thief), it should be understood in the same way. Just as with parents, these tetrads should be understood regarding Arahants as well. The *ānantariya-kamma* (an action with immediate retribution) is incurred only by killing a lay Arahant; killing a non-human (yakkha) Arahant does not incur *ānantariya-kamma*, but it is a grave kamma similar to *ānantariya-kamma*. Even if a weapon is used or poison is given while a future Arahant is still a worldling (*puthujjana*), if that person dies from that wound or poison after attaining Arahantship, it is indeed the killing of an Arahant (*arahantaghāta*). However, if an offering given while one was a worldling is consumed after attaining Arahantship, that offering is considered as given to a worldling only. For one who kills other noble persons (*ariya*), there is no *ānantariya-kamma*, but it is a grave kamma similar to *ānantariya-kamma*.

In the decision regarding causing the blood of a Tathāgata to flow (*lohituppāda*), because the Tathāgata has an unbreakable body, it is impossible for blood to flow by cutting the skin through another's effort. Blood only collects in one place within the body. A splinter of stone that broke off from the rock rolled down by Devadatta struck the Tathāgata's toe. Just as if struck by an axe, there was internal blood congestion within the foot. For one who does such an act, *ānantariya-kamma* is incurred. However, the physician Jīvaka, according to the Tathāgata's wish, cut the skin with a small knife, removed the bad blood from that place, and made Him comfortable. For one who does such an act, it is only a meritorious deed.

Now, what happens to those who, after the Tathāgata has attained Parinibbāna, destroy a shrine (*cetiya*), cut the Bodhi tree, or act against the relics? It is a grave kamma similar to *ānantariya-kamma*. However, it is permissible to cut a Bodhi branch that is obstructing a shrine or an image containing relics. Even if birds perched on that Bodhi branch drop excrement on the shrine, it is permissible to cut it. This is because a bodily shrine (*sarīra-cetiya*) is more noble than a shrine of use (*paribhoga-cetiya*). It is also permissible to cut and remove a Bodhi root that is destroying the foundation of a shrine. However, a Bodhi branch that is damaging a Bodhi-house (*bodhighara*) cannot be cut to protect the house. This is because the house is for the Bodhi tree, not the Bodhi tree for the house. The same principle applies to an image-house (*āsanaghara*). But if relics are enshrined in that image-house, it is permissible to cut the Bodhi branch to protect that house. It is certainly permissible to cut a branch that saps the nutrients or a decayed part to tend to the Bodhi tree; like tending to the Buddha's body, it is a meritorious deed.

In the decision regarding schism in the Saṅgha (*saṅghabheda*), for one who, before the Saṅgha within the boundary (*sīmā*) has assembled, takes a separate group and performs the act of proclamation and taking of voting tickets (*anussāvana-salākaggāha*), or recites the Pātimokkha...
409:
...for the person reciting the Pātimokkha, both the schism and the *ānantariya-kamma* occur. However, it is permissible to do so with the perception of harmony (*samagga-saññā*). This is because for one who acts with the perception of harmony, neither schism nor *ānantariya-kamma* occurs. Likewise, in an assembly of fewer than nine, schism and *ānantariya-kamma* do not occur. However, at the minimum limit, the monk who divides the Saṅgha among nine monks incurs *ānantariya-kamma*. For the followers who speak contrary to the Dhamma (*adhamma-vādī*), it is a kamma of great fault; those who speak according to the Dhamma (*dhamma-vādī*) are faultless. Regarding the schism of the Saṅgha among nine monks, there is this Sutta: 'Upāli, on one side there are four monks, and on the other side there are four; the ninth monk makes them hear the word of schism and makes them take the voting tickets, saying: "This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this view, approve of this view." In this way, Upāli, there is both a crack in the Saṅgha (*saṅgharāji*) and a schism in the Saṅgha (*saṅghabheda*). Upāli, for nine monks or more than nine monks, there is both a crack in the Saṅgha and a schism in the Saṅgha.' (Thus it is stated in the Cūḷavagga Pali).

Among these five *ānantariya-kammas*, the act of schism is a verbal action (*vaci-kamma*), and the remaining are bodily actions (*kāya-kamma*). Thus, the decision should be understood by way of action (*kamma*).

Regarding 'by way of doors' (*dvāra*), all these *ānantariya-kammas* arise through both the bodily door (*kāya-dvāra*) and the verbal door (*vaci-dvāra*). However, among these, the first four actions, though arising from the verbal door by power of command or magical means (*vijjāmaya-payoga*), fulfill only the bodily door. The act of schism, for one who causes schism by hand gestures, though arising from the bodily door, fulfills only the verbal door. Thus, the decision should be understood by way of doors.

Regarding 'by way of lasting for an aeon' (*kappaṭṭhitiya*), among these actions, only the act of schism has the result of lasting for an entire aeon. This is because, whether the schism is made while the aeon is being established or in the middle of the aeon, one is released from hell only when the aeon is destroyed. Even if one causes a schism today, thinking 'the aeon will be destroyed tomorrow,' one is released tomorrow, having been cooked in hell for only one day. However, such an occurrence is impossible. The remaining four actions are only *ānantariya-kammas* and do not have the result of lasting for an entire aeon. Thus, the decision should be understood by way of lasting for an aeon.

Regarding 'by way of ripening' (*pāka*), if a person has committed all five of these *ānantariya-kammas*, only the act of schism ripens in terms of rebirth (*paṭisandhi*). The remaining actions fall into the category of 'there was kamma but no ripening of kamma,' and so on. If there is no act of schism, the act of causing the blood of a Tathāgata to flow ripens; if that is absent, the act of killing an Arahant ripens. If the father is virtuous and the mother is not, the act of killing the father (*pitughāta*) ripens in terms of rebirth. If the mother is virtuous, the act of killing the mother (*mātughāta*) ripens. If both parents are equally virtuous or non-virtuous, only the act of killing the mother ripens in terms of rebirth. This is because the mother performs what is difficult to do and is of great benefit to the children. Thus, the decision should be understood by way of ripening.

Regarding 'by way of commonality' (*sādhāraṇa*), the first four actions are common to both laypeople and monks. As for the act of schism, according to the teaching 'Upāli, a (layperson) cannot divide the Saṅgha,' by the aforementioned distinction...
410:
If the father is virtuous and the mother is not, or vice versa, the act of killing the father (pitughātaka kamma) ripens by way of rebirth-linking [if the father is the virtuous one]. If the mother is virtuous, the act of killing the mother (mātughātaka kamma) ripens. If both parents are equal in being virtuous or lacking virtue, only the act of killing the mother ripens by way of rebirth-linking. This is because the mother is one who performs what is difficult and is of great assistance to her children. Thus, in this matter, the decision (vinicchaya) should be understood by way of the result as well.

Regarding the term 'sādhāraṇādīhi', the four previously mentioned ānantariya kammas are common (sādhāraṇa) to all, both householders and monastics. However, as for the act of causing a schism in the Saṅgha (saṅghabheda), according to the statement: "Upāli, a bhikkhunī does not split the Saṅgha, nor a sikkhamānā, nor a sāmaṇera, nor a sāmaṇerī, nor a male lay follower, nor a female lay follower. Upāli, it is a bhikkhu who is of natural status (pakatatta), who belongs to the same communion (samānasaṃvāsaka), and who stays within the same boundary (samānasīmā), who splits the Saṅgha," it occurs only in a bhikkhu of the described type and not in anyone else. Therefore, it is uncommon (asādhāraṇa). By the word 'ādi', it should be understood that all these kammas are accompanied by painful feeling and are associated with hatred and delusion; thus, the decision should be understood here by way of 'common' and so forth.

Regarding the term 'aññaṃ satthāraṃ' (another teacher): the meaning is that it is impossible for [a noble disciple] to take another sectarian teacher as 'This is my teacher' even in another life, thinking 'This teacher of mine is capable of performing the duties of a teacher.'

Regarding the term 'aṭṭhamaṃ bhavaṃ nibbattayya' (would produce an eighth birth): even a person of the dullest wisdom among all noble ones cannot surpass the seventh birth and produce an eighth birth. It is only with reference to the seventh birth as the ultimate limit that this person is described as 'niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo' (assured of enlightenment). What is it that makes that person fixed (niyāma)? Is it past causes (pubbahetu) that make them fixed, or the attained path (paṭiladdhamagga), or the three higher paths? This is merely a name designated by the Fully Enlightened One. As for the person, there is no such thing as 'fixed' [inherently]. For if it were said 'past causes make them fixed,' it would mean the sufficing condition (upanissaya) for the three higher paths is stated, and it would follow that there is no sufficing condition for the first path (sotāpatti-magga). In that case, it would arrive at a state of arising without cause or condition. If it were said 'the attained path makes them fixed,' the three higher paths would be without function, and only the first path would have a function; one would have to exhaust the defilements and attain parinibbāna by the first path alone. If it were said 'the three higher paths make them fixed,' the first path would be without function and only the three higher paths would have a function; one would have to produce the three higher paths without having produced the first path, and defilements would have to be exhausted without having arisen through the first path. Therefore, nothing else makes them fixed; only the insight (vipassanā) of the three higher paths makes them fixed. If their...
411:
...insight is sharp and courageous and carries through, they produce only one more birth, reach Arahantship, and attain parinibbāna. A person with wisdom duller than that reaches Arahantship and attains parinibbāna in the second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth birth. A person with the dullest wisdom among all [Stream-enterers] produces a seventh birth and reaches Arahantship; there is no rebirth-linking in an eighth birth. Thus, this taking of names such as 'sattakkhattuparama' and so forth by the Fully Enlightened One is merely a name. In truth, the Teacher, having weighed with the Buddha's scale and delimited with the knowledge of omniscience, saw: 'This person has great wisdom and sharp insight, and having produced only one more birth, will attain Arahantship,' and designated the name 'ekabījī'. Seeing: 'This person, having produced a second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth birth, will attain Arahantship,' He designated the name 'kolaṅkola'. Seeing: 'This person, having produced a seventh birth, will attain Arahantship,' He designated the name 'sattakkhattuparama'.

However, there is no person who is [inherently] fixed to seven births. A noble disciple, even if they are of dull wisdom for some reason, attains parinibbāna in between without reaching an eighth birth. Even a Stream-enterer like Sakka, who greatly delights in the round of rebirths, goes only to a seventh birth. In the seventh birth, even for a Stream-enterer who dwells negligently in every way, their insight-knowledge reaches maturity. They become weary even with a slight object and reach the peace of the exhaustion of defilements. Even if that Stream-enterer, while sleeping or while going out of sight in the seventh birth, were to have their head cut off by someone standing behind with a sharp sword, or were killed by being submerged in water, or if a thunderbolt were to fall on their head—even at such a time, there is no such thing as a death that is followed by rebirth; they attain parinibbāna only after reaching Arahantship. Therefore, it was said: 'That he should produce an eighth birth—this is impossible.'

Regarding 'ekissā lokadhātuyā' (in a single world system): it means in the ten-thousandfold world system. Indeed, there are three fields: the field of birth (jātikhetta), the field of authority (āṇākhetta), and the field of range (visayakhetta). Among these, the 'field of birth' is the ten-thousandfold world system. For it trembles at the time the Bodhisatta descends into his mother's womb, at the time of his birth (or his renunciation), at the time of his enlightenment, at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, at the relinquishing of the life-force, and at his parinibbāna. The hundred-thousand-crore universe is the 'field of authority'. For the authority of the Āṭānāṭiya, Mora, Dhajagga, and Ratana Parittas, etc., prevails in this hundred-thousand-crore universe. As for the 'field of range', there is no limit. For the Buddhas, as far as the range of knowledge extends, so far extends the range of the knowable; as far as the range of the knowable extends, so far...
412:
“Knowledge has the limit of the knowable, and the knowable has the limit of knowledge” (Paṭisambhidāmagga, Mahāvagga 3, 5). According to this statement, there is nothing that is not an object (of knowledge for the Buddhas).

Among these three fields, excluding this cakkavāဠa (world system), there is no Sutta stating that Buddhas arise in other cakkavāဠas; however, there are Suttas stating that they do not arise. There are three Piṭakas: Vinaya Piṭaka, Suttanta Piṭaka, and Abhidhamma Piṭaka. There are three Councils (Saṅgīti): the Council of the Elder Mahākassapa, the Council of the Elder Yasa, and the Council of the Elder Moggaliputtatissa. In the Buddha's words of the Tipitaka established in these three Councils, there is no Sutta stating that Buddhas arise in places other than this cakkavāဠa; however, there are Suttas stating that they do not arise.

“Apubbaṃ acarimaṃ” means not before and not after; they do not arise simultaneously, but they arise either before or after. In that context of “apubbaṃ acarimaṃ,” the period from the time of sitting on the Bodhi throne with the thought, “I shall not rise until I attain Enlightenment,” back to the time of taking conception in the mother's womb, should not be regarded as “before” (pubba). This is because, at the very moment of the Bodhisatta's conception, the birth-field (jātikhetta) is already demarcated by the shaking of the ten thousand cakkavāဠas, and the arising of another Buddha is already prevented. From the time of Parinibbāna as long as relics (dhātu) even the size of a mustard seed remain, it should not be regarded as “after” (pacchā). As long as the relics remain, the Buddhas remain. Therefore, within this interval, the arising of another Buddha is prevented; however, when the relics disappear and the Dhātu-parinibbāna occurs, the arising of another Buddha is no longer prevented.

There are three kinds of disappearance (antaradhāna): disappearance of Pariyatti (scriptures), disappearance of Paṭivedha (realization), and disappearance of Paṭipatti (practice). Therein, “Pariyatti” refers to the three Piṭakas; “Paṭivedha” refers to the penetration of the Truths; “Paṭipatti” refers to the path of practice (paṭipadā). Among these three, Paṭivedha and Paṭipatti may or may not exist. At one time, there were many monks capable of Paṭivedha, such that one had to point a finger and say, “This monk is a puthujjana (worldling).” It is said that once on this island of Sīhaဠa (Sri Lanka), there was not a single monk known as a puthujjana. Those who fulfill Paṭipatti are also sometimes many and sometimes few. Thus, Paṭivedha and Paṭipatti may or may not exist.

For the endurance of the Sasana, however, Pariyatti alone is the standard. A wise monk, having heard and learned the Tipitaka, can fulfill both Paṭivedha and Paṭipatti. Just as our Bodhisatta, after attaining the five supernormal powers and the seven attainments (samāpatti) in the presence of the ascetic Āဠāra, asked about the preliminary work (parikamma) for the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and that ascetic Āဠāra said, “I do not know.” Then...
413:
He went to the presence of the ascetic Udaka, and after comparing the special attainments he had reached, he asked about the preliminary work for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. That ascetic Udaka explained it, and immediately upon the conclusion of his words, the Bodhisatta accomplished that attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. In the same way, a wise monk, having heard the Pariyatti, can fulfill both Paṭipatti and Paṭivedha. Therefore, as long as Pariyatti remains, the Sasana remains.

However, when that Pariyatti disappears, first the Abhidhamma Piṭaka vanishes. Within the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the Paṭṭhāna is the first of all Abhidhamma texts to vanish. Following the order of the texts, the Dhammasaṅgaṇī vanishes last. Even when the Abhidhamma Piṭaka has vanished, as long as the remaining two Piṭakas, the Suttanta and the Vinaya, remain, the Sasana is still considered to remain.

Between those two Piṭakas, when the Suttanta Piṭaka vanishes, first the Aṅguttara Nikāya vanishes, starting from the Book of the Elevens down to the Book of the Ones. After that, the Saṃyutta Nikāya vanishes, starting from the Cakkapeyyāla Sutta down to the Oghataraṇa Sutta. After that, the Majjhima Nikāya vanishes, starting from the Indriyabhāvanā Sutta down to the Mūlapariyāya Sutta. After that, the Dīgha Nikāya vanishes, starting from the Dasuttara Sutta down to the Brahmajāla Sutta. Although questions in one or two verses (gāthā) may remain for a long time, they are not able to sustain the Sasana, like the Sabhiya-pucchā and the Āဠavaka-pucchā. It is said that those questions existed during the time of Kassapa Buddha, but they were unable to sustain the Sasana during the interval between Buddhas.

Even when the two Piṭakas have vanished, as long as the Vinaya Piṭaka remains, the Sasana remains. When the Parivāra and the Khandhakas vanish, if the Ubhatovibhaṅga remains, the Sasana is still considered to remain. When the Ubhatovibhaṅga vanishes, if the Mātikā remains, the Sasana is still considered to remain. When the Mātikā vanishes, as long as the Pātimokkha, the procedure for novice ordination (pabbajjā), and the procedure for higher ordination (upasampadā) remain, the Sasana remains. The outward appearance (liṅga) of a monk remains for a long time. However, the lineage of recluses wearing white clothes, which started from the time of Kassapa Buddha, was unable to sustain the Sasana. From the time of the last person's penetration of the Four Noble Truths, and from the time of the last monk's breach of virtue, the Sasana is said to have declined. From that time onwards, the arising of another Buddha is no longer prevented.

There are three kinds of Parinibbāna: Kilesa-parinibbāna (extinction of defilements), Khandha-parinibbāna (extinction of the aggregates), and Dhātu-parinibbāna (extinction of the relics). Among these three, Kilesa-parinibbāna occurred at the Bodhi throne, Khandha-parinibbāna occurred at Kusinārā, and Dhātu-parinibbāna will occur in the future. Of the Sasana...
414:
At the time of the decline of the Dispensation, the relics in this island of Tambapaṇṇi will gather and go to the Mahācetiya. From the Mahācetiya, they will go to the Rājāyatana Cetiya in Nāgadīpa, and from there to the Mahābodhi throne (Mahābodhi-pallaṅka). Relics from the Naga realm, the deva world, and the Brahma world will also go only to the Mahābodhi throne. Even a relic as small as a mustard seed will not be lost on the way. All those relics will gather at the Mahābodhi throne and, becoming a single solid mass like a great block of gold, they will emit six-colored rays.
