Those rays will pervade the ten thousand world systems. 

Then, the deities from the ten thousand universes will gather and, saying, "Today the Teacher attains Parinibbāna; today the Dispensation declines; this is now our final sight [of him]," they will show a grief even greater than on the day the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) attained Parinibbāna. Except for Non-returners (Anāgāmīs) and those whose taints are destroyed (Arahants), others will not be able to restrain themselves. The fire element (tejo-dhātu) will arise from the relics and ascend as far as the Brahma world. As long as there is a relic the size of a mustard seed, it will exist as a single flame, and only when the relics are completely consumed will that flame be extinguished. Having shown such great supernatural power, when the relics disappear, the Dispensation is said to have disappeared. As long as it has not disappeared in this way, it is called "not the last." That Buddhas should arise neither before nor after (simultaneously)—this is not possible.

Why do two Buddhas not arise simultaneously? Because it would not be marvelous or extraordinary. This is because Buddhas are extraordinary human beings. As the Blessed One said: "Monks, when one person arises in the world, he arises as an extraordinary man. Who is that one person? Monks, it is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One." If two, four, eight, or sixteen Buddhas were to arise at the same time, they would no longer be extraordinary. For example, just as in a single monastery, if there are two shrines, the offerings and honor are not grand; and because of the abundance of monks, they are not seen as extraordinary; so it would be if there were many Buddhas. Therefore, they do not arise simultaneously. 

Furthermore, there would be no distinction in the teaching. For the Dhamma consisting of the foundations of mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhāna) and so on, which one Buddha teaches, would have to be taught by another even if he arose. Thus, it would not be extraordinary. However, when only one Buddha teaches the Dhamma, the teaching is extraordinary. Also, it is because disputes might arise. If many Buddhas were to arise, the disciples of various teachers might argue, saying, "Our Buddha is more inspiring, our Buddha has a sweeter voice, is more gainful, has more merit." Therefore, they do not arise simultaneously.
415:
This matter has already been explained in detail by the Elder Nāgasena when questioned by King Milinda. In that Milindapañhā, it is said:

"Venerable Nāgasena, it was said by the Blessed One: 'It is impossible, monks, it cannot happen, that in a single world system two Arahants, Fully Enlightened Buddhas, should arise simultaneously—this is not possible.' Venerable Nāgasena, all Tathāgatas, when teaching the Dhamma, teach only the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (Bodhipakkhiyadhamma); when speaking, they speak only of the four Noble Truths (Ariya-sacca); when training, they train only in the three Trainings (Sikkhā); when instructing, they instruct only in the practice of heedfulness (Appamāda). Venerable Nāgasena, if the teaching, the words, the training, and the instruction of all Tathāgatas are the same, for what reason do two Tathāgatas not arise at the same time? By the arising of even one Buddha, this world becomes full of light. If a second Buddha were to arise, this world would become even more intensely illuminated by the radiance of the two Buddhas. If two Tathāgatas were to give advice, they could do so easily and happily; if they were to instruct, they could do so easily and happily. Please show me the reason for this so that I may be free from doubt."

"Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system can support only one Buddha; it supports the virtues of only one Tathāgata. If a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world system could not support him; it would shake, tremble, bend, sink, tilt, scatter, be dispersed, and destroyed; it would not remain in its place.

Great King, suppose there were a boat that could carry only one man. When one man boards, that boat would float evenly. Then, a second man, equal in age, appearance, stature, size, and limbs to the first man, were to come and board that boat. Great King, would that boat be able to carry both men?"

"No, venerable sir. It would shake, tremble, bend, sink, tilt, scatter, be dispersed, and destroyed; it would not remain in its place and would sink into the water."
416:
“It would sink in the water,” he replied. “Even so, Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system can support only one Buddha; it can support the virtues of only one Tathāgata. If a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world system could not support him; it would shake... [pe]... it would not remain stable.

Great King, for example, suppose a man were to eat as much delicious food as he desired, filling himself up to the throat. When that man is satiated, full, with no room for more, and feeling heavy and stiff like a wooden post from overeating, if he were to eat that same amount of food again, Great King, would that man be at ease?” “No, Bhante, he would die after just one more mouthful.” “Even so, Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system can support only one Buddha... [pe]... it would not remain stable.”

“Bhante Nāgasena, does the earth shake because of the excessive weight of the Dhamma?” “Great King, suppose there were two carts filled with jewels up to the brim. If one were to take the jewels from one cart and pour them into the other, Great King, would that cart be able to carry the weight of the jewels from both carts?” “No, Bhante, its hub would shake, its spokes would break, its rim would fall off, and its axle would break.” “Great King, is it not because of the excessive weight of the jewels that the cart breaks?” “Yes, Bhante.” “Even so, Great King, the earth shakes because of the excessive weight of the Dhamma.

Furthermore, Great King, this reason is given to demonstrate the power of the Buddhas. Hear another suitable reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not arise at the same time. Great King, if two Perfectly Enlightened Ones were to arise at the same time, a dispute would arise among their followers, saying, ‘Your Buddha, our Buddha,’ and they would split into two factions. Just as, Great King, a dispute might arise among the followers of two powerful ministers, saying, ‘Your minister, our minister,’ and they would split into two sides; even so, Great King, if two Perfectly Enlightened Ones were to arise at the same time, a dispute would arise among their followers...”
417:
“...(If two Buddhas were to arise at the same time), a dispute would arise, saying, ‘Your Buddha, our Buddha,’ and they would split into two factions. This, Great King, is one reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not arise at the same time.

Hear another even more superior reason, Great King, why two Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not arise at the same time. Great King, if two Perfectly Enlightened Ones were to arise at the same time, the statement ‘The Buddha is the Foremost (Agga)’ would become false. The statements ‘The Buddha is the Eldest (Jeṭṭha)’, ‘The Buddha is the Best (Seṭṭha)’, ‘The Buddha is the Most Distinguished (Visiṭṭha)’, ‘The Buddha is the Supreme (Uttama)’, ‘The Buddha is the Most Excellent (Pavara)’, ‘The Buddha is the Peerless (Asama)’, ‘The Buddha is the Equal of the Unequaled (Asamasama)’, ‘The Buddha is the Incomparable (Appaṭisama)’, ‘The Buddha is the Matchless (Appaṭibhāgī)’, and ‘The Buddha is the Unique Individual (Appaṭipuggala)’ would all become false. Great King, accept this reason as the truth why two Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not arise at the same time.

Moreover, Great King, it is the natural characteristic of the Blessed Buddhas that only one Buddha arises in the world. For what reason? Because of the greatness of the qualities of an Omniscient Buddha. Great King, whatever is great in the world is unique. Great King, the earth is great, and it is unique. The ocean is great, and it is unique. Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, is great, and it is unique. The sky is great, and it is unique. Sakka is great, and he is unique. Mahābrahmā is great, and he is unique. Likewise, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is great, and He is unique in the world. Where these arise, there is no room for others. Therefore, Great King, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, arises as the only one in the world.”

“Bhante Nāgasena, the question has been well answered with similes and reasons,” the King replied.
418:
“In a single world-element” means in a single universe (cakkavāḷa). Below, by this very term, ten thousand universes are included. It is appropriate to define those ten thousand universes as a single universe. Indeed, when Buddhas arise, they arise only in this universe. Since the place of arising is restricted (to this universe), it is already prohibited that they arise in universes other than this one.

“Neither before nor after” (apubbaṃ acarimaṃ): in this phrase, “before” refers to the time prior to the appearance of the Wheel-treasure (cakkaratana), and “after” refers to the time following its disappearance. In this context, the disappearance of the Wheel-treasure occurs in two ways: either by the death of the Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) or by his renunciation. When that Wheel-treasure disappears, it vanishes on the seventh day from the day of death or the day of renunciation. After such disappearance, the appearance of a new Universal Monarch is not prohibited.

Why do two Universal Monarchs not arise simultaneously in a single universe? It is to prevent disputes, because it would not be marvelous, and because of the great power of the Wheel-treasure. Indeed, if two Universal Monarchs were to appear, disputes might arise, such as “Our king is great, our king is great.” Furthermore, if there were “a Universal Monarch on one island, and a Universal Monarch on another island,” it would no longer be marvelous. Moreover, the great power of the Wheel-treasure, which is capable of granting sovereignty over the four great islands together with their two thousand surrounding small islands, would diminish. Thus, to prevent disputes, because it would not be marvelous, and because of the great power of the Wheel-treasure, two Universal Monarchs do not appear simultaneously in a single universe.

“That a woman should be an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha”: in this statement, let alone the state of Buddhahood which is capable of delivering the world from the round of rebirths by producing qualities such as omniscience, even the mere aspiration (paṇidhāna) to become a Buddha cannot be fulfilled by a woman.

“The meeting of eight factors—being human, being male, having sufficient causes (tihetu), meeting a living Teacher, renunciation, possession of attainments (jhāna and abhiññā), extreme dedication, and strong desire—makes the aspiration successful.”

These are the causes for the fulfillment of the aspiration. For a woman who cannot even fulfill this aspiration, how could Buddhahood be possible? Therefore, it is said: “It is impossible, it cannot happen, that a woman should be an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha.” Alternatively, since a mass of merit that is complete in every aspect can only produce a physical form that is complete in every aspect, only a man can be an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha.
419:
“A woman might be a Wheel-turning Monarch,” and so on. In these statements, because a woman lacks the marks such as the ensheathed male organ (kosohitavatthaguyha), her marks are not complete. Because she is a “woman-treasure” (itthiratana), she cannot attain the state of being endowed with the seven treasures. Her physical form cannot be superior to all humans. Therefore, it is said: “It is impossible, it cannot happen, that a woman could be a Wheel-turning Monarch.” Since the three positions such as that of Sakka are also supreme, and the female gender is inferior, those positions such as that of Sakka are also prohibited for a woman.

Is it not the case that just as there is no female gender in the Brahma world, there is also no male gender? Therefore, should it not also be said: “That a man should exercise the role of a Brahmā—this is possible”? No, it should not be said so. Why? Because a man from this world is reborn in that Brahma realm. “The role of a Brahmā” refers to the status of a Great Brahma (Mahābrahmā). A woman, having developed jhāna in this life, can be reborn among the retinue of Brahma (brahmapārisajja) after death, but not as a Great Brahma. However, it cannot be said that a man is not born in that Great Brahma realm. Although both genders are absent there, the Brahmas have only a male appearance, not a female appearance. Therefore, this statement is well-spoken.

“Of bodily misconduct...”, and so on. Just as the seeds of the neem or the bitter melon do not produce sweet fruit, but produce only unpleasant and non-sweet fruit, likewise, bodily misconduct and so on do not produce sweet results, but produce only non-sweet results. And just as the seeds of sugarcane or hill-paddy produce only sweet and delicious fruit, and not unpleasant or bitter fruit, likewise, bodily good conduct and so on produce only sweet results, and not non-sweet results. It has also been said:

“According to the seed that is sown, so is the fruit that is reaped. The doer of good reaps good, and the doer of evil reaps evil.”

Therefore, it is said: “It is impossible, it cannot happen, that bodily misconduct (should result in a pleasant result)...”, and so on.

“One endowed with bodily misconduct,” and so on. “Endowment” (samangitā) is of five kinds: possession by accumulation (āyūhana-samangitā), possession by volition (cetanā-samangitā), possession by kamma (kamma-samangitā), possession by result (vipāka-samangitā), and possession by appearance (upaṭṭhāna-samangitā). Among these, the moment of striving for wholesome or unwholesome kamma is called “possession by accumulation.” “Possession by volition” is the same. As long as they have not reached Arahantship, all beings are called “endowed with kamma” (kamma-samangī) with reference to the kamma accumulated in the past that is liable to give results; this is “possession by kamma.” “Possession by result,” however, should be understood only at the moment of the result's fruition. As long as beings have not reached Arahantship...
420:
For those who, having passed away from various existences, are to be reborn in hell, the sign of hell appears through manifestations such as flames and large iron cauldrons. For those to be conceived in a mother's womb, the mother's womb appears. For those to be reborn among the devas, the deva world appears through manifestations such as wish-fulfilling trees and celestial mansions. Thus, the sign of rebirth (upapattinimitta) appears. Because these beings cannot escape from this appearance of the sign of rebirth, it is called 'possession of appearance' (upaṭṭhānasamaṅgitā). This possession of appearance is unstable; the remaining types of possession are stable. Indeed, even when the sign of hell has appeared, the sign of the deva world can change and appear. Even when the sign of the deva world has appeared, the sign of hell can change and appear. Even when the sign of the human world has appeared, the sign of the animal realm can appear. And even when the sign of the animal realm has appeared, the sign of the human world can indeed change and appear.

Regarding this change of signs, there is this story: It is said that at the Acela Monastery at the foot of Mount Soṇa, there was a Dhamma preacher named Elder Soṇa. His father was a hunter who bred dogs. Although the Elder tried to restrain him, he was unable to establish him in restraint. Thinking, "May this poor old man not perish," he had him ordained as a monk in his old age, even against his will. While that old monk was lying on his sickbed, the sign of hell appeared. Large dogs from the foot of Mount Soṇa seemed to come and surround him as if wanting to bite and eat him. Being terrified with great fear, he said, "Dear Soṇa, stop them! Dear Soṇa, stop them!" When asked, "Why, Venerable Sir?", he replied, "Dear son, don't you see?" and told him what was happening.

Elder Soṇa thought, "How could the father of someone like me be reborn in hell? I shall be a refuge for him." He had novices bring various flowers and arranged flower offerings and seat offerings at the courtyard of the stupa and the courtyard of the Bodhi tree. He had his father carried to the stupa courtyard on a couch, and while he was lying on the couch, the Elder said, "Venerable Sir, this offering has been made for your sake. Say, 'O Blessed One, this is my humble gift,' and having paid homage to the Blessed One, inspire faith in your heart." Seeing the offering and doing as instructed, the old monk inspired faith in his heart. Immediately, the sign of the deva world appeared to him. It was as if the Nandavana, Cittalata, Missaka, and Phārusaka gardens, celestial mansions, and celestial dancers stood surrounding him. He said, "Move aside, Soṇa! Move aside, Soṇa!" When asked, "Why is this, Venerable Sir?", he replied, "Dear son, these mothers of yours are coming." The Elder thought, "The sign of heaven has appeared to the Great Elder."
421:
(The Elder) thought, "It has appeared." Thus, it should be understood that the possession of appearance is unstable. Among these possessions, in this context, by way of the possession of accumulation (āyūhanasamaṅgitā), the possession of volition (cetanāsamaṅgitā), and the possession of kamma (kammasamaṅgitā), it is said, "one possessed of bodily misconduct," and so forth. In all the Suttas, the remaining meaning is clear.

## Explanation of the First Power (Paṭhamabalaniddesavaṇṇanā)

## The Second Power (Dutiyabalaniddesa)

In the description of the second power, "prevented by the success of destination" (gatisampattipaṭibāḷhāni) means those (kammas) that are prevented, rejected, or blocked by the success of destination. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Here, "success of destination" (gatisampatti) refers to a successful and good destination, namely the world of devas and Brahmas, and the human world. "Failure of destination" (gativipatti) refers to the failed destinations, the four woeful states. "Success of physical form" (upadhisampatti) refers to the perfection of the physical body. "Failure of physical form" (upadhivipatti) refers to having an inferior physical body. "Success of time" (kālasampatti) refers to a successful time, known as the time of good kings and good people. "Failure of time" (kālavipatti) refers to a failed time, known as the time of bad kings and bad people. "Success of effort" (payogasampatti) refers to right effort. "Failure of effort" (payogavipatti) refers to wrong effort.

Among these, such as success of destination, a certain person may have many evil kammas. Those evil kammas would ripen in the continuum of one established in a failure of destination; however, that person, due to a single wholesome kamma, is reborn in a success of destination, either among devas or humans. In such a place, there is no turn for the ripening of unwholesome kamma; indeed, it is only the turn for the ripening of wholesome kamma. Thus, He knows that those unwholesome kammas of that person are prevented by the success of destination and do not ripen.

Another person also has many evil kammas. Those evil kammas would ripen in the continuum of one established in a failure of physical form; however, that person, due to a single wholesome kamma, is established in a success of physical form, possessing well-proportioned limbs, an excellent appearance, and is beautiful to behold, having a physical form like that of a Brahma. Even if he is born as a slave from the womb of a slave woman, people think, "Such a physical form is not suitable for dirty work," and they do not make him do tasks such as being an elephant trainer, horse trainer, or cowherd. They clothe him in fine garments and place him in positions such as a treasurer. If it is a woman, they do not make her cook food for elephants and so forth. Giving her clothes and ornaments, they make her a guardian of the bed or place her in a position of a favorite, like Somadevī.

It is heard that during the reign of King Bhātika, many people who ate beef were captured and presented to the King. When asked, "Are you able to pay the fine?", they replied, "We are not able, Your Majesty." Then, the King made them scavengers in the palace courtyard. Among them, one daughter was beautiful, lovely to behold, and inspiring of joy. Seeing that maiden, the King took her into the palace and placed her in the position of a favorite. The remaining relatives also lived happily due to the influence of that maiden. Indeed, in such a physical form, evil kammas are unable to ripen. Thus, He knows that (evil kammas) are prevented by the success of physical form and do not ripen.

A person has many evil kammas. Those kammas would ripen in the continuum of one established in a failure of time; however, that person, due to a single wholesome kamma, (is born) at the time of the first people of the aeon, or at the time of a Cakkavatti King, or at the time when Buddhas appear...
422:
They were presented to the king. When asked, "Are you able to administer punishment?" they replied, "We are not able." Then, they were made to be sweepers in the royal courtyard. Among them, one daughter was very beautiful, lovely, and pleasing to behold. Upon seeing that maiden, the king took her into the inner palace and placed her in the position of a favorite. The remaining relatives also lived happily due to her influence. Indeed, in such a physical existence (attabhāva), evil kammas are unable to produce their results. Thus, he understands that unwholesome kammas obstructed by physical excellence (upadhi-sampatti) do not ripen.

A person may have many evil kammas. Those deeds would ripen for one who exists in a failure of time (kāla-vipatti). However, due to a single wholesome kamma, that person is born in the time of the first inhabitants of the world, or in the time of a Wheel-turning King, or in the time when Buddhas appear—a time of good kings and good people. For one born in such a time, there is no opportunity for unwholesome kamma to give its result; indeed, there is only the opportunity for wholesome kamma. Thus, he understands that unwholesome kammas obstructed by the excellence of time (kāla-sampatti) do not ripen.

Another person also has many evil kammas. Those deeds would ripen for one who exists in a failure of effort (payoga-vipatti). However, due to a single wholesome kamma, that person exists in the excellence of effort (payoga-sampatti), refraining from taking life and so on, and fulfilling good conduct in body, speech, and mind. In such a state, there is no opportunity for unwholesome kamma to ripen; indeed, there is only the opportunity for wholesome kamma. Thus, he understands that unwholesome kammas obstructed by the excellence of effort (payoga-sampatti) do not ripen.

Another person also has many evil kammas. Those deeds would not ripen for one who exists in the excellence of destination (gati-sampatti). However, due to a single evil kamma, that person is born in a failure of destination (gati-vipatti). There, those evil kammas approach and give their results turn by turn. Sometimes they cause rebirth in hell, sometimes in the animal realm, sometimes in the realm of hungry ghosts (petas), and sometimes in the realm of asuras. For a long time, they do not allow one to lift one's head from the states of deprivation (apāya). Thus, he understands that unwholesome kammas, which were unable to give results because they were obstructed by the excellence of destination (gati-sampatti), ripen upon reaching a failure of destination (gati-vipatti).

Another person also has many evil kammas. Those deeds would not ripen for one who exists in physical excellence (upadhi-sampatti). However, due to a single evil kamma, that person is established in physical failure (upadhi-vipatti), being of bad complexion, ugly, ill-formed, loathsome, and resembling a ghost. If that person were born as a slave from the womb of a slave woman, thinking, 'These tasks are suitable for this person,' all the dirty tasks to that person...
423:
...they make [that person] perform dirty tasks, starting from the lowest work of a scavenger. If it is a woman, thinking, 'These tasks are suitable for this woman,' they make her perform all dirty tasks such as cooking elephant fodder and so on. Even if born in a noble family, royal officials collecting taxes, perceiving her as a 'house-slave,' seize and mistreat her as they go, like the wife of the great householder in the village of Kotalavāpī. Thus, he understands that unwholesome kammas, which were unable to give results because they were obstructed by physical excellence (upadhi-sampatti), ripen upon reaching physical failure (upadhi-vipatti).

Another person also has many evil kammas. Those deeds would not ripen for one born in the excellence of time (kāla-sampatti). However, due to an evil kamma, that person is born in a failure of time (kāla-vipatti), a time of bad kings and bad people, a time of scarcity and lack of essence, when the lifespan is only ten years. At that time, the five bovine flavors are cut off, and kudrūsaka grain becomes the highest food. Although born in the human world, one lives like wild animals and beasts. In such a time, there is no opportunity for wholesome kamma to ripen, but only for unwholesome kamma. Thus, he understands that unwholesome kammas, which were unable to give results because they were obstructed by the excellence of time (kāla-sampatti), ripen upon reaching a failure of time (kāla-vipatti).

Another person also has many evil kammas. Those deeds would not ripen for one who exists in the excellence of effort (payoga-sampatti). However, existing in a failure of effort (payoga-vipatti), that person commits the ten unwholesome kammas such as taking life and so on. People seize him along with the stolen goods and present him to the king. The king inflicts many tortures and has him killed. Thus, he understands that unwholesome kammas, which were unable to give results because they were obstructed by the excellence of effort (payoga-sampatti), ripen upon reaching a failure of effort (payoga-vipatti). In this way, an evil kamma obstructed by the four excellences (sampatti) does not yet give its result, but gives its result upon reaching the four failures (vipatti).

For example, a certain man pleases the king through some deed. Then the king gives him a rank and a province to govern. Being unable to manage that province properly, he ruins it like a monkey ruining a packet of rice it has obtained. Whenever he sees anyone's fine vehicle, mount, male slave, female slave, garden, or land, he seizes them all by force. The people, thinking, 'This man is a royal favorite,' are unable to say anything. That man offends another high official who is even more of a favorite of the king. That high official seizes him, has him severely beaten, has him dragged out with his back rubbing against the ground, and approaching the king, says, 'Such and such a person...'
424:
“Your Majesty, this man is destroying your district,” they would say and have him arrested. The King would have him imprisoned and then have a drum beaten throughout the city, asking, “What property of whose has this person named so-and-so stolen?” People would come, and thousands of cries would arise: “He took this property of mine! He took this property of mine!” The King, becoming exceedingly angry, would cause that man to suffer in prison in various ways, have him executed, and then say, “Go, discard his corpse in the cemetery and bring back the iron shackles.” This should be understood according to this simile.

The time when a worldling (puthujjana) is reborn in heaven due to some meritorious deed should be understood as being like the time when that man pleased the King with some deed and received a high position. The time when unwholesome kamma finds no opportunity to ripen while he is in heaven should be understood as being like the time when he was destroying the district and taking people's property, and no one was able to say anything. The time when he passes away from heaven and is reborn in hell should be understood as being like the time when he offended a minister who was more favored by the King, and that angry minister had him beaten, reported him to the King, and had him imprisoned. The time when all unwholesome kammas gather to produce results when he is reborn in hell should be understood as being like the time when people cried out, “He took this property of mine!” The time when he suffers in hell for a whole aeon (kappa), unable to lift his head from hell due to the results of various kammas even when one kamma is exhausted, should be understood as being like the time when he was discarded in the cemetery and the shackles were brought back. Indeed, beings who perform kamma that lasts for an aeon and suffer in hell for a whole aeon are not just one, two, a hundred, or a thousand. Such beings suffering in hell are numerous beyond counting.

In passages such as “Some wholesome kammas are obstructed by failure of destination (gati-vipatti) and do not ripen,” the meaning should be understood in this same way. In this world, some person has many wholesome kammas. Those kammas would ripen when he is in the attainment of destination (gati-sampatti). However, due to one unwholesome kamma, he is reborn in a failure of destination, such as hell or the realm of asuras. In such a place, wholesome kamma is unable to produce its result; only unwholesome kamma is consistently able to produce results. Thus, it is understood that his wholesome kammas are obstructed by failure of destination and do not ripen.

Another person has many wholesome kammas. Those kammas would ripen when he is in the attainment of physical form (upadhi-sampatti). However, due to one unwholesome kamma, he is established in the failure of physical form (upadhi-vipatti) and becomes ugly like a demon (pisāca). Even if he is born into a royal family, when his father passes away, they say, “What is the use of this inglorious prince as king?” and he does not obtain the kingship. Even if born in the house of a general, etc., he does not obtain the position of a general. To clarify this meaning, the story of King Dīpa should be told. It is heard that when a prince was born, the King, being pleased with the Queen, gave her a boon. The Queen took the boon and kept it. When the prince was seven or eight years old, he engaged in cockfighting in the royal courtyard. A cock flew up and pecked out both of the prince's eyes. When the prince was fifteen or sixteen, the Queen Mother, wishing to claim the kingship for him, approached the King and said, “Your Majesty, you gave a boon when the prince was born. I kept that boon and now I wish to take it.” The King said, “Very well, Queen, take it.”
425:
When his father passes away, they say, “What is the use of this inglorious person as king?” and he does not obtain the kingship. Even if born in the house of a general, etc., he does not obtain the position of a general.

To clarify this meaning, the story of King Dīpa should be told. It is heard that when a prince was born, the King, being pleased with the Queen, gave her a boon. The Queen took the boon and kept it. When the prince was seven or eight years old, he had cocks fight in the royal courtyard. A cock flew up and pecked out the prince's eyes. When the prince was fifteen or sixteen, his mother, the Queen, thinking, “I will request the kingship,” approached the King and said, “Your Majesty, you gave a boon when the prince was born. I have kept that boon and now I wish to take it.” The King said, “Very well, Queen, take it.” She said, “Your Majesty, there is nothing I have not received from you. But now, please give the kingship to my son.” The King said, “Queen, your son is physically deformed. It is not possible to give him the kingship.” She replied, “Why did you give a boon if you are unable to give the boon I desire?” The King, being greatly pressured, said, “It is not possible to give your son the kingship over the whole of Lankādīpa. However, let him live in Nāgadīpa with the white parasol raised.” He sent him to Nāgadīpa. He became known as King Dīpa. If his eyes had not been destroyed, he would have obtained the kingship with all its wealth and retinue over the whole of Tambapaṇṇidīpa, which is three hundred leagues (yojana) in extent. Thus, it is understood that wholesome deeds obstructed by failure of physical form (upadhi-vipatti) do not ripen.

Another person has many wholesome kammas. Those kammas would ripen for one who is in the attainment of time (kāla-sampatti). However, due to one unwholesome kamma, he is born in the failure of time (kāla-vipatti), a time of bad kings and wicked people, a time that is worthless, lacking essence, short-lived, and at the end of a destination. In such a time, wholesome kamma is unable to produce its result. Thus, it is understood that wholesome deeds obstructed by failure of time (kāla-vipatti) do not ripen.

Another person has many wholesome kammas. Those kammas would ripen for one who is in the attainment of effort (payoga-sampatti). However, this person remains in the failure of effort (payoga-vipatti), practicing all forms of immorality such as killing living beings. Consequently, even families of the same caste do not enter into marriage alliances with him. People avoid him from afar, saying, “This is a wicked man, a womanizer, a drunkard, and a gambler.” Wholesome kammas are unable to ripen. Thus, it is understood that wholesome deeds obstructed by failure of effort (payoga-vipatti) do not ripen. In this way, the four...
426: Wholesome kamma that is capable of producing results upon reaching [the right] successes (sampatti) does not ripen because it is obstructed by the four failures (vipatti). Another person may also have many wholesome kammas. Those kammas would not ripen for one who is in a failure of destination (gati-vipatti). However, that person, due to a single wholesome kamma, is born in a success of destination (gati-sampatti). There, those [other] kammas reach him and give results in turn—sometimes causing rebirth in the human world, sometimes in the deva world. Thus, he knows that wholesome kammas which were unable to give results because they were obstructed by a failure of destination, ripen upon reaching a success of destination. Another person may also have many wholesome kammas. Those kammas would not ripen for one who is in a failure of physical appearance (upadhi-vipatti). However, that person, due to a single wholesome kamma, is established in a success of physical appearance (upadhi-sampatti), becoming handsome, attractive, pleasant to behold, and having an appearance like a Brahmā. Because he is established in a success of physical appearance, his wholesome kammas give results. If he is born into a royal family, even if there are other elder brothers, [people] consult, saying, 'This prince's physical form is perfect; if the white umbrella is raised for this prince, the happiness of the people will come to be,' and they consecrate only him as king. One born in the house of a viceroy and so on, upon the death of his father, receives the position of viceroy, general, treasurer, or merchant. Thus, he knows that wholesome kammas which were unable to give results because they were obstructed by a failure of physical appearance, ripen upon reaching a success of physical appearance. Another person may also have many wholesome kammas. Those kammas would not ripen for one who is in a failure of time (kāla-vipatti). However, that person, due to a single wholesome kamma, is born in a success of time (kāla-sampatti) when there are good kings and good people. For one born in such a success of time, wholesome kamma gives results. In this regard, the story of Mahāsoṇa Thera should be told—it is said that during the peril of Brahman Tissa, twelve thousand monks resided at Cittalapabbata. Likewise, [twelve thousand monks resided] at Tissamahāvihāra. In both great monasteries, large rats ate the three-year supply of grain (vatta) in a single night, leaving only the husks. The Saṅgha of monks at Cittalapabbata consulted, 'The grain supply will be available at Tissamahāvihāra; let us go and stay there,' and they left the monastery. The Saṅgha of monks at Tissamahāvihāra also consulted, 'The grain supply will be available at Cittalapabbata; let us go and stay there,' and they left the monastery.
427: The two groups of monks met on the bank of a deep ravine and, upon inquiring, learned that the grain supply was exhausted. Thinking, 'What shall we do by going to those monasteries?' the twenty-four thousand monks entered the forest of the deep ravine, sat down, and in that very sitting posture, attained Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder. Later, when the perils had subsided, the Saṅgha of monks brought Sakka, the King of Devas, collected the relics, and built a stupa. The rebel Brahman Tissa also destroyed the countryside. The Saṅgha assembled and consulted, then sent eight elders to Sakka to say, 'Please ward off the rebel.' Sakka, the King of Devas, said, 'Venerable sirs, I am unable to ward off the rebel who has arisen. Let the Saṅgha go to the other side of the ocean. I will provide protection on the ocean.' The Saṅgha went from all directions to Nāgadīpa and, at the port of Jambukola, had a three-story raft constructed. One level of the raft was submerged in the water. The Saṅgha of monks stayed on one level, and their bowls and robes were placed on another level. Three elders—the Saṃyutta-reciter Cūḷasīva Thera, Isidatta Thera, and Mahāsoṇa Thera—were the leaders of that assembly. Among them, two elders said to Mahāsoṇa Thera, 'Friend Mahāsoṇa, board the great raft.' Mahāsoṇa Thera asked, 'Will you not go, venerable sirs?' They replied, 'Friend, whether dying in the water or dying on land, it is the same. We will not follow. But depending on you, the lineage of the Sāsana will endure in the future. Go, friend.' Although he spoke up to three times, saying, 'Venerable sirs, if you do not go, I will not go either,' they were unable to make the elder board the raft, and they turned back. Then Cūḷasīva Thera said to Isidatta Thera, 'Friend Isidatta, in the future, the lineage of the Sāsana will endure depending on Mahāsoṇa Thera; do not let him go from your hands.' When asked, 'Will you not go, venerable sir?' he replied, 'I will worship the Mahācetiya.' After instructing the two elders, he traveled by stages and reached Mahāvihāra. At that time, Mahāvihāra was empty of monks. Castor oil plants were growing on the courtyard of the stupa, and the stupa was surrounded by creepers and covered with moss. The elder, as if showing the utmost respect to the living Buddha, worshipped the Mahācetiya, entered the rest house on the western side, and while looking out, sat down thinking, 'The site of the stupa for the bodily relics of the Blessed One, who reached the pinnacle of gain and fame, has indeed become desolate.'
428: At that time, a tree deity residing in a nearby tree, taking the form of a traveler and carrying a measure of rice and a lump of jaggery, approached the Elder and asked, "Venerable Sir, where are you going?" "Lay follower, I am going to the southern region," he replied. "Venerable Sir, I also wish to go to that southern region; let us go together," the deity said. "Lay follower, I am weak (having no strength as I have not eaten); I will not be able to keep up with your pace. You go on ahead," the Elder said. "I will also travel at your pace, Venerable Sir," the deity replied and took the Elder's bowl and robes. When they climbed the embankment of Tissavāpī, the deity asked for the bowl, prepared a drink, and offered it. As soon as the Elder drank it, some strength returned to him. The deity, shrinking the earth, reached an abandoned monastery near the Veṇu River, and having cleaned and prepared a place for the Elder to stay, offered it to him. On the following day, as soon as the Elder had washed his face, the deity cooked and offered gruel. After the gruel was finished, he cooked and offered rice. The Elder said, "Lay follower, keep some for yourself," and covered the bowl with his hand. "I do not have to go far," the deity replied, and placed the rice only in the Elder's bowl. After the meal was finished, he took the Elder's bowl and robes, and while traveling, he shrunk the earth and brought him near the Jajjara River. He said, "Venerable Sir, this is the dwelling place of the leaf-eating people; smoke can be seen. I shall go on ahead," and having paid homage to the Elder, returned to his own abode. The Elder lived depending on those leaf-eating people throughout the period of danger. The Venerable Isidatta Thera, wandering on his journey in due course, arrived at Aḷajanapada. In that district, people were splitting not-too-ripe Madhuka fruits, taking the seeds, and discarding the skins before leaving. The Elder said, "Friend Mahāsoṇa, alms-food has been found," and having his bowl and robes brought, he donned his robes, took out his bowl, and stood there. Seeing the Elder standing, the young boys thought, "There must be some benefit for this Venerable One," and having cleared away the sand, they put the Madhuka fruit skins into the bowl and offered them. The Elders partook of them. For seven days, those Madhuka fruit skins were their only food. In due course, they reached Coriyassara. People were taking Kumuda lotuses and discarding the lotus stalks before leaving. The Elder said, "Friend Mahāsoṇa, alms-food has been found," and having his bowl and robes brought, he donned his robes, took out his bowl, and stood there. The village boys cleaned the lotus stalks, put them into the bowl, and offered them. The Elders partook of them. For seven days, those lotus stalks were their only food.
429: Wandering in due course, those Venerable Ones arrived at a village gate in the dwelling place of the leaf-eating people. In that village, the parents of a young girl, while going to the forest, had instructed her, "Dear daughter, if any Venerable One should come, do not allow him to go elsewhere; tell the Venerable One about our dwelling place." Seeing the Elders, the girl took their bowls and invited them to sit. There was no grain of any kind in the house. However, taking a small knife, she pounded the bark of the Guñjā tree and the wild banana tree together with Guñjā vines and leaves, made three lumps, and placed one in the bowl of the Venerable Isidatta Thera and one in the bowl of the Venerable Mahāsoṇa Thera. Thinking, "I will place the extra lump in the bowl of the Venerable Isidatta Thera," she extended her hand. Her hand turned back and placed it only in the bowl of the Venerable Mahāsoṇa Thera. The Venerable Isidatta Thera said, "During the danger of Brāhmaṇatissa, how much fruit will this karma of offering these lumps of Guñjā and banana bark yield when the place and time are fulfilled?" Having partaken of those lumps, the Venerable Ones went to their dwelling place. The girl also told her parents when they returned from the forest, "Two Elders have arrived. I have told those Venerable Ones about our dwelling place." Both parents went to the Elders, paid homage, and requested, "Venerable Sirs, we will look after you with whatever food we obtain; please stay right here," and received their consent. The Elders lived depending on those people throughout the period of danger. When the rebel Brāhmaṇatissa died, King Pitumahārāja raised the white parasol and ascended the throne. Hearing that "The danger has subsided, and the country is prosperous again," the community of monks from across the ocean arrived by boat at the port of Mahātittha and asked, "Where does the Venerable Mahāsoṇa Thera reside?" and went to the Elder. The Elder, accompanied by five hundred monks, arrived at the Maṇḍalārāma Monastery in Kālakagāma. At that time, about seven hundred families resided in Kālakagāma. During the night, deities wandered about and told the people, "The Venerable Mahāsoṇa Thera has arrived at the Maṇḍalārāma Monastery with an entourage of five hundred monks. Let each person give alms-food worth one kahāpaṇa along with a nine-cubit cloth." On the following day, the Elders entered Kālakagāma for alms. The people invited them to sit and offered gruel. The Venerable Tissabhūti, who resided at Maṇḍalārāma, sat as the Elder of the Sangha. A great lay follower paid homage to him and asked, "Venerable Sir, which one is the Venerable Mahāsoṇa Thera?" At that time, the Elder was a junior monk sitting at the end of the line. The Venerable Tissabhūti extended his hand and said, "Mahāsoṇa..."
430: Elder Tissabhūti said, "Lay devotee, this person is named [Mahāsoṇa]." The lay devotee bowed to the Elder and reached for the bowl. The Elder did not give it. Elder Tissabhūti said, "Friend Soṇa, just as you do not know, we also do not know in this way. For those with merit, deities prepare [the recipient]. Give the bowl; perform an act of kindness for your fellow practitioners." The Elder gave the bowl. That great lay devotee took the bowl, filled it with alms-food worth one kahāpaṇa, made a base with a nine-cubit cloth, brought it back, and placed it in the Elder's hand. Another lay devotee also took the bowl of another monk, filled it with alms-food worth one kahāpaṇa, made a base with a nine-cubit cloth, brought it back, and placed it in the Elder's hand as well. In this way, the lay devotees offered seven hundred cloths and seven hundred portions of alms-food to the Elder alone. The Elder distributed them among the community of monks and eventually reached the Mahāvihāra. Having washed his face, paid homage to the Great Bodhi tree, and venerated the Great Stūpa (Mahācetiya), he stood at Thūpārāma and donned his robes. Surrounded by the community of monks, he entered the city through the South Gate. Between the gate and the Valañjanaka Hall, he received alms-food worth sixty kahāpaṇas. From that time on, there was no limit to the offerings and honors. Thus, during a time of adversity (kālavipatti), even the rind of a madhuka fruit and the stalks of a white water-lily were hard to find. But in a time of prosperity (kālasampatti), such great gain arose. During the time of Elder Vattabbaka Nigrodha as a novice, the Brāhmaṇatissa peril also occurred. The novice and his preceptor did not go to the other side of the ocean, thinking, "We shall live depending on people who eat leaves," and headed toward the border regions. While the novice had been without food for seven days, he saw a ripe palmyra fruit on a tree in a village and said to his preceptor, "Venerable Sir, please wait a moment; I will bring down the palmyra fruit." "Novice, you are weak; do not climb," the preceptor said. "I will climb, Venerable Sir," he replied. Taking a small knife, he climbed the palmyra tree and began to cut the cluster of fruit. The blade of the knife slipped from the handle and fell to the ground.
431: Having broken the palmyra fruit that had rolled away, the Elder said when the novice climbed down, "Novice, you are weak; eat this first." "Venerable Sir, I will not eat before you have eaten," he replied. Taking the small knife, he broke the palmyra fruits, took out his bowl, put the palmyra kernels inside, and offered them to the Elder; only then did he eat himself. They stayed in that place as long as there were palmyra fruits. When the fruits were exhausted, they eventually entered an abandoned monastery in the place where the leaf-eating people lived. The novice looked after the Elder's living quarters. The Elder gave instructions to the novice and entered the monastery. The novice thought, "There is no end to the number of existences wasted in improper places; I will perform service to the Buddhas." He went to the courtyard of the stūpa and cleared it of grass and shrubs. Being shaky due to seven days without food, he pulled out the grass even while falling and lying down. Some people wandering in the forest found honey, and while carrying wood and leafy vegetables, they saw the grass moving. Thinking, "Is that a wild animal?" they went near the novice and asked, "Novice, what are you doing?" "Lay devotees, I am gathering bundles of grass," he said. "Venerable Sir, is there anyone else?" they asked. "Yes, lay devotees, my preceptor is inside the chamber," he replied. "Venerable Sir, please eat after giving some to the Great Elder," they said, and having offered the honey to the novice, they told him their place of residence. "We will go, breaking branches [to mark the way]. Venerable Sir, please bring the Elder and come according to those signs," they said and departed. The novice took the honey, went to the Elder, and standing outside, said, "Venerable Sir, I pay my respects." The Elder thought, "The novice must have come because he is tormented by hunger," and remained silent. The novice said again, "Venerable Sir, I pay my respects." "Novice, why do you not allow weak monks to lie down in peace?" the Elder asked. "Venerable Sir, it is proper to open the door," he replied. The Elder stood up, opened the door, and asked, "Novice, what have you obtained?" "Venerable Sir, people have offered honey; it is proper to consume it," he replied. "Novice, if we consume it as it is, we will be exhausted; let us make a drink and drink it," the Elder said. The novice made the drink and offered it. Then the Elder asked him, "Novice, did you ask for the people's place of residence?" "Venerable Sir, they told me themselves," he replied. "Novice, if we go early in the morning, we will be exhausted; let us go this very day," the Elder said.
432:
Having had the bowl and robes taken, he departed. The teacher and pupil went and lay down in a place not far from where people lived.

During the night, the novice thought: "Since the time I ordained as a novice, I have never yet caused the dawn to rise near a village." Taking his bowl, he went to the forest to cause the dawn to rise. The Great Elder, not seeing the novice in his sleeping place, thought: "Could he have been seized by cannibals?" The novice, having caused the dawn to rise in the forest, returned taking water and tooth-sticks in his bowl. "Novice, where did you go? You have caused anxiety to elder monks; perform a penance," the Elder said. "I will perform it, venerable sir," he replied. The Elder washed his face and donned his robes. Both teacher and pupil went to the place where people lived. The people offered roots, tubers, fruits, and leaves, which were their own provisions. The Elder, having eaten, went to the monastery.

The novice brought water and said, "Venerable sir, I will wash your feet." "Novice, where did you go during the night? You caused us anxiety," the Elder said. "Venerable sir, I had never before caused the dawn to rise near a village; I went to the forest for the purpose of causing the dawn to rise," he replied. "Novice, it is not appropriate to give you a penance; it is only appropriate for us to be given a penance," the Elder said, and remained in that very place. He warned the novice: "We are old; it is impossible to know what might happen. You should protect yourself." It is said that the Elder was a Non-returner (Anāgāmī). Later, cannibals ate that Elder. The novice protected himself, and when the danger had subsided, he took a preceptor in such a place and attained higher ordination. Having learned the word of the Buddha and becoming a bearer of the Tipitaka, he became known as the Elder Vattabbakanigrodha.

King Pitumahārāja attained the kingship. Monks coming from across the ocean asked, "Where is the Elder Vattabbakanigrodha? Where is the Elder Vattabbakanigrodha?" and went to his presence. A great community of monks surrounded the Elder. Surrounded by that great community of monks, he eventually reached the Mahāvihāra, and after paying homage to the Great Bodhi tree, the Mahācetiya, and the Thūpārāma, he set out for the city. Even while walking as far as the South Gate, he received sets of triple robes in nine places. From the time he entered the city, great honor and offerings arose. Thus, in a time of adversity (kālavipatti), even palm fruits, roots, tubers, and leaves were hard to obtain. In a time of prosperity (kālasampatti), such great gain arose. Thus...
433:
He understands that kammas which are unable to give results because they are obstructed by the failure of time (kālavipatti) ripen when they reach the success of time (kālasampatti).

Another person also has many wholesome kammas. Those wholesome kammas would not ripen for one who stands in the failure of effort (payogavipatti). However, that person, established in right effort (sammāpayoga) through a single wholesome kamma, fulfills the three types of good conduct and observes the five precepts and the ten precepts. To one born in the success of time (kālasampatti), kings send princesses adorned with all ornaments, saying, "They are suitable for this man." They also send various gifts such as chariots, vehicles, elephants, horses, gems, gold, and silver, saying, "These are suitable for this man."

Even upon entering the monkhood, such a person becomes one of great fame and great power. In this regard, there is this story: It is said that King Kūṭakaṇṇa greatly cherished the Elder Cūḷasudhammā, who lived in Girigāmakaṇṇa. While the King was staying at Uppalavāpi, he sent for the Elder. The Elder came and stayed at the Mālārāma monastery. The King asked the Elder's mother, "What does the Elder like?" "Great King, he likes roots (tubers)," she replied. The King had roots brought and went to the monastery, but while offering them to the Elder, he did not dare to look up at the Elder's face. After leaving and coming to the outer precinct, he asked the Queen, "What is the Elder like?" The Queen replied, "If you, being a man, did not dare to look up, how should I be able to? I do not know what he is like." The King snapped his fingers and said, "In my own kingdom, I do not dare to look up even at the son of a householder who pays taxes. Great indeed is the Dispensation of the Buddha!" He also cherished the Elder Tipiṭakacūḷanāga. A boil appeared on that Elder's finger. The King, thinking "I will see the Elder," went to the monastery and, out of strong affection, took the finger in his mouth. The boil broke right inside his mouth; because of his love for the Elder, he did not spit out the pus and blood but swallowed it like nectar. That same Elder later lay on his deathbed. The King went and, placing the waste-pot on his head, wandered about lamenting, "The axle of the Dhamma-cart is breaking! The axle is breaking!" For a lord of the earth to wander about carrying a waste-pot on his head—whose path (practice) is this? It is the path of right effort (sammāpayoga). Thus, he understands that kammas which are unable to give results because they are obstructed by the failure of effort (payogavipatti) ripen when they reach the success of effort (payogasampatti). Thus, wholesome kamma obstructed by the four failures (vipatti) does not give results until it reaches the four successes (sampatti).

To illustrate this with an event that actually happened, here is a simile: It is said that a Great King, having become angry with a minister over a slight matter, had him bound in prison. That minister's relatives...
434:
The relatives, knowing the King's anger, remained silent. Only when his fierce wrath had subsided did they inform the King of the minister's innocence. The King then released the minister from prison and restored him to his original rank. Subsequently, the gifts arriving for the minister from various places were so numerous that they were beyond measure. Even the people tasked with receiving and storing them were unable to cope with the volume.

In this analogy, the period when the King, angered by a slight offense, had the minister imprisoned is like the time a worldling (puthujjana) is reborn in hell. The time when the relatives convinced the King and the minister's rank was restored is like the time that person is reborn in heaven. Just as the time when the gifts were too numerous to be received, so too, by encountering the fourfold success (sampatti), wholesome kammas lead one from a happy state to another happy state—from the deva world to the human world, and from the human world to the deva world—providing pleasant results for a hundred thousand aeons and ultimately leading to Nibbāna.

Thus, having first explained the Second Power according to the Pāli text, it should further be explained according to the method of the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "There was kamma, there was a result of kamma." In that text, "there was kamma" means kamma accumulated in the past occurred in the past. Regarding kamma that has already yielded its result in the past, it is said, "there was a result of kamma." Even though many kammas such as diṭṭhadhammavedanīya (kamma to be experienced in this life) are accumulated, only one yields a result in the present life; the rest are without result. Only one upapajjavedanīya (kamma to be experienced in the next life) draws one to rebirth; the rest are without result. Due to one ānantariya (weighty) kamma, one is reborn in hell; the rest are without result. Among the eight attainments (samāpatti), one causes rebirth in the Brahma world; the rest are without result. With reference to such kammas that do not yield results, it is said, "there was no result of kamma."

When a person, having performed many wholesome and unwholesome kammas, attains Arahantship by relying on a good friend (kalyāṇamitta), the result of that person's kamma is said to be "non-existent." Kamma that was accumulated in the past and yields a result now is called "Kamma was, the result of kamma is." Kamma that, according to the aforementioned method, reaches the state of not yielding a result is called "Kamma was, the result of kamma is not." Kamma that was accumulated in the past and will yield a result in the future is called "Kamma was, the result of kamma will be." Kamma that, according to the previous method, will reach the state of not yielding a result is called "Kamma was, the result of kamma will not be."
436:
How is it? For even when all the villagers together deprive a pig or a deer of its life (kill it), the volition of all of them has the life-faculty of another as its object. However, that kamma is different even at the moment of its accumulation. Indeed, among them, one performs it with respectful desire. One performs it because of being pressured (urged) by others, saying, "Come, you do it too." One wanders about as if having the same desire, without being restrained. Among them, one is reborn in hell because of that very kamma, one in the animal kingdom, and one in the realm of hungry ghosts (petas). The Tathāgata knows this even at the moment of accumulation: "Because of being accumulated in this manner, this person will be reborn in hell; this one in the animal kingdom; this one in the realm of hungry ghosts." Even for one being reborn in hell, He knows: "This one will be reborn in the eight great hells; this one will be reborn in the sixteen prominent (Ussada) hells." Even for one being reborn in the animal kingdom, He knows: "This one will be a footless animal, this one will be a two-footed animal, this one will be a four-footed animal, this one will be a many-footed animal." Even for one being reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts, He knows: "This one will be a Nijjhāmataṇhika peta, this one will be a Khuppipāsika peta, this one will be a Paradattūpajīvī peta." Among those kammas, He knows: "This kamma will not be able to draw forth rebirth-linking; it is weak; it will only be a result of physical excellence (upadhivepakka) for the rebirth-linking already given."

Similarly, when all the villagers together offer alms-food, the volition of all of them has the alms-food as its object. However, that kamma is different even at the moment of its accumulation, according to the previous method. Among them, some will be reborn in the celestial realm, some in the human world. The Tathāgata knows this even at the moment of accumulation: "Because of being accumulated in this manner, this person will be reborn in the human world; this one in the celestial realm." Even for those being reborn in the celestial realm, He knows: "This one will be reborn among the Paranimmitavasavattī devas, this one among the Nimmānarati devas, this one among the Tusita devas, this one among the Yāma devas, this one among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, this one among the Cātumahārājika devas, this one among the Bhummadevas. This one will be reborn as a chief deva king; this one will be reborn as an attendant performing the second or third rank of office for this deva king." Even for those being reborn among humans, He knows: "This one will be reborn in a Khattiya family, this one in a Brāhmaṇa family, this one in a Vessa family, this one in a Sudda family. This one will be reborn as a king among humans; this one will be reborn as an attendant performing the second or third rank of office for this king."
437:
(The Buddha) knows. Among those kammas, He knows: "This kamma will not be able to draw forth rebirth-linking; because it is weak, it will have a result of physical excellence (upadhivepakka) in the rebirth-linking already given."

Similarly, among those who are currently practicing Vipassanā, according to the manner in which Vipassanā is undertaken, He knows: "This person will reach the fruit of Arahantship; this person will not be able to reach the fruit of Arahantship; this person will only be an Anāgāmī; this person only a Sakadāgāmī; this person only a Sotāpanna. This person will not be able to realize either the path or the fruit; he will remain only in Vipassanā that takes characteristics such as impermanence as its object. This person will remain only in the knowledge of discerning causes (paccayapariggaha); this person only in the knowledge of discerning mind and matter (nāmarūpapariggaha); this person only in the knowledge of discerning the immaterial (arūpapariggaha); this person only in the knowledge of discerning the material (rūpapariggaha); this person will define only the great elements; this person will not be able to note even a single phenomenon."

Also among those performing preliminary work for Kasina, He knows: "For this person, there will be only the preliminary work; he will not be able to produce the sign (nimitta). This person will be able to produce the sign but will not be able to reach attainment (appanā). This person, having reached attainment, making the jhāna the basis and developing Vipassanā, will attain the fruit of Arahantship."

## Explanation of the Third Power (Tatiya-bala-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

## The Fourth Power (Catuttha-bala-niddesa)

In the explanation of the fourth power, 'diversity of aggregates' (khandha-nānatta) means He knows the various distinctions of the five aggregates thus: "This is called the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) ... this is called the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha)." Among those aggregates, He knows the diversity of each aggregate thus: "The aggregate of form exists in one way ... the aggregate of form exists in eleven ways. The aggregate of feeling exists in one way ... the aggregate of feeling exists in many ways ... the aggregate of perception exists in one way ... the aggregate of mental formations exists in one way ... the aggregate of consciousness exists in one way ... the aggregate of consciousness exists in many ways." 'Diversity of bases' (āyatana-nānatta) means He knows the various distinctions of the bases thus: "This is called the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) ... this is called the mind-object-base (dhammāyatana). Among those bases, ten bases are of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), and two belong to the four planes." 'Diversity of elements' (dhātu-nānatta) means He knows the various distinctions of the elements thus: "This is called the eye-element (cakkhudhātu) ... this is called the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu). Among those elements, sixteen elements are of the sense-sphere, and two belong to the four planes."
438:
Furthermore, the phrase "anekadhātunānādhātulokanānatta" is employed to show that the Tathāgata knows not only the diversity of the world of sentient (upādinnaka) formations, but also the diversity of the world of non-sentient (anupādinnaka) formations. Indeed, Paccekabuddhas and the two Chief Disciples know the diversity of the world of sentient formations only partially and not exhaustively, whereas they do not know the diversity of the non-sentient world at all.

The Omniscient Buddha, however, knows the diversity of the world of non-sentient formations thus: "Due to the predominance of such and such an element, the trunk of this particular tree is white, the trunk of this one is black, and the trunk of this one is smooth; this tree has thick bark, and this tree has thin bark. Due to the predominance of such and such an element, the leaf of this tree has such a nature in terms of color and shape. Due to the predominance of this element, the flower of this tree is blue, yellow, red, white, fragrant, or malodorous. Due to the predominance of such and such an element, the fruit is small, large, long, short, round, well-shaped, ill-shaped, smooth, rough, fragrant, malodorous, sweet, bitter, sour, pungent, or astringent. Due to the predominance of such and such an element, the thorn of this tree is sharp, very sharp, straight, curved, red, black, blue, or white." In this way, He knows the various diversities of the world of non-sentient formations. This power of knowing is the power of the Omniscient Buddhas alone, and not of others.

## Description of the Fourth Power.

## The Fifth Power

In the description of the fifth power, "hīnādhimuttikā" means those of low inclinations. "Paṇītādhimuttikā" means those of noble inclinations. "Sevanti" means they associate with or cling to. "Bhajanti" means they resort to. "Payirupāsanti" means they attend upon repeatedly. If teachers and preceptors are not virtuous while the resident pupils are virtuous, those pupils do not resort even to their own teachers and preceptors, but resort only to suitable monks who are like themselves. If the teachers and preceptors are suitable monks but others are unsuitable, they also do not resort to the teachers and preceptors, but resort only to those of low inclinations who are like themselves.
439:
To show that such approaching [associating] occurs not only at present but also in the past and future, he said "atītampi addhānaṃ" and so forth. The meaning of that is clear. However, what is it that determines that the non-virtuous associate only with the non-virtuous, the virtuous with the virtuous, the unwise with the unwise, and the wise with the wise? It is the element of inclination (ajjhāsayadhātu) that determines it. It is said that many monks were wandering for alms as a group in a village. People brought much food, filled their bowls, and said, "Venerable sirs, please enjoy according to your own affinity," and after giving, they sent them off. The monks also said, "Friends, people are performing actions connected with elements (dhātu)." Also, while the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya was traveling with five hundred monks to worship the shrine in Nāgadīpa, he was invited by people in a village. Along with the Elder, there was one unsuitable monk. In the monastery of that village, there was also one unsuitable monk. When the two groups of monks entered the village, those two persons—even though the visitor had never seen the resident, nor the resident the visitor—became one, laughing and talking, and stood to one side. Seeing this, the Elder said, "The Fully Enlightened One, knowing this, taught the Dhātusaṃyutta."

Having said "the element of inclination determines it" in this way, this very meaning should be illustrated by the Dhātusaṃyutta. Indeed, the Blessed One, while lying down on his sickbed at Gijjhakūṭa Mountain, saw the Elders such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna, who were staying around to protect him, walking to and fro (caṅkamanta) each with his own assembly, and addressed the monks: "Monks, do you see Sāriputta walking to and fro with many monks?" "Yes, Bhante." "Monks, all these monks are of great wisdom" (Saṃ. Ni. 2.99). The rest should be understood in detail.

## Description of the Fifth Power.

## The Sixth Power

In the description of the sixth power, "āsaya" (disposition) refers to that in which beings dwell or reside; it is their dwelling place, which is either a wrong view or knowledge as it really is. "Anusaya" (latent tendency) means...
440:
Anusaya refers to the defilements that lie latent repeatedly because they have not yet been abandoned by the Path. Carita refers to the wholesome and unwholesome deeds conditioned by the body and so forth. Adhimutta refers to the excessive desire (ajjhāsaya).

The meaning should be understood in the terms beginning with 'apparajakkha'. Because the dust of greed, hatred, and delusion in the eye of wisdom of those beings is little, they are called 'apparajakkha' (those with little dust). Because that same dust is abundant, they are called 'mahārajakkha' (those with much dust). By both these terms, the Buddha shows beings with few defilements and beings with many defilements. Those beings whose faculties such as faith are sharp are called 'tikkhindriya' (those with sharp faculties). Those whose faculties are dull are called 'mudindriya' (those with dull faculties). Those whose groups of inclinations and so forth are good are called 'svākāra' (those with good attributes). Those who are the opposite are called 'dvākāra' (those with bad attributes). Those who can remember the taught reasons and can be easily made to understand are called 'suviññāpaya' (those easy to teach). Those who are the opposite are called 'duviññāpaya' (those difficult to teach). Those who are endowed with the strong supporting condition (upaniṣsaya) suitable for the penetration of the Noble Path are called 'bhabba' (those who are capable). Those who are the opposite are called 'abhabba' (those who are incapable).

Having thus established the matrix (mātikā) of the sixth power, and now wishing to analyze it in order, He said: "Katamō ca sattānaṃ āsayō" (What is the inclination of beings?), and so forth. Therein, the meaning of the terms beginning with "sassatō lokō" (the world is eternal) has already been stated below in the commentary on the Nikkhepa-kaṇḍa. "Bhavadiṭṭhisannissitā vā" means they rely on the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi) in this way. Here, the eternalist view is taught as the view of existence (bhava-diṭṭhi), and the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi) is taught as the view of non-existence (vibhava-diṭṭhi). Since all views are encompassed by the eternalist and annihilationist views, all beings with wrong views rely only on these two views. Thus the Buddha also taught: "Kaccāna, this world mostly relies on the duality of existence (atthitā) and non-existence (natthitā)." Here, existence is eternalism, and non-existence is annihilationism. This is the inclination of worldlings who rely on the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa).

Now, to show the inclination of pure beings who rely on the cessation of the cycle (vivaṭṭa), He taught: "ēte vā pana ubhō antē anupagamma" (without approaching these two extremes), and so forth. Therein, "ēte vā pana" refers only to these parts. "Ubhō antē" refers to the two extremes called eternalism and annihilationism. "Anupagamma" means without clinging. "Idappaccayatā paṭiccasamuppannēsu dhammēsu" means in specific conditionality (the cause) and in dependently arisen phenomena (the effect). "Anulomikā khanti" is insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa). "Yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇaṃ" is Path knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). This is what is meant: the insight knowledge obtained without approaching the two extremes of eternalism and annihilationism regarding dependent origination (the cause) and dependently arisen phenomena (the effect), and the Path knowledge that is superior to that, is the inclination of beings. This is the inclination of all beings, both those relying on the cycle and those free from the cycle; this is the dwelling place. This is the uniform explanation of the teachers.
441:
A Vitaṇḍavādī (sophist) says: \"Does not the Path go about destroying the dwelling (vāsa)? Did you not say the Path is a dwelling?\" That person should be asked: \"Are you a reciter of the Ariyavāsa Sutta or not?\" If he says, \"I am not,\" he should be told: \"Because you are not a reciter, you do not know.\" If he says, \"I am a reciter,\" he should be told: \"Then present that Sutta.\" If he can present it, that is good. If he cannot, one should present it oneself: \"Monks, there are these ten noble dwellings (ariyavāsa) in which the Noble Ones have dwelt, are dwelling, or will dwell.\" This Sutta shows that the Path is a dwelling. Therefore, this statement is well-spoken indeed.

The Blessed One, knowing this inclination of beings, knows it even at the moment when the insight knowledge and path knowledge of these people with wrong views have not yet arisen (as well as when they have arisen). Thus it has also been taught:

\"The Buddha knows a person who is currently indulging in sensual pleasure: 'This person values sensual pleasure, has an inclination for sensual pleasure, and is firmly committed to sensual pleasure.' He knows a person who is currently indulging in renunciation: 'This person values renunciation, has an inclination for renunciation, and is firmly committed to renunciation.' ... ill-will ... non-ill-will ... sloth and torpor ... the perception of light. He knows a person who is currently indulging in renunciation: 'This person values the perception of light, has an inclination for the perception of light, and is firmly committed to the perception of light.'\"

In the description of underlying tendencies (anusaya-niddesa), it is called 'kāmarāgānusaya' because it is sensual lust and also an underlying tendency in the sense of not being abandoned by the Path. In the remaining terms, the method is the same. \"Agreeable nature (piyarūpa) in the world\" means having a nature that is loved in this world. \"Pleasurable nature (sātarūpa)\" means having a nature that is pleasurable, a pleasant object (iṭṭhārammaṇa) which is the proximate cause for gratification (assāda). \"The underlying tendency to lust lies latent in this pleasant object\" means that the underlying tendency to lust follows and arises in this pleasant object because of the sense of not being abandoned.

For example, just as there is only water below, above, and all around a person submerged in water, similarly, the arising of lust in a pleasant object is a practice that beings have repeatedly and constantly cultivated. Likewise, the arising of aversion (paṭigha) in an unpleasant object is the same. \"Thus in these two things which have sensual lust and aversion, namely pleasant and unpleasant objects\" means that ignorance (avijjā) follows by way of making them an object, being associated with sensual lust and aversion. \"It stands in the same [mind] as that ignorance\" means with that ignorance...
442:
It is called 'established in one [mind]' (ekattha) because of its establishment in a single mind by way of being associated (sampayutta) with that ignorance (avijjā). Among conceit (māna), views (diṭṭhi), and doubt (vicikicchā), conceit is of nine kinds, views are of sixty-two kinds, and doubt has eight bases (such as doubt regarding the Buddha, etc.). In this Anusaya-niddesa, it should be understood that the latent tendency of lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya) is included within the latent tendency of lust for sensual pleasure (kāmarāgānusaya). In the Carita-niddesa, thirteen types of volition are called meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra), twelve types of volition are called demeritorious volitional formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), and four types of volition are called imperturbable volitional formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra). Among these volitional formations, those of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara) have a limited (inferior) plane, while the remaining formations of the fine-material and immaterial spheres have a great (superior) plane. Alternatively, among these three types of formations, those with little result are called parittabhūmaka (of limited plane), and those with much result are called mahābhūmaka (of great plane). 

The Adhimutti-niddesa has already been clearly explained below. Why is this adhimutti taken up again even though it was taught below? Below, this Adhimutti-niddesa was taken separately to show the power [of the Buddha]; here, however, it is taken for the purpose of showing the state of sharp faculties and dull faculties of beings. In the Mahārajakkha-niddesa, 'ussadagatāni' refers to states that have reached abundance. This Mahārajakkha-niddesa is presented out of order by way of the sequence of abandonment. 'Anussadagatāni' refers to states that have not reached abundance. In the Tikkhindriya-mudindriya-niddesa, the supporting faculties (upanissaya-indriya) which are the strong basis for the Path are taught. Here, the purpose of the out-of-order presentation should be understood in the same way as mentioned below. 

Furthermore, in the Dvākāra-niddesa and so on, 'pāpāsayā' refers to those whose basis is unwholesome. 'Pāpacaritā' refers to those who fulfill demeritorious volitional formations. 'Pāpādhimuttikā' refers to those who delight in the existing body (sakkāya) and have desires pertaining to the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). In the Svākāra-niddesa, because there is no such thing as a 'good latent tendency,' the Buddha did not say 'kalyāṇānusaya.' The remaining group of terms should be understood by the reversal of the meanings already stated. In the Bhabba-abhabba-niddesa, 'kammāvaraṇena' refers to being endowed with the five types of heinous kamma (ānantariya-kamma). 'Kilesāvaraṇena' refers to being endowed with fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi). 'Vipākāvaraṇena' refers to being endowed with rootless rebirth-linking (ahetuka-paṭisandhi). Since those with two-root rebirth-linking also lack the penetration of the Noble Path, two-root rebirth-linking (duhetuka-paṭisandhi) should also be understood as a resultant obstruction (vipākāvaraṇa).
443:
'Assaddhā' refers to those who lack faith in the Buddha and so on. 'Acchandikā' refers to those who lack the wholesome desire (kusalacchanda) to strive for the attainment of the Path. Humans living in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) fall into the category of those lacking desire. 'Duppaññā' refers to those who are deficient in life-continuum wisdom (bhavaṅga-paññā). Even if one is complete in life-continuum wisdom, if that life-continuum does not serve as a basis for supramundane states, that person is also called 'duppaññā' (of little wisdom). Those who are unworthy to enter the Path, known as the 'fixed path of rightness' (sammattaniyāma) among wholesome states, are called 'abhabba' (incapable).

The terms 'na kammāvaraṇena' and so on should be understood by the reversal of the meanings already stated.
