This passage is the detailed classification of two knowledges: the knowledge of the proficiency of faculties (indriyaparopariyatti-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa). Here, the knowledge of the proficiency of faculties is also classified in detail by the knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies. Thus, it should be noted that these two knowledges combined become the single Sixth Power of Knowledge (Chaṭṭhabala-ñāṇa).

## ဆဋ္ဌဗလနိဒ္ဒေသဝဏ္ဏနာ။

## သတ္တမဗလနိဒ္ဒေသော

In the Sattamabalaniddesa, one is called 'jhāyī' because of contemplating fixedly on objects such as kasinas. Four types of persons who frequently enter meditative absorptions are called 'jhāyino' (four types of meditators). Among them, in the first group of four, the first person, although having obtained an attainment (samāpatti), perceives, 'I have not obtained the attainment,' and although it is a meditation object (kammaṭṭhāna), perceives it as 'not a meditation object.' This person should be understood as one who has obtained a jhāna that is not thoroughly mastered (appaguṇajjhānalābhī). The second person, although not having obtained an attainment, perceives, 'I have obtained it,' and although it is not a meditation object, perceives it as 'a meditation object.' This person is called a 'sleeping meditator' (niddājhāyī). Upon waking from sleep, he thinks he has entered an attainment in this way. The third person, when obtaining an attainment, perceives, 'I have obtained the attainment,' and perceives the meditation object as 'a meditation object.' This person should be understood as one who has obtained a jhāna that is thoroughly mastered (paguṇajjhānalābhī). The fourth person, not having obtained [an attainment], perceives, 'I have not obtained it,' and perceives what is not a meditation object as 'not a meditation object.' Thus, among these four, two persons do not actually possess jhāna, but they are called 'jhāyī' because they are included within the category of meditators.

In the second group of four, one who enters [concentration] slowly by suppressing the defilements that are obstacles to concentration along with effort and application is said to 'enter slowly' (dandhaṃ samāpajjati). One who can emerge quickly after staying for only one or two thought-moments is said to 'emerge quickly' (khippaṃ vuṭṭhahati). One who can enter quickly by easily clearing the obstacles to concentration is said to 'enter quickly' (khippaṃ samāpajjati). One who cannot emerge at his predetermined time but emerges only after the time has passed is said to 'emerge slowly' (dandhaṃ vuṭṭhahati).
444:
One who emerges after the set time has passed is called one who emerges slowly. The other two individuals should also be understood in this same manner. All four of these individuals are indeed attainers of meditative attainments (samāpatti).

In the third tetrad, one who is skilled in defining the factors of jhāna, such as "This jhāna has five factors, this jhāna has four factors," is called 'skilled in concentration' (samādhi-kusala). However, one who is not skilled in placing the mind in the casket of the mind by suppressing the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) is not called 'skilled in attainment' (samāpatti-kusala). The other three individuals should also be understood in this same manner. These four individuals are also attainers of meditative attainments.

Now, to show those jhānas depending on which these individuals are called 'meditators' (jhāyī), the text says "cattāri jhānāni" and so on. Therein, the four jhānas and the three deliverances (vimokkha) have been clearly explained in terms of meaning in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā itself. The meaning of the remaining deliverances should also be understood according to the method stated there. A slight distinction to be mentioned here is that among these eight deliverances, the first seven in succession are called deliverances because they are freed from opposing states at the moment of attainment and because they are firmly intent upon the object. The eighth, however, is called 'departed deliverance' (apagata-vimokkha) because it is freed from all perceptions and feelings in every way. Among concentrations, in the fourfold and fivefold methods, the concentration of the first jhāna is called 'with initial application and sustained application' (savitakka-savicāra). In the fivefold method, the concentration of the second jhāna is called 'without initial application but with sustained application only' (avitakka-vicāramatta). In both the fourfold and fivefold methods, the concentration in the three higher jhānas is called 'without initial application and without sustained application' (avitakka-avicāra). Indeed, among the attainments, the eight attainments in succession are called both 'concentration' (samādhi) and 'attainment' (samāpatti). Why? Because of the presence of one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā). In the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), however, because that one-pointedness of mind is absent, it does not get the name 'concentration'.

The 'state leading to decline' (hānabhāgiya-dhamma) refers to the rushing of the perceptions and mental applications of one who has emerged from the first jhāna, etc., which has not been thoroughly mastered, towards lower objects such as sensual desires. The 'state leading to distinction' (visesabhāgiya-dhamma) refers to the rushing of the perceptions and mental applications of one who has emerged from the first jhāna, etc., which has been thoroughly mastered, towards higher objects such as the second jhāna. By the words "purification (vodāna) is also called emergence (vuṭṭhāna)", it is stated that thoroughly mastered purification is called emergence. Indeed, a lower jhāna that is thoroughly mastered is the proximate cause for the higher and higher jhānas. Therefore, it is said that purification is also called emergence. By the words "emergence from various concentrations is also called emergence", emergence as the falling into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is stated. Indeed, emergence from all jhānas occurs through the life-continuum. Specifically, from the attainment of cessation, they emerge only through the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). This emergence from the attainment of cessation is called 'emergence outside the Pāḷi' (pāḷimuttaka-vuṭṭhāna).

## Explanation of the Description of the Seventh Power.
446:
"He will say, 'In succession, seven knowledges are of the sense sphere, then two knowledges are of the fine-material sphere, and at the end, one knowledge of the destruction of taints is supramundane.' He will say, 'Omniscience, however, is only with initial and sustained application, only of the sense sphere, and only mundane.' Thus, the Ten Powers of Knowledge are one thing, and Omniscience is another; Omniscience is one thing, and the Ten Powers of Knowledge are another.

## In the Vibhaṅga Commentary named Sammohavinodanī,
## the Explanation of the Knowledge-Vibhaṅga is finished."
447:
## 17. Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga
## 1. Commentary on the Matrix of the Ones, etc.
After teaching the Ñāṇavibhaṅga, now in the Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga which follows it, the Matrix (Mātikā) is first established, and the detailed exposition (Niddesa) is made according to the sequence of the terms laid down. In laying down that Matrix, this is the definition of the layout. At the beginning, seventy-three 'Ones' (Ekakas) starting with intoxication with birth (jātimada) are laid down. After that, eighteen 'Twos' (Dukas) starting with anger and malice (kodha and upanāha); thirty-five 'Threes' (Tikas) starting with unwholesome roots (akusalamūla); fourteen 'Fours' (Catukkas) starting with taints (āsava); fifteen 'Fives' (Pañcakas) starting with lower fetters (orambhāgiyasaṃyojana); fourteen 'Sixes' (Chakkas) starting with roots of contention (vivādamūla); seven 'Sevens' (Sattakas) starting with latent tendencies (anusaya); eight 'Eights' (Aṭṭhakas) starting with bases of defilement (kilesavatthu); nine 'Nines' (Navakas) starting with bases of resentment (āghātavatthu); ten 'Tens' (Dasakas) starting with bases of defilement (kilesavatthu); and six 'Eighteens' (Aṭṭhārasakas) starting with the eighteen mental obsessions of craving (taṇhāvicarita) beginning with the internal, are laid down. Thus, it should be understood that all these one hundred and eight defilements are laid down. This is first the definition of the layout of the Matrix.

## (1.) Commentary on the Exposition of the Ones
843-844. Now, in the section of exposition (Niddesavāra) undertaken according to the Matrix as laid down, in the manner of "Therein, what is intoxication with birth?", the phrase "dependent on birth" (jātiṃ paṭicca) means relying on birth. Here, the word "paṭicca" is used in the sense of existence (atthi); therefore, "when there is birth" is the meaning here. The same method applies to the passages such as "dependent on clan" (gottaṃ paṭicca). "Intoxication" (mada) is by way of being intoxicated. "Intoxicating" (majjanā) is the manner of being intoxicated. "The state of being intoxicated" (majjitatta) is the condition of one who is intoxicated. The terms "Conceit" (māna), "Thinking" (maññanā), etc., have the same meanings as stated below in the Commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī. "This is called" (ayaṃ vuccati) means this conceit, which arises relying on birth when there is such birth, and which proceeds in the manner of being intoxicated, is called "intoxication with birth". This intoxication with birth arises in the continuity of the four classes, such as the Khattiyas. Indeed, a Khattiya endowed with birth thinks with conceit: "There is no other like me. Other kings are merely those who have arisen in the interval. But I am a true Khattiya come from a lineage." The same method applies to Brahmins (Brāhmaṇas), etc. In the exposition of intoxication with clan (gottamada), etc., the meaning should be understood in this same way. For a Khattiya also thinks with conceit: "I am of the Koṇḍañña clan, I am of the Ādicca clan." A Brahmin also...
448:
...thinks with conceit: "I am of the Kassapa clan, I am of the Bhāradvāja clan." A Vessa or a Sudda also thinks with conceit relying on his own family and clan. Even the eighteen guilds (seṇi) think with conceit: "We are born in the same guild."

Among the terms such as intoxication with health (ārogyamada): "I am healthy, others are full of diseases; I have no disease even for as long as it takes to milk a cow once"—conceit arising by way of such intoxication is called "intoxication with health".

"I am young, the bodies of other beings are like trees standing on a precipice, but I am established in the first stage of life"—conceit arising by way of such intoxication is called "intoxication with youth" (yobbanamada).

"I have lived long, I am living long, I shall live long; I have lived happily, I am living happily, I shall live happily"—conceit arising by way of such intoxication is called "intoxication with life" (jīvitamada).

"I am a gainer of gains, other beings have few gains, but for me there is no measure of gains"—conceit arising by way of such intoxication is called "intoxication with gain" (lābhamada).

"Other beings receive whatever ordinary things, but I receive well-made and exquisite requisites such as robes"—conceit arising by way of such intoxication is called "intoxication with honor" (sakkāramada).

"People who walk treading on the heels of other monks do not even pay homage, thinking 'This is a monk'; but as soon as they see me, they pay homage, regarding me with respect like a stone parasol, and considering me difficult to approach like a mass of fire"—conceit arising by way of such intoxication is called "intoxication with being revered" (garukāramada).

"An arisen problem is solved only by my mouth; even when going for alms, they go surrounding me, putting me in the front"—conceit arising by way of such intoxication is called "intoxication with being prominent" (purekkhāramada).

For a layman with a large retinue: "A hundred men, a thousand men surround me"; and for a monk: "A hundred monks, a thousand monks surround me; others have few retinues, but I have a large retinue and a pure retinue"—conceit arising by way of such intoxication is called "intoxication with retinue" (parivāramada).
449:
Wealth (bhoga) is actually included under the term "gain" (lābha), but here it refers to an accumulated store of wealth. Therefore, the pride that arises through intoxication, thinking, "Other beings do not even get enough for their own consumption, but for me, there is no limit to my buried treasure," is called intoxication with wealth (bhogamada).

Based on appearance (vaṇṇa) means based on physical appearance as well as reputation. The pride that arises through intoxication, thinking, "Other beings are ugly and unattractive, but I am very beautiful and inspiring. Other beings have no virtues and no fame, but the sound of my fame is well-known among devas and humans—thus, this elder is very learned, thus he is virtuous, thus he is endowed with the dhutanga qualities," is called intoxication with appearance (vaṇṇamada).

The pride that arises through intoxication, thinking, "Other beings have little learning, but I am very learned," is called intoxication with learning (sutamada).

The pride that arises through intoxication, thinking, "Other beings have no ready wit (paṭibhāna), but there is no limit to my ready wit," is called intoxication with ready wit (paṭibhānamada).

The pride that arises through intoxication, thinking, "I am one of long standing (rattaññū); I know such and such lineage of the Buddhas, the lineage of kings, the history of the districts, the history of the villages, the divisions of night and day, and the conjunctions of constellations and moments," is called intoxication with seniority (rattaññumada).

The pride that arises through intoxication, thinking, "Other bhikkhus have become alms-food eaters only occasionally, but I have been a constant alms-food eater (jātipiṇḍapātika) since becoming a monk," is called intoxication with alms-food practice (piṇḍapātikamada).

The pride that arises through intoxication, thinking, "Other beings are looked down upon and despised, but I am recognized and not despised," is called intoxication with not being despised (anavaññātamada).

The pride that arises through intoxication, thinking, "The deportment (iriyāpatha) of others is not inspiring, but mine is inspiring," is called intoxication with deportment (iriyāpathamada).

The pride that arises through intoxication, thinking, "Other beings are like crows with clipped wings, but I have great psychic power and great majesty," or "Whatever task I perform, that task succeeds," is called intoxication with psychic power (iddhimada).

Although fame (yasa) is already included by the mention of retinue (parivāra) below, in this context, intoxication with having attendants (upaṭṭhākamada) is taken. That intoxication should be shown through both laypeople and monks. Indeed, a certain layperson is the head of one of the eighteen guilds; to him, "I appoint the remaining men, I..."
450:
...manage [them]." Even among those who are not householders (monks), a certain person might be a leader in some place. To him, the pride that arises through intoxication, thinking, "The remaining monks abide in my exhortation; I am the leader," is called intoxication with status (yasamada).

The pride that arises through intoxication, thinking, "Other beings have no virtue, but I am virtuous," is called intoxication with virtue (sīlamada). The pride that arises through intoxication, thinking, "Other beings do not have one-pointedness of mind even for the duration of a chicken drinking water, but I am an attainer of access concentration and fixed absorption," is called intoxication with jhāna (jhānamada).

The pride that arises through intoxication, thinking, "Other beings have no skills, but I am skilled," is called intoxication with skills (sippamada). The pride that arises through intoxication, thinking, "Other beings are short, but I am tall," is called intoxication with stature (ārohamada). The pride that arises through intoxication, thinking, "Other beings may be short or tall, but I have a body as well-proportioned as a banyan tree," is called intoxication with proportion (pariṇāhamada). The pride that arises through intoxication, thinking, "The physical form of other beings is deformed and loathsome, but my physical form is pleasing and inspiring," is called intoxication with physical form (saṇṭhānamada). The pride that arises through intoxication, thinking, "There are many defects in the bodies of other beings, but in my body, there is not even a defect the size of a hair-tip," is called intoxication with physical perfection (pāripūrimada).

Having explained pride with its objective basis through this much of the Pali text, now, wishing to show only the pride that arises without an objective basis, the text says, "Tattha katamo mado" and so on. The meaning of those words is clear.

In explaining negligence (pamāda), "letting the mind go" means letting the mind go without restraining it with mindfulness in these many instances. It means a lack of mindfulness. "Vossaggānuppadāna" means repeatedly letting go, repeatedly abandoning. "Acting without respect" (asakkaccakiriyatā) refers to the manner of acting without respect toward either the person or the gift when developing these wholesome states such as giving (dāna). Constant occurrence is called "sātacca." That which is not constant is called "asātacca." Not acting with perseverance is called "asātaccakiriyatā." Not acting with steadfastness is called "anaṭṭhitakiriyatā." For example, a chameleon stops for a while after going a little, and does not go continuously; in the same way, a person who performs an act of giving, makes an offering, listens to the Dhamma, or practices the monk's path on one day and then does it again only after a long time, not maintaining it continuously, his...
451:
Such an action (performed only after a long interval without continuity) is called instability of action (anatthitakiriyatā). Sluggish behavior (olīnavuttitā) is the state of being withdrawn due to the absence of expansion, known as continuous performance. Abandoning of desire (nikkhittachandatā) is the relinquishing of the desire for effort in performing wholesome deeds. Laying down the burden (nikkhittadhuratā) means the putting down of the burden of energy, or it means having a regressive mind. Lack of resolution (anadhiṭṭhāna) is the absence of stability in performing wholesome deeds. Lack of application (ananuyoga) is the failure to apply oneself repeatedly. Negligence (pamāda) is heedlessness. The phrase "negligence of such a nature" is an indication of its modes, because the variations of meaning and phrasing are endless. The meaning is this: the negligence shown from the beginning, and any other negligence of such a mode and such a kind, which is known as "neglecting" (pamajjanā) by way of the mode of neglecting, and as "the state of being negligent" (pamajjitatta) by way of the state of being negligent—this is called negligence (pamāda). By its characteristic, however, this negligence has the characteristic of letting go of mindfulness regarding the five cords of sensual pleasure; it should be understood as the mode of mindfulness being released in those very sensual pleasures.

In the description of stubbornness (thambha), it is called thambha because of its rigid meaning. Here, the rigidity and harshness of the mind is spoken of, like a cloth stiffened by starch. The mode of being stubborn is thambhanā. The state of being stubborn is thambhitatta. The state of a callous person is kakkhaḷiya (callousness). The state of a harsh person is phārusiya (harshness). The state of a mind kept erect by not performing the proper duties such as salutation is called ujucittatā (erectness of mind). Amudutā (non-gentleness) is the state of a person who is rigid and not mild. This state is called thambha. A person endowed with this stubbornness is like a python that has swallowed the head of a plow, or like a bellows filled with air; even upon seeing a pagoda or those more senior in age, he is unable to bow down and moves only by skirting around the edges. This stubbornness should be understood as having the characteristic of the mind being puffed up and rigid.

In the description of rivalry (sārambha), it is called sārambha by way of excessive grasping (or striving to excel others). Repeatedly grasping is paṭisārambha. The mode of rivalry is sārambhanā. Repeatedly grasping is paṭisārambhanā. The state of one who repeatedly grasps is paṭisārambhitta. This state is called sārambha. By its characteristic, it is called the characteristic of "doing more than others" (karaṇuttariya). A person endowed with this quality does twice as much as another. If he is a layman, when one person prepares one house-site, another prepares two, and another prepares four.
452:
Another prepares eight, and another sixteen. Even being a monk, when one monk learns one Nikāya, another thinks, "I shall not be inferior to this monk," and learns two; another learns three, another four, and another five. Indeed, it is not proper to learn by way of rivalry. This is the side of the unwholesome and is the path leading to hell. However, by way of the wholesome side, if one person gives one ticket-meal (salākabhatta) it is proper to give two; if he gives two, it is proper to give four. Also, for a monk, when another monk learns one Nikāya, if he stands on the side of liberation (vivaṭṭa) and thinks, "It is pleasant for me to recite having learned two Nikāyas," it is proper to learn more than that.

In the description of excessive desire (atricchatā), in the Ariyavaṃsa Sutta, the term itaritara (any whatever) is defined as "inferior and inferior." Without taking it that way, it refers to a monk who is dissatisfied and discontented with whatever requisites such as robes he has received (meaning he desires something special). Or, it refers to a layman who is discontented with whatever objects he has received among sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles. Bhiyyokamyatā is the state of desiring something special. By way of desiring, it is called icchā (desire). Icchā itself is icchāgatā, or it is the mode of desiring. Desiring beyond what one has obtained is aticchatā. Terms such as rāga (lust) have the same meanings as stated below. This (excessive desire) is called aticchatā. Atricchatā is also a name for this very aticchatā. By its characteristic, discontent with one's own gains and longing for the gains of others is the characteristic of atricchatā. Indeed, to a person with excessive desire, even the excellent things he has obtained seem inferior, while the inferior things obtained by others seem excellent. Even gruel, rice, or cakes cooked in the same pot seem inferior when placed in his own bowl, but seem excellent when placed in another's bowl. This excessive desire occurs among monks, laypeople, and even animals.

Regarding this excessive desire, there are these stories: It is said that a householder invited thirty bhikkhunīs and offered them rice along with cakes. The senior nun (saṅghattherī) caused the cakes in the bowls of all the other bhikkhunīs to be exchanged (thinking they might be better than hers), but in the end, she only got to eat the cakes she had originally received. Also, the King of Benares, thinking "I shall eat meat roasted on embers," took his queen and entered the forest. Seeing a Kinnarī, he abandoned the queen and followed the Kinnarī. The queen turned back, went to a hermitage, performed the preliminary exercises for kasina meditation, and attained the eight meditative attainments and five mundane superknowledges...
453:
Seeing the King approaching while she was sitting, Princess Asitābhū flew up into the sky and departed. The tree deity dwelling in the tree uttered this verse:

"Through excessive desire and through the intoxication of excessive greed, one thus falls away from one's own welfare, just as I have been separated from Princess Asitābhū."

Just as the King of Bārāṇasī, longing for the female Kinnarī, fell away and was deprived of Princess Asitābhū, so too does a person with excessive desire fall away and perish from their own welfare due to excessive greed; thus the deity joked with the King.

In the time of Kassapa Buddha, there was a merchant's son named Mittavindaka who was faithless and without devotion. His mother said, "Dear son, observe the Uposatha today and listen to the Dhamma at the monastery all night; I will give you a thousand coins." Driven by greed for wealth, he undertook the Uposatha precepts and went to the monastery. Thinking, "This place is safe," he noted it and lay down under the Dhamma-seat, slept all night, and then returned home. In the early morning, the mother prepared rice gruel and offered it to him. He drank the gruel only after taking the thousand coins. Then the thought occurred to him, "I will accumulate wealth." He wished to go to sea by boat. Then his mother forbade him, saying, "Dear son, there are forty crores of wealth in this family; there is no need to go." Disregarding his mother's words, he went anyway. The mother stood in front of him to block his way. Then, becoming angry at her, he said, "This woman stands in my way," and kicked her. Leaving his fallen mother behind, he departed. The mother stood up and said, "O foolish son, for you who go after doing such a deed to a mother like me, will there be happiness wherever you go? Who could think such a thing?"

While he was traveling by boat, on the seventh day, the boat stopped. Then the people said, "Surely there is an unlucky person here; let us draw lots." When the lots were drawn, they fell on him three times. They gave him a raft and cast him into the ocean. He reached an island and enjoyed luxury with Vimānika-petīs. Although they said, "Do not go further," he wished to see double the luxury and, proceeding in order, saw a man carrying a razor-wheel. To his mind, that razor-wheel appeared like a lotus flower. He said to that man, "Friend, this [is yours]..."
454:
"Give me this lotus flower that you are wearing," Mittavindaka said. "Sir, this is not a lotus; it is a razor-wheel," the man replied. Then Mittavindaka said, "You are deceiving me. Have I never seen a lotus before?" and added, "You do not want to give me the lotus flower that you are wearing, having anointed yourself with red sandalwood." The man thought, "This man also wishes to experience the result of a deed similar to the one I committed." Then, saying, "Here, fellow," he placed the wheel on Mittavindaka's head and fled. Knowing this matter, the Teacher uttered this verse:

"From four he went to eight, from eight to sixteen,
From sixteen to thirty-two, the greedy one reached the razor-wheel;
The wheel revolves on the head of the man overcome by desire." (Jā. 1.1.104)

Another greedy minister also overstepped his own territory and entered another's territory. Being beaten there, he fled and entered the dwelling of an ascetic, where he undertook the Uposatha precepts and lay down. When asked by the ascetic, "What have you done?" he spoke these verses:

"Greatly despising my own home,
Out of excessive greed, I went to Mallagāma village;
Then the people came out from the village,
And beat me all over with sticks.

With my head broken and my limbs smeared with blood,
I have returned to my own home;
Therefore, I observe the Uposatha,
May excessive greed never come again." (Jā. 1.14.138-139)

In the Exposition on Greatness of Desire (Mahicchatā-niddesa): One is called 'Mahiccha' (one of great desire) because of desiring many objects or because of having great desire. The state of such a person is 'Mahicchatā' (greatness of desire). By characteristic, it is the pretending to have virtues that one does not possess, and lack of moderation in both receiving and using requisites—this is the characteristic of Mahicchatā. Indeed, a person of great desire is like a peddler who carries a bundle of goods under his arm, holding ornaments in his hand, putting as much as should be put into his lap, and while the public is watching, manages with his voice, saying, "Mothers, take this item, take that item." In the same way, even with his own small amount of virtue, or mastery of scriptures, or ascetic qualities, or at the very least, merely living in the forest, while the public knows...
455:
(That person) desires to be praised, and after being praised, he accepts requisites brought even by carts without saying "Enough." Indeed, three things cannot be satisfied: fire with fuel, the ocean with water, and a greedy person with requisites.

A mass of fire, the ocean, and a person of great desire;
Even if given many requisites, these three cannot be filled.

Indeed, a person of great desire cannot even satisfy the mind of his own biological mother, let alone his supporters.

In this regard, there are these illustrative stories. It is said that a certain young monk was very fond of cakes. Then his mother, wishing to test his conduct, thought: "If my son knows moderation in receiving, I will support him with these cakes for the entire three months of the Rains Retreat." She tested him on the day of entering the Rains. First, she gave one cake; when that was finished, a second; when that too was finished, a third. The young monk ate them without saying "Enough." Realizing his lack of moderation, the mother thought: "Today alone, my son has eaten three months' worth of cakes," and from the second day onwards, she did not give him even a single cake.

King Tissa also used to give daily alms to the Saṅgha of monks at Cetiyapabbata. When the country folk asked, "Great King, why do you frequent only this one place? Is it not proper to give elsewhere?", on the second day, he had a great alms-giving held in Anurādhapura. One monk did not know moderation in receiving. The food and snacks received by that single monk had to be lifted and carried by two or three people. The next day, after inviting the Saṅgha of monks at Cetiyapabbata, the King said upon their arrival at the royal palace, "Give me your bowls." Not a single monk gave his bowl, saying, "Enough, Great King, we will take alms according to our own measure." All of them received only what was proportionate. Then the King said, "Look, among your monks, not even one is ignorant of moderation. Yesterday, nothing at all was left over. Today, what was taken is little, and the remainder is much." He was delighted by their moderation and displeased by the lack of moderation in the others.

## Pāpicchatā-niddesa
In the Pāpicchatā-niddesa, regarding the words beginning with "Being without faith, he desires, 'Let people know me as one who has faith,'" the meaning is as follows: One without faith displays the characteristics of one with faith. Those without virtue and so on display the characteristics of those with virtue and so on. How do they display them?

Firstly, a monk without faith, on a day of a great festival when people come to the monastery, takes a broom and sweeps the monastery grounds and discards the rubbish. When he knows people have seen him, he goes to the stupa terrace and there too, he sweeps, discards rubbish, levels the sand, washes the seats, and pours water on the Bodhi tree. When people see this, they think, "There is no one who cleans the monastery like this monk; this venerable one is very faithful," and when they return, they invite him for alms. An immoral person also, in the presence of his supporters, approaches a Vinaya expert and says, "Venerable sir, while I was walking, a cow was startled and ran away, and because of that cow, some blades of grass were broken. While I was sweeping, blades of grass were broken. While I was walking on the cloister..."
456:
A monk lacking faith, on a day of great celebration, at the time when people are coming to the monastery, first takes a broom and sweeps the monastery, discarding the rubbish. When he knows he has been seen by the people, he goes to the pagoda courtyard and there too, he sweeps, discards rubbish, levels the sand, washes the seats, and pours water at the Bodhi tree. When the people see him, they think, 'It seems there is no other monk who cleans the monastery but this one; only this monk looks after this monastery. The elder is indeed faithful.' Thinking thus, they invite him for a meal and depart.

An immoral monk, also in the presence of his lay supporters, approaches a Vinaya expert and asks, 'Venerable sir, while I was walking, a cow was startled and ran away, and the grass was broken. While I was sweeping, the grass was broken. While I was walking on the walkway, small insects died. While I was spitting, I did so unmindfully and it fell on the tips of the grass. What offense is there in these various acts?' When told, 'Friend, since it was done without intention, unmindfully, and without knowing, there is no offense (anāpatti),' he says, 'Venerable sir, it feels to me like a grave offense; please investigate it thoroughly.' Hearing these words, the people think, 'Our lord is remorseful even over such minor matters; how could he ever do anything coarse? There can be no one as virtuous as this lord,' and they show him honor and offerings.

An unlearned monk, also sitting in the midst of his lay supporters, says, 'Such and such a Tipitaka-dhara monk and such and such a master of the four Nikāyas are my resident pupils; they learned the Dhamma from me.' The people think, 'There is no one as learned as our lord; it is said that such and such famous persons learned the Dhamma from him,' and they show him honor and offerings.

A monk fond of company, also on a day of great celebration, has a long bench and a backrest carried for him and goes to stay at the foot of a tree at the edge of the monastery during the day. When people come and ask, 'Where is the elder?' his deceitful disciples say, 'The elder does not stay here at such busy times; he stays in the long walkway at the day-quarters on the edge of the monastery.' That monk, having spent the day there, attaches spiderwebs to his forehead, has the bench carried back, and returns to sit at the gate of the monastery compound. When the people say, 'Venerable sir, where have you been? We came but did not see you,' he informs them of his secluded nature, saying, 'Lay devotees, the inner monastery is very crowded; this is the place where young monks and novices wander about, so I stayed at the sixty-cubit walkway in the day-quarters.'

A lazy monk, also sitting in the midst of his supporters, asks, 'Lay devotees, did you see the meteor fall?' When they ask, 'We did not see it, venerable sir; at what time did it happen?' he says, 'It happened while we were on the walkway.' He asks, 'Did you hear the sound of the earthquake?' and when they say, 'We did not hear it,' he says, 'It happened at midnight while we were standing leaning against the backrest.' He asks, 'Did you see the great light?' and when they say, 'We did not see it,' he says, 'It happened at the time I was descending from the walkway.' The people think, 'Our elder is on the walkway throughout all three watches of the night; there is no one as energetic as this lord,' and they show him honor and offerings.

A forgetful monk, also sitting in the midst of his supporters, says, 'At that time I learned the Dīgha Nikāya; at that time I learned the Majjhima Nikāya, Saṃyutta Nikāya, and Aṅguttara Nikāya. As for looking at books in between...'
457:
"...did it happen?" when asked, he says, "It happened while we were on the walkway." He asks, "Did you hear the sound of the earthquake?" When asked, "Venerable sir, we did not hear it; at what time did it happen?" he says, "It happened during the middle watch of the night while we were standing leaning against our backrest." He asks again, "A great light appeared; did you see that light?" When asked, "Venerable sir, at what time did it happen?" he says, "It happened at the time I was descending from the walkway." The people think, "Our elder is on the walkway throughout all three watches of the night; there is no one with such exerted energy as this lord," and they show him honor and offerings.

A monk who has lost his mindfulness, also sitting in the midst of his lay supporters, says, "At such a time I learned the Dīgha Nikāya; at such a time I learned the Majjhima Nikāya, Saṃyutta Nikāya, and Aṅguttara Nikāya. There is no such thing as having to look back at the texts; the Pali comes to my mind just as I desire. But these other monks live like sheep, moving their mouths (muttering constantly for fear of forgetting)." The people think, "There is no one with such established mindfulness as this lord," and they show him honor and offerings.

An unconcentrated monk, also in the presence of his lay supporters, asks the teachers of the Commentaries, "How does one develop what is called a Kasina? By how much is the sign (nimitta) said to have arisen? By how much does access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) occur? By how much does absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) occur? How many factors are there in the first jhāna? How many factors are there in the second, third, and fourth jhānas?" When the teachers of the Commentaries speak according to what they have learned, he smiles and when asked, "Friend, is it not so?" he says, "It is appropriate, venerable sir," thus indicating his own attainment of meditative absorptions. The people think, "The lord is an attainer of meditative absorptions," and they show him honor and offerings.

An unwise monk, also sitting in the midst of his supporters, says, "While I was looking at the Pañcattaya Sutta in the Majjhima Nikāya, the Path (Magga) arrived along with psychic powers. Scriptural study (pariyatti) is not difficult for us; however, considering that one who is preoccupied with scriptural study is not released from suffering, I have abandoned scriptural study," and so on, showing off his great wisdom. By speaking in this way, that monk strikes a blow against the Sasana. There is no great thief like this monk. This is because it is not true that one who bears the scriptures is not released from suffering (on the contrary, they are released). A monk who is not an Arahant, seeing the village children, asks, "What do your parents say about us?"
458:
"Venerable sir, (people) say you are an Arahant," they said. "Householders are very clever; they cannot be deceived," he replied, indicating his state of being an Arahant.

In this context, other deceivers such as the 'Jar-Arahant' and the 'Aerial-root-Arahant' should also be known. It is said that a certain deceitful monk buried a large jar (cāṭi) inside an inner chamber and would enter it when people arrived. People would ask, "Where is the elder?" When told, "He is in the inner chamber," they would enter and search but, finding no one, would come out and say, "The elder is not there." When told again, "The elder is indeed in the inner chamber," they would enter once more. By then, the monk would have emerged from the jar and be sitting on a bench. When the lay devotees said, "Venerable sir, we did not see you before and left; where did you go?" he would indicate his state of being an Arahant by saying, "Monks go to whatever place they desire."

Another deceitful monk lived in a leaf-hut on a mountain. Behind the leaf-hut, at a precipice, there was a Kacchaka tree. Its aerial root (pāroha) reached down to the ground on the other side. People would come by the regular path and invite him. That monk, taking his bowl and robes, would descend by the aerial root and show himself at the village gate. When people arrived later and asked, "Venerable sir, by which path did you come?" he would indicate his state of being an Arahant by saying, "It is not proper to ask the path by which monks come; they come by whatever path they desire." A learned layman, realizing this, thought, "I will catch him." One day, seeing him descending by the aerial root, he cut it from behind, leaving only a tiny bit. The monk, intending to descend, fell with a "thud" as soon as he stepped on it, and his clay bowl broke. Thinking, "I have been found out," he fled. The state of having evil desires is called pāpicchatā. In terms of characteristics, it is the desire to be praised for qualities one does not possess and lack of moderation in receiving requisites. This should be known as the characteristic of pāpicchatā.

In the explanation of singa (horn), it is called singa because of its piercing nature. This is a name for the 'horn of defilement' (kilesa-singa), which is known as the habit of city-dwellers. The state of affectation is singāratā, or the manner of acting with affectation. The state of being elegant is caturatā. Similarly, it is called cāturiyam. The state of being well-groomed is parikkhatatā; this is a name for the state of firm affectation, like something that has been dug around and established.
459:
That name is a synonym for parikkhatatā itself. Thus, by all these terms, only the state of the 'horn of defilement' is described.

In the explanation of tintiṇa, tintiṇa means disparaging. Tintiṇāyanā is the manner of disparaging. Tintiṇāyitatta is the state of one who is full of disparagement. Loluppa is the state of one who is fickle and greedy. The other two are explanations of the manner and the state. Pucchañjikatā is the state of trembling and low livelihood in places where gains are expected. Sādhukamyatā is the longing for excellent gains. Thus, by all these terms, the manner of disparaging and quarreling out of defilement—saying "This is yours, this is mine"—is described, like a dog drinking sour gruel from a trough and growling "bhū-bhū" upon seeing another dog.

In the explanation of cāpalya (frivolity), decorating the robes by beating, folding, etc., is called cīvara-maṇḍanā. Decorating the bowl by making it shine like a gem, etc., is called patta-maṇḍanā. Decorating private lodgings with paintings, carvings, etc., is called senāsana-maṇḍanā. "Of this foul body" refers to this human body. Just as a newborn jackal is called an "old jackal," and a Galo-cilatā creeper as thick as a thigh is called a "foul creeper" (pūtilatā), so too the human body, even if golden-colored, is called a "foul body." Decorating that body at intervals with red or pale-colored garments and robes is called maṇḍanā. "Of external requisites" refers to the remaining requisites, excluding the bowl and robes. Alternatively, the decoration called cīvara-maṇḍanā and patta-maṇḍanā is maṇḍanā in the sense of decorating the body with those requisites or keeping those external requisites decorated; thus the meaning should be understood here. In these terms maṇḍanā and vibhūsanā, maṇḍanā should be understood as filling in deficiencies, and vibhūsanā as making the skin attractive. Keḷanā means playing. Parikeḷanā means repeated playing. Giddhikatā is the state of being associated with greed. Giddhikatta is a synonym for that same term. Capalatā is the state of a fickle person. Similarly, cāpalya is also the state of a fickle person. "This is called cāpalya" means that a person endowed with this frivolity, even if a hundred years old, becomes like a newborn child (childish).

In the explanation of asabhāgavutti (inappropriate conduct), vippaṭikūlaggāhitā is the state of taking what is unsuitable. Vipaccanīkasātatā is finding pleasure in doing what is contrary. Anādariya is the state of being disrespectful. Similarly, anādariyatā is also the state of being disrespectful. Agāravatā is the state of having no reverence. Appatissavatā is not acting towards elders (lack of obedience).
460:
This taking of the opposite, taking what is improper, and so forth, is called 'asabhāgavutti' (incompatible conduct). It means the state of having an incompatible livelihood. A person endowed with this incompatible conduct does not even look back at his mother or father when they are ill. He quarrels with his mother for the sake of his father's property, and with his father for the sake of his mother's property. He lives an incompatible life. For the sake of his parents' property, he quarrels with his elder or younger brothers. He speaks shameless words. He does not perform the major and minor duties toward his teacher or preceptor. He does not attend to his sick teacher or preceptor. In a place where the shrine (cetiya) of the Blessed Buddha can be seen, he commits the act of defecating or urinating. He spits or blows his nose there. He holds an umbrella. He walks wearing sandals (footwear). He is not ashamed before the disciples of the Buddha. He does not show respect to the Saṅgha. He does not manifest moral shame and moral dread (hiri-ottappa) toward those worthy of respect, such as those who are like his mother or father. All these actions of such a person, in relation to objects such as his mother, are called 'asabhāgavuttitā' (the state of incompatible conduct).

In the explanation of Arati (Aversion), 'pantesu' means in monasteries that are far away or secluded from people. 'Adhikusalesu' refers to the dhammas of Samatha (tranquillity) and Vipassanā (insight). 'Arati' is the rejection of delight (discontent). 'Aratitā' is the manner of being discontented. 'Anabhirati' is the state of not being delighted. 'Anabhiramaṇā' is the manner of not delighting. 'Ukkaṇṭhitā' is the manner of being dissatisfied or bored. 'Paritassitā' is the longing or anxiety arising from that very dissatisfaction.

In the explanation of Tandī (Sloth), 'tandī' is natural laziness. 'Tandiyanā' is the manner of being lazy. 'Tandimanakatā' is the state of having a mind overcome by laziness. The state of a lazy person is 'ālasyaṃ'. The manner of existing as a lazy person is 'ālasyāyanā'. The state of a person who exists as a lazy person is 'ālasyāyitattaṃ'. Thus, by all these terms, the laziness of the mental body (nāmakāya) arising through the power of defilements is described.

In the explanation of Vijambhitā (Stretching), 'jambhanā' is quivering (stretching of limbs). Repeated quivering is 'vijambhanā'. 'Ānamanā' is bending forward. 'Vinamanā' is bending backward. 'Sannamanā' is bending all around. 'Paṇamanā' is the straightening of the body upward, just as a weaver rising from his loom holds onto something and straightens his body. 'Byādhiyakaṃ' is the state of having an arisen illness. Thus, by all these terms, only the quivering of the physical body arising through the power of defilements is described.
461:
## Bhattasammadaniddesa
In the explanation of food-stupor (Bhattasammada), 'bhuttāvissā' refers to one who has finished eating. 'Bhattamucchā' is the illness (faintness) caused by food; indeed, it is because one becomes as if in a faint due to heavy food. 'Bhattakilamatho' is the state of fatigue caused by food. 'Bhattapariḷāho' is the distress (burning sensation) caused by food. At that time, because of the arising of distress, the faculties are impaired and the body becomes as if decaying. 'Kāyaduṭṭhullaṃ' is the unfitness (badness) of the body for work, depending on food.

Regarding the explanation of the sluggishness of the mind (līnatta), it is exactly as stated in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā mentioned below. It should be understood that by all these terms, the manner of the mind's illness arising through the power of defilements is described.

## Kuhanāniddesa
In the explanation of scheming (Kuhanā), 'lābhasakkārasilokasaannissitassa' refers to the state of one who depends on (longs for) gain, honor, and fame. 'Pāpicchassa' is the state of one who has evil desires, wishing to display qualities he does not possess. 'Icchāpakatassa' is the state of one who is oppressed by evil desires (made to deviate from his natural state).

Following this, since three types of scheming (kuhanavatthu) appear in the Mahāniddesa—namely, those based on the use of requisites (paccayapaṭisevana), indirect talk (sāmantajappana), and postures (iriyāpathasannissita)—the text begins with 'paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātena vā' and so forth to demonstrate these three. Among these three, when invited with robes and so forth, even though he actually desires those requisites, he rejects them based on evil desire. Then, knowing that those lay devotees have firm faith in him, and when they think, 'Oh, the venerable one has so few desires; he does not wish to accept anything. It would be a great gain for us if he would accept even a little,' and they bring excellent robes and so forth by various means, he accepts them while making it appear as if he is doing so only out of a desire to favor the donors. From that point on, the act of causing wonderment so that requisites amounting to eighty cartloads are offered is to be known as the scheming based on the use of requisites (paccayapaṭisevana). This is also stated in the Mahāniddesa:

"What is the scheming based on the use of requisites? Here, lay devotees invite a monk with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. That monk, being of evil desire, being oppressed by evil desire, even though he desires the requisites..."
462:
Based on a great desire for the four requisites such as robes and so forth, he rejects robes, rejects alms-food, rejects lodgings, and rejects medicinal requisites for the sick. That monk speaks thus: "What use does a monk have for expensive robes? It is only fitting for a monk to collect rags from a cemetery, or from a rubbish heap, or from a shop, and having made them into a double-layered robe (saṅghāṭī), to wear them. What use does a monk have for expensive alms-food? It is only fitting for a monk to make a living by gathering morsels of food through the practice of seeking scraps. What use does a monk have for expensive lodgings? It is only fitting for a monk to be a tree-root dweller, or a cemetery dweller, or an open-air dweller. What use does a monk have for expensive medicinal requisites? It is only fitting for a monk to make medicine with fermented urine or pieces of yellow myrobalan."

Based on that evil desire, he wears coarse robes, consumes coarse alms-food, uses coarse lodgings, and uses coarse medicinal requisites. Lay devotees, knowing him thus—"This monk has fewness of wishes, is contented, secluded, not associated with others, possesses aroused energy, and is one who speaks of the dhuta practices"—invite him again and again with requisites such as robes and so forth. That monk speaks thus: "Due to the presence of three factors, a faithful son of a good family generates much merit. Due to the presence of faith, a faithful son of a good family generates much merit; due to the presence of the gift... due to the presence of the recipients, a faithful son of a good family generates much merit. You have this faith, the gift is available, and I am the recipient. If I do not accept, you will be excluded from merit. I have no need for this requisite, yet I accept it only out of compassion for you."

Based on such speaking, he accepts many robes, and accepts many alms-food... and medicinal requisites. Such frowning, grimacing, scheming, deceiving, and the state of deception is called the basis of scheming (kuhanavatthu) consisting of the use of requisites.

Furthermore, for one who has evil desires, making others marvel by speech that indicates the attainment of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) through various means is to be known as the basis of scheming consisting of indirect talk (sāmantajappana). As it is said: "What is the basis of scheming consisting of indirect talk?"
463:
## The Basis of Scheming (Kuhanavatthu)
In this Dispensation, a certain monk, being of evil desires, overcome by bad intentions, and desiring the praise of others, thinks, "In this way, people will praise me," and speaks words based on the noble states (ariyadhamma). He says, "A monk who wears such a robe is a monk of great influence." He says, "A monk who carries such a bowl, a bronze vessel, a water-filter, a cloth-filter, a bolt-key, sandals, a waist-band, or a shoulder-strap is a monk of great influence." He says, "A monk who has such a preceptor, a teacher, a fellow-preceptor, a fellow-teacher, a friend, an acquaintance, an intimate, or a companion is a monk of great influence." Or he says, "A monk who lives in such a monastery—a lean-to, a long mansion, a gabled house, a cave, a mountain cleft, a hut, a pinnacled house, a watchtower, a hall, a storehouse, a long hall, an attendance hall, a pavilion, or at the foot of a tree—is a monk of great influence."

Alternatively, one who is a restrainer of repulsive and useless movements of body and speech, a great frowner, a great boaster, a great talker near the four requisites, and one who makes others praise him with his own mouth, speaks such profound, hidden, subtle, concealed, supramundane (lokuttara) speech connected with emptiness (suññatā) so that others will think, "This monk is an attainer of such peaceful attainments of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti)." Such frowning, making others marvel, and having the behavior that causes marveling is called the basis of scheming consisting of indirect talk (sāmantajappana).

Furthermore, for one who has evil desires, making others marvel by means of postures (iriyāpatha) performed with the desire for praise is to be known as the basis of scheming based on postures. As it is said: "What is the basis of scheming consisting of postures? In this Dispensation, a certain monk, being of evil desires, overcome by bad intentions, and desiring praise, thinks, 'In this way, people will praise me,' and composes his walking, composes his lying down; he walks with a fixed intention, stands with a fixed intention, sits with a fixed intention, and lies down with a fixed intention, thinking, 'May they know me as an Arahant.' He walks as if he were composed, stands, sits, and lies down as if he were composed. He appears as if he were absorbed in jhāna in the presence of people. Such solemnity, arrangement, and composition of postures, frowning, making others marvel, and having the behavior that causes marveling is called the basis of scheming consisting of postures."
464:
Among those words (spoken by way of using the four requisites), "spoken by way of using the four requisites" means by using the four requisites as described. "By speaking in the vicinity" means by words spoken nearby. "Of the posture" means of the four postures. Āṭhapanā means setting up from the beginning or setting up with respect. Ṭhapanā is the manner of placing. Saṇṭhapanā means well-arranging, making it pleasant to behold. Bhākuṭikā means frowning or wrinkling the face to show oneself as important or at the forefront. One who habitually frowns is called bhākuṭika, and the state of such a person is bhākuṭiya. Kuhanā means causing wonder. The act of causing wonder or the behavior of one who causes wonder is called kuhāyanā. The state of one who possesses the quality of causing wonder is called kuhitatta.

In the exposition of talking (lapanā), ālapanā (addressing) means, upon seeing people coming to the monastery, speaking from the very beginning such as: "Sirs, for what purpose have you come? Have you come to invite the monks? If so, go ahead; I will bring the monks and follow later." Or, it is ālapanā when one brings oneself forward and speaks boastfully of oneself: "I am Tissa; the King is pleased with me; such and such a great royal minister is pleased with me." Lapanā (talking) is the same kind of speaking as mentioned above when one is asked. Sallapanā (conversing) is speaking well by giving others a chance to speak, fearing that they might get bored. Ullapanā (extolling) is speaking by exalting others as "Great merchant, great ship-owner, great donor." Samullapanā is exalting from all sides. Unnahanā (hinting) means exalting and binding, such as saying: "Lay followers, in the past you gave gifts at such a time; why do you not give now?" until the lay followers say, "Venerable sir, we will give, we just haven't had the opportunity yet." Or, seeing someone with a bundle of sugar-cane in hand, one asks, "Lay followers, where have you come from?" They reply, "From the sugar-cane field, Bhante." "Is the sugar-cane there sweet?" "One must eat it to know, Bhante." "Lay followers, it is not proper for a monk to say 'Give me sugar-cane'." Such talk that binds them to give even while appearing to explain is called unnahanā. Repeatedly binding from all sides is samunnahanā. Ukkācanā (boasting) is exalting and presenting oneself such as: "This family knows only me; if any gift arises here, they give it only to me." This is also called uddīpanā.

The story of Telakandarikā should be told here. It is said that two monks entered a village and, while sitting in the rest house, saw a young girl and called her.
465:
Seeing the girl who had come, one of the two monks asked, "Venerable sir, whose daughter is this girl?" The other replied, "Friend, this girl is the daughter of our supporter, Telakandarikā. When I go to her house, her mother gives ghee by the jarful; this girl also gives by the jarful just like her mother." Thus he boasted and showed off.

Repeatedly boasting from all sides is called samukkācanā. Anuppiyabhāṇitā (flattery) is repeatedly saying only pleasant things without considering whether they are true or in accordance with the Dhamma. Cāṭukamyatā (fawning) is the state of being humble, acting by placing oneself in a low position. Muggasūpyatā (bean-soup-ness) is the state of being like green-gram soup. Just as when green grams are being cooked, some do not cook while the rest do; similarly, in the speech of a person, only some words are true while the rest are false (lies)—such a person is called muggasūpyo (one like bean-soup). The state of such a person is muggasūpyatā. Pāribhaṭayatā is the state of a pāribhaṭaya. A monk who carries young children of families in his arms or on his shoulders like a nurse (meaning he carries them about), the work of such a monk is called pāribhaṭaya, and the state of being a pāribhaṭaya is pāribhaṭayatā.

In the exposition of hinting (nemittikatā), nimitta (a sign) is any bodily or verbal action that links others to the giving of requisites. Nimittakamma (making a sign) is skill in making such signs.

Regarding this nimittakamma, there is this story: A monk who practiced the dhutanga of alms-round went to the door of a blacksmith who was his supporter. When asked, "What do you need, Bhante?", he took his hand out from within his robes and made a gesture as if striking with a billhook. The blacksmith said, "I understand, Bhante," and having made a billhook, he offered it. Obhāsa (intimation) is talk connected with the four requisites. Obhāsakamma (the act of intimation) is like seeing young cowherds and asking, "Are these calves of a milk-giving cow or a buttermilk-giving cow?" When told, "They are calves of a milk-giving cow, Bhante," he says, "They cannot be calves of a milk-giving cow; if they were, the monks would also receive milk." In this way, he informs the parents of those children and causes them to offer milk, etc. Sāmantajappā (indirect talk) is talking by bringing oneself close to the requisites.

The story of the Elder who recited the Jātakas should also be told here: An Elder who recited the Jātakas, wishing to eat, entered the house of a female supporter and sat down. She, not wishing to give, said, "There is no rice," and went to a neighbor's house as if she were going to fetch rice. The monk entered the inner room and looked around...
466:
The Elder saw sugar cane in the corner of the door, jaggery in a vessel, salted fish in a basket, rice in a pot, and ghee in a jar; he then went outside and sat down. The housewife returned, saying, "I did not get any rice." Then the Elder said, "Laywoman, today almsfood will not be obtained; I have already seen an omen earlier." When she asked, "What omen did you see, Bhante?", he replied, "I saw a snake like the sugar cane leaning in the corner of the door. Looking to strike it, I saw a stone like the lump of jaggery kept in the vessel. When struck with the stone, the snake showed its hood like the salted fish kept in the basket. Wanting to bite, it showed its teeth like the rice in the rice pot. Then, being angry, it showed venomous saliva coming out of its mouth like the ghee placed in the ghee jar." The laywoman thought, "It is no longer possible to deceive this shaven-headed one," and after offering the sugar cane and cooking the rice, she offered it together with the ghee, jaggery, and fish. Such speaking by approaching near the object is to be understood as sāmantajappa (indirect talk). Parikathā means speaking in a roundabout way so as to obtain the object.

In the explanation of nippesikatā: Akkosanā means insulting by way of the ten grounds for insult. Vambhanā means speaking disparagingly. Garahanā means blaming by saying, "He is faithless, without devotion," and so on. Ukkhepanā means extolling by speech, saying, "Do not say such things about this person." Extolling in every way along with a reason and a cause is called samukkhepanā. Alternatively, extolling one who does not give by saying, "Oh, what a great donor!" is ukkhepanā. Extolling well as a "great benefactor" is samukkhepanā. Khipanā means mocking by saying, "What is the use of the life of this one who eats the seed-corn?" Saṅkhippanā means mocking even more intensely by saying, "Why do you call this person a non-giver, who always gives the word 'there is none' to all?" Pāpanā means bringing one to the state of a non-giver or to ill-repute. Bringing to ill-repute in every way is sampāpanā. Avaṇṇahārikā means carrying dispraise from house to house, village to village, and district to district, thinking, "He will give out of fear of my dispraise." Parapiṭṭhimaṃsikatā means speaking sweetly in front but speaking dispraise behind one's back. This is called parapiṭṭhimaṃsikatā because it is like eating the flesh of the back of those whose faces one dare not look at. This is called nippesikatā. It is called nippesikatā because it scrapes off the virtues of others like a bamboo splinter scrapes off ointment, or because it seeks gain by oppressing others like one seeks scent by grinding a perfume-substance.
467:
Seeking gain by grinding and crushing the virtues of others is thus called nippesikatā (seeking gain by grinding down others).

In the explanation of seeking gain with gain (lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā), 'nijigīsanatā' means seeking. 'Obtained from here' (ito laddhaṃ) means obtained from this house. 'There' (amutra) means in that house. 'Eṭṭhī' means desiring. 'Gaveṭṭhī' means seeking. 'Pariyeṭṭhī' means seeking repeatedly. Here, the story of the monk who, from the beginning, gave whatever almsfood he obtained to the young boys in various houses and finally obtained and left with milk-gruel should be told. The terms 'esanā' and so on are synonyms for 'eṭṭhī' and so on; therefore, eṭṭhī is esanā (seeking), gaveṭṭhī is gavesanā (searching), and pariyeṭṭhī is pariyesanā (repeated searching). Thus should the connection of meaning be understood here.

In the explanation of seyyamāna (the conceit 'I am superior'): 'By birth' (jātiyā) means by the accomplishment of birth such as being of the Khattiya caste. 'By lineage' (gottena) means by a noble lineage such as the Gotama lineage. 'By noble birth' (kolaputtiyena) means by being of a great family. 'By beauty of complexion' (vaṇṇapokkharatāya) means by having a body endowed with beauty. Indeed, the body is called 'pokkhara'; the meaning is by way of being handsome due to the accomplishment of the body's complexion. The terms 'by wealth' (dhanena) and so on have clear meanings. 'He arouses pride' (mānaṃ jappeti) means he maintains or produces pride by way of any one of these things, thinking, "I am superior."

In the explanation of sadisamāna (the conceit 'I am equal'): 'He arouses pride' (mānaṃ jappeti) means he maintains pride by way of any one of these things, thinking, "I am equal." This is the distinction in meaning here. In the Pali text, however, there is no difference.

In the explanation of hīnamāna (the conceit 'I am inferior'): 'He arouses lowly pride' (omānaṃ jappeti) means he maintains a lowly pride. 'Omāna' is a low, inferior pride. 'Omaññanā' and 'omaññitatta' are explanations of the manner and the state. 'Hīḷanā' means loathing oneself on account of birth and so on. 'Ohīḷanā' means excessive loathing. 'Ohīḷitatta' is the explanation of that state. 'Attuññā' means knowing oneself as inferior. 'Attāvaññā' means despising oneself as low-class. 'Attaparibhava' means thinking with self-contempt, "The accomplishments of birth and so on have not arisen for me."

Thus, these three types of pride are taught by way of objects such as birth, without depending on the individual. Each of these types of pride can arise in all three kinds of persons: the superior, the equal, and the inferior. Among them, the pride thinking "I am superior" is a pride according to reality (yāthāvamāna) only for the superior person; for the others, it is a pride not according to reality. The pride thinking "I am equal"...
468:
The conceit that arises as 'I am equal' towards one who is equal is indeed true conceit (yāthāvamāna); towards others, it is false conceit (ayāthāvamāna). The conceit that arises as 'I am inferior' towards one who is inferior is indeed true conceit; towards others, it is false conceit.

Among those conceits, the nine types of conceit such as 'I am superior to the superior' are taught with reference to persons. Among these nine types of conceit, three types arise for each person. In that Pali, 'dahati' means 'reckons' or 'considers.' 'Taṃ nissāya' means based on that reckoning of being superior (developing conceit). Among these, the conceit of 'I am superior' to the superior arises in kings and renunciants. A king develops this conceit thinking, 'Who is equal to me in terms of country, wealth, or vehicles?' A renunciant also develops this conceit thinking, 'Who is equal to me in terms of virtue (sīla), ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and so on?'

The conceit of 'I am equal' to the superior also arises in these same kings and renunciants. A king develops this conceit thinking, 'What is the difference between me and other kings in terms of country, wealth, or vehicles?' A renunciant also develops this conceit thinking, 'What is the difference between me and another bhikkhu in terms of virtue, ascetic practices, and so on?'

The conceit of 'I am inferior' to the superior also arises in these same persons. A king whose country, wealth, or vehicles are not complete develops this conceit thinking, 'For me, there is only the mere designation of being a king; how can I truly be called a king?' A renunciant also develops this conceit when gain and honor are scarce, thinking, 'Being a Dhamma-teacher, one of great learning, or a Great Elder is just mere words; how can I, who have no gain and honor, be called a Dhamma-teacher, one of great learning, or a Great Elder?'

The conceits such as 'I am superior' to an equal arise in ministers and others. A minister or a governor develops these conceits thinking, 'Who is another royal official equal to me in terms of possessions and vehicles?' or 'What is the difference between me and others?' or 'For me, there is only the name of a minister, but I do not even have enough for food and clothing; how can I be called a minister?'

The conceits such as 'I am superior' to the inferior arise in slaves and others. A slave thinks, 'From the mother's side or the father's side, who is another person equal to me...'
469:
...there is no such slave.' There are those who have become slaves for the sake of their bellies because they were unable to make a living. Regarding them, he develops these conceits thinking, 'I am superior because I have descended from a lineage of slaves,' or 'What is the difference between me and such-and-such a slave, since I am a slave of pure descent from both the mother's and father's sides?' or 'I have entered into slavery only for the sake of my belly; however, from the perspective of my parents, I have no status as a slave; how can I be called a slave?' Just like a slave, basket-makers (pukkusa), outcasts (caṇḍāla), and others also develop these conceits.

Among these three types of conceit, only the conceit that arises as 'I am superior' towards the superior is true conceit (yāthāvamāna). The other two are false conceits (ayāthāvamāna). Similarly, the conceit that arises as 'I am equal' towards an equal, and 'I am inferior' towards the inferior, is true conceit. The other two are false conceits. Among those, true conceits are to be abandoned by the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga). False conceits are to be abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga).

Having thus taught the conceits together with their bases, he now says 'Tattha katamo māno' and so forth to show the conceit that arises without a base (purely as ultimate conceit).

In the exposition of over-pride (atimāna-niddesa), he points it out by way of bases such as birth (jāti) and so on, without considering the person as superior, etc. There, 'atimanyati' means thinking by surpassing others, 'There is no one equal to me in terms of birth and so on.'

In the exposition of pride and over-pride (mānātimāna-niddesa), 'yo evarūpo' refers to the conceit that arises as 'This person was equal to me before; now I am superior, I am much inferior.' This is said to show 'mānātimāna' because it arises based on the previous conceit of equality (sadisamāna), like a burden upon a burden.

The exposition of inferiority-conceit (omāna-niddesa) is just like the exposition of the conceit of being inferior (hīnamāna). However, by way of those who are to be disciplined, the conceit called 'I am inferior' is termed 'omāna.' A slight distinction here is that in this exposition of omāna, it should be understood as omāna because it occurs by way of lowering oneself, thinking, 'You have a birth, but your birth is like that of a crow; you have a lineage, but your lineage is like that of an outcast; you have a voice, but your voice is like the cawing of a crow.'
470:
In the explanation of adhimāna (overestimation), "perceiving what has not been reached as reached" means perceiving the Four Truths as reached when they have not been reached. "What has not been done" means the task to be performed by the four paths has not yet been done. "What has not been attained" means the Dhamma of the Four Truths has not yet been attained. "What has not been realized" means not yet having realized through Arahatship. This kind of conceit is called adhimāna; it is also called adhigatamāna (the conceit of thinking one has attained).

To whom does this adhimāna arise, and to whom does it not? Firstly, it does not arise in a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka). This is because that noble disciple, by reviewing the paths, fruits, Nibbāna, the defilements abandoned, and the remaining defilements, experiences joy and is free from doubt regarding the penetration of noble qualities. Therefore, in persons such as Stream-winners (sotāpanna), conceit does not arise in the form of "I am a Once-returner," and so on. It also does not arise in an immoral person (dussīla), because such a person has no hope of attaining noble qualities. Even for a virtuous person, it does not arise if they have abandoned meditation and delight in sleep and such.

However, it can arise in an insight meditator (vipassaka) who possesses pure virtue, is diligent in meditation, has overcome doubt by discerning mind and matter and grasping their causes, and is contemplating formations (saṅkhāra) by applying the three characteristics. When it arises, one who has attained pure tranquillity (samatha) or pure insight (vipassanā) may stop in the middle before reaching Arahatship. Such a person, not seeing the occurrence of defilements for ten, twenty, or thirty years, may think, "I am a Stream-winner," or "a Once-returner," or "a Non-returner." But one who has attained both tranquillity and insight usually stops only at Arahatship. This is because, by the power of concentration, defilements are suppressed, and by the power of insight, formations are well-grasped. Therefore, for sixty, eighty, or even a hundred years, defilements do not arise, and the mental process remains like that of an Arahant. Such a person, not seeing the occurrence of defilements for such a long time, may think "I am an Arahant" even before reaching Arahatship, like the Elder Mahānāga who lived in Uccamālaṅka, the Elder Mahādatta who lived in Haṅkanaka, or the Elder Cūḷasumana who lived in the Niṅkapoṇṇapadhānaghara at Cittalapabbata.

Regarding this matter, I shall present this story. It is said that an Elder named Dhammadinna, who lived in Talaṅgara, was a great Arahant who had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and was a teacher to a large community of monks. One day, while sitting in his daytime resting place, he reflected, "Has our teacher, the Elder Mahānāga of Uccataliṅka, finished the task of monkhood?" He saw that his teacher was still a worldling (puthujjana). Realizing, "If I do not go, the teacher will die as a worldling," he flew through the air by psychic power, descended near the Elder, paid respects, performed his duties, and sat in a suitable place. When the teacher asked, "Friend Dhammadinna, why have you come at an unusual time?" he replied, "Venerable Sir, I have come to ask some questions." The teacher said, "Ask, friend; if I know, I shall answer." He then asked a thousand questions, and the teacher answered them all without hesitation. Then he said, "Venerable Sir, your wisdom is very sharp. When did you attain this Dhamma?"
471:
...reflecting whether the task of monkhood of his teacher, the Elder Mahānāga who resided in Uccataliṅka, had reached its end or not, he saw only the teacher's state as a worldling (puthujjana). Knowing, "If I do not go, he will die as a worldling," he flew through the air by psychic power, descended near the Elder who was in his daytime resting place, paid respects, performed the major and minor duties, and sat in a suitable place. When asked, "Friend Dhammadinna, for what purpose have you come at an unusual time?" he replied, "Venerable Sir, I have come to ask some questions."

When told, "Ask, friend; if I know, I shall answer," he asked a thousand questions. The Elder answered every question asked without any hesitation. After that, he said, "Venerable Sir, your wisdom is very sharp. When did you attain this Dhamma?" The Elder replied, "Friend, I attained it sixty years ago." He then asked, "Venerable Sir, do you also make use of concentration (samādhi)?" The Elder replied, "Friend, making use of this concentration is not a heavy burden (not a difficult task)." He then requested, "If so, Venerable Sir, please create an elephant." The Elder created an entirely white elephant. He then requested, "Venerable Sir, now make this elephant come towards you with its ears pricked, its tail extended, its trunk in its mouth, and making a terrifying trumpeting sound like a heron. When the Elder did so and saw the terrifying appearance of the elephant rushing towards him, he stood up and prepared to run. At that moment, the Arahant Elder Dhammadinna reached out his hand, caught the corner of the Elder's robe, and said, "Venerable Sir, is there such a thing as fear for an Arahant?" Only then did the Elder realize his state as a worldling and, saying, "Friend Dhammadinna, be my refuge and support," he sat down on his heels at Dhammadinna's feet. Dhammadinna replied, "Venerable Sir, I have come specifically to be your support; do not worry," and he taught him a meditation subject. The Elder took the meditation subject, stepped onto the walking path, and on the third step, he reached the highest fruit, Arahatship. It is said that this Elder was of a hateful temperament (dosacarita).

In the explanation of asmimāna (the conceit "I am"), the conceit "Form is I" means the conceit (perception) that arises as "I am form." "Desire" (chanda) is the desire that follows the conceit. The same applies to "underlying tendency" (anusaya). The same method should be understood for feeling (vedanā) and the rest.

In the explanation of micchāmāna (wrong conceit), in the phrases such as "by a lowly occupation," a lowly occupation (kammāyatana) refers to the work of fishermen, hunters, and so on. A lowly...
472:
Lowly field of arts (sippāyatana) means skill in casting fishing nets, making fish traps, setting snares, fixing stakes, and so forth. Lowly branch of knowledge (vijjā) means any kind of knowledge that leads to the killing of others. Lowly learning (suta) means learning connected with the Bharata war, the abduction of Queen Sītā, and so forth. Lowly intuition (paṭibhāna) means intuition that arises in connection with poorly spoken words, such as poetry, dancing, and the interactions between men and women. Lowly virtue (sīla) means the practice of goats or the practice of cows. Vows (vata) likewise mean the goat-vow and the cow-vow. Lowly view (diṭṭhi) refers to any of the sixty-two types of wrong views.
In the explanation of the thought concerning relatives (ñātivitakka) and so forth: 'My relatives live happily and are endowed with prosperity'—such a thought that arises concerning relatives, based on household affection rooted in the five cords of sensual pleasure, is called the thought concerning relatives (ñātivitakka). However, a thought such as 'They have reached their end, they have passed away; they were faithful and confident' is not called the thought concerning relatives.
'Our country is well-supplied with food and abounds in crops'—such a thought that arises through the power of household affection in one who is pleased is called the thought concerning the country (janapadavitakka). However, a thought such as 'In our country, people are faithful and confident; they have reached their end, they have passed away' is not called the thought concerning the country.
It is called Amarā-thought (amaravitakka) because it is a thought for the sake of immortality (amara), or because it is a thought like the Amarā fish. Among these, for one who performs difficult austerities, thinking, 'If suffering is exhausted through practices such as squatting, the self will be happy and immortal in the next life'—such a thought connected with those difficult austerities is called a thought for the sake of immortality. As for a person with wrong views, when asked 'Is it eternal?' and so forth, he falls into prevarication (vikkhepa), saying, 'I do not think it is thus, I do not think it is so, I do not think it is otherwise, I do not think it is not, I do not think it is not not' (D. i. 62); his thought connected with that wrong view is also Amarā-thought. Just as the fish called Amarā cannot be caught and killed in the water because it runs here and there and does not get caught, so too, because it does not settle on one side and is not finalized (does not die), it is called Amarā. Combining these two types, the Blessed One taught that this is called Amarā-thought.
Thought connected with sympathy for others means being connected with household affection that resembles sympathy (compassion). In the words 'sharing joy' (sahanandī) and so forth, when the lay supporters rejoice or grieve, he rejoices twice as much or grieves twice as much with them. When they are happy, he is twice as happy; when they are suffering, he is twice as...
473:
...suffering. 'When duties and tasks arise' (uppannesu kiccakaranīyesu) means when large or small tasks arise for those supporters.
