'He involves himself' (attanā vā yogaṃ āpazzati) means that while performing those various tasks, he transgresses the regulations and ruins the practice of effacement (sallekha). 'Which therein' (yo tattha) refers to the household-based thought that arises in such socializing with people or in such involvement in their affairs. This thought is called the thought connected with repeatedly looking after others.

'Connected with gain, honor, and fame' (lābhasakkārasilokapaṭisaṃyutta) means a thought connected with the power of making an object of gain such as robes, honor, and reputation.

'Connected with not being despised' (anavaññattipaṭisaṃyutta) means a thought that arises along with the desire not to be despised, such as 'O, may others not look down on me, may they not speak to me with abuse or harassment.' 'Which therein is household-based' (yo tattha gehasito) means the thought that arises based on the 'house' of the five cords of sensual pleasure within that mind which thinks 'May others not despise me.' The remaining meanings are clear in all places.

## Commentary on the Section of Ones (Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā).

## (2.) Commentary on the Section of Twos (Dukaniddesavaṇṇanā)

Among the 'twos', the explanation of anger (kodhaniddesa) and so forth should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. However, in the explanation of grudge (upanāhaniddesa) and so forth which have not appeared below: because it binds the anger that occurred in the earlier period, the anger that occurs in the later period is called grudge (upanāha). The manner of binding is called upanayhanā. The state of one who binds is called upanayhitatta. 'Aṭṭhapanā' means placing the anger that first arose immediately after, or placing it within limits. 'Ṭhapanā' means placing it in its natural state. 'Saṇṭhapanā' means repeatedly placing the enmity from all sides. 'Anusaṃsandanā' means making it one with the first-arisen anger without leaving any gap. 'Anuppabandhanā' means connecting the later anger with the former. 'Daḷhīkamma' means making it firm. 'This is called' (ayaṃ vuccati) means this anger, which has the characteristic of binding a grudge and the function of not relinquishing enmity, is called upanāha. A person endowed with that grudge cannot relinquish the enmity; he binds it repeatedly, following it up, thinking, 'This person is not fit to speak to me in such a way.' Like a smoldering, rotting firebrand...
474:
It cannot be pure, like a burning log, like a washed snakeskin, or like an old cloth smeared with oil.

It is called 'makkha' (denigrating) because of its nature of smearing over the virtues of others. Although one strives to smear the virtues of another, it means that one first defiles oneself, just as excrement first smears the person who throws it. Following that, there are two terms indicating the mode and nature. The harsh nature is called 'niṭṭhuriya' (harshness). It means spitting, saying, 'There is not even this much benefit in depending on that person.' 'Niṭṭhuriyakamma' is the performance of harshness. Whether a layperson or a monk, while living in dependence on another layperson or monk, if they get angry over a small matter and spit, saying, 'There is not even this much benefit in depending on that person,' and act as if treading with their feet, it is called niṭṭhuriya. That action of that person is called niṭṭhuriyakamma. By way of characteristics, etc., this makkha has the characteristic of smearing the virtues of others; its function is the destruction of those virtues; and it manifests as the covering up of the good deeds performed by others.

It is called 'palāsa' (rivalry) because it acts in competition with others' virtues. It means that after (cutting down) or destroying the virtues of others, one acts to make them equal to one's own virtues. The occurrence of palāsa is called 'palāsāyanā'. Because it brings about one's own victory (being on par), it is both palāsa and a nutriment, thus it is called 'palāsāhāra'. 'Vivādaṭṭhāna' means the cause of dispute. 'Yugaggāha' means taking up the yoke equally. 'Appaṭinissagga' means not relinquishing the views one has taken up. By way of characteristics, etc., this palāsa has the characteristic of taking up equally (yugaggāha); its function is making one's own virtues equal to the virtues of others; and it manifests as standing close to the measure of others' virtues. Indeed, a person with rivalry does not give the position of superior to another but stands only by placing them on par with oneself. In a discussion, even if another monk brings forth many suttas and reasons, he says, 'What is the difference between your view and my view? Is not our speech identical, like gold split in the middle?' The explanations of 'issā' (envy) and 'macchariya' (stinginess) are exactly as previously stated.

In showing 'māyā' (deceit), 'vācaṃ bhāsati' means speaking like a peaceful person while knowing full well, 'Monks who transgress the regulations perform a heavy task, but for us, there is no such thing as a place of transgression.' 'Kāyena parakkamati' means performing minor and major duties with the body, thinking, 'Let no one know this evil deed I have done.' Because it hides existing faults and is like a magic trick that deludes the eyes, it is called 'māyā'. The state of one who has deceit is called 'māyāvitā'. Because it covers up an evil deed again after having committed it, it is called 'āsaraṇā'.
475:
Because beings transgress and cover up faults with this deceit, it is called 'accāsarā'. Because it deceives by showing one thing through bodily and verbal actions while being another, it is called 'vañcanā'. Because beings act wrongly through this nature, it is called 'nikati', which means acting wrongly. Because it casts away evil deeds by saying, 'I do not do such a thing,' it is called 'vikiaraṇā'. Because it evades by saying, 'I do not do such a thing,' it is called 'pariharaṇā'. Because it hides and conceals with the body and so on, it is called 'gūhanā'. Concealing from all sides is called 'parigūhanā'. Because it covers up evil with bodily and verbal actions, just as one covers excrement with grass and leaves, it is called 'chādanā'. Covering from all sides is called 'paṭicchādanā'. Not making it plain and showing it is called 'anuttānīkamma'. Not making it manifest and showing it is called 'anāvikamma'. Covering well is called 'vocchādanā'. Because of performing evil again by covering up the committed fault, it is called 'pāpakiriyā'. This nature, characterized by covering up the committed fault as described, is called 'māyā'. A person endowed with that deceit is like an ember covered by ash, like a stump covered by water, or like a weapon wrapped in a piece of cloth.

In the explanation of 'sāṭheyya' (fraud), 'saṭha' means not speaking according to the truth because of making manifest virtues that do not exist in oneself. One who is thoroughly crooked and fraudulent is called 'parisaṭha'. The fraudulence that exists in that person is called 'saṭha'. Showing non-existent virtues is called 'kerāṭiya' (guile). The mode of being crooked is called 'saṭhatā'. Being like the rough and harsh nature of a lotus stalk that is unpleasant to touch is called 'kakkaratā'. 'Kakkariya' is also a synonym for that same nature. By the two terms 'parikkhattatā' and 'pārikkhattiya', firm fraudulence is meant, like an object that has been dug in and placed in the ground. This nature, characterized by making manifest virtues that do not exist in oneself, is called 'sāṭheyya'. It is not easy to know the belly or the back of a person endowed with that fraudulence.

Looking from the left, he is like a pig;
Looking from the right, he is like a goat.
By voice, he is like a young calf;
By horns, he is like an old ox.

He is a person like the 'Yakkha-pig' described thus. The explanations of 'avijjā' (ignorance) and so on have the same meaning as already stated.

In the explanation of 'anajjava', 'anajjava' means the mode of being non-upright. The nature of lacking uprightness is called 'anajjavatā'. Being crooked at both ends like a crescent moon is called 'jimhatā'. Being crooked throughout like the path of cow's urine is called 'vaṅkatā'. Being crooked only on one side like the tip of a plow is called 'kuṭilatā'. By all these terms, only the crookedness of body, speech, and mind is expressed.

In the explanation of 'amaddava', the absence of gentleness is called 'amudutā'. The mode of being ungentle is called 'amaddavatā'. The harsh nature is called 'kakkhaḷiya'. The harsh nature due to the absence of the 'oil' (affection/gentleness) that produces softness is called 'phārusiya'. The state of a mind that stands only upright without a humble manner is called 'ujucittatā'. Again, the term 'amudutā' is taken to specify that the ungentle nature called amudutā is not the uprightness called ujucittatā.

The explanations of 'avijjā' and so on should be understood by way of their opposites, such as the explanation of 'khanti' (patience) and so on.

In the explanation of 'saṃyojana' (fetters), 'ajjhatta' (internal) means the sensual existence (kāmabhava). 'Bahiddhā' (external) means the fine-material existence (rūpabhava) and the immaterial existence (arūpabhava). Indeed, beings have to live in the sensual existence for only a short time. They live there for only about one-fourth of an aeon. During the remaining three parts of the time, the sensual realm remains empty and void of beings. In the fine-material and immaterial existences, however, they have to live for a long time. Nevertheless, the occurrences of death and rebirth for those beings in the sensual existence are numerous. The occurrences of death and rebirth in the fine-material and immaterial existences are few. Because death and rebirth are frequent in the sensual realm, attachment, longing, and desire are great in that realm. Because death and rebirth are few in the fine-material and immaterial realms, attachment, longing, and desire are less in those realms. Therefore, the sensual existence is called 'ajjhatta' (internal existence). The fine-material and immaterial existences are...
476:
The state of having a straight mind is called ujucittatā (rectitude of mind). Again, the inclusion of the word amudutā (non-mildness) serves the purpose of specifying that ujucittatā: "it is the rectitude of mind known as non-mildness, not the rectitude of mind known as uprightness (ajjava)."

The description of impatience (akkhanti) and so forth should be understood by way of the opposite of the description of patience (khanti) and so forth.

In the description of fetters (saṃyojana), 'internal' (ajjhatta) refers to the sensual realm (kāmabhava). 'External' (bahiddhā) refers to the fine-material and immaterial realms (rūpārupabhava). Even if beings reside in the sensual realm for only a short time, such as a fourth part of an aeon, and the sensual realm is empty and void of beings during the remaining three parts, while they reside in the fine-material and immaterial realms for a long time—nevertheless, because their deaths and rebirths are numerous in the sensual realm and few in the fine-material and immaterial realms [it is called internal]. In whichever realm deaths and rebirths are numerous, there attachment (ālaya), longing (patthanā), and desire (abhilāsa) are also numerous. In whichever realm they are few, these are also few. Therefore, the sensual realm is called 'internal' (ajjhatta), and the fine-material and immaterial realms are called 'external' (bahiddhā). Thus, the fetter that binds one to the sensual realm, which is called internal, is named the 'internal fetter' (ajjhattasaṃyojana). The fetter that binds one to the fine-material and immaterial realms, which are called external, is named the 'external fetter' (bahiddhāsaṃyojana). Among those fetters, each is of five kinds. Therefore, it is said: "pañcorambhāgiyāni pañcuddhambhāgiyāni" (five lower fetters and five higher fetters). In that context, the definition of the terms is: the sensual element (kāmadhātu) is called ora (the hither side); because they lead to the production of rebirth in that ora, they are called orambhāgiya. The fine-material and immaterial elements are called uddha (the upper side); because they lead to the production of rebirth in those upper elements, they are called uddhambhāgiya.

## Commentary on the Description of Dyads
## (3.) Commentary on the Description of Triads

In the description of triads (tikaniddesa), the occurrence of the root of the round of existence (vaṭṭamūla) by way of the three unwholesome roots is taught. In the unwholesome thoughts (akusalavitakka) and so forth, they should be understood as 'thought' (vitakka) by way of thinking, as 'perception' (saññā) by way of perceiving, and as 'element' (dhātu) in the sense of intrinsic nature (sabhāva). In the description of misconduct (duccaritaniddesa), the first method is analyzed by way of the paths of action (kammapatha); the second method by way of kamma that includes all [unwholesome states]; and the third method only by way of the volition (cetanā) produced from the paths of action and kamma.

In the description of taints (āsavaniddesa), only three taints are taught according to the Suttanta method.
477:
In the description of searches (esanāniddesa), in brief, the lust that searches for sensual pleasures, taught by the method beginning with "Among those searches, what is the search for sensual pleasures?", is called the search for sensual pleasures (kāmesanā). The lust that searches for existence, taught by the method beginning with "The desire for existence in the realms of existence", is called the search for existence (bhavesanā). The search for the holy life as designated by those with wrong views, taught by the method beginning with "The world is eternal", is to be understood as the search for the holy life based on views (diṭṭhibrāhmacariyāesanā).

Since not only lust and views are 'searches' (esanā), but the kamma associated with them is also a search, the second method is analyzed to show that kamma. In that second method, 'sharing the same basis' (tadekaṭṭha) should be understood as having the same meaning through association (biting/concomitance). Therein, kamma existing in the same mind as sensual lust occurs only in beings of the sensual sphere. However, kamma existing in the same mind as lust for existence occurs in the Great Brahmas.

When those who have emerged from a meditative attainment and are walking in meditation enjoy the factors of jhāna, unwholesome bodily kamma occurs. When they enjoy it by breaking into speech, saying "Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!", verbal kamma occurs. When they enjoy it only with the mind, without moving the limbs of the body or the organs of speech, mental kamma occurs. By the power of wrong views that grasp at extremes (antaggāhikadiṭṭhi), these [actions] such as walking in meditation and so forth occur for all those who hold wrong views.

In the description of modes (vidhaniddesa), in passages such as "What kind (kathaṃvidhaṃ) of virtuous person do they speak of? What kind of wise person do they speak of?", the form or manner (ākārasaṇṭhāna) is called vidhā. In passages such as "The objects of knowledge by way of one portion (ekavidhena)", a portion or group (koṭṭhāsa) is called vidhā. In passages such as "He does not waver among the modes [of pride] (vidhāsu)", pride (māna) is called vidhā. Here too, pride alone is called vidhā. For that pride is called vidhā because it arranges (vidahati) [beings] by way of 'superiority' and so forth. Or, vidhā is in the sense of 'establishing' (ṭhapana). Therefore, the mode of pride or the establishment of pride that arises as "I am superior" should be understood as the mode (vidhā) "I am superior". The same method applies to the other two terms.

In the description of fear (bhayaniddesa), 'fear in dependence on birth' means fear arisen with birth as a condition. 'Fearful' (bhayānaka) is a description of the aspect. 'State of trembling' (chambhitatta) is the shaking of the body due to fear. 'Horripilation' (lomahaṃsa) is the delight of the hairs, their standing on end. By these two terms, fear is shown by way of its function, and then by the term "terror of the mind" (cetaso utrāsa), it is shown by way of its intrinsic nature.

In the description of darkness (tamaniddesa), ignorance (avijjā) is taught with doubt (vicikicchā) as the heading. For, according to the statement, "Darkness is delusion (sammoha); the flood of ignorance is a great danger", ignorance is...
478:
Ignorance (*avijjā*) is called darkness (*tamo*). In teaching by way of the three periods of time, the instruction was given starting with doubt (*vicikicchā*) for the sake of ease of exposition. In that context, one who doubts, thinking, "Was I a kshatriya in the past, or a brahmin, a vaishya, or a shudra? Was I dark, fair, short, or tall?" is said to doubt regarding the past period. One who doubts, thinking, "Will I be a kshatriya in the future, or a brahmin, a vaishya... or tall?" is said to doubt regarding the future period. One who doubts, thinking, "Am I now a kshatriya, or a brahmin, a vaishya, or a shudra? Am I form, or feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?" is said to doubt regarding the present period.

In such doubting, there is indeed no kshatriya who does not know his own status as a kshatriya, nor a brahmin his status as a brahmin, nor a vaishya his status as a vaishya, nor a shudra his status as a shudra. However, a being who holds the view of a soul (*jīva*), upon hearing about the differences in color and so on of the souls of kshatriyas and others, doubts: "What is the nature of the soul within us? Is it blue, yellow, red, or white? Is it four-sided, six-sided, or eight-sided?" Such doubting is what is meant by 'doubts'.

*Titthāyatana* means the bases (*āyatana*) that are like fords (*tittha*), or the bases of the sectarians (*titthiyas*). Therein, *tittha* refers to the sixty-two wrong views. Those who delight in and accept those views are called sectarians (*titthiyas*). The meaning of *āyatana* has already been stated below. In this context, since all those who hold wrong views arise only in these three grounds (the cause of past deeds, the cause of creation by a Lord, and the absence of cause and condition), and when they converge, they converge and assemble only in these grounds, and these are the very reasons for their state of holding wrong views; therefore, they are called *titthāyatana* in the sense of being both fords and places of arising. By that same meaning, they are also called *titthāyatana* as the bases of the sectarians.

*Purisapuggala* means a being (*satta*). Although both 'man' (*purisa*) and 'person' (*puggala*) are used, they both refer to a being. However, this is conventional speech (*sammutikathā*); the teaching is given according to how a person understands. *Paṭisaṃvedeti* means knowing what has arisen in one's own continuity, making it clear, or experiencing it. *Pubbekatahetu* means having the cause in what was done in the past. The meaning is that one experiences only because of the condition of kamma performed in a previous life. This is the doctrine of the Niganthas. Those who speak thus reject the feeling during the act (*kammavedanā*) and the feeling associated with functional consciousness (*kiriyavedanā*), and accept only the single feeling that is the result (*vipākavedanā*). Regarding the eight kinds of diseases, such as those caused by bile...
479:
...regarding those diseases, they reject seven and accept only the eighth (disease born of kamma-result). Regarding the three types of kamma such as that to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*), they reject two and accept only the single kamma to be experienced in some subsequent life (*aparāpariyavedanīya*). Among the four types of volition (*cetanā*) known as wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional, they accept only the resultant volition.

*Issaranimmānahetu* means because of the cause of creation by a Lord. The meaning is that one experiences because of being created by a Lord who is either Brahmā or Pajāpati. This is the doctrine of the Brahmins. For this is their intention: these three kinds of feelings cannot be experienced through a cause created by oneself in the present, or by a cause of command, or by past deeds, or without cause or condition; rather, one experiences these feelings only because of the cause of creation by a Lord. Those who speak thus do not accept even one among the eight kinds of diseases mentioned above, but reject them all. Likewise, among all the portions of kamma such as that to be experienced in the present life, they do not accept even one, but reject them all.

*Ahetu-appaccayā* means experiencing without cause (*hetu*) and without condition (*paccaya*), entirely without a cause. This is the doctrine of the Ājīvakas. Those who speak thus also do not accept even one among the causes and diseases mentioned above, but reject them all.

*Kiñcana* means impediments (*palibodha*). Lust (*rāga*) is called an impediment because when lust arises, it binds and oppresses beings. The same method applies to hatred (*dosa*) and delusion (*moha*). *Angaṇa* (blemish): in the passage "*udaṅgaṇe tattha papaṃ avindu*," *angaṇa* refers to a piece of ground. In the passage "*tasseva rajassa vā aṅgaṇassa vā pahānāya vāyamati*," any speck of dust or impurity is called *angaṇa*. In the passage "*sāṅgaṇova samāno*," various kinds of intense defilements are called *angaṇa*. Here too, it is that blemish of defilements (*kilesaṅgaṇa*) that is intended. Therefore, it is said, "Lust is a blemish," and so on.

*Mala* (stains) means those things that cause tarnishing. Lust is a stain because when lust arises, it makes the mind tarnish and causes it to take on a stain. The same method applies to the other two, hatred and delusion.
480:
In the explanation of the uneven (visama), beings stumble in lust (rāga) and so forth, as well as in bodily misconduct (kāyaduccarita) and so forth. Those who stumble fall away from both the Dispensation (sāsana) and from the happy realms (sugati). Because it is the cause of such stumbling and falling, lust is called "uneven" (visama), "fire" (aggi), and so forth.

It is called fire (aggi) in the sense of burning continuously. When lust arises, it continuously burns and consumes beings. Therefore, it is called fire. The same principle applies to hatred (dosa) and delusion (moha). Regarding this burning, there are these stories—it is said that at the Cittalapabbata Monastery, a young nun went to the Uposatha hall and stood looking at the figure of a door-guardian. At that moment, lust arose within her. She was consumed by that very lust and passed away. When the other nuns were passing by, they said, "This young nun is standing there; call her." One nun went and asked, "Why are you standing?" and took her hand. As soon as she was touched, she fell over. This is the story regarding the burning nature of lust. Regarding the burning nature of hatred, the Manopadosika deities should be understood. Regarding the burning nature of delusion, the Khiḍḍāpadosika deities should be understood. Indeed, through the power of delusion, those deities become forgetful. Thus, through the power of play, they exceed the time for taking food and consequently pass away. Taint (kasāva) refers to states that are like dregs and lack essence. In lust and so forth, and in bodily misconduct and so forth, there is not a single refined or nutritious essence; therefore, lust is called a taint (kasāva) and so forth.

The view of gratification (assādaditthi) is the view associated with enjoyment. In saying "there is no fault in sensual pleasures," it means asserting that there is no fault in indulging in objective sensuality (vatthukāma) through defiled sensuality (kilesakāma). Drinkability (pātabyatā) means the state of being consumed, enjoyed, or swallowed. One who holds such a view enjoys objective sensuality as if drinking or swallowing defiled sensuality. The view of self (attānuditthi) is the view that follows the self. Wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is a base view. Now, since among these views, the first is eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi), the second is identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), and the third is annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi), the Teacher said "eternalism, gratification view," and so forth to demonstrate that meaning.

The explanations of aversion (arati) and cruelty (vihesā) have the same meanings as previously stated. Unrighteous conduct (adhammacariyā) means practicing what is not the Dhamma; it means the performance of unrighteousness. Uneven conduct (visamacariyā) means practicing unevenly, or the practice of uneven deeds. The explanations of unruliness (dovacassatā) and bad friendship (pāpamittatā) also have the same meanings as previously stated. Perception of diversity (nānattasaññā) is perception that occurs in many signs and objects, or in various objects. Alternatively, it is called perception of diversity because sensual perception (kāmasaññā) is one kind, and perceptions of ill-will (byāpāda) and so forth are of different kinds respectively.
481:
Therefore, because it is a perception of diverse natures, it is called nānattasaññā. In the expositions of sloth (kosajja) and negligence (pamāda), for one whose mind is loose among the five cords of sensual pleasure, the state of shrinking back due to lack of application in the development of wholesome states is sloth (kosajja). The state of being negligent through the power of negligence is to be understood as negligence (pamāda). The meanings of the expositions of discontent (asantuṭṭhitā) and so forth are just as already stated.

In the exposition of disrespect (anādariya), the state of having no respect due to not taking advice is anādariya. The manner of being disrespectful is anādaratā. The state of lack of reverence due to not living with those worthy of honor is agāravatā. The lack of obedience due to not living with elders is appatissavatā. Anaddā means not taking advice. Anaddāyanā is the manner of one who does not take advice. The state of one who exists by not taking advice is anaddāyitattaṃ. The state of one without virtue is asīlyaṃ. Acittīkāra means not performing acts of esteem.

The state of one without faith is assaddhiyaṃ. The manner of not believing is asaddhanā. Not grasping by reflecting and penetrating within is anokappanā. Because of not being devoted, it is anabhippasāda.

Avadaññutā (unresponsiveness) means not understanding the words "give" or "do" due to harsh stinginess.

In the phrase "the Buddha and the disciples of the Buddha," the term "Buddha" also includes Paccekabuddhas. Asametukamyatā means the desire not to approach them. Saddhammaṃ asotukamyatā means the desire not to hear the True Dhamma, namely the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma). Anuggahetukamyatā means the lack of desire to learn.

Upārambhacittatā means the state of one having a mind that attacks. Since that is essentially just a mind associated with anger that attacks, he said "therein, what is upārambha?" and so on, to show that state. Therein, it is upārambha because of attacking. Repeated attacking is anupārambha. The manner of attacking is upārambhanā. Repeatedly attacking is anupārambhanā. The state of one who attacks repeatedly is anupārambhitattaṃ. Uññā means knowing by looking down [on others]. Avaññā means knowing by looking down (disdain). Occurring by way of overwhelming is paribhava. Seeking for faults is randhagavesitā. Or, one who seeks for faults is randhagavesī; the state of such a person is randhagavesitā. This which is called upārambha has the characteristic of observing the faults of others; a person endowed with this upārambha is like, for example...
482:
Just as a tailor spreads out a cloth and looks only for the holes (to sew), in the same way, one conceals and destroys all the virtues of another and dwells only on their faults.

Unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) means attending in a way that is not a means to welfare (*anupāya-manasikāra*). It occurs as "this is permanent" regarding an impermanent object; the same method applies to attending to pleasure in suffering, and so on. All terms such as *cittassa āvaṭṭanā* (turning of the mind), which occur by way of not conforming to the Four Truths, are merely synonyms for adverting (*āvajjana*). Because adverting turns the *bhavaṅga* mind, it is called *cittassa āvaṭṭanā*. Because it turns it again and again, it is called *anāvaṭṭanā*. Because it bends towards the object, it is called *ābhoga*. Because it brings together an object other than the *bhavaṅga* object, it is called *samannāhāra*. Because it performs attention in the mind that arises following that very object, it is called *manasikāra*. "Kareti" means "thapeti" (establishes). *Ayoniso-manasikāra*, characterized by attending in a wrong way, is so called. Because of it, a person cannot reflect on the Truths such as suffering as they really are.

In the explanation of the description of following the wrong path (*kummagga-sevanā-niddesa*), the second question "What is the wrong path?" is asked to show the following of the wrong path. The remaining meanings are clear everywhere.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Triads is finished.

## (4.) The Explanation of the Description of the Tetrads

In the description of the tetrads, among the arisings of craving, craving arises because of robes, thinking, "Where shall I get a pleasing robe?" In the phrase "*iti-bhavābhava-hetu*", the word "*iti*" is a particle used in the sense of pointing out; the meaning is that just as craving arises because of robes and so on, it also arises because of *bhavābhava* (excellent things). Here, *bhavābhava* refers to excellent oil, honey, molasses, and so forth. It should be understood that the four noble lineages (*ariya-vaṃsa*) were taught in order to abandon these four arisings of craving.
483:
## On the Wrong Courses
Among the four wrong courses, "following the wrong course through favoritism (*chandāgati*)" means going on a wrong path that should not be taken or doing what should not be done because of desire or affection (*chanda*). The same method applies to the other terms like *dosāgati* (wrong course through hatred).

Among those wrong courses, one who, through the power of favoritism, makes a non-owner an owner, thinking, "This person is my friend, or an acquaintance, or a companion, or a relative, or he gives me a bribe," is said to follow the wrong course through favoritism. One who, through natural enmity or through anger arisen at that moment, makes an owner a non-owner, thinking, "This person is my enemy," is said to follow the wrong course through hatred (*dosāgati*). One who, through dullness or delusion, says whatever and makes a non-owner an owner, is said to follow the wrong course through delusion (*mohāgati*). One who, out of fear, thinking, "This person is a favorite of the king, or is dependent on an unjust person, and might do me harm," makes a non-owner an owner, is said to follow the wrong course through fear (*bhayāgati*).

Furthermore, when distributing something in a place of distribution, one who gives extra out of the power of affection (*pema*), thinking, "This person is my friend, acquaintance, or companion"; one who gives less out of the power of hatred, thinking, "This person is my enemy"; one who, due to great delusion, gives less to some and more to others without knowing what has been given or not; and one who gives extra to some out of fear, thinking, "If I do not give to this person, he might do me harm"—these four types of persons are also said to follow *chandāgati* and so on, respectively.

Because the Noble Ones do not go by way of these motives such as favoritism, it is called *agati* (wrong course). Because non-noble ones go to places they should not go by way of these motives, it is called *agati-gamana* (following the wrong course). Both these terms are used generally for all four wrong courses. Going because of affection is called *chanda-gamana*. This is a specific term not related to hatred and so on. Going discordantly, putting forward attachment to one's own side and hatred for the other side, is called *vagga-gamana* (partisan going). This is a term related to both favoritism and hatred. Going as water flows towards low ground (inclining towards favoritism, etc.) is called *vāri-gamana*. This is a term used generally for all four wrong courses.

## On Perversions
Among the perversions (*vipariyāsa*), they are so called because they seek objects such as the impermanent in a perverted way as permanent and so on. The perversion of perception (*saññā*) is *saññā-vipariyāsa*. The same method applies to the other two: perversion of mind (*citta-vipariyāsa*) and perversion of view (*diṭṭhi-vipariyāsa*). Thus, there are four perversions by way of the four objects, and in those objects, there are twelve perversions by way of perception, mind, and view.

Among those twelve, eight are abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*). The perversions of perception and mind that take the foul as beautiful are weakened by the Path of Once-returning (*sakadāgāmi-magga*) and are completely abandoned by the Path of Non-returning (*anāgāmi-magga*). It should be understood that the perversions of perception and mind that take suffering as pleasure are abandoned by the Path of Arahantship (*arahatta-magga*).
484:
In the ignoble modes of speech (anariya-vohāra), 'ignoble modes of speech' refers to the speech of those who are ignoble and base. 'Speaking of what is seen' (diṭṭha-vāditā) means saying, "I have seen." In these ignoble modes of speech, the meaning should be understood by the power of the volition (cetanā) that originates each particular speech. It is also said that volition is taught along with the sound. The same method applies to the second set of four. For a Noble One (Ariya) does not say "I have seen" without having seen, nor "I have not seen" having seen; only an ignoble person speaks in this way. Therefore, the eight volitions occurring with the sound of one who speaks thus should be known as ignoble modes of speech.

Among misconducts (duccarita), the first set of four is spoken of by way of the volition of enmity (vera-cetanā), and the second set by way of verbal misconduct (vacī-duccarita).

Among fears (bhaya), in the first set of four, the fear arising because of birth is called the fear of birth (jāti-bhaya). The same applies to the remaining fears. In the second set of four, the fear arising because of a king is called the fear of kings (rāja-bhaya). The same applies to the remaining fears.

In the third set of four, the four fears are those taught for one who descends into the waters of the great ocean. It is heard that in the great ocean, the wave called Mahinda rises to sixty leagues (yojana). The wave called Gaṅgā rises to fifty, and the wave called Rohana rises to forty leagues. The fear arising because of such waves is called the fear of waves (ūmi-bhaya). Fear because of crocodiles is the fear of crocodiles (kumbhīla-bhaya). Fear from whirlpools is the fear of whirlpools (āvaṭṭa-bhaya). A fierce fish is called susukā; fear because of that fish is the fear of susukā (susukā-bhaya).

In the fourth set of four, the fear of self-reproach (attānuvāda-bhaya) is the fear that arises when an evildoer reproaches himself. The fear of reproach by others (parānuvāda-bhaya) is the fear arising from the reproach of another. The fear of punishment (daṇḍa-bhaya) is the fear arising from the punishment inflicted by a king for a layperson, or the disciplinary punishment (vinaya-daṇḍa) for a monk. The fear of miserable states (duggati-bhaya) is the fear arising because of the four planes of misery. Thus, by these four sets of four, the sixteen great fears are taught.

In the set of four views (diṭṭhi), the view of Timbaruka is taught. Therein, "pleasure and pain are self-created" (sayaṅkataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ) is the wrong view arising for one who regards feeling (vedanā) as self (atta), thinking that feeling itself is created by feeling. In this case, since it follows that the feeling existed even before it was created, this is called the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi). "Truly and firmly" (saccato thetato) means in terms of truth and stability.
485:
"Created by another" (paraṅkataṃ) is the view arising for one who repeatedly regards a feeling-self as the cause of feeling, other than the present feeling, thinking, "This feeling is created by that other feeling." In this case, since it follows that the preceding causal feeling is annihilated, this is called the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi). "Both self-created and created by another" is the view arising for one who takes it as, "Half is self-created, half is created by another," according to the aforementioned meaning; this is called the eternalist-annihilationist view (sassata-uccheda-diṭṭhi). The fourth view is the view arising for one who takes it that "pleasure and pain occur without a cause." In this case, this is called the causeless view (ahetuka-diṭṭhi). The rest of the text here is clear in meaning, following the method already mentioned below.

## The Commentary on the Description of the Fours is finished.

## (5.) Commentary on the Description of the Fives

In the Description of the Fives, because the fetters such as the view of personal identity (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) have not yet been abandoned by certain individuals, even if they are reborn in the highest plane of existence (the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception), these fetters pull them down and cause them to fall into the sensual realm alone; therefore, they are called the lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana). Thus, these five do not prevent one who is going (to a higher plane), but they bring back one who has gone. The five (higher) fetters, such as lust for form (rūpa-rāga), also do not prevent one who is going to the lower sensual realm, but they do not allow for a return (to the sensual realm). The five, such as lust (rāga), are called 'attachments' (saṅga) in the sense of clinging, and 'darts' (salla) in the sense of entering successively.

Mental barrenness (cetokhila) refers to the state of the mind being stiff, like rubbish, or like a stump. "He doubts the Teacher" means he doubts the physical body or the qualities of the Teacher. One who doubts the physical body doubts, "Does a body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man really exist or not?" One who doubts the qualities doubts, "Does the Omniscient Knowledge, capable of knowing the past, future, and present, really exist or not?" "He is perplexed" (vicikicchati) means he becomes weary while investigating, falls into suffering, and is unable to decide. "He does not resolve" means he does not obtain the resolution (adhimokkha) that "it is just so." "He is not confident" means he is unable to be confident by entering into the qualities with a state free from doubt, and is unable to be undisturbed.

"In the Dhamma" means in the Dhamma of scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma) and the Dhamma of realization (paṭivedha-dhamma). One who doubts the Dhamma of scriptures doubts, "They say the Buddha's word, the Three Piṭakas, consists of eighty-four thousand Dhamma aggregates; does this really exist or not?" One who doubts the Dhamma of realization [doubts], "The Path, which is the result of insight..."
486:
The consequence of the Path is called Fruition (*phala*); the relinquishment of all conditioned things is called Nibbāna. One doubts, 'Do these (Path, Fruition, Nibbāna) exist or not?'

'Doubts regarding the Saṅgha' means one doubts whether there exists a Saṅgha, which is the community of eight types of individuals—the four who stand on the Path and the four who stand in Fruition—who have practiced such a way of life by virtue of terms such as 'practicing uprightly' (*ujuppaṭipanna*).

One who doubts regarding the training (*sikkhā*) doubts, 'They speak of the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*), the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-sikkhā*), and the training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññā-sikkhā*); do these trainings exist or not?'

'Mental shackles' (*cetosovinibandha*) are so called because they bind the mind and seize it as if holding it in a fist. 'In sensual pleasures' (*kāme*) refers to both the objects of sensuality (*vatthu-kāma*) and the defilements of sensuality (*kilesa-kāma*). 'In the body' (*kāye*) refers to one's own body. 'In form' (*rūpe*) refers to external forms. 'As much as one desires' (*yāvadatthaṃ*) means eating as much as one wants. 'Filling the belly' (*udarāvadehakaṃ*) means filling the stomach to the brim. Such eating as much as one desires is called *udarāvadehakaṃ* because it causes the belly to be distended. 'The happiness of lying down' (*seyyasukkha*) is the pleasure of sleeping on a couch or bench, or the pleasure of the season. 'The happiness of reclining' (*passasukha*) is the kind of pleasure experienced by one who lies turning from side to side, on the right side and the left side. 'The happiness of torpor' (*middhasukha*) is the pleasure found in sleepiness. 'Devoted to' (*anuyutto*) means living with great exertion. 'Having aspired' (*paṇidhāya*) means having made a wish.

Among the terms beginning with 'by virtue' (*sīlena*), 'virtue' (*sīla*) refers to the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*). 'Vow' (*vata*) refers to the undertaking of ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*). 'Austerity' (*tapa*) refers to the practice of ascetic duties. 'Holy life' (*brahmacariya*) refers to abstinence from sexual intercourse. 'I shall become a god' means I shall become a great and powerful deity. 'Or one among the gods' means I shall become one among the lesser deities. They are called 'hindrances' (*nīvaraṇa*) because they obstruct and block wholesome states.

'Depriving the mother of life' means a human being deprives their own biological human mother of life (killing her). The father is also a human father. The Arahant is also a human Arahant. 'With a malicious mind' means with the intent to kill.

'Percipient' (*saññī*) means being endowed with perception. 'Healthy' (*arogo*) means permanent. 'Thus some proclaim' means that some proclaim firmly; this is the meaning. By this much, the sixteen doctrines of percipient existence (*saññīvāda*) have been taught. 'Non-percipient' (*asaññī*) means being devoid of perception. By this term, the eight doctrines of non-percipient existence (*asaññīvāda*) have been taught. By the third term, the eight doctrines of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient existence (*nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda*) have been taught. 'Or of an existing being' (*sato vā pana sattassa*) means of a being who is clearly present. 'Annihilation' (*uccheda*) means cutting off; 'destruction' (*vināsa*) means disappearance; 'non-existence' (*vibhava*) means the departure from one's inherent nature. All these terms are synonyms for one another. In that doctrine of annihilation, two types of persons hold the view of annihilation:
487:
Those who have attained [supernormal knowledge] and those who have not. Both types hold the view of annihilation. Among them, the one who has attained knowledge, though seeing the death (*cuti*) of an Arahant with the divine eye, does not see the rebirth (*upapatti*); or because they can see only the death and not the rebirth, they hold the view of annihilation (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*). The one who has not attained knowledge holds the view of annihilation either out of excessive greed for sensual pleasures, thinking, 'Who can know the world beyond?', or through reasoning such as, 'Just as leaves fallen from a tree do not grow again, so it is with beings.' Here, seven types of annihilationist doctrines are taught, which arise through various speculations by the power of craving and views. This statement is a summary of those seven types of annihilationist doctrines.

In the passage, 'Some proclaim Nibbāna in the present life,' 'present life' (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to the immediate nature (or the present state of existence). It is a designation for the state of existence (*attabhāva*) obtained in various realms. 'Nibbāna in the present life' (*diṭṭhadhammanibbāna*) means the cooling of suffering in the present state of existence. The meaning is that sufferings are stilled in this very state of existence. This is a summary statement of the five types of doctrines of Nibbāna in the present life.

'Enmity' (*vera*) refers to the intention that causes hostility. 'Ruin' (*byasana*) means destruction. 'Intolerance' (*akkhanti*) means not enduring (not allowing something to dwell within oneself). 'Unpleasant' (*appiya*) refers to a person who should not be loved because they are repulsive to see or hear. Because even thinking of them is repulsive, the mind does not apply itself to that person, thus they are called 'disagreeable' (*amanāpa*). 'Full of enmity' (*verabahulo*) means one who has much hostility. 'Full of faults' (*vajjabahulo*) means one who has many defects.

'Fear regarding livelihood' (*ājīvaka-bhaya*) is the fear that arises on account of one's means of living. This fear can occur to both householders and monastics. Regarding the householder, if they have committed many unwholesome acts for the sake of livelihood, fear arises at the time of death when signs of hell appear. For the monastic as well, if they have engaged in much improper seeking (*anesanā*), fear arises at the time of death when signs of hell appear. This is called the fear regarding livelihood. 'Fear of ill-repute' (*asiloka-bhaya*) is the fear of being blamed. 'Fear of embarrassment in an assembly' (*parisasārajja-bhaya*) is the fear characterized by embarrassment that arises when a person who has committed evil approaches a gathered assembly. The other two fears (fear of death and fear of an unhappy destination) are quite clear.

In the sections on Nibbāna in the present life, 'with the five strands of sensual pleasure' means with the five portions of sensuality (or bonds of sensuality) such as pleasing forms and so on. 'Fully provided' (*samappito*) means being well-attached or clinging. 'Endowed' (*samaṅgībhūto*) means being possessed of. 'Indulges' (*paricāreti*) means causing one's faculties to roam as one pleases among those strands of sensual pleasure, or playing and enjoying oneself. Here, sensual pleasures are of two kinds: human and divine. Human sensual pleasures should be understood as being like those of King Mandhātu; divine sensual pleasures should be understood as being like those of the king of the *Paranimmitavasavatti* gods. Those recluses and brahmins say of one enjoying such sensual pleasures, 'He has reached the supreme Nibbāna in the present life.'
488:
Those recluses and brahmins say that a person who has attained sensual pleasures has reached supreme Nibbāna in the present life (parama-diṭṭhadhamma-nibbāna). In that phrase, 'parama-diṭṭhadhamma-nibbāna' means the supreme cooling of all suffering in the visible existence.

In the second turn, they should be understood as impermanent (anicca) in the sense of non-existence after having been; as suffering (dukkha) in the sense of being oppressive; and as subject to change (vipariṇāmadhamma) in the sense of abandoning their original nature. The 'change and becoming otherwise' (vipariṇāma-aññathābhāva) of those sensual pleasures means their becoming otherwise, which is called change from their original nature. Sorrow (soka), lamentation (parideva), pain (dukkha), grief (domanassa), and despair (upāyāsa) arise according to the method stated: "What I once had, I no longer have." Among these, sorrow is characterized by inner burning. Lamentation is characterized by the loud wailing based on that sorrow. Pain is characterized by bodily oppression. Grief is characterized by mental affliction. Despair is characterized by the lack of mental clarity and joy (or affliction).

'Thought' (vitakkita) is initial thought (vitakka) occurring by way of directing the mind to the object. 'Examined' (vicārita) is sustained thought (vicāra) occurring by way of rubbing the object. Because of this initial and sustained thought, this first jhāna appears as if it were coarse or as if it had thorns.

'Gone to joy' (pītigata) is simply joy (pīti). 'Elation of mind' (cetaso uppilāvita) means making the state of the mind uplifted. 'Advertence of mind' (cetaso ābhoga) means the repeated attention or advertence of the mind to that happiness after emerging from jhāna. The remaining terms have clear meanings in all places.

## The Explanation of the Niddesa of the Fives is finished.

## (6.) The Explanation of the Niddesa of the Sixes

In the Niddesa of the Sixes, because an angry person, through the power of anger (kodha), or one who clings to their own views, through the power of such clinging, falls into quarrels, disputes, and contention, anger and so forth are called 'roots of dispute' (vivādamūla).

In the Niddesa of desire and lust (chandarāga), having stated collectively that desire and lust are 'household-based states' (gehassita-dhamma) because they rely on the house of sensual pleasures, the Teacher said "in pleasant forms" and so forth to show them again by way of division. In that passage, 'pleasant' (manāpiya) refers to desirable objects (iṭṭhārammaṇa) that increase the mind's excitement. Opposing states are themselves 'objects of opposition' (virodhavatthu). 'Unpleasant' (amanāpiya) refers to undesirable objects (aniṭṭhārammaṇa).

Among the states of disrespect, 'disrespect' (agārava) means being devoid of respect. 'Lack of reverence' (appatissa) means having no one to revere or rely upon, or a lack of humble conduct. Here, a monk who does not go to attend on the Teacher at the three times while the Teacher is alive; who walks with sandals while the Teacher walks barefoot; who walks on a higher path while the Teacher walks on a lower path; who stays on an upper floor while the Teacher stays on a lower floor; who covers both shoulders, carries an umbrella, wears sandals, bathes, or relieves himself in a place within the Teacher's sight.

Furthermore, after the Teacher has attained Parinibbāna, he does not go to worship the stupa. In the place where the stupa stands, he performs all the aforementioned disrespectful acts as if in the presence of the Teacher. This monk is called 'disrespectful' (agārava) toward the Teacher. A monk who does not go respectfully to the time of hearing the Dhamma or to assemblies, and does not listen to the Dhamma respectfully, is disrespectful toward the Dhamma.
489: ...walks. While the Teacher is walking on a lower cloister, he walks on a higher cloister; while the Teacher is staying on a lower floor, he stays on an upper floor; in a place where the Teacher can see him, he covers both shoulders, wears an umbrella, wears shoes, bathes, or relieves himself. After the Teacher has attained Parinibbāna, he does not go to worship the shrine (cetiya). In a place where the shrine is visible, he performs all the aforementioned acts as if in the presence of the Teacher—this is called disrespect (agārava) towards the Teacher. When the signal for hearing the Dhamma is given, not going respectfully, not listening to the Dhamma respectfully, sitting while talking, not learning it respectfully in mind, not teaching it respectfully—this is called disrespect towards the Dhamma. Teaching the Dhamma or answering questions without being invited by an elder monk; walking, standing, or sitting while bumping into elder monks; sitting with knees clasped by cloth or hands (āyogapaṭṭa); covering both shoulders, wearing an umbrella, or wearing shoes in the midst of the Saṅgha—this is called disrespect towards the Saṅgha. Indeed, if disrespect is shown even to a single monk, it is considered disrespect towards the Saṅgha. Not fulfilling the three trainings is called disrespect towards the training (sikkhā). Not cultivating the characteristic of heedfulness (appamāda) is called disrespect towards heedfulness. Not performing the two kinds of hospitality is called disrespect towards hospitality (paṭisanthāra). States that lead to decline (parihāniya-dhamma) are those that cause one to fall away. Delight in work (kammārāmatā) means being excessively devoted to and engaged in new construction (navakamma) or tasks such as managing robes. Delight in talk (bhassārāmatā) means being excessively devoted to talk by way of 'animal talk' (tiracchānakathā). Delight in sleep (niddārāmatā) means being excessively devoted to sleeping. Delight in company (saṅgaṇikārāmatā) means being excessively devoted to congregating with others. Delight in socializing (saṃsaggārāmatā) means being excessively devoted to the five kinds of socializing: socializing by hearing, by seeing, by talking together, by using things together, and by physical contact. Delight in proliferation (papañcārāmatā) means being excessively devoted to the proliferations of craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and views (diṭṭhi). In terms like 'somanassupavicāra' (mental exploration accompanied by joy), they are called so because one explores closely along with joy (somanassa). "Having seen a form with the eye" means having seen a form with eye-consciousness. 'Somanassaṭṭhāniya' means the form which is the cause of joy by way of being its object. 'Upavicarati' means one explores closely by the occurrence of sustained application (vicāra) therein. Initial application (vitakka) associated with that is also to be understood in the same way; thus the meaning should be understood in all three sets of six. 'Home-based' (gehassita) refers to states based on the cords of sensual pleasure. 'Somanassas' refer to mental happiness (cetasika-sukha). 'Domanassas' refer to mental pain (cetasika-dukkha). Equanimity (upekkhā) is...
490:
Equanimity feeling not associated with knowledge (associated with delusion) is also named aññāṇupekkhā.

In all the phrases such as "I have a self," the word "or" (vā) has the sense of an alternative (distinction). It means that the wrong view arises in this way or that way. In this view "I have a self," eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) takes the self to exist in all times. "By way of truth, by way of stability" means taking it with extreme firmness in the sense of "this view is true," both in terms of reality and in terms of permanence. This view "I have no self" is annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi), because it takes the destruction of the existing being (or self) in various lives. Alternatively, the former view (I have a self) is eternalism because it takes the self to exist in the three periods of time. If one takes it to exist only in the present, it is annihilationism. The latter view (I have no self) is also annihilationism because it takes the self not to exist in the past and future, like those with wrong views who hold that "offerings end in ashes." If one takes it not to exist only in the past, it is eternalism like the view of the fortuitous-originationist (adhiccasamuppannika).

"With the self, I perceive the self" means taking the aggregates as the self, headed by the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha), and perceiving the remaining aggregates through perception; thus it occurs as "with this self, I perceive this self." "With the self, I perceive the non-self" means taking only the aggregate of perception as the self and the other four aggregates as non-self, and perceiving those aggregates through perception. "With the non-self, I perceive the self" means taking the aggregate of perception as non-self and the other four aggregates as the self, and perceiving those aggregates through perception. All these are only eternalism and annihilationism.

"The self that speaks, the self that experiences," etc., are modes of fixed attention belonging only to eternalism. In that text, it is called "speaker" (vada) because it speaks; it means the doer of vocal action. It is called "experiencer" (vedeyya) because it knows and experiences; it means it knows and it feels. Now, to show the benefit experienced by that self, it is said: "in this and that [existence], for a long time, [it experiences the results] of good and bad deeds," etc. Therein, "in this and that" means in those various modes of birth (yoni), destinations (gati), stations of consciousness (viññāṇatthiti), abodes of beings (sattāvāsa), and classes of beings (sattanikāya), or in objects. "For a long time" means for a long night. "Experiences" means it feels repeatedly. "That self has never arisen, has never existed" means that because the self does not have the nature of arising, it is not said to have arisen; it means it is always manifest. For that very reason, it did not exist in the past, and will not exist in the future. For only a self that has arisen is said to have existed, and only a self that will arise is said will exist. Alternatively, "that self has never arisen, has never existed" means that because the self is always manifest, in the past it certainly...
491:
...did not not exist, and in the future also it will certainly not not exist (it always exists). 'Permanent' (nicca) means being free from arising and passing away. 'Stable' (dhuva) means being a firm essence. 'Eternal' (sassata) means existing at all times. 'Of a non-changing nature' (avipariဏāmadhamma) means having the nature of not abandoning its original state, not reaching various different states like a chameleon. Thus, the wrong views mentioned in this Sabbāsava Sutta have been explained. In all the remaining Pali, the meaning is clear.

## Commentary on the Exposition of the Sixes.

## (7.) Commentary on the Exposition of the Sevens

In the Exposition of the Sevens, they are called 'underlying tendencies' (anusaya) because they lie dormant, having reached strength and not having been abandoned by the Path. They are called 'fetters' (saṃyojana) because they bind and connect beings to the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). They are called 'obsessions' (pariyuṭṭhāna) because they arise and obsess all around by way of manifestation. Sensual lust itself is a state that obsesses all around, thus it is 'obsession of sensual lust' (kāmarāga-pariyuṭṭhāna). In the remaining terms, the method is the same.

They are called 'false teachings' (asaddhamma) because they are the teachings of those who are not virtuous (wicked people), or because they are teachings that should not be praised due to their low meaning. They are called 'misconduct' (duccarita) because they are practices corrupted by faults such as lust. They are called 'conceit' (māna) because one imagines through various modes.

In the Exposition of Views, 'material' (rūpī) means having form. 'Consisting of the four great elements' (cātumahābhūtika) means being made of the four great elements. It is called 'belonging to mother and father' (mātāpettika) because it is the property of the parents. What is that property of the parents? It is semen and blood. It is called 'born of mother and father' (mātāpettika-sambhava) because it arises from the parents' semen and blood. Here, taking the material body as the head, the human state of existence is called "self." The second person rejects that first view and calls the divine state of existence "self." 'Divine' (dibba) means arising in the deva world. 'Belonging to the sense sphere' (kāmāvacara) means being included among the six classes of sense-sphere devas. It is called 'feeding on physical food' (kabaḷīkārabhakkha) because it eats nutriment. 'Mind-made' (manomaya) means produced by the mind of jhāna. 'Having all limbs and parts' (sabbanga-paccangī) means being endowed with all large and small limbs. 'With unimpaired faculties' (ahīnindriya) means having complete faculties. This is said in terms of the faculties that exist in the Brahma world and in terms of the shape of the other faculties. 'Attained to the base of infinite space' (ākāsānañcāyatanūpaga) means having reached the state of the base of infinite space. In the remaining terms, the method is the same. In all the remaining Pali, the meaning is clear.

## Commentary on the Exposition of the Sevens.
492:
## (8.) Aṭṭhakaniddesa-vaṇṇanā

In the Aṭṭhakaniddesa, the defilements themselves are the bases of defilements (kilesavatthu) that will arise in the future. "Kusītavatthu" (bases of laziness) refers to the bases or causes of laziness for a person who is indolent or sluggish in everything. "Work should be done" means that there is work to be performed, such as the preparation of robes and so forth. "Does not exert effort" means not exerting both physical and mental effort. (He does not exert effort) for the sake of reaching the Dhamma of Jhanas, Vipassana, Paths, and Fruits that have not yet been reached; for the sake of attaining those that have not yet been attained; and for the sake of realizing those that have not yet been realized. "This is the first" means that the first base of laziness (cause of indolence) is sinking into the thought, "I will sleep now."

In the phrase "māsācitaṃ maññe," "māsācitaṃ" refers to wet beans. Just as wet beans are heavy, it means "heavy." "Gilānā vuṭṭhito hoti" refers to one who has recovered from an illness.

In the phrase "aṭṭhasu lokadhammesu," they are called worldly conditions (lokadhamma) because they are the conditions of the world. There is no one who is free from these worldly conditions; they occur even to the Buddhas. Therefore, they are called "lokadhamma." "Paṭighāta" refers to the state of being troubled or distressed. "Lust for gain" means the lust that arises through the power of householder-based joy (gehasita-somanassa) thinking, "I have obtained a gain"; that lust oppresses the mind. "Aversion to loss" means the opposition that arises through the power of grief (domanassa) thinking, "I have not obtained a gain"; that opposition also oppresses the mind. Therefore, it is called "paṭighāta." In other worldly conditions such as fame (yasa) and so forth, the manner of their occurrence should be understood as: "I have many followers, I have few followers; I have attained praise, I have attained blame; I have attained happiness, I have attained suffering." "Anariyavohāra" refers to the expressions of non-Aryans (worldlings).

"Purisadosa" refers to the faults of men. "I do not remember" is an excuse made through lack of mindfulness, saying, "I do not remember or notice the place where I performed this action," thus attempting to be released from the charge. "Attacks the accuser" means being antagonistic and lashing out, standing as one who talks back. By the words "What benefit is there for you?" he shows, "What benefit is there in the words of an ignorant and unskilled person like you, who knows neither the basis of the offense nor the procedure of accusation?" He overwhelms the accuser by saying, "Even someone like you thinks it is appropriate to speak without knowing anything."
493:
"Maññissasī" means overwhelming or oppressing. "Paccāropeti" means counter-accusing by saying things such as "You too..." "Paṭikarohi" means to confess an offense that can be cleared by confession (desanāgāminī), or to emerge from an offense that requires a period of penance (vuṭṭhānagāminī); it indicates that only after being established in purity should one accuse another.

"Aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati" means concealing one reason or statement with another reason or statement. When told, "You have committed an offense," he says, "Who committed it? What was committed? How was it committed? For what reason was it committed? To whom are you speaking? What are you saying?" When asked, "Did you see anything of this nature?" he says, "I do not hear," and turns his ear away. As for "How does he divert the conversation to external matters?", when asked, "Have you not committed such-and-such an offense?" he says, "I went to Pāṭaliputta." When told again, "We are not asking about your journey to Pāṭaliputta," he says, "From there I went to Rājagaha." When told, "Go to Rājagaha or to a Brahmin's house if you wish, but have you not committed an offense?" he says, "I obtained pork there," and so forth, thus tossing the conversation to external matters. "Kopa" is anger. "Dosa" is the nature of malice. Both of these are names for anger (kodha). "Appaccaya" is the manner of dissatisfaction, and it is a name for grief (domanassa). "Pātukaroti" means to show or to make manifest. "Bāhāvikkhepakaṃ bhaṇati" means speaking shameless words while waving one's arms. "Viheseti" means to harass or oppress. "Anādiyitvā" means not taking seriously, acting without respect or disregarding.

"Atibāဠhaṃ" means excessively or extremely. "Mayi vyāvaṭā" means they are concerned with my affairs. "Hīnāyāvattitvā" means returning to the low state of a layman, i.e., disrobing. "Attamanā hotha" means saying "Be joyful" with the sense of: "Enjoy the gains I should have received, live in the place where I should have lived, I have made your living comfortable."

The doctrine that arises as "non-percipient" (asaññī) is called the doctrine of non-perception (asaññīvāda); those who hold that doctrine are called non-percipients (asaññīvādā). In phrases such as "the self has form" (rūpī attā), those who have attained Jhana take the kasina-form as the self, and thus the wrong view "it has form" arises. For those who have not attained Jhana, it arises through mere reasoning, like the Ājīvakas. Those who have attained Jhana take the sign of formless attainment (arūpasamāpatti) as the self, and thus the wrong view "it is formless" arises. For those who have not attained Jhana, it arises through mere reasoning, like the Nigaṇṭhas. In this doctrine of non-perception, however, one should certainly not search for a root cause.
494:
One who holds a wrong view, like a madman, grasps at whatever [view]. The view 'Self has form' and 'Self is formless' is spoken of by way of grasping at a self mixed with materiality and immateriality. This view arises for one who has attained the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) attainments, as well as for a reasoner (takki). The view 'Neither having form nor formless,' however, is purely the view of a reasoner. 'Finite' is the view of one grasping a limited kasina as the self. 'Infinite' is the view of one grasping an immeasurable kasina as the self. 'Both finite and infinite' is the view arising from grasping the self as a kasina that is limited above and below but unlimited horizontally. 'Neither finite nor infinite' is purely the view of a reasoner. The rest of the words are clear in meaning everywhere.

## Commentary on the Exposition of the Eights.

## (9.) Commentary on the Exposition of the Nines

In the Exposition of the Nines, the nine bases of malice (āghātavatthu) are spoken of only by way of their occurrence in beings. 'Purisamalāni' means the stains of men. 'Ninefold' means having nine parts or nine divisions.

'Dependent on craving' means relying on craving. 'Seeking' (pariyesanā) means seeking objects such as visible forms. Indeed, that seeking exists when there is craving. 'Gain' (lābha) means the acquisition of objects such as visible forms. Indeed, that gain exists when there is seeking. 'Decision' (vinicchaya), however, is of four types: decision by knowledge (ñāṇa), decision by craving (taṇhā), decision by view (diṭṭhi), and decision by thought (vitakka). Among these, 'One should know the decision of happiness; having known the decision of happiness, one should pursue internal happiness'—this is decision by knowledge. 'Decision is twofold: decision by craving and decision by view'—thus the 108 modes of craving are decision by craving. The sixty-two views are decision by view. In this Sakkapañha Sutta, however, 'decision' is spoken of as thought (vitakka) alone. Indeed, after obtaining gain, one decides by thought whether it is desirable or undesirable, good or bad: 'This much will be for the purpose of visible objects, this much for sounds, etc., this much will be for me, this much for others, this much...'
495:
"...I will use, this much I will store up." Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Dependent on gain, decision arises."

Desire and lust (chanda-rāga) means the arising of weak lust and strong lust for the object thought about with unwholesome thought. Here, 'desire' (chanda) is a designation for weak lust. 'Attachment' (ajjhosāna) means the decision made with strong craving as 'I' and 'mine'. 'Possession' (pariggaha) means the act of possessing by the power of craving and views. 'Stinginess' (macchariya) means the inability to tolerate sharing with others. Therefore, the ancient teachers give this definition: "Let this wonderful thing be mine alone, let it not be another's"—because it occurs in this way, it is called stinginess. 'Guarding' (ārakkha) means protecting well by way of closing doors, storing in boxes, etc. 'Adhikaraṇa' means that which brings about an effect; it is a name for a cause. 'Ārakkhādhikaraṇa' is a neuter noun used in the sense of 'because of the cause of guarding'. Among 'taking up sticks' (daṇḍādāna), etc., taking up a stick to ward off others is daṇḍādāna. Taking up a weapon with a single edge, etc., is taking up a weapon (satthādāna). 'Quarrel' (kalaha) means both physical and verbal quarrels. The very first opposition is strife (viggaha); the subsequent opposition is dispute (vivāda). 'Tuvaṃ tuvaṃ' is a disrespectful way of speaking, meaning 'you, you'.

'Iñjita' means movements or fluctuations. By all the terms such as 'I am' and 'this is a movement,' conceit (māna) alone is spoken of. Indeed, conceit occurring as 'I' is a movement (iñjita); conceit occurring as 'this is I' or 'they will be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient' is also [a movement]. By the remaining nines also, conceit alone is spoken of. Conceit is called 'movement' (iñjita) because it moves, 'thinking' (maññita) because it thinks, 'palpitation' (phandita) because it throbs, and 'proliferation' (papañcita) because it expands [samsara]. It is also called 'conditioned' (saṅkhata) because it is conditioned by various causes. The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.

## Commentary on the Exposition of the Nines.

## (10.) Commentary on the Exposition of the Tens.

In the Exposition of the Tens, the defilements (kilesa) themselves are the bases of defilements (kilesavatthu). Here, the bases of malice (āghātavatthu) are spoken of together with the malice that arises in inappropriate places such as stumps and thorns, where one should not be angry, by way of 'he has done me harm,' etc.

Among wrongnesses (micchatta), wrong knowledge (micchā-ñāṇa) is the delusion (moha) that arises in the form of reflection after performing an evil deed through the planning of means for evil actions, thinking 'I have done well'.
496:
False liberation (micchāvimutti) means the perception of being liberated while one is not yet liberated from the defilements. The remaining words are clear in meaning in all places.

## Commentary on the Exposition of the Tens (Dasakaniddesa).

## Commentary on the Exposition of the Mental Wanderings of Craving (Taṇhāvicariṭaniddesa)

In the Exposition of the Mental Wanderings of Craving, 'mental wanderings of craving' (taṇhāvicariṭāni) refers to the activities and occurrences of craving. 'Grasping the internal' (ajjhattikassa upādāya) means grasping the five aggregates occurring within one's own continuity. Here, the genitive case 'ajjhattikassa' stands in the sense of the accusative case. 'I am' (asmi) occurs: this means that by grasping these five internal aggregates through the power of craving, conceit, and wrong view as a collective whole, the thought 'I am' arises. It means when those five aggregates exist, 'I am' occurs.

In the terms beginning with 'I am thus' (itthasmi), when there is such a grasping of 'I' as a collective whole, thereafter two types of grasping occur: without comparison and with comparison. Among these, 'grasping without comparison' means taking one's own nature as the object without relating to any other mode, thinking 'I am of such a kind.' In the case of kings and so on, it means the thought 'I am of this kind' arises through the power of craving, conceit, and wrong view. This is grasping without comparison.

Grasping with comparison is of two types: by way of equality and by way of inequality. To show these two, 'I am like this' (evasmi) and 'I am otherwise' (aññathasmi) are stated. Among them, 'I am like this' is grasping by comparison in terms of equality; it means 'Just as this person is a king, just as this person is a brahmin, so too am I.' 'I am otherwise' is grasping in terms of inequality; it means 'Just as this person is a king, just as this person is a brahmin, I am different from them, being either inferior or superior.'

These four are the mental wanderings of craving occurring by way of the present. The four beginning with 'they will be' (bhavissantic) are stated by way of the future. The remaining meaning should be understood in the same way as the first four.

'I am' (asmi) is grasping 'I am' by way of permanence. 'I am pleasant' (sātasmī) is grasping 'I am' by way of impermanence. There is also a reading 'asasmī' or 'satasmī'. In that reading, 'asaṃ' is so-called because of the meaning 'it exists' (atthi); this is a designation for a permanent self. 'Sataṃ' is so-called because of the meaning 'it perishes' (sīdati); this is a designation for an impermanent self. Thus, these two should be understood as being stated by way of eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) and annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi).

Following this, the four beginning with 'I might be' (siyaṃ) are stated by way of speculative thought through doubt. Their meaning should be understood in the same way as the first four. The four beginning with 'Would that I were' (appahaṃ siyaṃ) are stated by way of the proliferation of longing, as in 'Would it not be good if I were to be.' These too should be understood in the same way as the first four. Thus, among these mental wanderings of craving—
497:
Two headed by wrong view, four purely headed, and those rooted in the primary terms are twelve, in groups of three. These eighteen should be explained.

Among them, the two stated by way of eternalism and annihilationism are called 'headed by wrong view' (diṭṭhisīsa). These four—'I am' (asmi), 'I shall be' (bhavissaṃ), 'I might be' (siyaṃ), and 'Would that I were' (appahaṃ siyaṃ)—are 'purely headed' (suddhasīsa). The twelve terms in groups of three beginning with 'I am thus' (itthasmi) are called 'rooted in the primary terms' (sīsamūlaka). Thus, the eighteen mental wanderings of craving consisting of two headed by wrong view, four purely headed, and twelve rooted in the primary terms should be understood.

Now, to show those states by analyzing them in order, the passage beginning with 'How does "I am" (asmi) occur?' is undertaken. In that passage, 'without discarding any state' means without separating any single state among form, feeling, and so on, not taking them individually, but taking them only as a collective whole. To 'obtain the desire' (chanda) that 'I am' means to grasp the five aggregates without remainder and obtain the craving 'I [am].' The same method applies to conceit and wrong view. Although this is the Exposition of the Mental Wanderings of Craving, because conceit and wrong view cannot occur without craving, they are stated here as being of the same standing as craving. Or, all three types of proliferation (papañca) are indicated with craving as the head. To explain them in detail according to that indication, conceit and wrong view are also included. Or, while showing the proliferation of craving, the remaining proliferations are also shown along with it; thus it is stated.

'When that exists, these proliferations occur' means when the three proliferations stated by the method beginning with 'obtains the desire that "I am"' exist, then these proliferations beginning with 'or "I am thus"' (itthasmīti vā) occur.

In the words beginning with 'I am a king' (khattiyosmi), the meaning should be understood in this way: 'I am a king' by way of being consecrated, having an army, ministers, etc.; 'I am a brahmin' (brāhmaṇa) by way of reciting mantras, being a chaplain, etc.; 'I am a merchant' (vessa) by way of farming, cattle-breeding, etc.; 'I am a servant' (sudda) by way of being one who carries a sickle and a yoke; 'I am a householder' (gahaṭṭha) by way of the appearance of a layman. Thus, 'I am thus' occurs means that having produced in oneself the mode of a king, etc., among kings and so on, the thought 'I am of this kind' arises.

In the words beginning with 'Just as that king is,' the meaning should be understood in this way: 'Just as that person is a king by way of being consecrated, having an army, ministers, etc., so too am I a king.' In the second method, the meaning should be understood thus: 'Just as that person is a king by way of being consecrated, having an army, ministers, etc., I am not a king in that way; I am either inferior or superior to that person.' In the expositions beginning with 'I shall be' (bhavissaṃ), the method is the same.
498:
The meaning should be understood in this way: "Or". The same method applies to the expositions beginning with "bhavissanti" (they will be) and so forth.

Having thus analyzed the craving-behaviors (taṇhā-vicarita) based on the internal collection of the five aggregates, the text now says "Tattha katamāni" (Therein, which are they?) and so forth to analyze the craving-behaviors based on the external five aggregates. In that Pali passage "Tattha katamāni" etc., "bāhirassa upādāya" means based on the external collection of the five aggregates. Indeed, this word "bāhirassa" is a genitive case used in the sense of the accusative case. "Iminā" means "by this material form" ... etc ... "by this consciousness" (I am). The remaining collection of words should be understood exactly as explained in the Summary Section (Uddesa-vāra).

In the Exposition Section (Niddesa-vāra), "avakāriṃ karitvā" means having made a distinction. In the Pali passages such as "iminā asmi" (by this I am), one obtains desire (chanda), etc.; taking the five aggregates partially as "by this material form aggregate" ... etc ... "by this consciousness aggregate", the meaning should be understood as "by this aggregate, I am", thus obtaining desire and so forth.

In the Pali passages such as "iminā khattiyo'smi" (by this I am a Khattiya), the meaning should be understood according to the previous method: "By this white parasol, or by this sword, or by the consecration, the army, the ministers, etc., I am a Khattiya." Here, only the word "iminā" is the distinction.

In "yathā so khattiyo" (as that Khattiya) and so forth, only the word "iminā" is the distinction. Therefore, by the power of that word "iminā", it should be connected in all passages as: "Just as that person is a Khattiya because of consecration, the army, the ministers, etc., so too am I a Khattiya because of this sword, or this white parasol, or the consecration, the army, the ministers, etc." Thus the meaning should be understood. "Iminā nicco'smi" (by this I am eternal) means without distinguishing the five aggregates individually, taking only one phenomenon among material form, etc., as "I", one perceives: "Because of this sword or this white parasol, I am permanent, I am stable." The same method applies to annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi). All remaining meanings should be understood as previously explained.

"Thirty-six past craving-behaviors of such nature" refers to the thirty-six craving-behaviors in the past of each individual.
