"Thirty-six future" refers to the thirty-six craving-behaviors in the future of each individual. "Thirty-six present" refers to the thirty-six craving-behaviors in the present of each individual, or of many individuals according to what is obtained. For all beings, it should be understood as thirty-six in the past, thirty-six in the future, and thirty-six in the present. Indeed, beings with various types of craving, conceit, and wrong view are infinite. In the phrase "there are one hundred and eight craving-behaviors", the meaning should be noted as there being craving-behaviors numbered as one hundred and eight. In all sections, the remaining meaning is clear.

## Commentary on the Exposition of Craving-Behavior.
499:
## Commentary on the Exposition of Wrong Views
In the Exposition of Wrong Views, "Brahmajāle Veyyākaraṇe" means (taught) in the discourse named Brahmajāla, which is the first sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya. "Vuttāni Bhagavatā" means (the words) spoken specifically by the Blessed One himself. In the passages such as "cattāro sassatavādā" (four eternalist views), the types and meanings of wrong views should be understood according to the method taught in the Brahmajāla Sutta (D. i. 29-30): "On what grounds and dependent on what do these honorable recluses and brahmins, being eternalists, proclaim the self and the world to be eternal in four ways?"

## 1. Commentary on the Universal Inclusion Section
## 18. Dhammahadaya-vibhaṅga (The Heart of the Teaching Analysis)
Now, in the Dhammahadaya-vibhaṅga which follows the Khuddakavatthu-vibhaṅga, the division of the Pali text should first be understood thus: Here, at the very beginning, the Universal Inclusion Section (Sabba-saṅgāhika-vāra) is taught by way of the twelve categories such as the aggregates. The second section is the section showing the arising and non-arising (Uppattānuppatti-dassana-vāra) of those same phenomena in the sense-sphere, etc. The third section is the section showing the included and non-included (Pariyāpannāpariyāpanna-dassana-vāra) in those same spheres. The fourth section is the section showing the phenomena present and not present (Vijjamānāvijjamāna-dhamma-dassana-vāra) at the moment of rebirth in the three planes. The fifth section is the section showing those phenomena by way of the different planes (Bhūmantara-vasena dassana-vāra). The sixth section is the section showing the productive kamma and the life-span (Uppādaka-kamma-āyuppamāṇa-dassana-vāra) in the destinations. The seventh section is the section on things to be fully known (Abhiññeyyādi-vāra), etc. The eighth section is the section on those with objects and those without objects (Sārammaṇānārammaṇa-vāra). The ninth section is the section showing those phenomena such as aggregates by including them by way of the seen, heard, etc. (Diṭṭhasutādi-vasena saṅgahetvā dassana-vāra). The tenth section is the section showing them by including them by way of the wholesome triads, etc. (Kusalattikādi-vasena saṅgahetvā dassana-vāra).

In the Pali text thus divided into ten sections, first, in the first section, the Universal Inclusion Section, when it is asked: "From the Avīci hell to the peak of existence, how many aggregates are there within this range?", the Buddha, demonstrating the power of his own knowledge, gave the answer according to the question: "Five aggregates", without saying "one", or "four", or "six", as no one else is capable of saying "five". Answering according to the question is called the explanation of the Omniscient One. The same method applies to the twelve bases (āyatana) and so forth. The distinctions of the material form aggregate, etc., should be understood exactly as explained in the Khandha-vibhaṅga, etc.

## 2. Commentary on the Arising and Non-arising Section
In the second section, whatever phenomena arise in the sense-sphere existence, or in the continuity of beings born in the sense-sphere—whether included or not included in the sense-sphere—all those phenomena are collected and taught as "five aggregates in the sense-sphere", and so on. The same method applies to the fine-material sphere (rūpa-dhātu), etc. However, because of the absence of the nose-base (ghānāyatana), etc., in the continuity of beings included in the fine-material sphere, the odor-base (gandhāyatana), etc., cannot perform the function of a base, etc. Therefore, it is taught as "six bases, nine elements", etc., in the fine-material sphere.
502:
Observing the Uposatha endowed with eight factors on days such as the fourteenth is called "having performed the Uposatha act." Now, because a small amount of merit such as giving is the cause of human prosperity, and merit performed moderately is a superior cause of human prosperity, and even when it is merit of superior measure, it becomes the cause for various states such as being a Khattiya-mahāsāla due to various distinctions; therefore, wishing to show the distinctions of rebirth by the power of that kamma, it is said: "some householder-mahāsālas," and so forth. In that context, they are called mahāsāra because they have great (mahā) essence (sāra) of wealth. By changing the letter 'r' to 'l', it is stated as mahāsāla. They are called gahapati-mahāsāla because the householders themselves are mahāsālas, or because they are mahāsālas among householders. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Among them, a householder in whose house at least forty crores of wealth are buried, and whose daily expenditure is five ambaṇas of coins, is called a gahapati-mahāsāla. A brahmin in whose house at least eighty crores of wealth are buried, and whose daily expenditure is ten ambaṇas of coins, is called a brāhmaṇa-mahāsāla. A king in whose house at least one hundred crores of wealth are buried, and whose daily expenditure is twenty ambaṇas of coins, is called a khattiya-mahāsāla.

"Companionship" (sahabyataṃ) means the state of being together; it means they are born having a similar portion. The Cātumahārājika gods reside in the middle of Mount Sineru. Among those gods, there are those who dwell on the mountain and those who dwell in the sky. The succession of those sky-dwelling gods reaches the Cakkavāḷa mountains. The Khiḍḍāpadosika gods, Manopadosika gods, Sītavalāhaka gods, Uṇhavalāhaka gods, the young deva Candima, and the young deva Suriya—all these are also dwellers in the Cātumahārājika deva world.

They are called Tāvatiṃsa because thirty-three individuals were born there. Alternatively, it is said that Tāvatiṃsa is simply the name of those gods. They also include mountain-dwellers and sky-dwellers. Their succession reaches the Cakkavāḷa mountains. The same applies to the Yāma gods and others. Indeed, even in a single deva world, there is no such thing as the succession of gods not reaching the Cakkavāḷa mountains. Among them, they are called Yāma because they have reached (yāta) or attained divine happiness. They are called Tusita because they are contented and joyful. They are called Nimmānarati because, when they wish to enjoy themselves beyond their naturally prepared objects, they create whatever enjoyments they desire and delight in them. They are called Paranimmitavasavatti because, knowing the intentions of others, they exercise control over the enjoyments created by others.
503:
## (2.) Lifespan

"A little more or less" means a lifespan that exceeds one hundred years by 20, 30, 40, 50, or 60 years, without reaching the second hundred years. Although it exceeds one hundred years, because it does not fully reach the second hundred years, this total number of years is called "a little."

In the realms such as Brahmapārisajjā, they are called Brahmapārisajjā because they are the attendants and retinue of the Great Brahmas (Mahābrahmā). They are called Brahmapurohitā because they stand as the chaplains of those Great Brahmas. They are called Mahābrahmā because they are great Brahmas due to their beauty and long life. All these three types of beings live on the same level in the first jhāna plane, but their lifespans are different from one another.

They are called Parittābhā because they have limited radiance. They are called Appamāṇābhā because they have immeasurable radiance. They are called Ābhassarā because the radiance from their bodies streams out and spreads like the flickering flames of a torch. These three types of beings also live on the same level in the second jhāna plane, but their lifespans are different from one another.

They are called Parittasubhā because they have limited beautiful radiance. They are called Appamāṇasubhā because they have immeasurable beautiful radiance. They are called Subhakiṇhā because they are pervaded with beautiful aura, because they have a solid mass of aura, and because they have the splendor of a glowing gold nugget placed in a golden box. These three types of beings also live on the same level in the third jhāna plane, but their lifespans are different from one another.

The state of the diversity of objects is called the diversity of objects (ārammaṇanānattatā). The same principle applies to the diversity of attention and so forth. In this context, for one person, the earth kasina is the object, ...pe... for another person, the white kasina is the object; this is the diversity of objects. One person attends to the earth kasina, ...pe... another person attends to the white kasina; this is the diversity of attention. For one person, there is desire for the earth kasina, ...pe... for another person, there is desire for the white kasina; this is the diversity of desire (chanda). One person makes an aspiration for the earth kasina, ...pe... another person makes an aspiration for the white kasina; this is the diversity of aspiration (paṇidhi). One person resolves by means of the earth kasina, ...pe... another person resolves by means of the white kasina; this is the diversity of resolution (adhimokkha). One person directs the mind by means of the earth kasina, ...pe...
504:
One person directs the mind by means of the white kasina; this state is the diversity of directing the mind (abhinīhāranānattatā). For one person, there is wisdom that defines the earth kasina ... for another person, there is wisdom that defines the white kasina; this state is the diversity of wisdom (pajñānānattatā). Among those, such as the diversity of objects, the diversity of object and attention are taught as the preliminary stage. Desire (chanda), aspiration (paṇidhi), resolution (adhimokkha), and directing the mind (abhinīhāra) should occur both at the moment of absorption (appanā) and at the moment of access (upacāra). Wisdom, however, is taught as a mixture of mundane and supramundane.

Asaññasattānaṃ refers to (the state of) beings who are devoid of perception. Indeed, some individuals, having gone forth in the teachings of heretics with wrong views, see the faults in the mind, thinking, 'Attachment, aversion, and delusion occur depending on the mind,' and they generate disgust for perception, thinking, 'The state of mindlessness alone is beautiful; this mindlessness is Nibbāna in this very life.' They then develop the fifth jhāna attainment that leads to that Asaññasatta realm and are reborn there. At the moment of rebirth of those Asaññasatta Brahmas, only the form aggregate (rūpakkhandha) arises. A Brahma who is reborn while standing remains only standing; a Brahma reborn while sitting remains only sitting; a Brahma reborn while lying down remains only lying down. Being like painted or sculpted statues, they remain for five hundred aeons. At the end of their lifespan, that form aggregate disappears, and sense-sphere perception (kāmāvacarasaññā) arises. Because of the arising of perception here in the sense-sphere, it is known that those Brahmas have passed away from that assembly of Asaññasatta Brahmas.

They are called Vehapphala because they have abundant fruit. They are called Avihā because they do not fall away from their own prosperity. They are called Atappā because they do not torment any being. They are called Sudassā because they have a beautiful appearance and are pleasant to behold. They are called Sudassī because they see well (or because they have a beautiful vision). They are called Akaniṭṭhā because they are the greatest in all virtues and in the prosperity of existence, and there are no 'younger' (lower) ones among them.

They are called Ākāsānañcāyatanūpagā because they have reached the realm of the sphere of infinite space. The same principle applies to the remaining formless (āruppa) realms. Thus, there are 6 sense-sphere deva realms, 9 Brahma worlds, 5 Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), and 4 formless realms, which together with Asaññasatta and Vehapphala make 26 deva and Brahma worlds. Including the human world, there are 27.

In showing that lifespan (āyuppamāṇa), when the Fully Enlightened One defined the lifespan of humans and devas, He did not define the lifespan of the four woeful states and the earth-bound devas (bhummadeva). Why did He not define them? In hell (niraya), kamma alone is the measure. As long as the kamma is not exhausted, they do not pass away. It is the same in the remaining woeful states. For the earth-bound devas as well, kamma alone is the measure. Those who are reborn in that realm...
505:
Some beings remain for only seven days, some for half a month (fifteen days), some for a month; there are even earth-dwelling devas (Bhummadeva) who remain for an entire aeon (kappa).

Among those beings, there are those who, while remaining in the state of laypeople among humans, become Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna); they also reach the Fruit of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmiphala), the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala), and the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala). Among those noble ones, those such as Stream-enterers remain for the duration of their lives. Arahants, however, either attain Parinibbāna or go forth into homelessness (ordain). Why is this? Because Arahatship is a supreme quality, while the lay form is inferior; because of its inferiority, the lay form is unable to sustain the supreme quality of Arahatship. Therefore, those laypeople who have become Arahants either desire to attain Parinibbāna or desire to ordain.

Earth-dwelling devas, however, remain for the duration of their lives even after reaching Arahatship. Among the six heavens of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), devas who are Stream-enterers and Once-returners remain for the duration of their lives. A deva who is a Non-returner (Anāgāmī) should go to the fine-material realm (rūpabhava), and a deva who is an Arahant should attain Parinibbāna. Why is this? Because there is no place for concealment. In the fine-material realm (rūpāvacara) and the immaterial realm (arūpāvacara), all noble Brahmas also remain for the duration of their lives. Stream-enterers and Once-returners born in the fine-material realm do not return to this sense realm again, but attain Parinibbāna right there. This is because those Stream-enterer and Once-returner Brahmas are called "Non-returners through Jhāna" (Jhāna-Anāgāmī).

For those who have attained the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti), what determines their rebirth? Mastered jhāna (paguṇajjhāna) determines it. Whichever jhāna is mastered by that person, they are reborn by means of that jhāna. If all jhānas are mastered, what determines it? Aspiration (patthanā) determines it. In whichever realm they aspire to be reborn, they are reborn in that very realm. If there is no aspiration, what determines it? The attainment entered at the time of death determines it. If there is no attainment entered at the time of death, what determines it? The attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-samāpatti) determines it. This is because that person is certainly reborn in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. For noble disciples (ariyasāvaka) born in the nine Brahma worlds, there is rebirth in that same realm or rebirth in a higher realm, but no rebirth in a lower realm. For worldling (puthujjana) Brahmas, however, there is rebirth in that same realm, rebirth in a higher realm, and also rebirth in a lower realm. In the five Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) and the four immaterial realms, noble disciples have rebirth in that same realm and rebirth in a higher realm. A Non-returner born in the first jhāna realm, after purifying the nine Brahma worlds and staying in the supreme Vehapphala realm, attains Parinibbāna. These three Brahma realms—Vehapphala, Akaniṭṭha, and Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana—are called the supreme realms. Non-returner Brahmas born in these three places go neither up nor down, but attain Parinibbāna right there. This is the miscellaneous discussion on this section.
506:
## 7. Commentary on the Section on Things to be Known by Higher Knowledge, etc.
In the seventh section (vāra), the state of being known by higher knowledge (abhiññeyyatā) should be understood by means of higher knowledge (abhiññā) that discerns individual and general characteristics. The state of being fully understood (pariññeyyatā) should be understood by means of full understanding as the known (ñātapariññā), full understanding as investigation (tīraṇapariññā), and full understanding as abandoning (pahānapariññā). That pariññeyyatā, in such passages as "The aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) is to be known by higher knowledge, is to be fully understood, and is not to be abandoned," should be understood only by means of full understanding as the known and as investigation. In such passages as "The truth of the origin (samudayasacca) is to be known by higher knowledge, is to be fully understood, and is to be abandoned," it should be understood by means of full understanding as abandoning.

In the eighth section, the state of having an object or not having an object (sārammaṇā-anārammaṇatā) should be understood by means of eye-consciousness and so on, which have visible forms and so on as their objects. The ninth section has a clear meaning. In the tenth section also, whatever should be said has all been said in the respective sections of the Questioning (Pañhāpucchaka) such as the Khandha Vibhaṅga.

## The Commentary on the Dhammahadaya Vibhaṅga
## in the Sammohavinodanī is finished.
507:
## Concluding Discourse
And by this much—

While teaching the Abhidhamma to the devas in the city of devas (Tāvatiṃsa), the Protector (the Buddha), who honors the Dhamma and is surrounded by thousands of hosts of devas, the Peerless Man, taught that second book of the Vibhaṅga, which is adorned with eighteen Vibhaṅgas and possesses qualities worthy of being an ornament.

For the purpose of explaining its meaning, I was requested by the monk Buddhaghosa, who possesses steady virtue, whose intellect is not slow, and who has good wisdom. I, Buddhaghosa, have exerted effort to compose this commentary named Sammohavinodanī, because it is able to dispel confusion regarding very subtle and profound meanings.

Taking the essence of the ancient commentaries (Porāṇaṭṭhakathā), this [work] has reached its conclusion without obstacles, consisting of forty-one recitation sections (bhāṇavāra) in the Pali text. Just as this book has reached its conclusion, may all the pure desires of all beings reach fulfillment.

Whatever merit I have gained by composing this work for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dhamma, may the world together with the devas reach the same fulfillment through that merit. May the Dhamma endure for a very long time; may the world always delight in the Dhamma; and may the districts always be endowed with prosperity, such as freedom from danger and abundance of food.

[This was written by the Great Poet] who is adorned with supreme and pure faith, wisdom, and energy; who is endowed with a collection of virtues such as morality, conduct, integrity, and gentleness; who is capable of diving into the depths of his own and others' doctrines; who possesses clarity of wisdom; who has unhindered power of knowledge in the Teacher's Dispensation consisting of the Tipiṭaka and its commentaries; who is a great grammarian; who is endowed with the beauty of sweet and noble speech arising from the happiness produced by perfection of vocal instruments; who speaks what is appropriate and liberated; who is the best of speakers; who is a great poet; who is surrounded by the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā); who is adorned with qualities such as the six higher knowledges (chaḷabhiññā) and analytical insights; who is well-established in the qualities of a superior human (uttarimanussadhamma); and who is a lamp of the lineage of the Elders (Theravaṃsa).
508:
This Vibhaṅga Commentary named Sammohavinodanī was composed by the Elder who is an ornament to the lineage of the Elders residing in the Mahāvihāra, who possesses vast and pure wisdom, and who was given the name Buddhaghosa by his teachers—

May this scripture remain in the world, showing the path of the purification of wisdom to the sons of good family who seek liberation from the world.

As long as the very name "Buddha" of that Exalted One—who is pure in mind, the foremost in the world, and the seeker of the great virtue—endures in the world, (may it remain).

## The Vibhaṅga Commentary named Sammohavinodanī is finished.
